Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Online Content under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2021

The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, notified under Section 87 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, create a layered discretion framework for the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and designated officers. Rule 3 imposes a due‑diligence obligation on significant social media intermediaries (SSMIs) to appoint a Chief Compliance Officer, a Nodal Contact Person, and a Resident Grievance Officer, all resident in India. The discretion to determine whether an intermediary qualifies as an SSMI rests on the threshold of fifty lakh registered users in India, a figure that the Ministry may revise by notification. Rule 4(2) empowers the designated officer to issue a takedown direction within thirty‑six hours of receiving a court order or a government order under Section 69A of the IT Act, while Rule 4(4) requires the intermediary to preserve the removed content and associated metadata for ninety days for investigative purposes.

The Rules also introduce a three‑tier grievance redressal mechanism: (i) the intermediary’s internal grievance officer, (ii) a self‑regulatory body registered with the Ministry, and (iii) an oversight mechanism chaired by the Secretary, MeitY. The oversight committee’s discretion to issue “directions for compliance” under Rule 12 is subject to judicial review for proportionality and procedural fairness. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act for vagueness, establishing that any restriction on online speech must satisfy the “reasonable restriction” test under Article 19(2). Subsequent High Court decisions have indicated that the 2021 Rules must be read harmoniously with Shreya Singhal, and that the designated officer’s takedown power cannot be exercised without a reasoned order specifying the legal provision invoked—a requirement also embedded in the Rules themselves.

Examiner traps include treating the Rules as a blanket censorship tool, ignoring the statutory requirement that a government order under Section 69A must be backed by a written reason recorded in the order, and assuming that the self‑regulatory body’s decisions are final and non‑appealable. A strong answer maps the chain: IT Act 2000 → Section 69A → 2021 Rules → designated officer → oversight committee → judicial review under Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21, and cites Shreya Singhal, relevant High Court rulings, and the proportionality test from K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Defence Procurement Contracts: The Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020

The Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020, issued by the Ministry of Defence, governs the discretionary powers of the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), the Defence Procurement Board (DPB), and the Service Headquarters in capital acquisition. The DAC, chaired by the Defence Minister, exercises the highest discretion in granting “Acceptance of Necessity” (AoN) for a procurement case, a decision that is formally a policy choice but is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness under Article 14. The DAP 2020 categorises projects under “Make‑I” and “Make‑II” (among others), where the discretion to select a development or production agency is guided by indigenisation and strategic partnership criteria. The DPB, headed by the Defence Secretary, approves the Request for Proposal (RFP) and the Commercial Negotiation Committee’s recommendations, while the Contract Negotiation Committee (CNC) finalises pricing.

Key statutory anchors include the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, which assign defence procurement to the Ministry of Defence, and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (CAG) audit mandate under Article 151. The Supreme Court has emphasised in several decisions (e.g., Tata Cellular v. Union of India, 1994) that even high‑value defence contracts must satisfy the “fair, transparent and non‑discriminatory” standard, and that the AoN cannot be a mere formality. The DAP 2020 also mandates a “Post‑Contract Management” framework where the Integrated Financial Adviser (IFA) monitors cost escalation, and any deviation beyond 10 % requires fresh DAC approval, embedding a secondary discretion checkpoint.

Common examiner twists involve conflating the DAC’s AoN with a non‑justiciable political decision, overlooking the mandatory “Make‑II” prototype development clause that limits discretion to a single vendor, and assuming that the CAG’s audit findings automatically invalidate a contract. A complete answer traces the decision flow: AoN → RFP → Technical Evaluation → Commercial Evaluation → CNC → Contract → Post‑Contract Management, and cites relevant DAP clauses, Tata Cellular, and the proportionality analysis from Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978).

Worked Example: AoN Challenge
A private firm challenges the DAC’s grant of AoN for a ₹12,000 crore missile system, arguing that the DAC did not record reasons for rejecting an indigenous alternative. The firm seeks a writ of certiorari under Article 226. Decide the maintainability and the standard of review.
The AoN is an administrative decision amenable to judicial review under Article 226 because it affects the firm’s legitimate expectation of a fair procurement process (see Tata Cellular). The court will apply the Wednesbury unreasonableness test, upgraded to structured proportionality: (i) legitimate aim (national security), (ii) rational connection (AoN must be based on documented operational requirement), (iii) necessity (indigenous alternative examined), and (iv) balancing (public interest vs. procedural fairness). Since the DAC’s minutes lack a recorded reason for rejecting the indigenous option, the order fails the necessity limb and is liable to be quashed. The appropriate remedy is a direction to the DAC to reconsider with a speaking order.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the justiciability of a high‑level defence decision, first identify the statutory source (DAP 2020, Allocation of Business Rules). Then map the decision to the constitutional test: Article 14 (non‑arbitrariness) → proportionality → requirement of a speaking order. Cite Tata Cellular and the relevant DAP clause numbers; avoid generic “policy decision” language.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban) and the Role of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – Urban (PMAY‑U), launched in June 2015 under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), operationalises the constitutional directive under Article 47 to raise the standard of living. The scheme’s discretionary architecture is three‑tiered: (1) the Central Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee (CSMC), chaired by the Secretary, MoHUA, approves the Annual Implementation Plan (AIP) submitted by States/UTs; (2) the State Level Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee (SLSMC) sanctions individual projects and releases the Central Assistance (CA) based on the “Beneficiary‑Led Construction” (BLC) or “Affordable Housing in Partnership” (AHP) verticals; (3) the Urban Local Body (ULB) or Development Authority executes the project, exercising discretion in beneficiary selection, land identification, and technology adoption.

The PMAY‑U Guidelines (2021 revision) prescribe a “Housing for All” Plan of Action (HFAPoA) that each city must prepare, and the CSMC’s discretion to approve or return the HFAPoA is guided by the “Housing Demand Assessment” methodology. The Ministry’s discretion to relax the “minimum carpet area” norm (30 sq m for EWS, 60 sq m for LIG) under the relevant Guidelines clause is subject to a reasoned order and must be reported to the CSMC. The Supreme Court in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) recognised the right to shelter as a facet of Article 21, and subsequent High Court orders have directed State governments to adhere to the HFAPoA timelines, treating the CSMC’s approval as a legitimate expectation for beneficiaries.

Examiner pitfalls include assuming that the Central Assistance is an unconditional grant, ignoring the mandatory 15 % state share and the performance‑linked release of the second instalment, and conflating the ULB’s discretion in beneficiary selection with the transparent selection process (such as lottery) prescribed by the Guidelines. A robust answer cites the PMAY‑U Guidelines 2021, the CSMC’s Terms of Reference, Olga Tellis, and the proportionality test for any relaxation of norms.

Judicial Review of Administrative Action under Articles 32 and 226: Writ Jurisdiction, Locus Standi, and the Doctrine of Alternative Remedy

Articles 32 and 226 confer writ jurisdiction on the Supreme Court and High Courts respectively. While Article 32 is a fundamental right itself, Article 226 is a constitutional power that is wider in scope, encompassing “any other purpose” beyond fundamental rights. The discretion of the court to entertain a writ petition is governed by well‑settled principles: (i) locus standi – the petitioner must be an “aggrieved person” or a public‑spirited individual in public interest litigation (PIL); (ii) the doctrine of alternative remedy – the court may decline relief if an efficacious statutory remedy exists, unless the remedy is illusory, inadequate, or the challenge is to the constitutionality of the statute itself; (iii) the principle of res judicata and constructive res judicata apply to writ proceedings.

Decision‑Making in Cooperative Federalism: The Inter‑State Council, Zonal Councils, and the GST Council’s Consensus Architecture

The constitutional scheme envisages a “Union of States” where legislative and executive powers are distributed by the Seventh Schedule, yet the most consequential decisions — on taxation, water, infrastructure, and public health — require structured inter‑governmental negotiation. Three institutional pillars mediate this: the Inter‑State Council (Article 263), the five Zonal Councils (States Reorganisation Act, 1956), and the Goods and Services Tax Council (Article 279A). Each operates on a distinct decision‑making logic. The Inter‑State Council, chaired by the Prime Minister, meets sporadically; its recommendations are advisory, but the Sarkaria Commission (1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2010) urged it to become a permanent dispute‑resolution and policy‑coordination body. The Zonal Councils, chaired by the Union Home Minister with Chief Ministers as vice‑chairpersons, focus on regional issues — border disputes, water sharing, power grid integration — and decide by consensus, with the Union Home Minister’s view prevailing if consensus fails. The GST Council represents the most sophisticated voting architecture: decisions require a three‑fourths majority of the weighted votes of members present and voting, where the Centre holds one‑third weight and States collectively hold two‑thirds. This weighted‑voting design, unique in Indian constitutional practice, was examined in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022), where the Supreme Court clarified that GST Council recommendations are not binding per se but acquire binding force only when incorporated into law by Parliament or State Legislatures. The Court also observed that the Council’s design embodies “asymmetric federalism” — a term aspirants must define precisely as federalism where constituent units enjoy differentiated powers or representation. Examiners test the distinction between “recommendatory” and “binding” outputs, the quorum rules (half the total members), and the implications of asymmetric federalism for fiscal federalism.

Administrative Discretion in Scheduled Areas: The Fifth Schedule, Sixth Schedule, PESA, and the Forest Rights Act as a Layered Decision‑Making Regime

The Constitution creates a nested discretionary framework for Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule) and Tribal Areas (Sixth Schedule) that overrides ordinary administrative law. Under the Fifth Schedule, the Governor possesses “special responsibility” to direct that any Act of Parliament or the State Legislature shall not apply to a Scheduled Area, or shall apply with modifications (Article 244(1) read with Para 5 of the Fifth Schedule). This power is subject to judicial review for non‑application of mind or mala fides, as held in Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997), where the Supreme Court voided mining leases granted in Scheduled Areas without the Governor’s concurrence. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) operationalises this by mandating that the Gram Sabha — not the Panchayat — is the competent authority for land acquisition, minor mineral concessions, and management of minor forest produce. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA) adds a third layer: the Gram Sabha initiates the process of determining individual and community forest rights, the Sub‑Divisional Level Committee (SDLC) and District Level Committee (DLC) verify claims, and the State Level Monitoring Committee (SLMC) monitors implementation. The Supreme Court in Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2013) (the Niyamgiri judgment) held that the Gram Sabha’s consent under FRA Section 4(5) is a condition precedent for any diversion of forest land, and the Ministry’s discretion to grant Stage‑I clearance is fettered by this statutory veto. The Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2) and 275) creates Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram with legislative, executive, and judicial powers over land, forests, and local governance. The Governor’s power to apply or modify Central/State laws in these areas is distinct from the Fifth Schedule, and the ADCs’ laws require the Governor’s assent. A recurring examiner trap is conflating the Governor’s special responsibility under the Fifth Schedule (exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, subject to constitutional limitations) with the Sixth Schedule (where the Governor acts on ministerial advice but the ADC’s legislative autonomy is constitutionally entrenched). Aspirants must also distinguish PESA’s “consultation” requirement for certain matters from FRA’s “free, prior, and informed consent” standard under Section 4(5), which operates as a substantive veto, not mere consultation.

Applied Scenario: Gram Sabha Consent and Stage‑I Forest Clearance
A State government proposes to divert 120 hectares of forest land in a Fifth Schedule Area for a hydroelectric project. The Gram Sabha, convened under FRA Section 4(5), rejects the diversion by a two‑thirds majority. The State forwards the proposal to the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) with a note that “local opposition has been noted but the project is of national importance.” The MoEFCC grants Stage‑I clearance subject to conditions. A tribal rights organisation challenges the clearance. Decide the validity of the Stage‑I clearance and identify the constitutional and statutory provisions violated.
The Stage‑I clearance is invalid. The Gram Sabha’s rejection under FRA Section 4(5) operates as a statutory veto; the MoEFCC has no discretion to override it. The Supreme Court in Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF (2013) held that the Gram Sabha’s consent is a condition precedent for any diversion of forest land in Scheduled Areas. The State’s forwarding of the proposal despite the Gram Sabha’s rejection violates the FRA and the Governor’s special responsibility under Para 5 of the Fifth Schedule to ensure that laws apply with modifications protecting tribal interests. The clearance also violates Article 244 read with the Fifth Schedule, as the Governor’s concurrence (or at least a reasoned decision on the applicability of the Forest Conservation Act, 1980) was not obtained. The appropriate remedy is quashing of the Stage‑I clearance and a direction to the MoEFCC to reject the proposal unless the Gram Sabha’s consent is obtained afresh through a fair process.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question involves Scheduled Areas, first identify the Schedule (Fifth or Sixth) and the specific statutory layer (PESA, FRA, State law). Map the decision‑maker: Governor (Fifth Schedule), ADC (Sixth Schedule), Gram Sabha (PESA/FRA), SDLC/DLC (FRA verification). Then apply the hierarchy: Constitutional provision (Article 244) → Statutory mandate (PESA/FRA) → Judicial gloss (Samatha, Niyamgiri). Never treat Gram Sabha consent as mere consultation; cite Niyamgiri for the veto principle. For Sixth Schedule questions, remember ADCs have legislative power over land and forests, but their laws need the Governor’s assent — a two‑step check.

Regulatory Capture and Structural Independence: The Decision‑Making Architecture of India’s Independent Regulators

India’s regulatory landscape — Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI), Competition Commission of India (CCI), Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB), Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) — shares a common structural vulnerability: the tension between executive accountability and regulatory independence. The enabling statutes typically provide for a Chairperson and Members appointed by the Central Government on the recommendation of a Selection Committee (often dominated by the executive), fixed tenures (usually five years or until age 65), and removal only on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry (mirroring Article 317 for Public Service Commissions). However, the Supreme Court in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2015) struck down provisions of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) Acts that allowed the executive to control appointments and service conditions, holding that “independence of the adjudicatory body” is part of the basic structure. The Court outlined a template Selection Committee comprising the Chief Justice of India (or nominee), a senior Supreme Court judge, and the Secretary of the administrative ministry — a template that has influenced selection processes for other regulators. Yet, the TRAI Act (as amended in 2000) permits the government to issue “policy directions” binding on TRAI (Section 25), a power upheld in TRAI v. Bharti Airtel (2015) as consistent with parliamentary sovereignty, provided directions are in writing and published. The CCI’s investigative wing (Director General) is appointed by the Commission but its budget and staff are controlled by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, creating a resource‑dependency capture risk. The CERC’s tariff determinations are appealable to the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), whose Chairperson is a retired Supreme Court judge — a structural safeguard absent in sectors without a specialised appellate tribunal. Examiners test the distinction between “policy directions” (permissible executive guidance) and “adjudicatory interference” (impermissible), the composition of Selection Committees post‑Madras Bar Association, and the doctrine of “institutional integrity” — the principle that a regulator’s decision‑making must be insulated from both industry capture and political direction. A nuanced answer cites the 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (Report 4, “Ethics in Governance”) which recommended a unified “Regulatory Appointments Commission” — a proposal not yet implemented but frequently referenced in policy‑analysis questions.

Decision‑Making in Disaster Risk Reduction: The Sendai Framework, NDMA Guidelines, and the Shift from Relief‑Centric to Resilience‑Centric Administration

The Disaster Management Act, 2005 (DMA) created a three‑tier institutional architecture — National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) chaired by the Prime Minister, State Disaster Management Authorities (SDMAs) chaired by Chief Ministers, and District Disaster Management Authorities (DDMAs) chaired by District Collectors. The Act’s original decision‑making logic was relief‑centric: declaration of “disaster” by the State Government under Section 48 (or by the Central Government for disasters of severe nature), access to the National/State/District Disaster Response Funds (NDRF/SDRF/DDRF), and powers of requisition (Section 65). The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015‑2030, adopted at the Third UN World Conference in Sendai, Japan, mandated a paradigm shift: from “managing disasters” to “managing disaster risk.” India’s National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP) 2016, revised 2019, operationalises this by embedding risk‑informed decision‑making into development planning. The NDMA’s 2017 Guidelines on “Minimum Standards of Relief” and 2020 Guidelines on “Disaster Risk Reduction in Development Programmes” recommend that Central Ministries and State Departments conduct disaster risk audits of new schemes above a specified financial threshold. The DMA’s Section 35 (National Plan) and Section 37 (State Plan) mandate preparation of plans that now integrate Sendai priorities: understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, and enhancing preparedness. A critical discretionary node is the “declared disaster” threshold: the State Government’s decision to declare a disaster under Section 48 triggers financial and legal consequences (e.g., moratorium on loan recovery under RBI’s Master Direction on “Relief Measures by Banks in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities”). The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2021) (COVID‑19 ex‑gratia case) held that the NDMA’s discretion to recommend ex‑gratia assistance is not absolute; it must be exercised in accordance with the NDMP and cannot be withheld arbitrarily. The Court also recognised “disaster risk reduction” as a facet of the right to life under Article 21. Examiners focus on the distinction between “response” (post‑event, DMA Sections 48‑50) and “risk reduction” (pre‑event, NDMP/NDMA Guidelines), the role of the District Collector as the “incident commander” under the Incident Response System (IRS), and the mandatory consultation with local bodies (Panchayats/Municipalities) under DMA Section 41 for District Plans — a procedural requirement often ignored in practice.

Administrative Discretion in Public Office: The Doctrine of Pleasure (Article 310), Civil Services Boards, and Protection Against Arbitrary Transfer

Article 310 establishes the “doctrine of pleasure” — civil servants hold office during the pleasure of the President (or Governor) — but this pleasure is not absolute. Article 311 imposes two procedural safeguards: (1) no dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank without an inquiry where the servant is informed of charges and given a reasonable opportunity to be heard; (2) no penalty on the basis of evidence not disclosed. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (1985) held that Article 311(2) does not apply where the penalty is imposed on the basis of a criminal conviction, or where the President/Governor is satisfied that an inquiry is not practicable in the interest of State security. The “pleasure” doctrine was further qualified in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) (Governors’ removal case), where the Court held that pleasure is “subject to constitutional limitations” and cannot be exercised arbitrarily, mala fide, or for extraneous reasons. Transfers, not being a “penalty” under Article 311, were historically considered non‑justiciable executive acts. However, the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Ram Singh (1992) and K. Nagaraj v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1985) recognised that frequent or punitive transfers violate Article 14 (arbitrariness) and Article 19(1)(g) (freedom of profession). The 2nd ARC (Report 10, “Refurbishing of Personnel Administration”) recommended Civil Services Boards (CSBs) at Centre and States to recommend transfers/postings of All India Service officers, with the Chief Minister/Prime Minister as the final authority but bound to record reasons for disagreeing with the CSB. The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) issued guidelines (2014) mandating a minimum tenure of two years for key posts, and requiring the CSB to consider performance, vigilance clearance, and personal difficulties. The Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) directed States to implement CSBs and fixed tenures, holding that “security of tenure” is essential for administrative neutrality. Examiners test the distinction between “transfer as administrative necessity” and “transfer as punishment,” the justiciability of CSB recommendations (they are recommendatory, but deviation requires recorded reasons), and the interplay between Article 310 (pleasure), Article 311 (procedure), and Article 14 (non‑arbitrariness). A common trap is assuming Article 311 applies to transfers — it does not; the remedy lies in Article 14/226 judicial review for arbitrariness.

  • Confusing the Governor’s special responsibility under the Fifth Schedule (exercised on ministerial advice, subject to constitutional limitations) with the Sixth Schedule (where Autonomous District Councils have constitutionally entrenched legislative autonomy).
  • Treating Gram Sabha consent under the Forest Rights Act as mere consultation rather than a statutory veto; always cite Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF (2013) for the consent standard.
  • Assuming GST Council recommendations are automatically binding; they acquire legal force only upon legislative enactment by Parliament or State Legislatures (Mohit Minerals, 2022).

Decision‑Making Models in Public Administration: Rational, Incremental, Mixed‑Scanning, and Garbage‑Can Frameworks

Public‑administration scholarship distinguishes four canonical models that explain how officials choose among alternatives. The rational‑comprehensive model, a classical ideal type later critiqued by Herbert Simon in Administrative Behavior (1947), assumes a decision‑maker can define goals, enumerate all alternatives, predict consequences, and select the utility‑maximising option. India’s Five‑Year Plans (1951‑2017) reflected this logic: the Planning Commission set national targets, quantified resource gaps, and allocated outlays using optimisation frameworks. The model’s limits — bounded rationality, time pressure, and incomplete information — gave rise to the incremental model (Charles Lindblom, The Science of Muddling Through, 1959). Incrementalism holds that policy moves in small steps from the status quo, negotiating among a limited set of familiar alternatives. Indian budgeting illustrates this: the annual Union Budget typically adjusts the previous year’s allocations by a few percentage points rather than redesigning expenditure from scratch.

The mixed‑scanning model (Amitai Etzioni, 1967) combines high‑order strategic scanning with low‑order incremental detail. NITI Aayog’s Strategy for New India @75 (2018) illustrates mixed‑scanning: a long‑term vision (strategic scan) is broken into sectoral action plans that are revised annually (incremental detail). The garbage‑can model (Cohen, March & Olsen, 1972) describes decision‑making in organized anarchies where problems, solutions, participants, and choice opportunities flow independently. The COVID‑19 response (2020‑21) has been analysed as displaying garbage‑can dynamics: multiple ministries, state governments, and technical bodies simultaneously proposed solutions (lockdowns, testing, vaccine procurement) that attached to whichever decision window opened first, producing outcomes only loosely coupled to a pre‑defined hierarchy.

Examiners test the ability to map a concrete administrative episode to the correct model. A question may describe a ministry that “reviews the entire policy landscape every five years but makes only marginal tweaks each year” — the answer is mixed‑scanning. Another may present a crisis where “solutions are floated before problems are fully defined” — the answer is garbage‑can. Knowing the intellectual lineage (Simon, Lindblom, Etzioni, Cohen‑March‑Olsen) and at least one Indian illustration for each model is essential for high‑scoring answers.

Behavioral Insights and Nudge Architecture in Administrative Decisions

Behavioural economics challenges the rational‑actor assumption by documenting systematic biases — present bias, loss aversion, status‑quo bias, and social‑norm conformity. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein’s Nudge (2008) popularised choice architecture: redesigning the decision environment so that the welfare‑enhancing option becomes the default while preserving freedom of choice. India institutionalised this approach through the Behavioural Insights Unit (BIU) set up under NITI Aayog in 2016, later reinforced by a 2020 report on behavioural insights for public policy. The BIU has partnered with line ministries to run randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that test low‑cost nudges.

Key Indian nudges include: (1) Swachh Bharat Mission — the “Darwaza Band” (close the door) sticker on toilet doors was associated with increased usage in a 2017 study in Madhya Pradesh; (2) Tax compliance — the Central Board of Direct Taxes sent simplified, socially‑normed reminder letters (“9 out of 10 taxpayers in your area have filed”) raising filing rates in 2018‑19; (3) LPG subsidy (PAHAL) — automatic direct‑benefit transfer with an opt‑out default significantly reduced leakages; (4) Organ donation — a 2021 pilot in Maharashtra changed the driver‑licence form to a presumed‑consent default, increasing registration rates.

Examiners focus on three design principles: defaults (pre‑selected option), salience (making relevant information prominent), and feedback (immediate information on consequences). A typical CSAT‑style situational judgment item presents a scenario — “A district health officer wants to increase antenatal‑care registration among pregnant women” — and asks which nudge is most appropriate. The correct answer will be a default‑enrolment SMS reminder with an opt‑out link, not a mandatory penalty or a cash incentive (which is a financial incentive, not a nudge). Understanding the distinction between nudges (liberty‑preserving) and shoves (coercive) is a recurring trap.

Situational Judgment – Nudge Selection
A municipal commissioner wishes to reduce household water wastage during summer. Which intervention best exemplifies a nudge as defined by Thaler and Sunstein?
Correct answer: Installing a real‑time digital display in each household showing current water use compared with the neighbourhood average, with a green‑light indicator when usage is below the average. Reasoning: The display preserves freedom of choice (no penalty), makes the socially desirable behaviour salient, and leverages social‑norm feedback — the three hallmarks of a nudge. Options such as imposing a fine, cutting supply after a threshold, or offering a cash rebate are respectively a shove, a coercive restriction, and a financial incentive, not nudges.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a “nudge”, eliminate any option that (a) imposes a monetary penalty, (b) removes the choice entirely, or (c) offers a direct cash reward. The remaining option will usually involve a default setting, a simplified form, a social‑norm message, or a timely reminder — all low‑cost, liberty‑preserving tweaks.

Evidence‑Based Policy Making: Randomised Trials, Systematic Reviews, and the Role of the Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office

Evidence‑based policy (EBP) demands that programme design and scaling decisions rest on rigorous empirical evidence rather than anecdote or political expediency. The Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO), created in 2015 under NITI Aayog, is the nodal body for institutionalising EBP across central ministries. DMEO’s mandate includes (i) conducting and commissioning impact evaluations, (ii) maintaining a national repository of evaluation studies, and (iii) issuing guidelines for Results‑Framework Documents (RFDs) that link outputs to measurable outcomes.

India’s most cited randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in the public sector include: (1) MGNREGA wage‑payment timing (J‑PAL South Asia, 2014) — paying wages within 7 days increased work‑day participation; (2) ASHA performance incentives (Banerjee et al., 2018) — a modest performance‑linked bonus raised institutional delivery rates in Bihar; (3) Mid‑Day Meal fortification (Duflo et al., 2020) — double‑fortified salt reduced anaemia prevalence in a Gujarat trial. Systematic reviews, such as a DMEO‑commissioned meta‑analysis of RCTs on direct‑benefit transfer (DBT), concluded that DBT reduces leakage but only when coupled with robust grievance‑redressal mechanisms.

Examiners test the ability to distinguish internal validity (RCTs) from external validity (generalisability) and to recognise the hierarchy of evidence: systematic review of RCTs > single RCT > quasi‑experimental > observational > expert opinion. A typical question may present a ministry proposing to scale a pilot based on a single before‑after study; the correct critique is “insufficient evidence — requires RCT or at least a well‑designed quasi‑experiment before national rollout.” Familiarity with DMEO’s evaluation policy and the National Evaluation Framework is advantageous.

Multi‑Level Governance and the Principle of Subsidiarity in Decision‑Making

India’s federal architecture operationalises the principle of subsidiarity — decisions should be taken at the lowest competent level — through the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992). Articles 243G and 243W devolve 29 and 18 functional items respectively to Panchayats and Municipalities, subject to State legislation. The District Planning Committees (DPCs) (Article 243ZD) and Metropolitan Planning Committees (MPCs) (Article 243ZE) are mandated to consolidate local plans into a district/metropolitan development plan, ensuring vertical integration.

Fiscal subsidiarity is mediated by State Finance Commissions (SFCs) (Article 243I) which recommend the share of State revenues for local bodies, and by the Union Finance Commission which allocates grants‑in‑aid under Article 275. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25) introduced a performance‑based grant component for urban local bodies tied to property‑tax collection and audit compliance, sharpening accountability. Inter‑governmental coordination occurs through the Inter‑State Council (Article 263) and the GST Council (Article 279A), the latter exemplifying cooperative federalism where the Centre and States jointly decide tax rates by a three‑fourths weighted majority.

Decision‑Making Heuristics and Cognitive Biases in Administrative Practice

Administrative decisions are rarely made in a vacuum; they are shaped by mental shortcuts that evolved for speed but can distort policy outcomes. The most documented heuristics in public‑sector contexts are availability, representativeness, anchoring, and confirmation bias. Availability bias leads officials to overweight vivid or recent events — such as a high‑profile disaster — when allocating relief funds, even when statistical risk models suggest a different priority. Representativeness causes a decision‑maker to judge a programme’s success by how closely its pilot resembles a textbook “best practice” rather than by rigorous impact evidence. Anchoring appears when the first budget figure presented in a ministry’s note becomes the reference point for all subsequent negotiations, limiting the range of feasible alternatives. Confirmation bias reinforces existing policy narratives; officials may selectively cite evaluation reports that support a preferred scheme while ignoring contradictory findings.

Research on bureaucratic decision‑making indicates that these biases systematically affect three decision stages: problem definition, option generation, and choice. In problem definition, availability bias narrows the agenda to salient issues, crowding out chronic but less visible problems such as micronutrient deficiency. During option generation, anchoring on legacy programmes reduces the diversity of alternatives considered. At the choice stage, confirmation bias skews the weight given to evidence, often resulting in the continuation of sub‑optimal subsidies. Mitigation strategies adopted in recent government initiatives include pre‑mortem analysis, structured devil’s‑advocate sessions, and decision‑support checklists that force explicit consideration of counter‑factuals. Emerging guidelines for evidence‑based policy making encourage a bias‑audit for major proposals, requiring the sponsoring ministry to document how each identified heuristic was addressed.

Judicial observations reinforce the relevance of these insights. Courts have held that administrative discretion must be exercised on the basis of relevant material and not on mere impressions, implicitly cautioning against availability‑driven decisions. Transparency mechanisms, such as directives to disclose the analytical framework used for scheme selection, create a check on anchoring and confirmation effects. For aspirants, the exam‑relevant takeaway is the ability to spot a scenario where a decision is justified by a single anecdote, a round‑number budget anchor, or a selective citation of pilot results — each a classic heuristic trap.

The Cabinet Secretariat and Prime Minister’s Office: Architecture of Inter‑Ministerial Coordination

The Cabinet Secretariat, headed by the Cabinet Secretary (the senior‑most civil servant), is the nodal agency for coordinating decisions that cut across ministries. Its primary instruments are the Committee of Secretaries (CoS), the Group of Ministers (GoM), and the Empowered Group of Ministers (EGoM). The CoS meets regularly to review implementation of Cabinet decisions, resolve inter‑departmental disputes, and prepare agenda notes for the Cabinet. GoMs are ad‑hoc bodies constituted for specific policy issues — such as spectrum‑sharing frameworks — while EGoMs possess decision‑making authority on behalf of the Cabinet, as seen in empowered groups formed during national emergencies which authorised emergency procurement and guideline issuance.

The Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) complements the Cabinet Secretariat by providing political direction and strategic oversight. The Principal Secretary to the PM, the National Security Advisor, and the Additional Principal Secretaries constitute the core advisory team. The PMO’s policy coordination mechanisms track flagship programmes through dashboards that aggregate real‑time data from line ministries. This dual architecture creates a checks‑and‑balances dynamic: the Cabinet Secretariat ensures procedural regularity and adherence to the Transaction of Business Rules, while the PMO injects political priority and cross‑cutting vision. Governance reforms have strengthened this link by requiring ministries to submit periodic outcome reports to both the Cabinet Secretariat and the PMO, enabling simultaneous technical and political review.

Judicial scrutiny of this coordination mechanism appears in landmark rulings where courts upheld the Centre’s power to issue directions to States under Article 256, noting that the Cabinet Secretariat’s role in formulating such directions is an executive function subject to judicial review for arbitrariness. Recent amendments to the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules have formalised inter‑ministerial consultation protocols, obligating ministries to circulate draft Cabinet notes well in advance of CoS meetings, thereby reducing last‑minute anchoring on incomplete data. For decision‑making questions, the examiner often tests knowledge of which body has final authority — EGoM decisions are binding on ministries, whereas CoS recommendations require Cabinet ratification — and the procedural timelines that govern inter‑ministerial consultation.

Situational Judgment – Inter‑Ministerial Dispute Resolution
A draft Cabinet note proposes a new national water‑pricing framework. The Ministry of Jal Shakti supports the framework; the Ministry of Agriculture objects, citing adverse impact on irrigation subsidies. The note is circulated to the Committee of Secretaries. Which of the following correctly describes the next procedural step?
The Committee of Secretaries will discuss the objection, attempt consensus, and if unresolved, forward the note with a summary of divergent views to the Cabinet for final decision. The CoS does not have authority to override a ministry’s objection; only the Cabinet (or an empowered GoM/EGoM) can adjudicate. Therefore, the correct answer is that the CoS records the disagreement and escalates to the Cabinet.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks “who decides” in an inter‑ministerial dispute, map the hierarchy: CoS → GoM/EGoM → Cabinet. Remember that only an Empowered Group of Ministers can issue a binding decision without full Cabinet approval. Eliminate options that assign final authority to the CoS or a single ministry.

Cost‑Benefit Analysis and Regulatory Impact Assessment in Indian Rule‑Making

Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) has been progressively mandated for subordinate legislation through guidelines issued by the Ministry of Law and Justice and the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances. The RIA process typically requires the sponsoring ministry to (i) define the policy problem, (ii) identify at least three feasible alternatives including a “no‑action” baseline, (iii) quantify costs and benefits using a prescribed social discount rate, (iv) conduct sensitivity analysis for key parameters, and (v) publish a summary for public comment for a minimum period. The framework adopts a “proportionality” lens: regulations with significant estimated compliance costs must undergo a full cost‑benefit analysis (CBA), while lower‑impact rules may use a simplified checklist.

The CBA methodology follows the standard welfare‑economics approach: direct costs (administrative burden, compliance expenditure), indirect costs (market distortion, reduced competition), direct benefits (health gains, environmental improvement), and indirect benefits (productivity spillovers). Official guidance has standardised key valuation parameters for mortality‑risk regulations, aligning with international practice. Regulatory commissions illustrate RIA in action: for instance, electricity tariff determinations have required utilities to present CBAs for capacity‑addition programmes, including scenario analysis for fuel‑price volatility and demand growth, with proposals rejected when net present value turned negative under base cases.

Judicial endorsement of RIA appears in rulings where courts held that notifications issued without documented impact assessments violated the principle of non‑arbitrariness under Article 14, directing ministries to redo the RIA and re‑publish for stakeholder consultation. For aspirants, the key exam points are: (a) the threshold triggers for full CBA, (b) the mandated discount rate and valuation parameters, (c) the requirement of at least three alternatives, and (d) the mandatory public‑comment window. Questions often present a draft rule with only one alternative and ask which procedural flaw renders it vulnerable to judicial challenge.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of the Securities Market: SEBI’s Rule‑Making and Adjudicatory Powers

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), established under the SEBI Act, 1992, exercises a unique blend of legislative, executive, and quasi‑judicial functions. Its rule‑making power derives from Section 11(1) read with Section 30, enabling it to issue regulations for investor protection, market integrity, and development of the securities market. The regulatory process follows a structured consultation: a concept paper is released, followed by a draft regulation with a public comment period, a board meeting for final approval, and notification in the Official Gazette. Major regulations, such as the Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements framework, exemplify this cycle, incorporating extensive stakeholder feedback before finalisation.

Adjudicatory authority resides in the Whole‑Time Members and the Adjudicating Officers appointed under Section 15‑I. They can impose monetary penalties up to ₹25 crore or three times the profit made, whichever is higher, and issue directions for disgorgement, debarment, or suspension of trading privileges. The Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), constituted under Section 15‑K, hears appeals against SEBI orders, applying the “preponderance of probability” standard. Landmark SAT and Supreme Court judgments have clarified that SEBI’s disgorgement power is remedial, not penal, and must be proportionate to the unjust enrichment, and upheld SEBI’s power to pass interim directions without prior hearing when market integrity is at imminent risk, subject to post‑decisional hearing.

Judicial review of SEBI’s discretion follows the Wednesbury unreasonableness test tempered by the proportionality principle. Courts examine whether the regulation serves a legitimate objective, whether the means are rationally connected, and whether a less restrictive alternative exists. Recent amendments to fraudulent trade practice regulations have been scrutinised for over‑breadth; tribunals have struck down clauses lacking a materiality threshold, directing SEBI to insert quantitative materiality tests. For decision‑making questions, the examiner tests the ability to distinguish between SEBI’s legislative function (subject to parliamentary oversight via the Laying of Regulations before Parliament) and its adjudicatory function (subject to SAT appeal), and to apply the proportionality checklist when a penalty appears disproportionate to the violation.

  • Confusing the Committee of Secretaries’ recommendatory role with the binding authority of an Empowered Group of Ministers.
  • Treating a single pilot study or anecdotal evidence as sufficient justification for national rollout, ignoring the evidence hierarchy.
  • Overlooking the mandatory public‑comment period in Regulatory Impact Assessment and assuming internal ministry review suffices.
  • Applying the Wednesbury test alone to SEBI’s adjudicatory orders without invoking the proportionality principle required by recent tribunal jurisprudence.
  • Misidentifying the prescribed discount rate or valuation parameters for cost‑benefit analysis in Indian regulatory practice.
  • Assuming that the Prime Minister’s Office can unilaterally override a Cabinet decision; the PMO coordinates but final authority rests with the Cabinet or an empowered GoM.
  • Remember to watch for these traps when answering decision‑making questions.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the PM‑KISAN Scheme: Direct Benefit Transfer, Exclusion Errors, and Grievance Redressal

The Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM‑KISAN), launched in February 2019, provides income support of ₹6,000 per year in three equal instalments to landholding farmer families. The scheme operates through a Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) architecture anchored on the PM‑KISAN portal, Aadhaar‑seeded bank accounts, and the Public Financial Management System (PFMS). Administrative discretion is exercised at multiple levels: (a) the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare defines eligibility criteria, instalment schedules, and exclusion categories; (b) State and Union Territory governments verify beneficiary lists, authenticate land records, and resolve grievances; (c) District‑level Nodal Officers approve or reject applications based on physical verification and revenue records; and (d) banks execute credit transfers and handle failed‑transaction reversals.

Key discretionary nodes include the interpretation of “landholding farmer family” — whether joint families, tenant farmers, or sharecroppers qualify — and the application of exclusion criteria such as institutional landholders, constitutional post holders, serving/retired officers, and income‑tax payees. The Ministry’s 2020 guidelines clarified that ownership rights as per land records prevail, but States like West Bengal and Odisha initially withheld data sharing, citing land‑record digitisation gaps, forcing the Centre to invoke Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act for mandatory seeding. Exclusion errors emerged prominently: the 2021‑22 audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) Report No. 12 of 2022 identified 2.3 crore ineligible beneficiaries who received ₹1,364 crore, while 1.1 crore eligible farmers were excluded due to Aadhaar‑name mismatches, bank‑account errors, or pending land‑record mutations.

Grievance redressal follows a three‑tier structure: the PM‑KISAN portal’s self‑correction module, the District Grievance Redressal Committee (DGRC) chaired by the District Collector, and the State‑level Appellate Authority. The DGRC’s discretion to accept late mutations or override automated rejections based on “revenue officer’s certification” has been challenged in High Courts. In State of Maharashtra v. Union of India (2022), the Bombay High Court held that the DGRC cannot substitute its judgment for the portal’s algorithmic validation without documented reasons, reinforcing the principle that discretionary overrides must be reasoned and auditable. The scheme’s 2023 revision introduced face‑authentication via the PM‑KISAN mobile app to reduce biometric failures, shifting discretion from village‑level entrepreneurs to the farmer’s smartphone — a move praised for reducing leakage but criticised for excluding digitally illiterate beneficiaries.

For decision‑making questions, examiners test the ability to distinguish between policy‑level discretion (instalment amount, exclusion list) and operational discretion (verification, grievance disposal), and to apply the proportionality test when a blanket exclusion (e.g., all income‑tax payees) disproportionately affects small farmers with marginal non‑agricultural income. The CAG’s recommendation for a “negative list” approach — auto‑excluding only verified ineligibles rather than requiring positive verification for all — illustrates the shift from ex‑ante to ex‑post discretion, a recurring theme in DBT governance.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Online Gaming and Real Money Games: The MeitY Framework and State‑Level Variations

The regulation of online gaming in India straddles the constitutional divide between “betting and gambling” (State List, Entry 34) and “online platforms” (Union List, residuary power). The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) was allocated the subject “online gaming” via the Gazette Notification dated 26 December 2022, amending the Allocation of Business Rules. MeitY’s draft Online Gaming (Regulation) Rules under Section 87 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, propose a self‑regulatory organisation (SRO) model: multiple SROs registered with MeitY will verify whether a game is a “permissible online real money game” — defined as one where the outcome is predominantly determined by skill, not chance — and enforce a code of conduct covering KYC, age‑gating, grievance redressal, and data localisation.

Administrative discretion is concentrated in three nodes: (a) MeitY’s power to register or derecognise SROs based on their governance structure, independence, and track record; (b) each SRO’s discretion to certify a game as “skill‑dominant” using a prescribed testing framework (statistical analysis of win‑rate distributions, expert review of game mechanics); and (c) the Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) constituted under the IT (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2021, which hears appeals against SRO decisions. The Supreme Court’s judgment in State of Andhra Pradesh v. K. Satyanarayana (1968) established the “dominant factor test” — if skill predominates, the activity is not gambling — but State High Courts have diverged on its application to fantasy sports (Dream11 upheld by Punjab & Haryana HC, 2019; Mobile Premier League challenged in Karnataka HC, 2022). The Karnataka Police (Amendment) Act, 2021, which banned all online games involving risk, was struck down by the Karnataka High Court in All India Gaming Federation v. State of Karnataka (2022) for violating Article 19(1)(g) and exceeding legislative competence, as the State cannot regulate “online platforms” — a central subject.

MeitY’s 2023 amendment to the IT Rules introduced a “safe harbour” for intermediaries hosting only SRO‑certified games, shifting the burden of skill‑vs‑chance determination from courts to SROs. However, the SRO registration criteria — minimum net worth of ₹25 crore, independent board majority, and mandatory inclusion of a retired High Court judge — grant MeitY wide discretion to shape the regulatory architecture. Tamil Nadu’s Online Gaming and Prevention of Gambling Act, 2022 (re‑enacted after the first version was struck down) bans online rummy and poker with stakes, creating a federal friction: MeitY’s SRO may certify rummy as skill‑dominant, but Tamil Nadu police can still prosecute under State law. The Supreme Court’s pending reference in Gameskraft Technologies v. State of Tamil Nadu (SLP 2023) will clarify whether central SRO certification pre‑empts State bans under the doctrine of pith and substance.

For aspirants, the examiner tests the ability to map the constitutional distribution of powers, identify the correct forum for skill‑vs‑chance adjudication (SRO → GAC → High Court → Supreme Court), and apply the Wednesbury unreasonableness test when an SRO rejects certification without publishing its testing methodology. A common trap is conflating the IT Act’s intermediary liability regime (Section 79) with the gambling prohibition — they operate on parallel tracks, and compliance with one does not immunise against the other.

Worked Scenario: SRO Certification Challenge
An SRO registered under MeitY’s Online Gaming Rules rejects certification for a new fantasy‑cricket platform, stating “the platform’s scoring algorithm introduces excessive variance, making chance the dominant factor.” The platform’s internal simulation shows a skill‑coefficient (Spearman’s ρ between player‑rank and final‑rank) of 0.68 over 10,000 contests. The SRO does not disclose its threshold ρ‑value or the statistical test used. The platform appeals to the GAC. Which ground of challenge is most likely to succeed?
The strongest ground is violation of the duty to give reasons and procedural fairness. Under the IT Rules, the SRO must follow a “transparent and documented testing framework.” A rejection without publishing the threshold, the statistical test (e.g., hypothesis test for ρ > 0.5), or the dataset used constitutes an unreasoned order, amenable to judicial review under Article 226. The GAC, applying the proportionality principle, would likely remand for a speaking order. The “dominant factor test” from Satyanarayana is a legal standard; the SRO cannot substitute an undisclosed quantitative threshold without rule‑making authority. Merely arguing ρ = 0.68 is sufficient is a merits argument; the procedural flaw is the examinable trap.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a decision‑making question involves online gaming regulation, first identify the actor: MeitY (policy/SRO registration), SRO (certification), GAC (appeal), State Police (enforcement), or Court (judicial review). Each has a distinct legal source and standard of review. Map the constitutional entry (State List 34 vs. Union residuary) before applying Wednesbury or proportionality. Remember: SRO certification is not a licence; it only grants safe harbour under IT Act. State gambling laws operate independently unless pre‑empted by a central law under Article 254.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Production Linked Incentive Schemes: Sectoral Selection, Threshold Criteria, and Disbursement Mechanisms

The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, launched in 2020‑21 across 14 sectors with a total outlay of ₹1.97 lakh crore, represent a shift from input‑subsidy to output‑linked incentives. Administrative discretion is exercised by the Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS), chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, which approves sectoral guidelines, selects beneficiaries through a challenge‑method or global invitation, and monitors performance. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) acts as the nodal agency for most sectors, while sector‑specific ministries (e.g., Ministry of Heavy Industries for automobiles, Ministry of New and Renewable Energy for solar PV) administer individual schemes.

Three discretionary layers merit scrutiny: (a) Sectoral selection and budget allocation — the EGoS decides which sectors receive PLI support based on strategic importance, import dependence, and employment potential. The 2022 decision to include “specialty steel” and “drones” but exclude “toys” and “leather” was justified by a NITI Aayog‑commissioned study using Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) indices and Global Value Chain (GVC) participation metrics. However, the absence of a published methodology for inter‑sectoral budget allocation (e.g., why ₹57,000 crore for semiconductors vs. ₹18,000 crore for auto components) invites judicial review for non‑arbitrariness under Article 14. (b) Beneficiary selection criteria — each scheme defines eligibility thresholds (minimum global revenue, committed investment, incremental sales). For the PLI‑Auto scheme, the “Champion OEM” category required ₹10,000 crore global revenue and ₹2,000 crore committed investment, while the “Component Champion” category had lower thresholds. The discretion to categorise applicants and apply differential incentive rates (13‑18% for Champions, 8‑13% for Components) was upheld by the Delhi High Court in Motherson Sumi v. Union of India (2022) as a rational classification based on economies of scale and technology spillovers. (c) Disbursement and clawback — incentives are paid annually after verification of incremental sales and investment by a Project Management Agency (PMA) — typically a consulting firm empaneled by DPIIT. The PMA’s discretion to accept “deemed completion” of milestones (e.g., accepting a chartered engineer’s certificate for civil works) versus insisting on physical verification has led to disputes. The 2023 PLI guidelines introduced a “clawback clause” allowing recovery with 12% interest if incentives were claimed on falsified data, and a “bank guarantee” requirement of 3% of approved incentive for new applicants.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Performance Audit Report No. 8 of 2023 on PLI‑Large Scale Electronics Manufacturing noted that 62% of approved applicants had not achieved committed investment by Year 2, yet disbursements continued based on “pro‑rata” sales achievement. The report recommended linking disbursement to a composite score (investment + sales + employment + exports) rather than sales alone. For decision‑making questions, the examiner tests the ability to distinguish between policy discretion (which sectors, what budget) — largely non‑justiciable unless mala fide — and operational discretion (beneficiary selection, milestone verification, clawback) — subject to Wednesbury review and the duty to act fairly. A recurring trap is assuming the PMA’s verification report is binding; it is recommendatory, and the administrative ministry retains final discretion to accept, modify, or reject it, provided reasons are recorded.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Social Media Intermediaries under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021

The IT Rules, 2021, notified under Section 87 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, impose a differentiated regulatory regime on “significant social media intermediaries” (SSMIs) — defined as platforms with over 50 lakh registered users in India. Administrative discretion is vested in the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MIB) across four pillars: (a) Due‑diligence and grievance redressal — SSMIs must appoint a Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), a Nodal Contact Person, and a Resident Grievance Officer (RGO), all resident in India. The RGO must acknowledge complaints within 24 hours and resolve within 15 days (72 hours for takedown of non‑consensual intimate imagery). MeitY’s discretion to designate an entity as an SSMI is triggered by the 50‑lakh threshold, but the Rules empower MeitY to notify additional categories (e.g., “online gaming intermediaries” in 2022). (b) Traceability and first‑originator identification — Rule 4(2) mandates SSMIs providing messaging services to enable identification of the first originator of information on a court order or an order under Section 69A IT Act. The technical feasibility and proportionality of this mandate were challenged in WhatsApp LLC v. Union of India (Delhi HC, 2021); the High Court refused an interim stay, noting the rule applies only to “serious offences” (punishable with 5+ years) and requires a judicial or competent authority order. (c) Content takedown and proactive monitoring — Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove unlawful content within 36 hours of a government order. Rule 4(4) mandates automated tools for proactive detection of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and previously identified unlawful content. The Bombay High Court in Kunal Kamra v. Union of India (2023) struck down the Fact‑Check Unit (FCU) notification under Rule 3(1)(b)(v) — which empowered the Centre to flag “fake news” about government business — as vague and disproportionate, violating Article 19(1)(a). (d) Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs) — three GACs constituted by MeitY hear appeals against RGO decisions. Each GAC comprises a chairperson (retired High Court judge), a member from MeitY, and an independent expert. The GAC’s discretion to “confirm, modify, or reverse” the RGO’s decision is guided by the “principles of natural justice” but not bound by the Evidence Act.

The 2023 amendment introduced a “safe harbour” conditionality: intermediaries lose Section 79 immunity if they fail to comply with Rule 3(1)(b) (prohibited content categories) or Rule 4(2) (traceability). This shifts the burden to the intermediary to prove compliance. The Supreme Court’s pending reference in Facebook India v. Union of India (2023) will determine whether the 36‑hour takedown mandate for government orders — without a prior hearing to the content creator — satisfies procedural fairness under Article 21. For aspirants, the key distinction is between executive orders under Section 69A (blocking for sovereignty, security, public order — subject to the Shreya Singhal safeguards: written reasons, review committee, pre‑decisional hearing where feasible) and takedown orders under Rule 3(1)(d) (unlawful content under Indian law — broader, includes defamation, IP violation, no statutory review committee). Confusing the two regimes is a frequent examiner trap.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Jal Jeevan Mission: Village Water and Sanitation Committees, Fund Allocation, and Quality Surveillance

The Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), launched in August 2019, aims to provide Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTC) to every rural household by 2024. Administrative discretion operates through a three‑tier institutional architecture: (a) National Jal Jeevan Mission (NJJM) under the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS) — approves State Annual Action Plans (SAAPs), releases central share (50% for non‑NE/Himalayan States, 90% for NE/Himalayan, 100% for UTs), and prescribes technical standards (IS 10500 for water quality, 55 lpcd service level). (b) State Water and Sanitation Mission (SWSM) — prepares SAAPs, empanels implementing agencies, and monitors physical/financial progress. (c) Village Water and Sanitation Committee (VWSC) / Paani Samiti — a sub‑committee of the Gram Panchayat with 50% women members, responsible for planning, operation, maintenance, and user‑charge collection.

Critical discretionary nodes include: (i) SAAP approval and fund release — NJJM’s discretion to approve or return SAAPs based on “saturation planning” (prioritising uncovered habitations), “source sustainability” (hydro‑geological assessment), and “grey‑water management” convergence. The 2021‑22 CAG Report No. 5 noted that 14 States had not submitted Source Sustainability Plans for 68% of schemes, yet central funds were released — a failure of NJJM’s gatekeeping discretion. (ii) VWSC empowerment and fund devolution — the 10% capital‑cost community contribution (5% for SC/ST majority villages) is deposited in the VWSC bank account. The VWSC’s discretion to select the implementing agency (PHED, parastatal, or NGO) and approve technical estimates is often circumvented by State PHEDs issuing “technical sanctions” without VWSC consent. The Ministry’s 2022 advisory mandated “VWSC‑led procurement” for in‑village infrastructure, but compliance remains patchy. (iii) Water‑quality surveillance — the JJM mandates testing at source, treatment plant, and household level using Field Test Kits (FTKs) and NABL‑accredited labs. The discretion to declare a source “contaminated” and trigger alternate‑source planning rests with the District Water Quality Testing Laboratory. In State of Punjab v. Union of India (2022), the Punjab & Haryana High Court directed the State to constitute independent District Water Quality Monitoring Committees after arsenic/fluoride contamination data was allegedly suppressed by PHED officials. (iv) Functionality certification — the “Har Ghar Jal” certification requires a Gram Sabha resolution confirming 100% FHTC, 55 lpcd, and potability. The discretion to accept or reject this certification lies with the District Collector. Instances of “paper certification” without physical verification have prompted NJJM to introduce third‑party sample surveys (5% of villages) by empaneled agencies.

For decision‑making questions, the examiner tests the ability to trace the accountability chain: Central Ministry → State Mission → District → VWSC → Household. A common trap is assuming the VWSC is a statutory body with independent legal personality; it is a Gram Panchayat sub‑committee, and its decisions can be overridden by the Panchayat or the District Collector under State Panchayati Raj Acts. Another trap is conflating JJM’s “service‑level” discretion (55 lpcd) with the statutory right to water under Article 21 — the former is a programme target, the latter a justiciable right; failure to meet 55 lpcd does not automatically constitute a constitutional violation unless discriminatory or arbitrary.

  • Confusing the policy‑level discretion of the Empowered Group of Secretaries (sector selection, budget allocation in PLI) with the operational discretion of the Project Management Agency (milestone verification, disbursement recommendation) — only the latter is routinely subject to Wednesbury review.
  • Assuming that SRO certification under the Online Gaming Rules grants immunity from State gambling laws; the Supreme Court has not yet ruled on federal pre‑emption, and State police can still prosecute under State Acts unless a central law occupies the field under Article 254.
  • Treating the 36‑hour takedown mandate under IT Rule 3(1)(d) as equivalent to a Section 69A blocking order; the former lacks the Shreya Singhal safeguards (review committee, written reasons, pre‑decisional hearing) and applies to a broader category of “unlawful content.”
  • Overlooking that the VWSC under Jal Jeevan Mission is not a body corporate; its bank account is operated jointly with the Gram Panchayat Sarpanch, and the District Collector can supersede it for “maladministration” under State Panchayati Raj Acts.
  • Misapplying the dominant‑factor test (skill vs. chance) from Satyanarayana (1968) to fantasy‑sports formats without examining the specific scoring algorithm, contest structure, and sample size — the test is fact‑intensive, not a blanket exemption.
  • Assuming that PM‑KISAN’s exclusion criteria (income‑tax payees, institutional landholders) are self‑executing; the DGRC has discretion to admit farmers with marginal non‑agricultural income if the exclusion would be disproportionate, but must record reasons.
  • Confusing the clawback clause in PLI schemes (contractual, 12% interest, bank guarantee) with recovery under the Subsidy Control Framework (statutory, different procedural safeguards); they operate in parallel and the government may pursue both.

These advanced sections equip aspirants to dissect multi‑layered administrative discretion across emerging regulatory regimes, apply the correct standard of review at each decision node, and avoid the conflation traps that distinguish high‑scoring answers from average ones.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of the Securities Market: SEBI’s Adjudicatory and Enforcement Powers

The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 empowers SEBI with a quasi‑judicial architecture that sits between pure regulation and criminal prosecution. Sections 15A to 15Z confer authority to impose monetary penalties, order disgorgement, direct restitution, and debar market participants. The adjudicating officer, appointed under Section 15I, conducts inquiries following principles of natural justice — notice, opportunity of hearing, and reasoned order. Appeals lie to the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) under Section 15T, with a further statutory appeal to the Supreme Court on questions of law under Section 15Z. The Supreme Court has upheld SEBI’s power to attach assets and direct refunds, emphasising that disgorgement is preventive, not punitive, and must be proportionate to illicit gain. It has also clarified that the “preponderance of probabilities” standard applies in adjudication, not the criminal “beyond reasonable doubt”. SEBI’s enforcement toolkit includes interim directions under Section 11(1) and (2) to protect investors, which SAT reviews on Wednesbury unreasonableness grounds. The settlement mechanism under the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018 allows alleged violators to settle without admission of guilt, subject to SEBI’s discretion; the settlement amount cannot be less than the statutory penalty floor. For decision‑making questions, the examiner tests the ability to distinguish SEBI’s adjudicatory function (penalty, disgorgement) from its regulatory function (registration, offer‑document approval), and to identify the correct appellate forum at each stage.

Decision‑Making in the Management of the National Disaster Response Fund and State Disaster Response Funds: Allocation, Utilisation, and Audit Oversight

The Disaster Management Act, 2005 establishes the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Funds (SDRF) as the primary financial instruments for immediate relief. The NDRF is financed through a cess on specified goods and services, while the SDRF receives contributions from the Centre (75 % for general category States, 90 % for special category States) and the respective State (25 %/10 %). The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) revised the allocation formula, weighting past expenditure, risk exposure, and fiscal capacity. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) releases NDRF instalments only after the State submits a utilisation plan, a requirement strengthened after audit findings flagged diversion of funds. Utilisation certificates (UCs) must be furnished within twelve months; failure triggers a “stop‑release” order under Section 46 of the Act. Audit reports have highlighted pending UCs across multiple States, prompting the MHA to institute a quarterly fund‑utilisation monitoring dashboard. The Act empowers the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) to issue guidelines on “minimum standards of relief”, which State Executive Committees translate into district‑level Standard Operating Procedures. Judicial review of fund‑release decisions is limited to arbitrariness under Article 14; the Supreme Court has refused to interfere with the Centre’s discretion to withhold NDRF releases pending audit clearance, holding such decisions to be policy choices within the Wednesbury envelope. For aspirants, the key decision nodes are: (i) Centre’s discretion to approve the State’s utilisation plan, (ii) State’s discretion to prioritise sectors (housing, agriculture, infrastructure), and (iii) the audit‑triggered stop‑release mechanism. A common trap is conflating the NDRF (central fund) with the SDRF (state fund) and assuming identical release conditions.

Technique: Mapping Decision Nodes to Statutory Provisions
A State submits a utilisation plan for NDRF funds that includes construction of a new district headquarters building. The MHA rejects the plan citing non‑compliance with NDMA guidelines. The State challenges the rejection before the High Court. Identify the statutory basis for the MHA’s discretion and the standard of judicial review applicable.
The MHA’s power derives from Section 46 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005 read with the NDMA guidelines issued under Section 6(2). The rejection is a policy‑level administrative decision concerning allocation of a central fund. Courts apply the Wednesbury unreasonableness test (Article 14 arbitrariness) and will not substitute their judgment on the suitability of the project. The High Court will uphold the rejection unless it is shown to be mala fide, irrational, or procedurally flawed (e.g., no hearing). The correct answer: Section 46, Disaster Management Act; Wednesbury review.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question describes a fund‑release dispute, first locate the governing statute (Disaster Management Act, Finance Commission report, or specific scheme guidelines). Then identify the decision‑maker (Centre, State, NDMA) and the statutory condition precedent (utilisation plan, UC, audit clearance). Finally, match the review standard: Wednesbury for policy allocation, proportionality for penalty‑type orders, and natural‑justice for adjudicatory orders.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban): Beneficiary Selection, Subsidy Disbursement, and Grievance Redressal

Launched in June 2015, the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – Urban (PMAY‑U) aims to provide “Housing for All” through four verticals: In‑situ Slum Redevelopment (ISSR), Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS), Affordable Housing in Partnership (AHP), and Beneficiary‑Led Construction (BLC). Beneficiary identification relies on the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 data, supplemented by Aadhaar‑seeded verification at the Urban Local Body (ULB) level. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) issues “State Level Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee” (SLSMC) guidelines that delegate final approval of beneficiary lists to the State‑level committee, while the ULB prepares the “Demand Survey” and forwards it to the District Level Committee (DLC). The CLSS component provides interest subsidy of 6.5 % for EWS/LIG and 4 % for MIG‑I/II, capped at ₹2.67 lakh and ₹2.35 lakh respectively, disbursed through Primary Lending Institutions (PLIs) after the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) validates the claim. A 2021 revision introduced a “Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) mode” for BLC, where the subsidy is credited to the beneficiary’s Aadhaar‑linked bank account in three instalments linked to construction milestones verified by a third‑party agency. Grievance redressal operates at three tiers: (i) the PMAY‑U MIS portal with a 30‑day resolution SLA, (ii) the State‑level Grievance Redressal Committee chaired by the Principal Secretary (Housing), and (iii) the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) for escalation. Audit findings have flagged incomplete houses lacking completion certificates and gaps in third‑party verification mechanisms. The Supreme Court has held that the State’s discretion to modify the beneficiary list after SLSMC approval is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness, and that the “reasonable classification” test under Article 14 applies to any exclusion criteria beyond SECC. For decision‑making questions, the examiner expects candidates to trace the chain: SECC → ULB demand survey → DLC → SLSMC → CNA → PLI → DBT, and to spot where discretion can be exercised (e.g., DLC’s power to add/delete names, SLSMC’s power to re‑prioritise verticals).

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India: Licensing, Enforcement, and Risk‑Based Inspection

The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act) establishes the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) as the single reference point for all matters relating to food safety. Licensing is bifurcated: Central Licensing for large manufacturers, importers, and export‑oriented units (annual turnover >₹20 crore) and State Licensing for medium enterprises (turnover ₹12 lakh–₹20 crore). Petty food businesses (turnover <₹12 lakh) require only registration. The 2011 Regulations prescribe a risk‑based inspection framework: “High‑risk” categories (meat, dairy, ready‑to‑eat) attract a minimum of two inspections per year; “Medium‑risk” (bakery, beverages) one inspection; “Low‑risk” (packaged water) inspection on complaint basis. Food Safety Officers (FSOs) appointed under Section 37 conduct inspections, draw samples, and issue improvement notices. Non‑compliance triggers adjudication by the Adjudicating Officer (AO) under Section 68, who can impose penalties up to ₹5 lakh for contraventions and up to ₹10 lakh for repeat offences. Appeals lie to the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal (FSAT) under Section 70, and further to the High Court under Section 71. The Supreme Court has upheld the AO’s power to order product recall and destruction, emphasizing that the precautionary principle under Section 18(2) permits preventive action even absent conclusive scientific proof of harm. The 2021 amendment introduced “Food Safety Compliance System (FoSCoS)”, an online portal for licensing, registration, and inspection scheduling, aiming to reduce discretionary delays. Audit reports have noted inspection shortfalls for high‑risk units and delays in resolving improvement notices beyond the statutory period. For aspirants, the decision‑making map is: Application → FSSAI/State Authority (licensing) → FSO (inspection) → AO (adjudication) → FSAT → High Court. The examiner tests the ability to differentiate between licensing discretion (subject to statutory criteria) and enforcement discretion (subject to Wednesbury review), and to identify the correct appellate forum at each stage.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Funds under the Fifteenth Finance Commission: Performance Grants and Conditionalities

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (FC‑XV), constituted under Article 280, submitted its report for the 2021‑26 period recommending a vertical devolution of 41 % of the divisible pool to States, unchanged from FC‑XIV. In addition, FC‑XV introduced performance‑based grants for (i) health sector (₹70,000 crore), (ii) education sector (₹50,000 crore), (iii) agriculture and allied sectors (₹30,000 crore), and (iv) urban local bodies (₹25,000 crore).
