Each grant carries conditionalities: the health grant requires States to achieve a minimum utilisation of National Health Mission funds and to maintain a functional Health Management Information System; the education grant is linked to the “Learning Outcomes” index and the implementation of the National Education Policy 2020 reforms; the agriculture grant is contingent on the adoption of the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act and the establishment of a State‑level Farmer Producer Organisation registry. The Commission also recommended a “Fiscal Consolidation Roadmap” limiting the fiscal deficit to 3 % of GSDP by 2025‑26, with a glide path for States exceeding the threshold. The Centre’s discretion to release performance grants is exercised through the Ministry of Finance’s “Grant Release Order” after verification by the concerned line ministry and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (CAG) certification of utilisation. The Supreme Court has held that the Centre’s decision to withhold a performance grant for non‑fulfilment of conditionalities is a policy decision amenable only to Article 14 arbitrariness review, not to a proportionality test. Audit reports have highlighted shortfalls in health‑grant utilisation across several States. For decision‑making questions, the candidate must map the flow: FC‑XV recommendation → Ministry of Finance (release) → Line Ministry (verification) → CAG (certification) → State (utilisation). The key discretion points are the line ministry’s assessment of “satisfactory performance” and the Ministry of Finance’s final release order. A frequent trap is assuming that the FC‑XV recommendations are legally binding; they are advisory until accepted by the President, after which the conditionalities become executable through executive orders.

  • Confusing SEBI’s adjudicatory penalties (Sections 15A‑15Z) with its regulatory directions under Section 11; the former attract SAT appeal, the latter are reviewed on Wednesbury grounds.
  • Treating NDRF and SDRF release conditions as identical; NDRF requires Centre’s approval of a State utilisation plan, SDRF follows a pre‑agreed sharing formula.
  • Assuming PMAY‑U beneficiary selection is solely SECC‑driven; ULBs and DLCs exercise discretion to add or delete names, which is subject to Article 14 review.
  • Equating FSSAI licensing discretion with enforcement discretion; licensing follows statutory eligibility criteria, enforcement follows risk‑based inspection and Wednesbury review.
  • Believing Fifteenth Finance Commission performance grants are automatically released; they require line‑ministry verification and CAG certification, and the Centre may withhold them for non‑compliance.
  • Overlooking that the Settlement Mechanism under SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018 is optional and does not extinguish the right to appeal to SAT.
  • Misapplying the precautionary principle under the FSS Act to all food categories; it is invoked primarily for high‑risk products where scientific uncertainty exists.

Ethical Decision‑Making in International Obligations: Treaty Implementation and Domestic Administrative Action

India’s constitutional scheme places the power to implement international treaties primarily in the executive, subject to parliamentary ratification where legislation is required. Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws for giving effect to treaties, while Article 51(c) directs the State to foster respect for international law. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969) reflects customary international law binding on India; it obliges a state to perform its treaty obligations in good faith (pacta sunt servanda) and prohibits invoking domestic law as justification for non‑compliance (Article 27). In practice, the executive often issues notifications, rules, or executive orders to align domestic administration with treaty commitments without awaiting fresh legislation, provided the treaty is self‑executing or the Constitution permits such action.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly clarified the justiciability of treaty‑derived obligations. In Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1970) the Court held that a treaty ratified by the President becomes part of the law of the land only when implemented by legislation; however, where a treaty creates rights that are directly enforceable, courts may give effect to them. Jolly George Varghese v. Bank of Cochin (1980) reinforced that international conventions ratified by India can be invoked to interpret domestic statutes, especially when the statute is ambiguous. The landmark Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) judgment imported the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) to fill a legislative vacuum on sexual harassment, establishing that international norms can shape administrative guidelines pending domestic law.

More recently, National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) recognized the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) as a guiding principle for interpreting the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), the Court referred to the Yogyakarta Principles on the application of international human rights law in relation to sexual orientation and gender identity, illustrating how soft‑law instruments influence constitutional adjudication. Administrative decision‑makers must therefore trace the chain: treaty → ratification → domestic legislation or executive action → administrative rule → implementation. Discretion arises at the stage of translating treaty standards into operational guidelines, and such discretion is subject to judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness (Article 14) and violation of fundamental rights (Articles 19, 21).

Key practical checkpoints for a civil servant: (1) verify whether the treaty is self‑executing or requires enabling legislation; (2) identify the competent authority (Ministry, Department, or statutory body) designated to issue implementing rules; (3) ensure that any administrative order cites the specific treaty provision and the domestic legal basis; (4) maintain a record of stakeholder consultation, especially when the treaty mandates participatory processes (e.g., the Aarhus Convention on access to information); (5) anticipate judicial scrutiny by aligning the decision with the principle of proportionality and the doctrine of legitimate expectation where treaty‑based rights create enforceable expectations.

Legitimate Expectation in Government Contracts and Procurement

The doctrine of legitimate expectation, rooted in administrative law, protects a person’s reasonable expectation of a benefit or procedural fairness arising from a consistent practice or an explicit promise by a public authority. In the context of government contracts and procurement, the doctrine operates at two levels: (a) substantive expectation — where a bidder or contractor expects renewal, extension, or award based on past conduct; and (b) procedural expectation — where a participant expects adherence to published tender conditions, transparency norms, and the principles of natural justice.

The Supreme Court in Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994) held that a public authority’s decision to grant a licence creates a legitimate expectation of renewal if the authority has consistently renewed similar licences without policy change. In State of Punjab v. Ramdev Singh (2003), the Court ruled that a contractor who had been awarded successive contracts on the basis of a standing policy could not be arbitrarily excluded without a reasoned order. The General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017 and the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, 2017 codify procedural expectations: equal treatment, non‑discrimination, and a fair opportunity to compete. The Government e‑Marketplace (GeM) platform further institutionalises these expectations by mandating electronic bidding, real‑time evaluation, and automated award letters.

Substantive expectation does not confer a vested right; it merely obliges the authority to consider the expectation and provide cogent reasons for departure. In M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. v. Union of India (2005), the Court held that a change in policy must be prospective, publicly notified, and backed by a rational nexus to public interest. Competition law jurisprudence has also recognised that unilateral alteration of contract terms by a dominant enterprise may violate the reasonable expectations of business users.

For decision‑making questions, the examiner expects candidates to map the following sequence: (i) identification of the representation or practice creating the expectation; (ii) assessment of whether the expectation is legitimate (reasonable, induced by authority, not contrary to law); (iii) determination of whether the authority’s departure is justified by a compelling public interest, policy shift, or statutory mandate; (iv) verification that the affected party was afforded a hearing or written reasons. A frequent trap is conflating legitimate expectation with estoppel; estoppel requires detrimental reliance, whereas legitimate expectation can arise from a consistent practice alone.

Technique: Mapping Expectation to Review Standard
A State Transport Corporation has renewed a private bus operator’s permit annually for ten years under a policy that permits renewal “subject to satisfactory performance”. In the eleventh year, the Corporation issues a new policy limiting permits to State‑owned operators only, and refuses renewal without a hearing. The operator challenges the refusal. Identify the legitimate expectation, the applicable standard of review, and the likely outcome.
1. Legitimate expectation arises from the consistent ten‑year renewal practice and the published policy wording, creating a reasonable expectation of renewal subject to performance. 2. The standard of review is Wednesbury unreasonableness coupled with procedural fairness (right to be heard). 3. Because the new policy is a substantive policy change affecting vested expectations, the Corporation must demonstrate a compelling public interest, provide prior notice, and afford a hearing. Absent these, the refusal is likely to be quashed as arbitrary under Article 14 and violative of natural justice.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question presents a factual pattern of repeated administrative action, first label the expectation (substantive vs procedural). Then ask: “Was there a clear representation or consistent practice?” “Is the departure backed by a published policy change?” “Was the affected party heard?” Answering these three sub‑questions in order yields the correct review standard and outcome in >90 % of CSAT decision‑making items.

Regulatory Sandbox Framework under the RBI and SEBI: Design, Exit Criteria, and Judicial Oversight

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) launched its Regulatory Sandbox for FinTech in August 2019 through the “Enabling Framework for Regulatory Sandbox” notification. The framework defines a sandbox as a controlled environment where eligible entities — start‑ups, banks, NBFCs — can test innovative products, services, or technology under relaxed regulatory requirements for a limited period. Eligibility criteria include a minimum net‑owned fund of ₹25 lakh (as per latest audited balance sheet) and a viable business plan addressing a genuine financial inclusion or efficiency gap, alongside compliance with data‑localisation and consumer‑protection norms. The sandbox operates in three cohorts per year, each with a testing window of up to six months, extendable by three months on justified grounds.

SEBI introduced its own sandbox in May 2020 via the “SEBI (Regulatory Sandbox) Regulations, 2020”. The SEBI sandbox targets securities‑market innovations such as algorithmic trading platforms, distributed ledger‑based settlement, and robo‑advisory services. Participants must be registered intermediaries or entities sponsored by a registered intermediary, with a minimum net worth of ₹1 crore. The testing phase lasts up to twelve months, with a mandatory “exit plan” that specifies how customers will be migrated to a fully regulated environment or how the product will be wound down. Both regulators require a “sandbox coordinator” — a designated compliance officer — and periodic reporting of incidents, consumer complaints, and risk metrics.

Exit criteria are the most scrutinised design element. The RBI framework mandates that at the end of the testing period the entity must either (a) obtain the requisite licence/authorisation to operate at scale, (b) cease operations and return customer funds, or (c) demonstrate that the innovation has been integrated into an existing regulated product. SEBI adds a “graduated exit” where the regulator may impose additional capital, governance, or audit requirements before full authorisation. Judicial oversight has been limited but instructive. In Internet and Mobile Association of India v. Reserve Bank of India (2020), the Supreme Court set aside the RBI’s 2018 circular restricting banking services to virtual‑currency businesses, noting that the sandbox framework provides a lawful avenue for innovation without circumventing banking regulation. The Court emphasised that sandbox participation does not confer immunity from existing statutes such as the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.

For decision‑making questions, candidates should be able to: (1) distinguish the RBI sandbox (financial‑services‑wide) from the SEBI sandbox (securities‑specific); (2) identify the mandatory exit‑plan components — customer protection, data‑handling, and regulatory reporting; (3) recognise that sandbox relaxation is conditional and revocable, and that the regulator retains Wednesbury‑type discretion to terminate participation for non‑compliance; (4) apply the proportionality test when a participant challenges termination — the regulator must show that the restriction is necessary, suitable, and not excessive relative to the risk identified.

Corporate Governance of Public Sector Undertakings: Board Autonomy, Government Nominee Directors, and DPE Guidelines

Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in India are governed by the Companies Act, 2013, supplemented by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) Guidelines issued periodically (2010, 2014, 2020). The DPE classifies PSUs into Maharatna, Navratna, and Miniratna categories based on net worth, turnover, and profit criteria, granting graded autonomy in investment, joint‑venture formation, and human‑resource decisions. Maharatna firms (e.g., ONGC, Indian Oil) may invest up to ₹5,000 crore without prior government approval; Navratna firms up to ₹1,000 crore; Miniratna‑I up to ₹500 crore (subject to net‑worth ceilings).

Board composition is a critical decision‑making node. The Companies Act mandates at least one‑third independent directors for listed PSUs. The DPE Guidelines further require that government nominee directors (usually Joint Secretaries from the administrative ministry) not exceed one‑third of the board strength. In practice, nominee directors often dominate strategic decisions, raising concerns about “dual loyalty”. The Supreme Court in Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd v. Union of India (2003) held that while the government may issue policy directives, it cannot micromanage day‑to‑day operations, and the board retains fiduciary duty to the company and its shareholders, including minority shareholders.

The 2020 DPE Guidelines introduced a “Board Evaluation Framework” requiring annual performance evaluation of the board, its committees, and individual directors, including nominee directors. The framework also mandates a “Code of Conduct for Directors” aligned with the Nolan Principles. The Public Enterprises Survey (annual) tracks compliance, and the CAG conducts performance audits that assess whether board decisions adhere to the principles of commercial prudence and public accountability.

Key decision‑making checkpoints for a PSU board: (i) verify that any capital expenditure beyond delegated limits receives prior approval from the administrative ministry and the DPE; (ii) ensure that related‑party transactions are cleared by the Audit Committee and disclosed in the annual report; (iii) confirm that the appointment of the Chairman‑cum‑Managing Director follows the “Search‑cum‑Selection Committee” process prescribed by the DPE; (iv) document dissent notes of independent directors when nominee directors push for non‑commercial objectives. Failure to observe these safeguards exposes the board to judicial review under Article 14 (arbitrariness) and relevant provisions of the Companies Act governing fraud and mismanagement.

Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and the Role of the CAMPA Authority

The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 requires that any diversion of forest land for non‑forest purposes be compensated by afforestation on an equivalent area of non‑forest land or degraded forest land. The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 operationalised this by establishing the National Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (National CAMPA) and State CAMPAs. The Fund receives money from user agencies (mining, infrastructure, hydropower) as “Net Present Value” (NPV) of the diverted forest, compensatory afforestation charges, and penal charges for violations.

Decision‑making flow: (1) Project proponent submits a diversion proposal to the State Forest Department; (2) the State Government forwards it to the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) with a site‑specific compensatory afforestation plan; (3) the Forest Advisory Committee (FAC) examines the proposal and recommends approval, conditional approval, or rejection; (4) upon approval, the user agency deposits the NPV and afforestation charges into the National CAMPA account; (5) the State CAMPA prepares an Annual Plan of Operations (APO) detailing afforestation works, which is approved by the National CAMPA; (6) funds are released to the State Forest Department for implementation; (7) the State CAMPA monitors survival rates, submits utilisation certificates, and the CAG audits the accounts.

The Supreme Court’s “Godavarman” series (starting with T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India, 1995) established that compensatory afforestation is not a mere financial transaction but an ecological obligation. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996), the Court directed that the NPV rates be revised periodically to reflect ecological value. The Central Government notified NPV rates in 2018 for different forest types (e.g., ₹9.39 lakh/ha for very dense forest, ₹5.65 lakh/ha for moderately dense forest) and mandated that at least 80 % of the Fund be spent on afforestation and forest‑related activities, with the remainder for capacity building and monitoring.

For CSAT decision‑making items, the examiner tests the ability to sequence the above steps, identify the discretionary nodes (FAC recommendation, State CAMPA’s APO approval, MoEFCC’s final clearance), and spot violations such as: (a) releasing funds before APO approval; (b) using Fund money for non‑forestry purposes; (c) ignoring survival‑rate thresholds (minimum 70 % at the end of the third year). The CAG’s 2022 report highlighted significant diversions of CAMPA funds to non‑afforestation heads, prompting the MoEFCC to issue a 2023 directive tightening fund‑utilisation monitoring.

  • Confusing the RBI sandbox’s six‑month testing window with SEBI’s twelve‑month window and assuming identical exit criteria.
  • Treating legitimate expectation in procurement as a vested right that cannot be overridden by any policy change.
  • Assuming that treaty obligations automatically become enforceable domestic law without checking for enabling legislation or self‑execution.
  • Believing that government nominee directors on PSU boards have veto power over all commercial decisions.
  • Overlooking the requirement that State CAMPA’s Annual Plan of Operations must be approved by National CAMPA before fund release.
  • Misapplying the proportionality test to sandbox termination when the regulator’s action is reviewed only on Wednesbury grounds.
  • Ignoring the distinction between NPV charges and compensatory afforestation charges when calculating the total deposit for forest diversion.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana: Beneficiary Selection, Fund Flow, and Monitoring

The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY) was launched in June 2015 with two verticals — PMAY‑Urban (PMAY‑U) under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and PMAY‑Gramin (PMAY‑G) under the Ministry of Rural Development. The scheme aims to provide “Housing for All” by 2022 (later extended to 2024) through four components: In‑situ Slum Redevelopment (ISSR), Credit‑Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS), Affordable Housing in Partnership (AHP), and Beneficiary‑Led Construction (BLC). Decision‑making authority is distributed across three tiers: (i) the Central Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee (CSMC) approves annual action plans and releases central assistance; (ii) State Level Sanctioning and Monitoring Committees (SLSMC) validate beneficiary lists, approve project‑level Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), and monitor physical progress; (iii) Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) or Gram Panchayats execute construction, verify completion, and upload geo‑tagged photographs on the PMAY‑MIS portal.

Beneficiary identification relies on the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 data, supplemented by state‑specific surveys. Guidelines provide for preference to women‑headed households or joint ownership with women under BLC. Fund flow follows a Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) model: central assistance for BLC is ₹1.5 lakh per house for EWS category (with varying shares for other components); the amount is credited to the beneficiary’s Aadhaar‑linked bank account in instalments linked to construction stages — typically on sanction, plinth completion, and final completion certified by the ULB/Gram Panchayat. Cost‑sharing ratios differ: PMAY‑U follows a 60:40 Centre‑State split for most states (90:10 for North‑Eastern and Himalayan states); PMAY‑G follows a 60:40 split for plain areas and 90:10 for special category states.

Monitoring mechanisms include the PMAY‑MIS dashboard, third‑party quality audits by designated institutions, and a grievance redressal module integrated with CPGRAMS. Audit reports have flagged delays in fund release due to mismatched SECC data, non‑compliance with geo‑tagging norms, and instances of “ghost beneficiaries.” The Ministry has responded with directives mandating Aadhaar‑based authentication at instalment stages and timelines for state‑level sanction after CSMC approval.

For CSAT decision‑making items, examiners test the ability to sequence the approval chain (CSMC → SLSMC → ULB/Gram Panchayat), identify discretionary nodes (state‑level addition of beneficiaries beyond SECC, relaxation of women‑ownership clause in exceptional cases), and spot violations such as releasing the second instalment before plinth‑level geo‑tag verification or diverting central assistance to non‑housing heads. A common twist is to present a scenario where a state government proposes to use PMAY‑U funds for slum rehabilitation under a state‑specific scheme; the correct answer hinges on the requirement that any deviation from the four approved components requires prior CSMC clearance.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Coal Blocks under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015: Auction Design, Eligibility, and Judicial Oversight

The Supreme Court’s 2014 judgment in Manohar Lal Sharma v. Union of India cancelled 214 coal block allocations made between 1993 and 2011 on grounds of arbitrariness and lack of transparency. In response, Parliament enacted the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 (CMSP Act) to provide a statutory framework for transparent allocation through competitive bidding. The Act empowers the Central Government to notify coal mines for auction, specify eligibility criteria, and define the bidding parameters — primarily the “floor price” (minimum bid per tonne) and the “revenue share” (percentage of sale value payable to the state). The auction process is conducted on the Ministry of Coal’s e‑auction platform, managed by MSTC Limited, a public sector undertaking.

Eligibility is restricted to companies incorporated in India meeting prescribed net‑worth thresholds and prior experience in mining or related infrastructure. The bidding document requires a technical bid (company credentials, mine development plan, environment clearance status) and a financial bid (quoted revenue share). Evaluation follows a two‑stage process: (1) technical qualification — only bidders meeting net‑worth, experience, and environment‑clearance thresholds proceed; (2) financial ranking — the highest revenue share wins, subject to the floor price. The successful bidder signs a Coal Mine Development and Production Agreement (CMDPA) with the nominated authority, committing to achieve “peak rated capacity” within stipulated timelines that differ for captive and commercial mines.

Discretionary nodes include: (a) the Central Government’s power to decide which mines are placed in Schedule II (captive) versus Schedule III (commercial) — a policy choice reviewed only for manifest arbitrariness under Article 14; (b) the Nominated Authority’s discretion to grant extensions for achieving peak capacity on grounds of force majeure or regulatory delays; (c) the Ministry’s authority to modify the floor price after stakeholder consultation, provided the change is published before the bid submission deadline. The Supreme Court has upheld the auction framework but struck down provisions allowing allocation to state‑owned enterprises without auction, reiterating that the CMSP Act’s core mandate is competitive bidding.

Monitoring and compliance are enforced through the Coal Controller’s Organisation (CCO), which verifies production data, conducts periodic inspections, and can impose penalties for shortfalls. Audit reports have highlighted that a portion of auctioned mines had not commenced production within stipulated timelines, mainly due to delays in forest clearance and land acquisition — areas where state government discretion intersects with central auction outcomes. For CSAT items, the examiner often asks to arrange the chronological order: (i) notification of mines, (ii) publication of bid document, (iii) technical bid evaluation, (iv) financial bid opening, (v) signing of CMDPA, (vi) achievement of peak rated capacity. Another trap is to confuse the “revenue share” model with the earlier “fixed royalty” regime; the correct answer always references the CMSP Act’s shift to revenue‑share bidding.

Technique: Sequencing Administrative Approvals
A state government proposes to allocate a coal block under Schedule III to a private company. The following steps are mentioned in random order: (1) Publication of bid document on the e‑auction portal; (2) Notification of the coal block in the Gazette; (3) Signing of the Coal Mine Development and Production Agreement; (4) Technical bid evaluation by the Nominated Authority; (5) Financial bid opening and ranking; (6) Achievement of peak rated capacity. Arrange the steps in the correct administrative sequence.
Correct sequence: (2) Notification of the coal block in the Gazette → (1) Publication of bid document on the e‑auction portal → (4) Technical bid evaluation by the Nominated Authority → (5) Financial bid opening and ranking → (3) Signing of the Coal Mine Development and Production Agreement → (6) Achievement of peak rated capacity. The notification precedes any bid document; technical evaluation must be completed before financial bids are opened; the CMDPA is executed only after the highest revenue‑share bidder is identified; production capacity is a post‑contract milestone.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question lists administrative steps out of order, first identify the statutory trigger (notification, gazette, rule publication). Then locate the decision‑making body that exercises discretion at each stage (Central Government, Nominated Authority, Coal Controller). Eliminate options that place a discretionary act before its legal prerequisite. Practice with at least three full‑length sequencing sets from previous years to internalise the pattern.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Medical Education: The National Medical Commission Act, 2019

The National Medical Commission (NMC) Act, 2019 replaced the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 and dissolved the Medical Council of India (MCI). The Act establishes the NMC as a 25‑member body comprising a Chairperson, ten ex‑officio members (including the Director General of Health Services, President of the Pharmacy Council, and representatives of the Ministry of Health), and fourteen part‑time members appointed by the Central Government on the recommendation of a Search Committee. Four Autonomous Boards — Under‑Graduate Medical Education Board (UGMEB), Post‑Graduate Medical Education Board (PGMEB), Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), and Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) — exercise regulatory functions under the NMC’s superintendence.

Key decision‑making powers: (i) UGMEB and PGMEB set minimum standards for curriculum, infrastructure, faculty, and admission processes; they grant permission for new medical colleges, increase of seats, and starting of post‑graduate courses after inspection by MARB. (ii) MARB conducts assessments and ratings of medical institutions; its rating determines eligibility for seat expansion and recognition of qualifications. (iii) EMRB maintains the National Medical Register, registers medical practitioners, and enforces the Code of Medical Ethics; it can suspend or cancel registration for professional misconduct. (iv) The NMC frames the National Exit Test (NExT) regulations — a single licentiate examination for MBBS graduates, replacing the erstwhile FMGE and serving as the basis for PG admission.

Discretionary nodes include: (a) the Central Government’s power to issue policy directions to the NMC on “matters of national importance” — subject to judicial review for arbitrariness; (b) the Search Committee’s composition and criteria for selecting part‑time members — the Supreme Court has upheld the Committee’s independence while requiring transparency in its proceedings; (c) MARB’s discretion to grant conditional permission for new colleges pending fulfillment of infrastructure norms within a prescribed timeline. The Act also introduces a “fee regulation” mechanism for 50 % of seats in private medical colleges and deemed universities, with the NMC fixing the fee ceiling based on a cost‑plus formula.

Monitoring and accountability: The NMC must submit an annual report to Parliament; the CAG audits its accounts. Recent amendments to the NMC Regulations mandated real‑time uploading of inspection reports on the NMC portal and introduced a “grievance redressal portal” for students and faculty. For CSAT decision‑making questions, examiners test the hierarchy: Central Government → NMC → Autonomous Boards → Medical Institutions. A frequent trap is to attribute the power to recognise foreign medical qualifications to the NMC; under the Act, that power rests with the Central Government on the NMC’s recommendation. Another twist involves the “bridge course” for AYUSH practitioners — the Act does not provide for it; any such proposal requires a separate legislative amendment.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Funds under the Fifteenth Finance Commission: Vertical Devolution, Horizontal Formula, and Performance Grants

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (FC‑XV), constituted in November 2017 under the chairmanship of N. K. Singh, submitted its final report for the award period 2021‑22 to 2025‑26. The Commission recommended a vertical devolution of 41 % of the divisible pool of central taxes to states — a reduction from the 42 % recommended by the Fourteenth Finance Commission, reflecting the Centre’s enhanced expenditure responsibilities after the GST rollout. The horizontal distribution formula assigns weights: 45 % to population (2011 Census), 15 % to area, 15 % to forest and ecology, 10 % to income distance, 10 % to demographic performance, and 5 % to tax effort. This formula replaces the earlier 1971‑Census‑based population weight, addressing concerns of states with successful population control.

Performance‑based grants constitute a conditional layer: (i) Health sector grants — released to states that meet defined output indicators (e.g., functional Health and Wellness Centres, immunisation coverage). (ii) Grants for local bodies — conditional on timely audited accounts, publication of service‑level benchmarks, and adoption of the Model Municipal Law. (iii) Disaster risk management grants — linked to the preparation of State Disaster Management Plans and mitigation projects approved by the National Disaster Management Authority. (iv) Sector‑specific grants for agriculture, education, and judiciary, each with measurable milestones.

Decision‑making flow: The Union Finance Ministry accepts the Commission’s recommendations (with or without modifications) and issues the “Finance Commission Grants Order” under Article 275. States submit utilisation certificates (UCs) and performance reports to the Ministry of Finance and the concerned line ministries. The Comptroller and Auditor General audits the grants; the Commission itself monitors outcomes through a dedicated “Performance Monitoring Unit”. Budget executions have seen shortfalls in health grant releases where states failed to operationalise the required number of Health and Wellness Centres within stipulated timelines — illustrating the conditional nature of performance grants.

For CSAT items, the examiner may ask to compute a state’s share given its population, area, and forest cover, or to identify which grant is “unconditional” (the vertical devolution share) versus “conditional” (performance grants). A common trap is to treat the 2011 Census population weight as 100 % of the horizontal formula; the correct answer always references the multi‑criteria weights. Another twist involves the “income distance” criterion — it measures the distance of a state’s per‑capita GSDP from the highest per‑capita GSDP state (currently Goa), not the national average.

Administrative Discretion in the Enforcement of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010: Registration, Prior Permission, and Cancellation Procedures

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (FCRA) governs the acceptance and utilisation of foreign contributions by individuals, associations, and NGOs in India. The Act was substantially amended in 2020 (FCRA Amendment Act, 2020) to tighten oversight. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is the nodal authority; it maintains the FCRA online portal for registration, prior permission, and annual returns. An entity seeking to receive foreign contributions must obtain either (i) registration under Section 12 (valid for five years, renewable) or (ii) prior permission under Section 11 for a specific project (valid for the project duration). Registration eligibility requires the entity to be in existence for at least three years, have a track record of societal work, and not be prohibited under any law.

Decision‑making nodes: (a) The MHA’s discretion to grant or refuse registration — the 2020 amendment introduced a “fit and proper” test for office‑bearers, including verification of criminal antecedents and source of funds. (b) The requirement that all foreign contributions be received only in a designated FCRA bank account (opened with the State Bank of India, New Delhi Main Branch) — a measure to enable real‑time monitoring. (c) The cap on administrative expenses at 20 % of total foreign contributions received in a financial year (reduced from 50 % pre‑2020). (d) The power to suspend or cancel registration under Section 14 for violations such as non‑filing of annual returns, diversion of funds, or activities prejudicial to national interest. The MHA must issue a show‑cause notice, provide an opportunity of hearing, and record reasons in writing — a procedural safeguard upheld by the Supreme Court.

Monitoring mechanisms: The FCRA portal auto‑generates alerts for delayed returns; the MHA conducts periodic “risk‑based” inspections. Audit reports have observed that a significant portion of registered NGOs had not filed annual returns for consecutive years, prompting the MHA to initiate cancellation proceedings. The 2020 amendment also barred public servants and political parties from receiving foreign contributions, and prohibited the transfer of foreign contributions to any other entity — a provision that has been challenged in courts but remains in force.

For CSAT decision‑making questions, the examiner tests the sequence: (i) application for registration/prior permission → (ii) MHA scrutiny and “fit and proper” verification → (iii) grant of registration with unique FCRA number → (iv) opening of designated bank account → (v) receipt of foreign contribution → (vi) filing of annual return (Form FC‑4) within nine months of financial year end. A frequent trap is to assume that prior permission can be converted into registration automatically; the Act requires a fresh registration application after three years of operation under prior permission. Another twist involves the “administrative expense” ceiling — candidates often confuse the 20 % cap with the earlier 50 % limit; the correct answer references the 2020 amendment.

Common Traps

  • Assuming that the Central Government can allocate coal blocks to state‑owned enterprises without auction after the 2019 amendment — the Supreme Court struck down that provision.
  • Treating the NMC’s power to recognise foreign medical qualifications as autonomous — it requires Central Government approval.
  • Confusing the vertical devolution share (unconditional) with performance‑based grants (conditional) in Finance Commission questions.
  • Believing that prior permission under FCRA automatically matures into registration after three years — a fresh application is mandatory.
  • Overlooking the requirement that the second instalment under PMAY‑BLC is released only after plinth‑level geo‑tag verification, not merely on a utilisation certificate.
  • Misapplying the 20 % administrative expense cap to foreign contributions received before the 2020 amendment — the cap applies prospectively.
  • Neglecting the multi‑criteria horizontal formula of the Fifteenth Finance Commission and using only population weight for share calculations.

Administrative Discretion in Coal Block Allocation under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015

The Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 (CMSP Act) replaced the earlier ordinance route and established a statutory framework for the allocation of coal blocks through transparent auction. The Central Government, acting through the Ministry of Coal, exercises discretion in three distinct stages: (i) identification of blocks for auction, (ii) setting of reserve price and eligibility criteria, and (iii) approval of the successful bidder’s mining plan and lease deed. The Act empowers the Central Government to notify blocks for auction after considering the recommendations of the Coal Controller and the Standing Committee on Coal. The reserve price is fixed based on the average market price of the relevant grade of coal, adjusted for quality, location, and infrastructure deficits. The Act mandates a two‑stage bidding process — technical qualification followed by financial bid — and requires the successful bidder to achieve commercial production within a prescribed period, extendable on justified grounds.

Judicial scrutiny has focused on the “reasonableness” of the reserve price and the “non‑arbitrariness” of block selection. In a 2020 Supreme Court decision, the Court upheld the auction methodology but struck down a clause allowing re‑allocation to a state‑owned enterprise without fresh auction, holding it violative of Article 14. The Court emphasised that the discretion to select blocks must be guided by objective geological data, not by political considerations. A subsequent amendment introduced a “commercial viability” test, requiring the Ministry to publish a viability report before notification, thereby narrowing discretion.

For decision‑making questions, the examiner often tests the sequence: (a) geological survey → (b) block identification → (c) reserve price fixation → (d) auction → (e) mining plan approval → (f) lease execution. A common trap is to assume that the Ministry can directly allocate a block to a public sector undertaking after the 2015 Act; the Act permits such allocation only if the block was previously allotted under the old regime and the allottee fails to develop it, in which case the block returns to the auction pool. Another twist involves the “force‑majeure” extension — candidates must recall that the extension is discretionary and requires a written order with reasons, not an automatic grant.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of the Insurance Sector: IRDAI Decision‑Making Framework

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) derives its decision‑making powers from the Insurance Act, 1938 (as amended in 2015) and the IRDA Act, 1999. The Authority exercises discretion in licensing, product approval, solvency monitoring, and enforcement. Under the IRDA Act, the Chairperson and whole‑time members are appointed by the Central Government, but the Authority functions as a quasi‑judicial body when adjudicating disputes under the Insurance Act. Licensing discretion is governed by the “fit and proper” criteria laid down in the IRDAI (Registration of Insurance Companies) Regulations, which require a minimum paid‑up capital, promoter background checks, and a viable business plan. Product approval follows a “file‑and‑use” regime for most life products, while health and general insurance products require prior clearance; the Authority may reject a product if the pricing assumptions breach the “principle of equivalence” or if the policy wording is ambiguous.

Solvency supervision is anchored in the “Solvency Margin” regulations. The Authority can direct an insurer to augment capital, restrict new business, or appoint an administrator under the Insurance Act. Enforcement discretion includes imposing penalties per contravention, suspending or cancelling registration, and issuing directions under the Act. The Supreme Court has affirmed that the Authority’s power to appoint an administrator is subject to the principles of natural justice — a show‑cause notice and hearing are mandatory before a final order.

In CSAT situational judgment items, the examiner may present a scenario where an insurer launches a health product without prior clearance, claiming the “file‑and‑use” route. The correct response is to identify that health products are excluded from the file‑and‑use regime and require prior approval under the relevant Health Insurance Regulations. Another frequent twist concerns the “promoter lock‑in” period — the regulations mandate a lock‑in period for promoters holding significant equity; candidates often confuse this with the lock‑in applicable to banking licenses.

Technique: Sequential Elimination
A state government proposes to allocate a coal block to a state‑owned power utility without auction, citing urgent power demand. The Ministry of Coal has already notified the block for auction under the CMSP Act, 2015. Which of the following actions is legally permissible? (a) Direct allocation under Section 4(2) of the CMSP Act. (b) Allocation after a fresh auction with the utility as a bidder. (c) Allocation by the Central Government under the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973. (d) Allocation by the state government under its own mining policy.
The CMSP Act, 2015 mandates that all coal blocks be allocated through auction (Section 4). The Act does not contain a provision for direct allocation to a state‑owned entity after notification; the only exception is for blocks previously allotted under the old regime that revert to the auction pool. Therefore, option (a) is impermissible. Option (c) is obsolete because the 1973 Act was repealed by the CMSP Act. Option (d) exceeds state competence — coal is a Union subject. The legally permissible route is (b): conduct the auction as notified, allowing the utility to participate as a bidder. The correct answer is (b).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question describes a statutory scheme with a mandatory auction or licensing step, first identify the governing Act and the specific section that makes the process compulsory. Eliminate any answer that bypasses that mandatory step. Look for keywords such as “notified for auction”, “prior approval required”, or “fit and proper test” — they signal a non‑discretionary procedural requirement.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Fertiliser Subsidies under the Nutrient Based Subsidy Scheme

The Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) Scheme, introduced in 2010 and revised in 2022, governs the distribution of subsidies on phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers. The Department of Fertilisers, under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers, exercises discretion in three core areas: (i) fixation of per‑nutrient subsidy rates for nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K) and sulphur (S); (ii) determination of the “maximum retail price” (MRP) ceiling for each grade; and (iii) allocation of the subsidy budget among manufacturers and importers based on production and import data. The subsidy rates are announced annually through a Gazette notification after consultation with the Fertiliser Industry Coordination Committee (FICC) and the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP). The 2022 revision linked the subsidy to the “nutrient content” rather than the product weight, aiming to incentivise balanced fertilisation.

Judicial review of NBS decisions is limited to the Wednesbury unreasonableness test. In a 2021 Delhi High Court decision, the Court upheld the rate revision, noting that the government had considered international price trends, domestic production costs, and the fiscal deficit target. However, the Court struck down a clause that allowed the Department to retrospectively reduce subsidy on already‑dispatched stocks without a hearing, holding it violative of the principle of legitimate expectation.

For decision‑making questions, the examiner may test the sequence: (a) international price benchmarking → (b) CACP recommendation → (c) FICC deliberation → (d) Gazette notification → (e) MRP fixation → (f) subsidy disbursement through the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) platform. A common trap is to assume that the subsidy is paid directly to farmers; under the DBT model the subsidy is transferred to the manufacturer/importer after the point‑of‑sale device authenticates the sale to a registered farmer. Another twist involves the “sulphur” nutrient — candidates often forget that sulphur was added as a fourth nutrient in a recent revision and carries a separate per‑kg rate.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban)

The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – Urban (PMAY‑U), launched in 2015, aims to provide “Housing for All” by 2024. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) exercises discretion in (i) approval of State Level Action Plans (SLAPs), (ii) release of central assistance under the four verticals — In‑situ Slum Redevelopment (ISSR), Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS), Affordable Housing in Partnership (AHP), and Beneficiary‑Led Construction (BLC) — and (iii) monitoring through the “Geo‑Tag” and “MIS” platforms. The Central Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee (CSMC) chaired by the Secretary, MoHUA, approves project proposals after appraisal by the State Level Nodal Agency (SLNA). Fund release follows a milestone‑based schedule: an initial tranche on sanction, a second tranche on plinth‑level geo‑tag verification, a third on roof‑level verification, and a final tranche on completion certificate.

The Supreme Court has examined the discretion to reject a SLAP on grounds of “non‑availability of land”. The Court held that while the Ministry may assess land availability, it cannot arbitrarily withhold approval without giving the state an opportunity to present alternative land parcels. The judgment reinforced the principle of “procedural fairness” in the disbursement of central assistance.

In CSAT situational judgment items, a typical scenario describes a municipal corporation that has completed plinth‑level construction but has not uploaded geo‑tagged photographs. The question asks which instalment can be released.

Decision‑Making in the Implementation of the National Urban Livelihoods Mission

The National Urban Livelihoods Mission (NULM), launched in 2013 as a centrally sponsored scheme, replaced the earlier Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) exercises discretion in three interlocking layers: (i) approval of State‑level Annual Action Plans (AAPs) that set physical and financial targets for each component; (ii) release of central assistance in tranches linked to the achievement of milestones such as formation of Self‑Help Groups (SHGs), skill‑training completion, and placement verification; and (iii) monitoring through the NULM‑MIS portal, which captures geo‑tagged photographs of training centres, micro‑enterprise units, and shelter homes.

The mission comprises four core components — Social Mobilisation and Institution Development (SM&ID), Employment through Skills Training and Placement (EST&P), Self‑Employment Programme (SEP), and Shelter for Urban Homeless (SUH). Discretion is most visible in the SEP component, where the State Level Nodal Agency (SLNA) evaluates project proposals for micro‑enterprise loans up to ₹2 lakh (individual) or ₹10 lakh (group). The appraisal criteria include viability of the business plan, creditworthiness assessed through the Credit Information Bureau, and adherence to the “priority sector” lending norms of the Reserve Bank of India. The central ministry can withhold subsequent tranches of funds if the utilisation certificate for the previous tranche is not submitted within the prescribed period, a condition that courts have upheld as a legitimate condition precedent.

A recurring situational‑judgment scenario tests the candidate’s ability to sequence the release of funds. For instance, a municipal corporation reports that 80 % of SHGs have been formed but only 40 % have completed the mandatory financial literacy module. The correct administrative response is to release the first tranche (which is linked to SHG formation) while flagging the literacy gap for the next review meeting; the second tranche, tied to skill‑training completion, must be withheld until the module is finished. This reflects the principle of “milestone‑based disbursement” that prevents front‑loading of expenditure without corresponding outputs.

Judicial review of NULM decisions is limited to the Wednesbury unreasonableness test, but courts have insisted on procedural fairness when a state’s AAP is rejected. High Courts have directed the ministry to provide a speaking order enumerating the specific deficiencies in the AAP rather than a blanket refusal. For CSAT‑type questions, the examiner often embeds a “trap” by suggesting that the central ministry can unilaterally redesign the component structure; the scheme guidelines, however, require any modification to be approved by the National Mission Directorate after consultation with the State Level Coordination Committee.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Online Gaming and Gambling

The regulation of online gaming in India straddles the legislative fields of “betting and gambling” (State List, Entry 34) and “information technology” (Union List, Entry 47). The Public Gambling Act, 1867, remains the primary statute, but most states have enacted their own amendments — for example, the Telangana Gaming (Amendment) Act, 2017, and the Andhra Pradesh Gaming (Amendment) Act, 2020 — which explicitly prohibit games of chance offered through electronic means. In contrast, states such as Nagaland and Sikkim have enacted licensing regimes for “games of skill” under the Nagaland Prohibition of Gambling and Promotion and Regulation of Online Games of Skill Act, 2016, and the Sikkim Online Gaming (Regulation) Act, 2008.

At the Union level, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) issued the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, amended in 2023 to require online gaming intermediaries to appoint a grievance officer, a chief compliance officer, and a nodal contact person. The 2023 amendment also introduced a “self‑regulatory body” (SRB) framework: any online gaming platform that offers “real‑money games” must obtain a certificate of registration from an SRB recognised by MeitY. The SRB is mandated to verify that the game’s outcome is predominantly determined by skill, using a statistical test prescribed by the Ministry (the “dominant factor test”).

Administrative discretion appears at three points: (i) the state government’s power to notify a game as “gambling” or “skill” under its amendment act; (ii) MeitY’s discretion to recognise or derecognise an SRB based on its governance structure, transparency norms, and conflict‑of‑interest policies; and (iii) the SRB’s own discretion to grant, suspend, or revoke a platform’s registration after a due‑process hearing. The Supreme Court has held that a state’s blanket ban on all online card games, without distinguishing skill from chance, violates Article 19(1)(g) and is therefore ultra vires, directing the state to formulate a skill‑test methodology within a specified period.

For decision‑making questions, a typical scenario presents a startup that has obtained an SRB certificate in Nagaland but wishes to operate in Maharashtra, where the state amendment treats the same game as gambling. The correct administrative answer is that the platform must comply with the more restrictive state law; the SRB certificate does not confer a pan‑India licence because gambling remains a state subject. Another common trap is the assumption that the 2023 IT Rules override state gambling laws — they do not; the Rules only impose due‑diligence obligations on intermediaries, while the substantive prohibition or licensing power stays with the state legislature.

Situational Judgment – Cross‑State Online Gaming Compliance
A company registered under the Nagaland Online Games of Skill Act obtains an SRB certificate in March 2024. It launches a real‑money rummy platform accessible nationwide. In June 2024, the Maharashtra Police issue a notice under the Maharashtra Prevention of Gambling Act, 1887 (as amended 2020) directing the company to cease operations in the state. The company argues that its SRB certificate grants it a valid licence across India. As the decision‑maker in the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, which of the following actions is legally sound?
The SRB certificate issued under the 2023 IT Rules only certifies that the platform meets the self‑regulatory body’s skill‑test and governance standards; it does not create a central licence that supersedes state gambling legislation. Since “betting and gambling” is a State subject, Maharashtra’s amendment classifying rummy as gambling prevails within its territory. The legally sound action is to advise the company that it must either (a) obtain a separate licence under Maharashtra law (if the state provides a skill‑game licensing route) or (b) geo‑block Maharashtra users to comply with the state prohibition. MeitY cannot direct the state to recognise the Nagaland certificate. Therefore, the correct response is to require geo‑blocking or state‑specific licensing, not to uphold the company’s claim of a pan‑India licence.
Exam‑Day Strategy for Federal‑Subject Overlap Questions
When a question pits a Union‑level regulatory framework against a State‑level prohibition, first identify the constitutional entry (List II vs List I). The Union law can only impose procedural obligations on intermediaries; it cannot legalise an activity that a State has validly prohibited. Eliminate any answer that suggests a central certificate overrides state law. Look for keywords such as “geo‑block”, “state‑specific licence”, or “subject to state legislation” — these signal the correct federal‑compliance approach.

Decision‑Making under the National Digital Health Mission: Data Governance and Consent Architecture

The National Digital Health Mission (NDHM), rebranded as the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) in 2021, creates a federated digital health ecosystem anchored on three building blocks: a unique Health ID (ABHA number), a Health Facility Registry (HFR), and a Health Professional Registry (HPR). The National Health Authority (NHA) exercises discretion in (i) defining the data‑sharing standards (FHIR‑R4 profiles) that all participating entities must adopt; (ii) accrediting Consent Managers (CMs) that enable patients to grant, revoke, and audit consent for each data‑access request; and (iii) enforcing the “privacy by design” principles laid down in the ABDM Sandbox Guidelines.

Consent under ABDM is granular, purpose‑bound, and time‑limited. A patient can authorise a hospital to view a specific encounter summary for 30 days, while denying access to the full longitudinal record. The Consent Manager logs every consent artefact as an immutable audit trail on the ABDM consent ledger. The NHA’s discretion to approve a CM hinges on the CM’s compliance with the “Consent Manager Certification Framework” — which mandates end‑to‑end encryption, tamper‑evident logs, and a grievance redressal mechanism with a defined response SLA.

Administrative decisions on data‑access requests are subject to the “minimum necessary” principle. When a research institution applies for de‑identified cohort data, the NHA evaluates the request against the “Data Access Policy”, which requires an Institutional Ethics Committee clearance, a data‑use agreement, and a demonstrable public‑health purpose. The NHA may grant “controlled access” through a secure data enclave rather than releasing raw datasets. Courts have upheld the NHA’s refusal to share identifiable health records with private entities, citing the absence of a valid consent artefact and the lack of a statutory exemption under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

For situational‑judgment items, a common scenario describes a district hospital that has integrated its HMIS with ABDM but has not yet onboarded a certified Consent Manager. The question asks what the hospital’s next step must be before it can share patient records with a tertiary centre. The correct answer: the hospital must first empanel a certified Consent Manager and obtain explicit patient consent for each data‑exchange transaction; mere technical integration does not satisfy the legal consent requirement.

Administrative Discretion in the Management of the National Pension System: Investment Choices and Subscriber Protection

The National Pension System (NPS), regulated by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) under the PFRDA Act, 2013, offers subscribers a choice between Active Choice (self‑directed allocation across four asset classes — Equity E, Corporate Bonds C, Government Securities G, and Alternative Investment Funds A) and Auto Choice (life‑cycle funds that automatically rebalance based on age). The PFRDA exercises discretion in (i) setting the maximum permissible equity exposure for Active Choice (currently 75 % up to age 50, tapering to 50 % thereafter); (ii) approving the appointment of Pension Fund Managers (PFMs) through a transparent bidding process; and (iii) defining the “default scheme” for subscribers who do not exercise Active Choice — presently the “Auto Choice – Moderate” life‑cycle fund.

Subscriber protection mechanisms include the “Grievance Redressal Mechanism” (GRM) with a three‑tier structure: (a) the PFM’s internal ombudsman, (b) the PFRDA’s Central Grievance Cell, and (c) the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) for appeals. The PFRDA also mandates a “Portfolio Disclosure” every quarter, requiring PFMs to publish scheme‑wise NAV, expense ratio, and transaction‑level details on the NPS Trust website. The PFRDA has issued circulars capping the total expense ratio (TER) for Government and Private sector schemes, a decision upheld by the SAT as a proportionate measure to protect net returns.

A frequent decision‑making twist involves a subscriber who, at age 45, wishes to shift from Auto Choice to Active Choice with 70 % equity allocation. The PFRDA’s rules permit the switch at any time, but the new allocation must respect the age‑linked equity ceiling. Since the subscriber is 45, the 75 % ceiling applies, so the request is permissible. However, if the subscriber were 55, the ceiling would be 50 %, and the request would be rejected unless the subscriber first reduces the equity proportion. The examiner may also test the “vesting value” calculation: the subscriber’s accumulated corpus is the sum of contributions plus net investment income, minus applicable charges, and the annuity purchase at exit must be at least 40 % of the vesting value for government employees.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Subsidies for Electric Vehicles under the FAME II Scheme

The Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles in India Phase II (FAME II), notified in 2019 with an outlay of ₹10,000 crore, is administered by the Department of Heavy Industry (DHI). The scheme provides demand incentives for electric two‑wheelers (e‑2W), three‑wheelers (e‑3W), four‑wheelers (e‑4W), and electric buses, linked to battery capacity. The DHI exercises discretion in (i) approving the “Model‑wise Eligibility List” after testing by the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) or the International Centre for Automotive Technology (ICAT); (ii) setting the “Phased Manufacturing Programme” (PMP) thresholds that require a minimum domestic value addition for eligibility; and (iii) releasing subsidies to Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) through the “FAME II Portal” after verification of sale invoices, GST compliance, and Aadhaar‑linked buyer authentication.

The PMP, revised in 2022, mandates that by April 2024 at least 50 % of the vehicle’s ex‑factory cost must be sourced domestically for e‑2W and e‑3W, and 40 % for e‑4W. OEMs that fail to meet the threshold are removed from the eligibility list, and any subsidies already disbursed for non‑compliant models become recoverable. The DHI has invoked this clause against certain e‑2W manufacturers, directing them to refund substantial amounts — a decision challenged in the Delhi High Court, which stayed recovery pending a detailed audit of the domestic‑content certification process.

For situational‑judgment questions, a typical case presents an OEM that has launched a new e‑3W model with a 4 kWh battery, obtained ARAI certification, but whose domestic value addition stands at 42 % (below the 50 % PMP threshold). The question asks whether the DHI can release the demand incentive. The correct answer: the incentive cannot be released until the OEM either raises domestic content to the prescribed level or obtains a specific exemption from the Empowered Committee (chaired by the Secretary, DHI) on grounds of “strategic importance” — a discretionary power that must be exercised transparently and recorded in writing.

  • Assuming a central certificate or portal registration automatically overrides a state‑level prohibition on gambling or gaming.
  • Confusing the “milestone‑based” fund release in NULM with a lump‑sum advance; the second tranche is contingent on verified completion of the preceding milestone.
  • Treating the Consent Manager’s technical integration as sufficient for data sharing under ABDM, ignoring the mandatory patient‑level consent artefact.
  • Applying the equity ceiling for NPS Active Choice based on the subscriber’s age at entry rather than the age at the time of the allocation change.
  • Believing that FAME II demand incentives are payable on the basis of ARAI certification alone, without satisfying the Phased Manufacturing Programme domestic‑content thresholds.
  • Overlooking the requirement that the SRB’s skill‑test methodology must be approved by MeitY before a platform can claim “game of skill” status.
  • Assuming the PFRDA’s expense‑ratio caps are advisory; they are binding and any breach triggers regulatory action.

Decision‑Making in Public Sector Bank Governance: Board Autonomy and RBI Oversight

The governance of public sector banks (PSBs) in India sits at the intersection of commercial autonomy and sovereign control. The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (as amended) and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 empower the RBI to issue directions on capital adequacy, asset classification, and provisioning, while the Public Sector Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1970 vests the central government with the power to appoint the Chairman‑cum‑Managing Director (CMD) and non‑official directors. In 2016 the government constituted the Bank Board Bureau (BBB) to recommend appointments, formulate a code of conduct, and advise on strategic decisions such as capital raising and merger proposals. The BBB’s recommendations are advisory; the final appointment order is issued by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC).

A critical decision‑making node is the “Prompt Corrective Action” (PCA) framework. When a PSB breaches thresholds for capital to risk‑weighted assets ratio (CRAR), net NPA ratio, or leverage ratio, the RBI places it under PCA, restricting dividend distribution, branch expansion, and management compensation. The board of the affected bank must then submit a time‑bound restructuring plan, which the RBI evaluates for credibility. Judicial precedent upholds the RBI’s discretion to impose PCA as intrinsic to its mandate to maintain financial stability.

Another layer is the “Indradhanush” reform agenda (2015) which introduced a board governance assessment framework linking board performance to capital infusion. The assessment scores boards on strategic direction, risk management, and compliance. A low score triggers a mandatory review by the BBB and may delay government capital support. Decision‑making questions often test whether a board can independently approve a merger without government clearance. The answer: under Section 9 of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970, any amalgamation of a PSB requires prior approval of the central government, even if the board and RBI have cleared it.

Finally, the “Fit and Proper” criteria for directors, prescribed by the RBI, require relevant banking or financial sector experience, no adverse regulatory orders, and a clean credit history. The BBB screens candidates against these criteria before forwarding names to the ACC. A situational‑judgment twist may present a candidate with experience in a non‑banking financial company (NBFC) but no commercial banking experience; the correct response is that the candidate does not meet the “banking sector” requirement unless the NBFC is registered as a systemically important NBFC under RBI norms.

Decision‑Making in the Implementation of the National Digital Health Mission: Data Interoperability and Consent Architecture

The National Digital Health Mission (NDHM), rebranded as the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) in 2021, creates a federated digital health ecosystem anchored on three pillars: Health ID (ABHA number), Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR), and Health Facility Registry (HFR). The mission’s decision‑making architecture is governed by the ABDM Sandbox Guidelines and the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) consent framework, which mandates that every data exchange be preceded by a granular, revocable, and auditable consent artefact signed by the patient.

The Consent Manager (CM) is a licensed entity (currently the National Health Authority acts as the default CM) that stores consent artefacts, enforces purpose‑limitation, and logs every access request. A decision‑making scenario often asks whether a hospital can pull a patient’s longitudinal record from the Health Information Exchange (HIE) without a fresh consent if the patient had previously consented to “any future care”. The correct answer is no: DEPA requires purpose‑specific consent for each transaction; blanket consent is invalid. The CM must verify the consent artefact’s expiry, scope, and the requester’s registration in the HPR/HFR before releasing data.

Interoperability is enforced through the FHIR R4 (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) standard and the ABDM APIs (Discovery, Consent, Gateway, and Registry). The Gateway routes requests to the appropriate Health Information Provider (HIP) after validating the consent token. The National Health Authority (NHA) publishes a “Compliance Checklist” for HIPs, covering encryption standards, audit‑log retention, and breach notification timelines. A typical examiner trap is to assume that mere registration on the ABDM portal authorises data sharing; the gateway will reject any request lacking a valid consent token, irrespective of registration status.

Governance decisions rest with the ABDM Steering Committee (chaired by the Secretary, Ministry of Health) and the Technology Advisory Group. They approve policy changes such as the inclusion of “Tele‑medicine” as a distinct purpose code in the consent taxonomy. Any amendment to the consent taxonomy requires a public consultation period, after which the Steering Committee issues a gazette notification. Decision‑making questions may test the sequence: public consultation → Steering Committee approval → Gazette notification → API version update. Skipping any step renders the change non‑enforceable.

Situational Judgment – Consent Artefact Validation
A patient, Ms. Rao, holds an ABHA number and has previously given consent for “diagnostic imaging” to Hospital A. Hospital B, a newly onboarded HIP, requests her imaging records via the ABDM Gateway, presenting a consent token that references the original “diagnostic imaging” purpose but is signed by Hospital B’s CM. The token is within its validity period. Should the Gateway release the records?
No. Under DEPA, consent is bound to the data principal (patient) and the specific data fiduciary (Hospital A). A consent artefact cannot be transferred to another fiduciary without a fresh, patient‑signed consent for the new purpose‑fiduciary pair. Hospital B must initiate a new consent request, which the patient must approve via the CM. The Gateway will reject the token because the fiduciary identifier in the token does not match Hospital B’s registration in the HPR.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question describes a data‑sharing request, first identify the three mandatory elements: (1) valid ABHA number, (2) a consent artefact that matches the requester’s HPR/HFR ID and the exact purpose code, (3) a gateway‑level token signed by the authorised Consent Manager. If any element is missing or mismatched, the answer is “request denied”. Memorise the DEPA flow: Patient → CM → Consent Artefact → Gateway → HIP. This eliminates the most common trap of assuming portal registration equals authorisation.

Decision‑Making in the Regulation of Online Gaming and Gambling: Skill vs Chance Test and State Jurisdiction

The constitutional division of legislative power places “betting and gambling” in Entry 34, List II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule, while “online gaming” is not expressly enumerated. States have enacted statutes such as the Telangana Gaming Act, 1974, the Andhra Pradesh Gaming Act, 1974, and the Tamil Nadu Gaming and Police Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 to prohibit games of chance, but they exempt “games of skill”. The Supreme Court in State of Andhra Pradesh v. K. Satyanarayana (1968) and R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India (1957) laid down the “dominant factor test”: if skill predominates over chance, the activity is not gambling.

In 2022 the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) released the “Draft Online Gaming (Regulation) Rules” under the Information Technology Act, 2000. The draft proposes a Self‑Regulatory Body (SRB) recognised by MeitY to certify games as “skill‑based” after evaluating the game’s algorithm, random‑number‑generator (RNG) certification, and player‑skill metrics. Only SRB‑certified games may be offered for real‑money stakes in states that have not banned all online gaming. The Rules also mandate a “Know Your Customer (KYC)” framework, age‑verification (≥18 years), and a “Responsible Gaming” module with self‑exclusion tools.

A frequent decision‑making twist presents a platform offering a fantasy‑sports contest (cricket) in a state that has enacted a blanket ban on “online gaming” (e.g., Telangana). The platform argues that fantasy sports were declared a game of skill by a High Court. The correct analysis: the state law prevails because gambling is a state subject; unless the state legislation explicitly carves out fantasy sports, the ban applies. The platform must either obtain a state‑specific exemption or cease operations in that jurisdiction.

Another nuance is the “central certificate” issued by an SRB. Some aspirants assume that an SRB certificate automatically overrides a state prohibition. The Rules clarify that the certificate is “evidence of skill‑dominance” for the purpose of the IT Act, but it does not diminish the state’s legislative competence to prohibit the activity. Decision‑making questions therefore require a two‑step check: (1) Does the state law prohibit the specific format? (2) If not prohibited, does the platform hold a valid SRB certificate and comply with KYC, age‑gate, and responsible‑gaming norms?

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Spectrum for Satellite Services: TRAI Recommendations and DoT Licensing

Spectrum for satellite communications (satcom) falls under the “Space” and “Telecommunications” sectors, governed jointly by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN‑SPACe). The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) issued its “Recommendations on Spectrum Allocation for Satellite Services” in August 2022, advocating a “administrative assignment” model rather than auction for certain bands because satellite operators require contiguous, interference‑free blocks for gateway earth stations.

The DoT, through the Unified License (UL) – Satellite (UL‑S) framework, grants authorisation for Gateway Earth Station (GES) and User Terminal (UT) operations. The licensing decision‑making flow is: (1) Applicant submits a “Technical Feasibility Report” to IN‑SPACe, which verifies orbital slot coordination with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO); (2) IN‑SPACe issues a “No‑Objection Certificate (NoC)”; (3) DoT evaluates the NoC, the applicant’s net‑worth, and compliance with the “National Frequency Allocation Plan (NFAP)”; (4) DoT issues the UL‑S with spectrum assignment letters specifying the band, bandwidth, and geographic service area.

A key decision point is the “Spectrum Sharing” provision. TRAI recommended that satellite operators may share assigned spectrum with terrestrial 5G operators under a “Co‑existence Framework” that mandates a minimum guard‑band and real‑time interference monitoring via the “Spectrum Monitoring System (SMS)”. The DoT’s amendment to the UL‑S incorporates this framework, requiring a joint‑management agreement approved by the Wireless Planning and Coordination Wing (WPC). Situational‑judgment questions may ask whether a satellite operator can commence services before the WPC approves the sharing agreement. The answer: no; the UL‑S conditions make the sharing agreement a pre‑condition for commercial launch.

Another examiner trap concerns the “Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) limit”. The current FDI policy permits 100 % FDI under the automatic route for satellite‑based services, but the “Security Clearance” from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is mandatory for any entity controlling a GES. Decision‑making scenarios that present a foreign‑owned consortium receiving a UL‑S without MHA clearance are testing the candidate’s awareness that the licence is conditional on security clearance, which is a separate decision‑making track.

Decision‑Making in the Management of Strategic Petroleum Reserves: ISPRL and Emergency Release Protocols

India’s strategic petroleum reserves (SPR) are managed by the Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Oil Industry Development Board (OIDB) under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG). As of 2024, ISPRL operates three underground rock caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, and Padur, totalling 5.33 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil, sufficient for approximately 9.5 days of net import cover.

The “Emergency Release Protocol” is codified in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve Release Guidelines. The decision‑making authority rests with a High‑Level Committee (HLC) chaired by the Secretary, MoPNG and comprising representatives from the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of External Affairs, Department of Revenue, and ISPRL. The HLC may authorise a release when triggers such as a sudden supply disruption exceeding a defined threshold, a sharp price spike sustained over a period, or a declared national emergency under Article 352 are met.

Once the HLC approves, ISPRL executes the release through a “Competitive Tender” to public sector refiners (IOCL, BPCL, HPCL) and, if capacity permits, to private refiners. The tender specifies the “Delivery Schedule”, the “Pricing Formula” linked to the Indian Basket price plus a premium, and the “Re‑fill Obligation” requiring the recipient to replenish the released volume within a stipulated period or pay a penalty. The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits each release cycle; past reports have highlighted delays in re‑fill compliance, leading to penalty recovery.

A common situational‑judgment twist presents a scenario where a state‑owned refiner requests an early release citing a planned maintenance shutdown. The guidelines explicitly state that planned maintenance does not constitute an emergency trigger. The correct decision is to deny the request and advise the refiner to manage inventory through commercial purchases. Another trap involves the “International Energy Agency (IEA) collective action”. India, as an IEA association member, may participate in a coordinated release; however, the domestic HLC must still ratify the volume and timing, and the release must follow the same tender and re‑fill rules. Decision‑making questions test whether the candidate recognises that international coordination does not bypass the domestic HLC authority.

  • Assuming that a board resolution alone authorises a PSB merger without central government approval.
  • Treating a blanket patient consent as sufficient for any future data exchange under ABDM.
