Because downstream speed equals boat speed plus stream speed, and upstream speed equals boat speed minus stream speed, adding the two equations eliminates the stream speed and yields twice the boat speed. Therefore, the boat speed in still water is exactly the arithmetic mean of the downstream and upstream speeds. Subtracting the upstream equation from the downstream equation eliminates the boat speed and yields twice the stream speed. Therefore, the stream speed is exactly half the difference between the downstream and upstream speeds. These derivation formulas—boat speed = (downstream + upstream)/2 and stream speed = (downstream - upstream)/2—are symmetric and allow instant calculation of the fundamental parameters from the observed effective speeds.

4.3 Round Trip Time and Average Speed in a Stream

A round trip covering the same distance downstream and upstream takes longer than the same round trip in still water because the time lost fighting the current upstream is greater than the time gained with the current downstream. The total time for a distance D each way is D/(B+S) + D/(B-S), which simplifies to 2BD/(B²-S²). The average speed for the round trip is total distance (2D) divided by total time, yielding (B²-S²)/B. This average speed is always less than the still water speed B, demonstrating that a current always increases the total travel time for a fixed round-trip distance. This result is independent of the distance D, depending only on the ratio of stream speed to boat speed.

4.4 Ratio-Based Problems and Time Comparisons

Many boat and stream problems are framed in terms of ratios rather than absolute speeds. If the ratio of upstream speed to downstream speed is given as U:D, then the ratio of boat speed to stream speed can be found by componendo and dividendo: (D+U)/(D-U) = B/S. Similarly, if the time taken to row a certain distance upstream is n times the time taken to row the same distance downstream, the ratio of speeds is the inverse, 1:n, so upstream speed : downstream speed = 1:n. Applying componendo and dividendo again yields the ratio of boat speed to stream speed as (n+1):(n-1). These ratio manipulations avoid the need for absolute speed values and are particularly useful when the problem asks for the ratio of speeds rather than their magnitudes.

Advanced Applications: Races, Variable Speed, and Meeting Points

5.1 Linear Races and Head Starts

In a linear race, contestants start from the same point and run towards a finish line. A head start can be given either in distance (one runner starts ahead of the starting line) or in time (one runner starts before the signal). If runner A gives runner B a start of x metres in a race of L metres, it means when A covers L metres, B covers only L-x metres in the same time. Since time is equal, the ratio of their speeds is L : (L-x). If A gives B a start of t seconds, then when A finishes the race in time T, B has been running for T+t seconds and has covered the full distance L. The speed ratio is then L/T : L/(T+t), which simplifies to (T+t):T. These equivalences allow conversion between distance starts and time starts, a common requirement in multi-part questions.

5.2 Variable Speed and Journey Segments

Real journeys often involve changes in speed—rest stops, speed reductions, or acceleration phases. The total time for such a journey is the sum of the times for each segment, where each segment time is its distance divided by its speed. The average speed for the whole journey is the total distance divided by this total time. It is never the average of the segment speeds unless the times are equal. A classic problem type involves a person travelling a certain distance at one speed and returning at another speed; the average speed is the harmonic mean of the two speeds because the distances are equal. If the problem states that a person covers one-third of the distance at speed S₁, one-third at S₂, and one-third at S₃, the average speed is the harmonic mean of the three speeds: 3 / (1/S₁ + 1/S₂ + 1/S₃).

5.3 Meeting Points and Distance Ratios

When two objects start simultaneously from two points and move towards each other, they meet at a point that divides the total distance in the ratio of their speeds. This follows because they travel for the same duration until meeting, and distance is proportional to speed when time is constant. If they continue to their destinations, turn around immediately, and move back, the subsequent meetings follow a predictable pattern: the total distance covered by both together between the start and the nth meeting is (2n-1) times the initial separation. The position of the nth meeting can be found by tracking the distance covered by one object, which is its speed multiplied by the total time, and then mapping that distance onto the back-and-forth path using the modulo operation with twice the track length. This technique transforms a seemingly complex bouncing problem into a simple linear distance calculation.
maths/simple-interest:
Simple & Compound Interest for the exam & the exam

Interest is the cost of borrowing money or the return on invested capital. In competitive exams, you will frequently encounter problems involving simple interest and basic compound interest calculations at a 10th standard level. To master this topic, you must understand the core concepts of principal, rate, time, and amount, as well as the specific formulas that govern these financial relationships.

Simple Interest: The Linear Approach

Simple Interest (SI) is calculated only on the original sum borrowed or invested, known as the Principal. Unlike compound interest, the interest earned does not add to the principal for future calculations; it remains constant every year. The formula is derived from the logic that interest is a fixed percentage of the principal for every unit of time.

The exact mathematical rule is: SI = (P × R × T) / 100. Here, P stands for Principal, R is the Rate of interest per annum, and T is the Time in years. The Amount you get back or owe is simply the sum of the Principal and the Simple Interest calculated.

Examiners typically ask questions where you are given three of these four variables (P, R, T, SI) and must find the fourth. Sometimes, they ask for the total Amount instead of just the interest, in which case you simply add the calculated SI to the Principal.

Compound Interest: The Exponential Growth

Compound Interest (CI) is often described as "interest on interest." In this method, the interest earned at the end of a period is added to the principal, so the next period's interest is calculated on this new, larger amount. This causes the growth to be exponential rather than linear.

The fundamental formula for the Amount in compound interest is: Amount = P(1 + R/100)^T. Consequently, Compound Interest itself is found by subtracting the Principal from this Amount: CI = Amount - P.

A crucial pattern often tested in competitive exams involves comparing Simple and Compound interest over a period of exactly two years. The difference between the two interests at the end of 2 years is mathematically equal to the simple interest earned on the first year's interest for the second year. The specific formula for this difference is: CI - SI = P(R/100)². This rule is a direct consequence of the compounding mechanism.

Solved Examples

Example 1: Mastering Simple Interest Calculation
Find the Simple Interest on ₹1000 at 8% per annum for 3 years.

a) ₹200 b) ₹220 c) ₹240 d) ₹260
Solution: The correct answer is option (c).

We use the formula SI = (P × R × T) / 100.
Substituting the values: P = 1000, R = 8, and T = 3.
SI = (1000 × 8 × 3) / 100
SI = (24000) / 100
SI = ₹240.

The total Amount would be Principal + SI = 1000 + 240 = ₹1240.
Example 2: The Two-Year Difference Trick
A sum of money amounts to ₹880 in 2 years at 5% per annum compound interest. What is the Simple Interest on this sum for the same period?

a) ₹40 b) ₹45 c) ₹50 d) ₹55
Solution: The correct answer is option (c).

First, find the Principal using the Compound Amount formula: Amount = P(1 + R/100)^T.
880 = P(1 + 5/100)²
880 = P(1.05)²
880 = P × 1.1025
P = 880 / 1.1025 ≈ ₹798 (approx).

A simpler way for exams is to calculate SI directly on the Principal derived from CI logic or use the difference formula if CI was given.

Common Traps

Students often fall into specific traps that lead to incorrect answers in competitive exams:

  • Mixing up SI and CI formulas: Applying the compound interest formula (P(1+R/100)^T) when the question explicitly asks for Simple Interest. Remember, SI is linear; CI is exponential.
  • Ignoring the "Per Annum" unit: If time is given in months, you must convert it to years by dividing by 12 before using the formula. Using months directly in the T variable will give a wrong answer.
  • The Two-Year Difference Error: Students often try to use the (CI - SI) formula for periods longer than 2 years or forget that this specific shortcut only works for exactly two years.
  • Calculation Errors with Decimals: In compound interest, squaring the rate (1+R/100)^2 introduces decimals. Always calculate the square of the decimal part first to maintain accuracy.

Memory Tricks

To recall these concepts quickly during the exam without panic:

  • The "PRT" Mantra: For Simple Interest, always remember the letters P, R, and T. If you see three of them, multiply them and divide by 100. It is a multiplication party.
  • The "Snowball Effect": Think of Compound Interest like a snowball rolling down a hill. The bigger it gets (principal increases), the faster it grows (interest increases). This visual helps remember that CI > SI over time.
  • The "Square Root" Rule: If you see a question with exactly 2 years and asks for the difference between CI and SI, immediately think of the square of the rate: P(R/100)². It's like a square shape appearing after two steps.
  • Units Check: Before multiplying, always check if Time is in months or days. If so, convert to years first. This prevents the most common calculation error.
Exam-Day Strategy
On exam day, read the question twice. First, identify if it asks for Principal, Interest, or Amount. Second, check the time unit (years vs months). If you see "2 years" and a difference between CI and SI is mentioned, use the shortcut formula immediately to save time. For Simple Interest problems, always write down P, R, T separately before multiplying to avoid confusion with the order of operations.

Variable Compounding Frequencies and Effective Annual Rate

When interest is compounded more frequently than once a year, the nominal annual rate no longer reflects the true growth of the principal. The standard formula Amount = P(1 + R/100)^T assumes annual compounding. If compounding occurs n times per year, the periodic rate becomes R/n percent and the number of periods becomes n × T. The generalized amount formula is therefore Amount = P(1 + R/(100n))^(nT). This adjustment captures the effect of interest being added to the principal multiple times within a single year, causing the effective yield to exceed the nominal rate.

The Effective Annual Rate (EAR) quantifies this difference. It is the single annual rate that would produce the same final amount if compounding were annual. Mathematically, EAR = (1 + R/(100n))^n - 1, expressed as a percentage by multiplying by 100. For example, a nominal rate of 12 % compounded monthly (n = 12) yields an EAR of (1 + 0.12/12)12 - 1 ≈ 0.1268, i.e. 12.68 %. The EAR is the figure that should be used when comparing financial products with different compounding frequencies, because it places them on a common annual basis.

In competitive examinations, questions often provide a nominal rate and a compounding frequency, then ask for the amount after a given time or the effective rate itself. A common shortcut is to compute the periodic factor (1 + R/(100n)) once, raise it to the power nT using logarithms or repeated squaring, and multiply by the principal. When the time T is not an integer number of years, convert the total number of periods directly: if the investment runs for 18 months and compounding is quarterly, the number of periods is 6 (since 18 months = 1.5 years, n = 4, periods = 4 × 1.5 = 6). Always verify that the exponent matches the total number of compounding intervals.

Another twist involves continuous compounding, where the limit as n → ∞ gives the formula Amount = P × e^(RT/100). Here e is the base of natural logarithms (≈ 2.71828). The corresponding effective annual rate becomes e^(R/100) - 1. Although continuous compounding is rare in standard banking, it appears in theoretical problems and in the valuation of certain derivatives. Recognising the continuous‑compounding formula and its derivation from the discrete formula is a useful differentiator for high‑difficulty questions.

Finally, be aware of the distinction between nominal rate (the quoted annual percentage) and periodic rate (the rate applied each compounding interval). The periodic rate is always R/n percent. When a problem states “12 % per annum compounded half‑yearly”, the periodic rate is 6 % per half‑year, not 12 % per half‑year. Misreading this detail is a frequent source of error.

Installment and Loan Amortisation Using Compound Interest

Many real‑world loans are repaid through equal periodic installments (EMIs) rather than a single lump sum. The present value of an annuity formula, derived from compound interest, gives the relationship between the loan principal P, the periodic installment X, the periodic interest rate i = R/(100n), and the total number of installments N = nT. The formula is P = X × [1 - (1 + i)^(-N)] / i. Rearranging yields the installment amount X = P × i / [1 - (1 + i)^(-N)]. This equation assumes that the first installment is paid one period after the loan is disbursed (ordinary annuity). If the first payment is immediate (annuity due), the denominator becomes [1 - (1 + i)^(-N)] / i × (1 + i).

To solve an EMI problem, first identify the compounding frequency, which usually matches the payment frequency (monthly payments → monthly compounding). Convert the annual nominal rate to the periodic rate i. Compute the total number of payments N. Then apply the formula. For example, a loan of ₹10 000 at 12 % per annum compounded monthly, to be repaid in 24 monthly installments, gives i = 0.12/12 = 0.01 and N = 24. The installment is X = 10000 × 0.01 / [1 - (1.01)^(-24)]. Evaluating (1.01)^(-24) ≈ 0.787, the denominator ≈ 0.213, so X ≈ 10000 × 0.01 / 0.213 ≈ ₹469.5. Rounding conventions vary; some exams expect the answer to the nearest rupee.

A related concept is the outstanding balance after k payments. The remaining principal equals the present value of the remaining N - k installments: Balance_k = X × [1 - (1 + i)^(-(N-k))] / i. This is useful for questions that ask for the principal repaid in a specific installment or the interest component of a particular payment. The interest portion of the k‑th installment is i × Balancek-1, and the principal repaid is X - interest.

When the installment amount is given and the principal or rate is unknown, the same formula can be solved iteratively or by using logarithms. For instance, if P, X, and N are known, the equation P = X × [1 - (1 + i)^(-N)] / i can be rearranged to isolate (1 + i)^(-N) and then solved for i using numerical methods (trial and error, interpolation, or a financial calculator). In exam settings, the rate is often a simple fraction (e.g., 10 %, 12 %) so that trial values quickly converge.

Another variation involves a balloon payment at the end of the term. The present value of the balloon payment B discounted at the periodic rate is added to the present value of the regular installments: P = X × [1 - (1 + i)^(-N)] / i + B × (1 + i)^(-N). This structure appears in certain hire‑purchase agreements and must be recognised to avoid treating the balloon as a regular installment.

Worked Example: Monthly EMI Calculation
A borrower takes a loan of ₹25 000 at 9 % per annum compounded monthly. The loan is to be repaid in 36 equal monthly installments. Find the monthly installment amount (rounded to the nearest rupee).

Step 1: Identify parameters. Principal P = 25000. Annual nominal rate R = 9 %. Compounding monthly ⇒ n = 12. Periodic rate i = R/(100n) = 9/(100×12) = 0.0075. Number of installments N = 36.

Step 2: Apply the ordinary annuity formula X = P × i / [1 - (1 + i)^(-N)].

Compute (1 + i) = 1.0075. Raise to power -N: (1.0075)^(-36). Using logarithms or a calculator, (1.0075)36 ≈ 1.309, so its reciprocal ≈ 0.764.

Denominator = 1 - 0.764 = 0.236.

Numerator = P × i = 25000 × 0.0075 = 187.5.

Installment X = 187.5 / 0.236 ≈ 794.5. Rounded to nearest rupee ⇒ ₹795.

Answer: ₹795 per month.

Exam‑Day Strategy for Installment Problems
When you see a loan repaid in equal installments, immediately write down the four variables P, i, N, X. Convert the annual rate to the periodic rate before doing any exponentiation. If the question asks for the outstanding balance after a certain number of payments, use the present‑value‑of‑remaining‑installments formula rather than recalculating the whole amortisation schedule. For balloon‑payment variants, treat the final lump sum as a separate present‑value term. Practise the shortcut (1+i)^N using the binomial approximation (1 + Ni) only when Ni is very small; otherwise use exact exponentiation to avoid cumulative error.

Growth of Principal under Mixed Simple and Compound Regimes

Some problems describe a scenario where a sum earns simple interest for an initial period and then switches to compound interest, or vice‑versa. The key is to treat each phase separately, using the amount at the end of one phase as the principal for the next. For instance, if ₹P is invested at R % simple interest for T₁ years, the amount becomes A₁ = P + (P × R × T₁)/100 = P[1 + (R T₁)/100]. This amount then serves as the principal for a compound‑interest phase of T₂ years at the same or a different rate R₂. The final amount is A₂ = A₁ × (1 + R₂/100)^T₂. The overall effective growth factor is the product of the simple‑interest factor and the compound‑interest factor.

A common twist is to ask for the equivalent single rate that would produce the same final amount if the whole period were under compound interest. Let the total time be T = T₁ + T₂. We need a rate R_eq such that P(1 + R_eq/100)^T = A₂. Solving gives R_eq = 100 × [(A₂/P)^(1/T) - 1]. This requires extracting a T‑th root, which can be done using logarithms: log(1 + R_eq/100) = (1/T) × log(A₂/P). In exam conditions, the numbers are often chosen so that the root is an integer or a simple fraction, allowing mental calculation.

Another variant involves a principal that earns compound interest for a certain period, after which the interest is withdrawn and the remaining principal continues at simple interest. Here the compound phase builds the amount A_c = P(1 + R/100)^T_c. The interest earned up to that point is I_c = A_c - P. If this interest is withdrawn, the principal reverts to P for the simple‑interest phase. The final amount becomes A_f = P + (P × R × T_s)/100. The total interest earned overall is I_c + (P × R × T_s)/100. Recognising whether the interest is reinvested or withdrawn changes the compounding base and is a frequent source of misinterpretation.

Problems may also combine different rates for the two phases. For example, a sum earns 8 % simple interest for 3 years, then 10 % compound interest for 2 years. Compute the simple‑interest amount: A₁ = P[1 + (8×3)/100] = P × 1.24. Then compound: A₂ = 1.24P × (1.10)2 = 1.24P × 1.21 = 1.4984P. The overall multiplication factor is 1.4984, i.e. a 49.84 % increase over the original principal. If the question asks for the principal given the final amount, divide the final amount by 1.4984.

When the simple‑interest phase follows the compound phase, the order of operations reverses. Suppose a sum grows at 12 % compound for 2 years, then the accumulated amount earns 6 % simple for 3 years. First compound factor: (1.12)2 = 1.2544. Then simple factor: 1 + (6×3)/100 = 1.18. Overall factor = 1.2544 × 1.18 = 1.4802. The sequence matters because the simple‑interest factor applies to a larger base when it comes after compounding.

Determining Unknown Rate or Time from Amount Data

Examiners frequently provide the principal, the final amount, and either the time or the rate, asking for the missing variable. The approach depends on whether the interest is simple or compound. For simple interest, the relationship is linear: A = P[1 + (R T)/100]. If R is unknown, rearrange to R = 100(A/P - 1)/T. If T is unknown, T = 100(A/P - 1)/R. Both formulas are direct and require only division.

For compound interest, the equation is A = P(1 + R/100)^T. Taking logarithms yields log(A/P) = T × log(1 + R/100). If R is unknown, log(1 + R/100) = log(A/P)/T, then 1 + R/100 = 10log(A/P)/T (or e... for natural logs), and finally R = 100(10log(A/P)/T - 1). If T is unknown, T = log(A/P) / log(1 + R/100). In many exam questions, the numbers are chosen so that A/P is a perfect power of (1 + R/100), making T an integer. For example, if a sum doubles in 5 years at compound interest, then 2 = (1 + R/100)5. Recognising that 2^(1/5) ≈ 1.1487 gives R ≈ 14.87 %. However, if the rate is a round number like 10 %, then (1.10)^T = 2 ⇒ T ≈ 7.27 years, which is not an integer; such a question would likely ask for the approximate time or provide options.

A useful shortcut for “doubling time” under compound interest is the Rule of 72: T ≈ 72 / R (with R in percent). This approximation works well for rates between 6 % and 10 %. For exact answers, logarithms are required. Similarly, the “tripling time” can be approximated by 114 / R. These rules are handy for quick elimination of options.

When the compounding frequency is not annual, the formula becomes A = P(1 + R/(100n))^(nT). The unknown could be the nominal rate R, the time T, or the frequency n. If n is unknown but the effective annual rate is given, use the EAR formula EAR = (1 + R/(100n))^n - 1 and solve for n by trial, since n is usually a small integer (2, 4, 12, 365). If the problem states “compounded quarterly” and asks for the nominal rate given the effective rate, rearrange R = 100n[(1 + EAR)^(1/n) - 1].

Another layer appears when the interest rate changes after a certain period. For instance, a sum amounts to ₹A₁ after T₁ years at rate R₁, then the amount is reinvested at rate R₂ for T₂ years to reach A₂. The equations are A₁ = P(1 + R₁/100)^T₁ and A₂ = A₁(1 + R₂/100)^T₂. If one of the rates is unknown, isolate it using the known amounts and times. This multi‑stage structure tests the ability to chain compound‑interest formulas correctly.

Comparative Analysis of Simple vs Compound Over Multiple Periods

Beyond the two‑year difference formula, examiners ask for the difference between simple and compound interest over three or more years, or for the ratio of the two interests. For a principal P, rate R, and time T (in years), simple interest is SI = P R T / 100. Compound interest is CI = P[(1 + R/100)^T - 1]. The difference CI - SI grows faster than the square of the rate because the compound factor includes higher‑order terms. Expanding the binomial (1 + r)^T where r = R/100 gives 1 + Tr + T(T-1)/2 r2 + T(T-1)(T-2)/6 r3 + …. Subtracting the linear term Tr leaves the difference as a polynomial in r starting with the quadratic term. For T = 3, CI - SI = P[3r2 + r3] (since 3(3-1)/2 = 3). For T = 4, the difference includes 6r2 + 4r3 + r4. Recognising these coefficients helps in quickly estimating the difference without full exponentiation.

The ratio CI / SI is another comparative metric. For small r and moderate T, the ratio is approximately 1 + (T-1)r/2. This approximation follows from the binomial expansion: CI ≈ P[Tr + T(T-1)/2 r2], so CI/SI ≈ 1 + (T-1)r/2. For example, at 10 % (r = 0.1) for 5 years, the ratio ≈ 1 + 4×0.1/2 = 1.2, meaning compound interest is about 20 % higher than simple interest. This mental shortcut is valuable for data‑interpretation sets where exact computation is time‑consuming.

Questions may also ask for the time at which compound interest exceeds simple interest by a given percentage. Set CI = k × SI where k > 1. Using the exact formulas, P[(1+r)^T - 1] = k × P r T. Cancel P and solve for T numerically. Because T appears both in the exponent and linearly, an analytical solution is rarely possible; trial with integer T values is the standard exam technique. For instance, find the smallest integer T such that CI is at least 50 % more than SI at 8 % (r = 0.08). Test T = 3: CI factor = (1.08)3 - 1 ≈ 0.2597, SI factor = 0.24, ratio ≈ 1.082. T = 4: CI factor ≈ 0.3605, SI factor = 0.32, ratio ≈ 1.126. T = 5: CI factor ≈ 0.4693, SI factor = 0.40, ratio ≈ 1.173. T = 6: CI factor ≈ 0.5869, SI factor = 0.48, ratio ≈ 1.223. T = 7: CI factor ≈ 0.7138, SI factor = 0.56, ratio ≈ 1.275. T = 8: CI factor ≈ 0.8509, SI factor = 0.64, ratio ≈ 1.329. T = 9: CI factor ≈ 0.9990, SI factor = 0.72, ratio ≈ 1.387. T = 10: CI factor ≈ 1.1589, SI factor = 0.80, ratio ≈ 1.449. T = 11: CI factor ≈ 1.3316, SI factor = 0.88, ratio ≈ 1.513. So T = 11 years is the first integer where CI exceeds SI by 50 %. This iterative method is expected in the exam.

Another comparative scenario involves two different principals invested at the same rate, one under simple interest and the other under compound interest, and the question asks when their amounts become equal. Let P₁ be the simple‑interest principal and P₂ the compound‑interest principal. Equate amounts: P₁(1 + rT) = P₂(1 + r)^T. If P₁ and P₂ are given, solve for T. If T is given, find the ratio P₁/P₂. This type of problem tests algebraic manipulation of the two growth laws simultaneously.

Finally, be aware of the “effective simple interest rate” concept: for a given compound interest rate and period, the simple interest rate that would yield the same final amount is R_eff = 100[(1 + R/100)^T - 1]/T. This is the average annual simple rate equivalent to the compound growth. It is always higher than the nominal compound rate for T > 1, and the gap widens with T. Recognising this equivalence helps in questions that mix simple‑interest language with compound‑interest data.

  • Assuming the two‑year difference formula works for any period; it is valid only for exactly two years.
  • Using the nominal annual rate directly in the periodic formula without dividing by the compounding frequency.
  • Forgetting to convert months or days into years before inserting into the simple‑interest formula.
  • Treating a balloon payment as a regular installment when calculating the present value of an annuity.
  • Applying the simple‑interest growth factor to a principal that has already been compounded, instead of using the compounded amount as the new principal.
  • Misidentifying whether the first installment is due immediately or after one period, leading to an off‑by‑one error in the annuity formula.
  • Rounding intermediate results too early, especially when raising (1 + i) to a high power, which amplifies the error.

Continuous Compounding and Force of Interest

When the compounding frequency tends to infinity, the discrete formula A = P(1 + r/n)n t converges to the continuous‑compounding expression A = P ert, where e ≈ 2.718281828. The constant r in this formula is called the force of interest (denoted δ) and equals the natural logarithm of the annual growth factor: δ = ln(1 + i) with i the effective annual rate. Conversely, the effective annual rate corresponding to a given force of interest is i = eδ – 1. This relationship is exact. In examinations, continuous compounding appears in two forms: (1) direct calculation of amount or present value using ert, and (2) conversion between a quoted nominal rate compounded m times a year and the equivalent force of interest. The conversion steps are: compute the effective annual rate i = (1 + r/m)m – 1, then δ = ln(1 + i). Because ln(1 + x) ≈ x – x²/2 + x³/3 – … for small x, the force of interest is always slightly smaller than the nominal rate when m is large. A typical question supplies a nominal rate of 12 % compounded monthly and asks for the force of interest; the answer is δ = ln[(1 + 0.12/12)12] ≈ 0.1194 or 11.94 %. Mastery of exponentials and natural logarithms is essential; examiners often test switching between discrete and continuous frameworks without a calculator using ln(1+x)≈x for small x.

Equivalent Nominal and Effective Rates across Compounding Frequencies

Financial instruments quote nominal annual rates with a stated compounding frequency (e.g., 10 % p.a. compounded quarterly). Two such quotes are equivalent if they produce the same effective annual rate (EAR). The EAR for a nominal rate r compounded m times per year is EAR = (1 + r/m)m – 1. To compare a quarterly quote with a monthly quote, compute each EAR and equate them. For instance, find the nominal monthly rate equivalent to 9 % p.a. compounded semi‑annually. First, EAR = (1 + 0.09/2)2 – 1 = 0.092025. Then solve (1 + rm/12)12 = 1.092025 → rm = 12[(1.092025)1/12 – 1] ≈ 0.0883 or 8.83 % p.a. compounded monthly. A second common task is to determine the nominal rate that yields a given EAR when compounding continuously: set eδ = 1 + EAR and δ = ln(1 + EAR). The nominal rate for continuous compounding is numerically equal to δ. Examiners also test the reverse: given a force of interest δ = 0.08, find the nominal rate compounded quarterly. Compute EAR = e0.08 – 1 ≈ 0.083287, then rq = 4[(1.083287)1/4 – 1] ≈ 0.0808 or 8.08 % p.a. quarterly. These conversions rely on the identity (1 + r/m)m = eδ. Practising the algebraic manipulation of roots and logarithms ensures speed; a useful shortcut is the approximation (1 + r/m)m ≈ er for large m, which shows that the nominal rate approaches the force of interest as compounding becomes continuous.

Worked Example: Rate Conversion
A bank offers a fixed deposit at 7.5 % p.a. compounded quarterly. Another bank offers a deposit at a nominal rate compounded monthly that is exactly equivalent. Find the nominal monthly rate (to two decimal places).
Step 1: Compute the effective annual rate of the quarterly offer. EAR = (1 + 0.075/4)4 – 1 = (1.01875)4 – 1 ≈ 1.077135 – 1 = 0.077135 (7.7135 %).
Step 2: Let the required nominal monthly rate be r. Then (1 + r/12)12 = 1.077135.
Step 3: Take the 12th root: 1 + r/12 = (1.077135)1/12 ≈ 1.006215.
Step 4: r/12 = 0.006215 → r = 12 × 0.006215 = 0.07458 ≈ 7.46 % p.a. compounded monthly.
Answer: 7.46 % p.a. compounded monthly.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a conversion question appears, first write the EAR formula for the given quote. Compute the EAR once, then set up the equation for the target frequency. Use the calculator’s yx key for roots (e.g., 1.077135 ^ (1/12)). Keep at least six decimal places during intermediate steps; rounding too early changes the final nominal rate by several basis points. If a calculator is not allowed, memorise the EAR for common nominal rates (6 %, 8 %, 10 %, 12 %) at standard frequencies to estimate quickly.

Present Value of Annuities with Growing Payments

Standard annuity formulas assume level payments. In many realistic scenarios — salary‑linked pensions, rental escalations, dividend growth models — payments increase at a constant rate g per period. The present value of a growing annuity immediate (first payment at end of period 1) with payment C, interest rate i per period, growth rate g (g ≠ i), and n periods is PV = C [1 – ((1+g)/(1+i))n] / (i – g). If g = i, the formula simplifies to PV = n C / (1+i). For a growing annuity due (first payment at time 0), multiply the immediate value by (1+i). The derivation uses the geometric series sum of discounted cash flows: each payment is C(1+g)k-1 discounted by (1+i)k. Examiners test two variants: (a) find the present value given C, i, g, n; (b) find the initial payment C required to fund a known present value. A typical twist: the payment growth rate is annual (e.g., 3 %) while the interest rate is quoted as a nominal monthly rate; the candidate must first convert to an effective annual rate matching the payment frequency. Another twist: the growth rate may exceed the interest rate, making the denominator negative; the formula still holds, but the present value grows with n and can exceed the sum of undiscounted payments. Candidates should recognise that a perpetuity with growth (n → ∞) has finite present value only when g < i, yielding PV = C / (i – g). This is the Gordon growth model used in equity valuation.

Sinking Fund and Capital Recovery Factor

A sinking fund is a reserve built by periodic deposits to accumulate a specified future sum, typically for debt redemption or asset replacement. If a future amount F is required after n periods at interest rate i per period, the level deposit R needed each period is R = F × i / [(1+i)n – 1]. The factor i / [(1+i)n – 1] is the sinking‑fund factor (SFF). Conversely, the capital recovery factor (CRF) gives the level payment that repays a present loan P over n periods: CRF = i(1+i)n / [(1+i)n – 1]. Note that CRF = SFF + i. This identity reflects that each loan payment consists of interest on the outstanding balance (i) plus a sinking‑fund deposit to retire the principal. Examiners often combine the two: a machine costs ₹10,00,000, earns 10 % p.a., and must be replaced after 8 years. The annual sinking‑fund deposit at 8 % p.a. is R = 10,00,000 × 0.08 / [(1.08)8 – 1] ≈ 10,00,000 × 0.08 / 0.85093 ≈ 94,000. If the same machine is financed by a loan at 10 % repaid over 8 years, the annual instalment is 10,00,000 × CRF(10 %,8) = 10,00,000 × 0.18744 ≈ 1,87,440. The difference (≈ ₹93,440) is the interest component. A common trap is to use the loan interest rate for the sinking‑fund calculation; the sinking fund earns its own rate, which may differ. Another trap: forgetting that the first deposit in a sinking fund is usually made at the end of the first period (ordinary annuity), whereas loan repayments may be due at the beginning (annuity due). Adjust the factor by multiplying by (1+i) for annuity‑due situations.

Using Logarithms to Solve for Time and Rate in Compound Interest

When the unknown is the number of periods n or the interest rate i in the compound‑interest equation A = P(1+i)n, logarithms provide the exact solution. Taking natural logs: ln(A/P) = n ln(1+i). Hence n = ln(A/P) / ln(1+i) and i = eln(A/P)/n – 1. Calculators with log functions are permitted, but candidates must also handle no‑calculator variants using common logarithms (base 10) or the approximation ln(1+x)≈x for small x. For example, find the time for ₹5,000 to become ₹8,000 at 9 % p.a. compounded annually. n = ln(8000/5000) / ln(1.09) = ln(1.6) / ln(1.09) ≈ 0.4700 / 0.08618 ≈ 5.45 years. Since n must be an integer number of compounding periods, the answer is 6 years (the amount first exceeds ₹8,000 after the 6th compounding). A second typical question: a sum doubles in 7 years under annual compounding; find the rate. 2 = (1+i)7 → 1+i = 21/7 → i = 21/7 – 1 ≈ 0.1041 or 10.41 %. When compounding is not annual, convert the nominal rate to the periodic rate first. For instance, “How many quarters for ₹10,000 to grow to ₹15,000 at 12 % p.a. compounded quarterly?” Periodic rate = 0.12/4 = 0.03. n = ln(1.5) / ln(1.03) ≈ 0.4055 / 0.02956 ≈ 13.72 quarters → 14 quarters (3.5 years). Examiners also test the reverse: given n and the growth factor, find the nominal rate compounded m times. The steps are identical: solve for the periodic rate, then multiply by m. Mastery of log properties (ln(a/b)=ln a – ln b, ln(ab)=b ln a) and the change‑of‑base formula ensures full marks even when the calculator only provides log10.

Common Traps in Advanced Interest Calculations

  • Using the nominal annual rate directly in the continuous‑compounding formula A = Pert without converting to the force of interest.
  • Equating two nominal rates with different compounding frequencies without first converting both to effective annual rates.
  • Applying the level‑annuity present‑value formula to a growing annuity, ignoring the growth rate g.
  • Assuming the sinking‑fund deposit earns the same rate as the loan interest rate; the two rates are independent unless explicitly stated.
  • Rounding the logarithmic quotient for n to the nearest integer instead of rounding up to the next whole period when the amount must reach or exceed a target.
  • Forgetting to adjust the sinking‑fund factor or capital‑recovery factor for annuity‑due timing (multiply by 1+i).
  • Treating the force of interest as equal to the nominal rate for any compounding frequency; the equality holds only in the limit of continuous compounding.

Piecewise Constant Interest Rates and Accumulation Factors

In many practical problems the interest rate is not constant for the whole term. A loan may carry 8 % for the first three years, 9 % for the next two years, and 10 % thereafter. The accumulation factor for a principal P over such a horizon is the product of the individual period factors: A = P × (1+i₁)ⁿ¹ × (1+i₂)ⁿ² × …. When the rates change at known dates, the time line can be split into sub‑intervals, each with its own effective rate per compounding period. The same principle applies to present‑value calculations: discount each cash flow by the product of the forward factors that apply from the cash‑flow date back to the valuation date. A common shortcut is to compute an equivalent constant rate i_eq that yields the same terminal amount over the total number of periods n = Σ n_k. This rate satisfies (1+i_eq)ⁿ = Π (1+i_k)ⁿᵏ, so i_eq = ( Π (1+i_k)ⁿᵏ )¹/ⁿ – 1. Examiners often ask for the equivalent annual rate when semi‑annual or quarterly rates vary, testing the candidate’s ability to convert each sub‑rate to the common compounding frequency before forming the product. Care must be taken to align the compounding frequency: if the first segment uses monthly compounding at 0.75 % per month and the second uses quarterly compounding at 2.5 % per quarter, convert both to an effective annual factor before multiplying, or convert everything to a common periodic basis (e.g., monthly) and then multiply the appropriate number of periods.

When the rate changes continuously (e.g., a force of interest that is a step function), the accumulation factor becomes an exponential of the integral of the force over time. For a piecewise constant force δ(t) the factor is exp( Σ δ_k × Δt_k ). This links directly to the continuous‑compounding framework already covered, but the piecewise version appears in questions on variable‑rate bonds or on loans with interest‑rate caps and floors. A typical trap is to average the nominal rates arithmetically instead of geometrically; the arithmetic average ignores compounding and leads to an under‑ or over‑statement of the true growth. Another trap is to forget that the number of compounding periods in each segment must be an integer; if a rate changes mid‑period, the segment must be split further or the exact day‑count convention (actual/360, actual/365, 30/360) must be applied.

Bond Valuation: Clean Price, Dirty Price, and Yield to Maturity

A bond is a series of fixed coupon payments plus a redemption (principal) payment at maturity. The theoretical price is the present value of all future cash flows discounted at the market yield (yield to maturity, YTM). If the bond pays a coupon C per period, has face value F, and there are n periods remaining, the price P satisfies P = Σk=1n C/(1+y)ᵏ + F/(1+y)ⁿ, where y is the periodic yield. In practice the quoted (clean) price excludes accrued interest since the last coupon date; the dirty (invoice) price equals clean price plus accrued interest. Accrued interest = C × (days since last coupon)/(days in coupon period) under the relevant day‑count convention. YTM is the internal rate of return that equates the dirty price to the present value of cash flows; it is found by solving the polynomial equation numerically (Newton‑Raphson, goal‑seek, or financial calculator). For a bond trading at par, YTM equals the coupon rate; for a premium bond YTM < coupon rate; for a discount bond YTM > coupon rate. The relationship between price and yield is convex: a given change in yield produces a larger price change when yields are low. Duration and convexity measure this sensitivity; modified duration = Macaulay duration/(1+y) and approximates the percentage price change for a small yield shift. Examiners may ask to compute the clean price given a dirty price and settlement date, or to find the YTM of a bond with semi‑annual coupons when the quoted yield is an annual nominal rate compounded semi‑annually. In such cases convert the nominal yield to a periodic rate before discounting. A frequent twist is a bond with a call feature: the yield‑to‑call uses the call date and call price instead of maturity, and the investor must compare YTM and yield‑to‑call to assess the worst‑case return.

Technique: Bond Price from Yield and Accrued Interest
A 10 % annual coupon bond with face value ₹1,00,000 pays coupons semi‑annually. The bond matures in 4 years. The market yield is 8 % p.a. compounded semi‑annually. Settlement occurs 45 days after the last coupon date; the coupon period is 182 days. Compute the clean price.
Periodic coupon = 10 % × 1,00,000 / 2 = ₹5,000. Periodic yield = 8 % / 2 = 4 % = 0.04. Number of periods = 4 × 2 = 8. Dirty price = Σk=18 5,000/(1.04)ᵏ + 1,00,000/(1.04)⁸. Using the annuity formula: PV of coupons = 5,000 × [1 – (1.04)⁻⁸]/0.04 = 5,000 × 6.7327 = ₹33,663.5. PV of principal = 1,00,000/(1.04)⁸ = 1,00,000 × 0.73069 = ₹73,069. Dirty price = ₹1,06,732.5. Accrued interest = 5,000 × 45/182 = ₹1,236.26. Clean price = 1,06,732.5 – 1,236.26 = ₹1,05,496.24.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a bond question appears, first list the cash‑flow timeline: coupon dates, settlement, maturity. Convert the quoted yield to the matching periodic rate before any discounting. Compute the dirty price using the annuity formula for coupons plus the lump‑sum principal. Then subtract accrued interest (coupon × days elapsed/days in period) to obtain the clean price. Keep a small table of day‑count conventions (actual/actual, 30/360) handy; the exam will state which one to use. If the yield is given as an effective annual rate, convert it to the periodic rate via (1+EAY)1/m – 1.

Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return for Non‑Uniform Cash Flows

Project appraisal often involves cash flows that are not level annuities. The net present value (NPV) at a discount rate r is NPV = Σt=0N CF_t/(1+r)ᵗ, where CF_t can be positive (inflows) or negative (outflows). The internal rate of return (IRR) is the rate r* that makes NPV = 0. Because the equation is a polynomial of degree N, there can be multiple IRRs when cash flows change sign more than once (Descartes’ rule of signs). In such cases the IRR is not a reliable decision criterion; the modified IRR (MIRR) assumes reinvestment at a safe rate and finance at a borrowing rate, yielding a unique solution. For mutually exclusive projects, NPV at the firm’s cost of capital is the correct ranking metric; IRR can give conflicting rankings due to scale and timing differences. Examiners test the ability to compute NPV for a given discount rate using a table of present‑value factors, and to approximate IRR by interpolation between two rates that give NPVs of opposite sign. The interpolation formula is IRR ≈ r₁ + (NPV₁/(NPV₁ – NPV₂)) × (r₂ – r₁). A typical twist is a project with an initial outlay, followed by a series of inflows, then a large terminal outflow (decommissioning cost). The candidate must include the terminal outflow in the cash‑flow stream and recognise that the IRR may be lower than the cost of capital even though early inflows are large. Another common variant: a lease‑versus‑buy analysis where the lease payments are an annuity due and the purchase involves a loan with a sinking fund; the NPV of each alternative must be computed on a common discount rate.

Tax‑Adjusted Yield and Post‑Tax Effective Rate

Interest income is often taxable, while certain investments (e.g., tax‑free bonds) are exempt. The post‑tax yield for a taxable instrument with nominal rate i and marginal tax rate t is i_post = i × (1 – t) when interest is taxed annually on an accrual basis. If tax is deducted at source (TDS) on the gross interest, the effective rate after tax is the same formula. For a tax‑free bond offering a coupon c, the taxable‑equivalent yield that would make an investor indifferent is c / (1 – t). When comparing a taxable deposit at 7 % with a tax‑free bond at 5.5 % for an investor in the 30 % bracket, the post‑tax deposit yield = 7 % × 0.70 = 4.9 %, so the tax‑free bond is superior. If the tax is levied only at maturity on the total interest earned (as in some cumulative deposits), the effective post‑tax rate solves (1+i_post)ⁿ = 1 + (1 – t)[(1+i)ⁿ – 1]. This yields a slightly higher post‑tax rate than the simple annual multiplication because the tax deferral allows interest to compound on the pre‑tax amount. Examiners may ask for the tax‑adjusted yield of a bond bought at a premium or discount, where the capital gain or loss may have a different tax treatment. In such cases separate the interest component (taxed at t_i) from the capital component (taxed at t_c) and compute the overall post‑tax yield by solving the equation Price = Σ (Coupon × (1 – t_i))/(1+r_post)ᵏ + (Redemption – Price) × (1 – t_c)/(1+r_post)ⁿ. A frequent trap is to apply the marginal tax rate to the coupon only and ignore the tax on the amortisation of premium or accretion of discount.

Deferred Annuities and Perpetuities with Delayed Start

A deferred annuity begins payments after a deferral period of d periods. Its present value at time 0 is the present value of an ordinary annuity of n payments evaluated at the start of the payment stream, then discounted back d periods: PV = R × [1 – (1+i)⁻ⁿ]/i × (1+i)⁻ᵈ. If the first payment occurs at the beginning of period d+1 (annuity due deferred), the factor becomes PV = R × [1 – (1+i)⁻ⁿ]/i × (1+i)⁻ᵈ⁺¹. A deferred perpetuity (a perpetuity that starts after d periods) has present value PV = R/i × (1+i)⁻ᵈ. When the perpetuity grows at rate g (with g < i), the formula is PV = R/(i – g) × (1+i)⁻ᵈ. These structures appear in pension valuation (deferred retirement annuities), endowment funds (spending begins after a build‑up phase), and real‑estate lease modelling (rent‑free periods). Examiners often combine deferral with a change in interest rate after the deferral period: for the first d periods the discount rate is i₁, thereafter i₂. The present value then splits into two discounting steps: discount the annuity at i₂ to the start of payments, then discount that lump sum at i₁ for d periods. A common error is to use a single rate for the whole horizon or to forget the extra factor of (1+i) when the first payment is immediate relative to the deferral date. Another trap is to treat a growing perpetuity with g ≥ i as having a finite present value; the formula only holds for g < i, otherwise the present value diverges.

  • Using arithmetic average of varying rates instead of geometric linking, leading to incorrect accumulation factors.
  • Confusing clean and dirty bond prices and omitting accrued interest when the settlement date falls between coupon dates.
  • Applying a single IRR to projects with multiple sign changes without checking for multiple roots.
  • Ignoring the tax treatment difference between coupon interest and capital gain/loss on bonds bought at premium or discount.
  • Forgetting the extra (1+i) factor for annuity‑due timing in deferred annuities and perpetuities.
  • Assuming a growing perpetuity has a finite present value when the growth rate equals or exceeds the discount rate.
  • Rounding the interpolated IRR to the nearest basis point without verifying that the NPV at that rate is sufficiently close to zero.
maths/ratio-proportion:
Fundamentals of Ratio

1.1 Definition and Notation of Ratio

A ratio expresses the relative size of two quantities of the same kind by showing how many times one quantity contains the other. It is written in the form a:b or as the fraction a/b, where the second term b is never zero because division by zero is undefined. The order of the terms matters; a:b is not the same as b:a unless the two quantities are equal. In practical problems the quantities may be lengths, weights, amounts of money, or any measurable attribute, provided they share the same unit of measurement.

1.2 Properties of Ratio

Ratios possess several algebraic properties that make them convenient for manipulation. Multiplying or dividing both terms of a ratio by the same non‑zero number leaves the ratio unchanged, which is the basis for simplifying ratios to their lowest terms. The sum of the terms of a ratio can be used to split a total quantity into parts that are proportional to the given ratio. If a ratio is expressed as a fraction, the usual rules of fraction arithmetic apply, allowing addition, subtraction, and comparison of ratios after bringing them to a common denominator.

1.3 Comparison of Ratios

To decide which of two ratios is larger, one can cross‑multiply the terms: for ratios a:b and c:d, the inequality a/b > c/d is equivalent to a·d > b·c, provided all terms are positive. This method avoids converting to decimals and is especially useful when the numbers are large. When ratios involve more than two quantities, they can be compared pairwise after making a common term equal, a technique that will be illustrated in the combined ratio problems later in the chapter.

1.4 Ratio in Real World Contexts

Ratios appear in everyday situations such as mixing ingredients in a recipe, scaling a map, or comparing financial metrics like debt‑to‑equity. In each case the ratio captures a relationship that remains constant even when the absolute amounts change. Understanding this invariance helps students recognise ratio problems hidden in word statements that do not explicitly use the word “ratio”.

Comparison of Ratio and Fraction Representations
AspectRatio (a:b)Fraction (a/b)
NotationColon separates termsSlash or horizontal bar
Order sensitivitya:b ≠ b:aa/b ≠ b/a
SimplificationDivide both terms by GCDDivide numerator and denominator by GCD
Addition of ratiosNot directly definedRequires common denominator

Proportion and Its Properties

2.1 Definition of Proportion

A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal. It is written as a:b = c:d or a/b = c/d. The four quantities a, b, c, d are called the terms of the proportion; a and d are the extremes, while b and c are the means. The equality of the two ratios implies a relationship among the four numbers that can be exploited to find an unknown term when the other three are known.

2.2 Fundamental Property of Proportion

The most important property of a proportion is that the product of the extremes equals the product of the means, expressed as a·d = b·c. This follows directly from cross‑multiplication of the equality a/b = c/d. The property provides a simple linear equation for the unknown term and is the foundation for solving all proportion problems, whether they involve direct variation, inverse variation, or continued proportion.

2.3 Types of Proportion

Proportions can be classified as direct, inverse, or continued. In direct proportion, an increase in one quantity causes a proportional increase in the other, so the ratio remains constant. In inverse proportion, an increase in one quantity causes a proportional decrease in the other, which means the product of the two quantities stays constant. Continued proportion occurs when three or more quantities are in proportion such that a:b = b:c = c:d, leading to the relationship b² = a·c, c² = b·d, and so on.

2.4 Applications of Proportion

Proportions are used to solve problems involving scaling, map reading, speed‑time‑distance relationships, and mixture calculations. For instance, if a car travels 150 kilometres in 3 hours, the distance covered in 5 hours can be found by setting up the proportion 150/3 = x/5 and solving for x. The same principle underlies the alligation rule for mixtures, which will be discussed in the next major section.

Worked Example: Finding a Missing Term in a Proportion
If 7:9 = 21:x, find the value of x.
The proportion 7:9 = 21:x means 7/9 = 21/x. By the fundamental property, the product of the extremes equals the product of the means, so 7·x = 9·21. Multiplying 9 by 21 gives 189. Dividing 189 by 7 yields 27. Therefore x = 27.
Exam‑Day Insight
When a proportion contains a variable in the denominator, cross‑multiply immediately to avoid dealing with fractions; the resulting linear equation is always easier to solve under time pressure.

Mixture and Alligation

3.1 Concept of Mixture

A mixture problem involves combining two or more components, each having a distinct value such as price per kilogram, concentration of a solution, or percentage of an alloy, to obtain a final mixture with a specified average value. The quantities of the components are usually unknown and must be determined from the given average. The underlying principle is that the total value of the mixture equals the sum of the values of the individual components, which leads to a linear equation in the unknown quantities.

3.2 Alligation Rule Derivation

The alligation rule is a shortcut derived from the weighted‑average equation. Suppose a cheaper ingredient costs C₁ per unit and a dearer ingredient costs C₂ per unit, with C₁ < C₂. If the mixture’s mean price is M, then the quantity of the cheaper ingredient multiplied by (M – C₁) equals the quantity of the dearer ingredient multiplied by (C₂ – M). Rearranging gives the ratio of quantities as (C₂ – M) : (M – C₁). This ratio is the inverse of the differences between each ingredient’s price and the mean price, which is why the rule is often remembered as “the difference opposite to the ingredient”.

3.3 Replacement Problems

Replacement problems are a special class of mixture questions where a portion of a homogeneous mixture is removed and replaced by another substance, often water, and the process may be repeated. After each operation the concentration of the original component decreases by a constant factor equal to the fraction that remains. If the initial quantity is Q, the fraction removed each time is f, and the operation is performed n times, the remaining quantity of the original component is Q·(1 – f)ⁿ. This formula follows from the fact that each operation leaves (1 – f) of the previous amount untouched.

3.4 Practical Examples

Consider a vessel containing 80 litres of a 40 % alcohol solution. If 20 litres are drawn off and replaced with water, the alcohol concentration drops because the removed portion contains alcohol in the same proportion as the whole. Applying the replacement formula with Q = 80, f = 20/80 = 1/4, and n = 1 gives a remaining alcohol volume of 80·(3/4) = 60 litres, which corresponds to a new concentration of 60/80 = 75 % of the original 40 %, i.e. 30 %. Repeating the operation once more would multiply by another factor of 3/4, yielding 45 litres of alcohol and a concentration of 22.5 %.

Alligation versus Algebraic Method for Two‑Ingredient Mixtures
CriterionAlligation RuleAlgebraic Method
SpeedVery fast once the rule is memorisedRequires setting up and solving a linear equation
ApplicabilityOnly for two ingredients with a single mean valueWorks for any number of ingredients and multiple constraints
Error riskLow if the differences are taken in the correct orderHigher if the equation is written incorrectly
Conceptual insightShows the inverse‑difference relationship directlyReveals the weighted‑average structure explicitly

Partnership and Profit Sharing

4.1 Simple Partnership

In a simple partnership all partners invest their capitals for the same duration. The profit or loss is divided in the ratio of the capitals contributed. If partner A invests ₹a and partner B invests ₹b for the whole period, the profit‑sharing ratio is a:b. This direct proportionality makes simple partnership problems straightforward applications of ratio concepts.

4.2 Compound Partnership

When partners invest for different lengths of time, the partnership is called compound. The effective capital of each partner is the product of the amount invested and the time for which it remains in the business, usually measured in months. The profit‑sharing ratio then becomes (Capital₁ × Time₁) : (Capital₂ × Time₂) : … . This adjustment ensures that a partner who keeps money in the venture longer receives a proportionally larger share of the profit.

4.3 Profit Distribution with Time Factor

Consider a business where A invests ₹50,000 for 12 months, B invests ₹60,000 for 8 months, and C invests ₹70,000 for 6 months. The effective capitals are 50,000×12 = 600,000; 60,000×8 = 480,000; 70,000×6 = 420,000. The profit‑sharing ratio simplifies to 600:480:420, which reduces to 10:8:7 after dividing by 60. If the total profit is ₹1,25,000, A receives (10/25)×1,25,000 = ₹50,000, B receives ₹40,000, and C receives ₹35,000.

4.4 Special Cases

Special situations arise when a partner joins or leaves mid‑year, when additional capital is introduced, or when a partner withdraws part of the investment. In each case the time‑weighted capital must be computed for every sub‑period and summed to obtain the total effective capital for that partner. The principle remains the same: profit share is proportional to the sum of (capital × time) over all sub‑periods.

Simple Partnership versus Compound Partnership
FeatureSimple PartnershipCompound Partnership
Investment durationIdentical for all partnersMay differ among partners
Profit‑sharing basisCapital amounts onlyCapital × Time for each partner
ComplexityLow, direct ratioHigher, requires time weighting
Typical exam frequencyCommon in basic arithmetic sectionsFrequent in advanced quantitative sections

Advanced Applications and Problem Solving Strategies

5.1 Combined Ratio Problems

Many examination questions require linking several ratios that share a common term. The standard technique is to equalise the common term by multiplying each ratio by the least common multiple of the two values that the common term takes. Once the common term is identical, the ratios can be concatenated to form a single chain ratio. This method extends naturally to three or more ratios and is essential for solving partnership problems where the profit‑sharing ratio must be derived from multiple investment ratios.

5.2 Multi‑Stage Mixture Problems

Multi‑stage mixture problems involve successive operations such as adding an ingredient, removing a portion, and then adding another ingredient. The key is to track the quantity of each component after every stage using the replacement formula or the alligation rule as appropriate. Because each stage changes the total volume and the composition, it is advisable to work with absolute quantities rather than percentages to avoid cumulative rounding errors.

5.3 Partnership with Changing Capitals

When a partner increases or decreases capital during the partnership period, the timeline must be split at the points of change. For each sub‑period the effective capital is calculated separately and then added. For example, if a partner invests ₹30,000 for the first 4 months, adds ₹10,000 for the next 5 months, and withdraws ₹5,000 for the final 3 months, the total effective capital is 30,000×4 + 40,000×5 + 35,000×3. This sum is then used in the profit‑sharing ratio alongside the other partners’ effective capitals.

5.4 Strategy for Time‑Bound Exams

In a timed test, identify the type of problem quickly: ratio, proportion, mixture, or partnership. For ratio and proportion, write the given equality and cross‑multiply immediately. For mixture, decide whether alligation or the replacement formula is faster; alligation is usually quicker for two‑ingredient problems, while the replacement formula is indispensable for repeated dilution. For partnership, compute effective capitals in a table to avoid missing any time segment. Practising these decision trees reduces hesitation and improves accuracy under pressure.

Mastering these interconnected topics equips you with a versatile toolkit for quantitative reasoning in competitive examinations.

Continued Proportion and Mean Proportional

A continued proportion is a sequence of three or more quantities where the ratio of the first to the second equals the ratio of the second to the third, and so on. For three numbers a, b, c in continued proportion we write a : b = b : c. The defining property is b² = a × c. The middle term b is called the mean proportional (or geometric mean) between a and c. The first term a is the first proportional, the third term c is the third proportional to a and b. If four numbers a, b, c, d satisfy a : b = b : c = c : d, they form a continued proportion of length four; then b² = ac, c² = bd, and ad = bc.

Mean proportionals appear in geometry (the altitude of a right triangle is the mean proportional between the segments of the hypotenuse) and in algebraic manipulation of quadratic equations. To find the mean proportional between two positive numbers p and q, compute √(p×q). The third proportional to p and q is q²/p. The fourth proportional to p, q, r (with p : q = r : x) is x = q×r/p. These formulas are direct consequences of cross‑multiplication and are frequently tested in disguised forms such as “find the number which when added to each of 6, 10, 14, 22 makes them proportional”.

When a problem states that three numbers are in continued proportion and gives either the sum or the product of the extremes, set up the equations b² = ac and the given condition, then solve the resulting quadratic. For example, if the sum of the extremes is 20 and the mean proportional is 8, then a + c = 20 and ac = 64. Solving yields a = 4, c = 16 (or vice‑versa). Recognising the symmetric nature of the equations avoids unnecessary trial‑and‑error.

Key Relationships

  • Mean proportional: √(a×c)
  • Third proportional: c = b²/a
  • Fourth proportional: d = b×c/a
  • Product of extremes = product of means in any proportion

Alligation with Three or More Ingredients

The classic alligation rule handles two ingredients by placing their costs on the left and the mean price in the centre, then taking differences to obtain the mixing ratio. For three or more ingredients the same principle extends through a pairwise or matrix approach. Suppose we have ingredients priced at C₁, C₂, C₃ per unit and we desire a mixture at mean price M. Write the costs in a column, place M to the right, and compute the absolute differences |Cᵢ − M|. The ratio of the quantities is proportional to these differences, but only when the mean lies between the minimum and maximum costs. If M lies outside that range, a feasible mixture does not exist without adding a fourth component or allowing negative quantities.

A systematic method is the alligation matrix. Create a table with rows for each ingredient and two columns: cost and difference from mean. Fill the differences, then the ratio of quantities is the inverse of the differences (larger difference → smaller share). For three ingredients A (₹30), B (₹40), C (₹50) targeting ₹42, the differences are 12, 2, 8. The inverse ratio is 1/12 : 1/2 : 1/8, which simplifies to 2 : 12 : 3 after multiplying by the LCM 24. Thus the required mixing ratio is 2 : 12 : 3. Verify by weighted average: (2×30 + 12×40 + 3×50) / (2+12+3) = (60+480+150)/17 = 690/17 = ₹40.59 — not ₹42. The discrepancy shows that the simple inverse‑difference rule works only when the mean is exactly between two adjacent costs; otherwise a linear combination of two‑ingredient alligations is needed.

The reliable technique for three ingredients is to treat the problem as two successive two‑ingredient alligations. First, combine the cheapest and the dearest to obtain an intermediate price that lies between the remaining ingredient and the target. Then alligate that intermediate with the third ingredient. This yields a unique ratio provided the target price lies within the convex hull of the given prices. The method also generalises to any number of ingredients by iteratively reducing the set.

Step‑by‑Step Procedure

  1. Arrange costs in ascending order.
  2. Check whether the desired mean lies between the minimum and maximum cost.
  3. Pick the two extreme costs and alligate them to produce an intermediate mean that equals the target or lies on the same side of the third cost.
  4. Alligate the intermediate mean with the remaining cost(s) until only the target remains.
  5. Multiply the ratios obtained at each stage to get the final proportion.
Alligation Matrix for Three Ingredients
A grocer has three varieties of tea costing ₹120, ₹150, and ₹180 per kg. In what ratio must he mix them to obtain a blend worth ₹160 per kg?

Step 1: Costs in ascending order: 120, 150, 180. Target 160 lies between 150 and 180.

Step 2: Alligate the extremes 120 and 180 to get an intermediate mean. Differences: |120−160| = 40, |180−160| = 20. Ratio of 120‑tea to 180‑tea = 20 : 40 = 1 : 2. This intermediate mixture has cost (1×120 + 2×180)/3 = 480/3 = ₹160, exactly the target.

Step 3: Since the intermediate already equals the target, the third variety (₹150) is not needed. The final ratio is 1 : 0 : 2, i.e., only the cheapest and dearest in 1 : 2.

If the target were ₹155, the intermediate from 120 and 180 would be (1×120+2×180)/3 = ₹160. Then alligate 160 with 150: differences |160−155| = 5, |150−155| = 5 → ratio 1 : 1. Combine with previous 1 : 2 gives overall ratio (1×1) : (1×1) : (2×1) = 1 : 1 : 2.

Exam‑Day Strategy for Multi‑Ingredient Alligation
When you see three or more costs, first verify that the target lies within the range. If it does, use the two‑stage alligation: pair the extremes, compute the intermediate, then alligate with the middle cost. Write the intermediate ratio clearly; examiners often award partial marks for correct intermediate steps even if the final arithmetic slips.

Partnership Admission, Retirement, and Goodwill Valuation

When a new partner is admitted, the existing partners sacrifice a portion of their profit share. The sacrifice ratio is the difference between the old profit‑sharing ratio and the new ratio for each continuing partner. Conversely, when a partner retires, the remaining partners gain a share; the gaining ratio is the difference between the new and old ratios for the continuing partners. Goodwill, the value of the firm’s reputation, must be valued and adjusted. Three standard valuation methods are:

  • Average Profit Method: Goodwill = Average annual profit × Number of years’ purchase. Average profit is computed after adjusting for abnormal items and partner remuneration.
  • Super Profit Method: Super profit = Average profit − Normal profit (where normal profit = Capital employed × Normal rate of return). Goodwill = Super profit × Number of years’ purchase.
  • Capitalisation Method: Goodwill = (Average profit × 100 / Normal rate of return) − Capital employed. Alternatively, goodwill = Super profit × 100 / Normal rate of return.

On admission, the incoming partner may bring goodwill in cash or kind. If goodwill is brought in cash, it is credited to the old partners in their sacrifice ratio. If goodwill is not brought in, the new partner’s capital account is debited with his share of goodwill and the old partners are credited in the sacrifice ratio. On retirement, the retiring partner’s share of goodwill is debited to the continuing partners in their gaining ratio and credited to the retiring partner’s account. All adjustments are made through the partners’ capital accounts; the firm’s books do not show a separate goodwill account unless the partnership deed requires it.

Illustrative Adjustment

Assume A and B share profits 3 : 2. C is admitted for 1/5 share, acquiring 1/10 from A and 1/10 from B. New ratio = A: 3/5 − 1/10 = 5/10, B: 2/5 − 1/10 = 3/10, C: 2/10 → 5 : 3 : 2. Sacrifice ratio = 1 : 1. If goodwill is valued at ₹50,000 and C brings ₹20,000 cash for goodwill, the remaining ₹30,000 is adjusted by debiting C’s capital ₹30,000 and crediting A and B ₹15,000 each.

Profit Sharing with Interest on Capital and Partner Salary

Partnership deeds often provide for interest on capital at an agreed rate and salary or commission to working partners. These items are appropriations of profit, not expenses. The profit‑and‑loss appropriation account is prepared after the profit‑and‑loss account. The sequence is:

  1. Calculate net profit from the profit‑and‑loss account.
  2. Charge interest on each partner’s opening capital (and on additional capital for the period it was employed) at the agreed rate.
  3. Allocate salary/commission to entitled partners.
  4. The residual profit (or loss) is distributed in the profit‑sharing ratio.

If the residual is a loss, interest and salary are still allowed unless the deed states they are payable only out of profits. In that case, the loss is shared in the profit‑sharing ratio after reversing the appropriations. The effective capital for interest calculation must reflect the time‑weighted capital, exactly as in compound partnership. For example, if A’s capital is ₹1,00,000 for 12 months and B adds ₹50,000 after 6 months, interest for A = 1,00,000 × 12/12 × r, for B = 50,000 × 6/12 × r.

Worked Example

Partners X and Y share profits 2 : 1. Capitals: X ₹2,00,000, Y ₹1,00,000. Deed allows 10% interest on capital and ₹12,000 annual salary to X. Net profit before appropriations = ₹1,20,000. Interest: X = 20,000, Y = 10,000. Salary to X = 12,000. Total appropriations = 42,000. Residual profit = 78,000. Distributed: X = 52,000, Y = 26,000. Final shares: X = 20,000 + 12,000 + 52,000 = ₹84,000; Y = 10,000 + 26,000 = ₹36,000.

Discounted Cash Flow Approach to Partnership Valuation

In advanced partnership problems, especially those involving buy‑out or dissolution, the value of a partner’s share is the present value of expected future profit distributions. The discounted cash flow (DCF) method estimates the stream of distributable profits for each future year, discounts them at an appropriate rate (often the firm’s weighted average cost of capital or a risk‑adjusted rate), and sums the present values. The steps are:

  1. Project the firm’s maintainable profit for each forecast year, adjusting for expected growth, capital expenditure, and working‑capital changes.
  2. Determine each partner’s share of the projected profit using the agreed profit‑sharing ratio (which may change if capital contributions change).
  3. Select a discount rate reflecting the risk of the partnership’s cash flows.
  4. Compute the present value of each partner’s profit share: PV = Σ (Profit_share_t / (1 + r)ᵗ).
  5. Add the present value of any terminal value (e.g., net assets on dissolution) if applicable.

This approach is superior to simple capital‑account valuation when profits are expected to grow or when the partnership has significant intangible assets. In examinations, a simplified version may appear: “A partner’s share of profit is ₹50,000 per year for the next 5 years. If the discount rate is 10%, find the present value of his share.” The answer uses the annuity formula PV = 50,000 × [1 − (1.10)⁻⁵] / 0.10 ≈ ₹1,89,540. Understanding the annuity factor table (or the formula) is essential for quick computation.

Key Points for Exams

  • DCF valuation is only required when the problem explicitly mentions “present value”, “discount rate”, or “buy‑out value”.
  • If the profit share is constant, use the annuity factor; if it grows at a constant rate g, use the growing annuity formula PV = C × [1 − ((1+g)/(1+r))ⁿ] / (r − g).
  • Always state the assumption that the discount rate remains constant over the projection horizon.
  • Confusing sacrifice ratio with gaining ratio when a partner is admitted versus when a partner retires.
  • Applying the simple inverse‑difference alligation rule to three ingredients without checking whether the target price lies between the extremes.
  • Forgetting to time‑weight capital when computing interest on capital in a compound partnership.
  • Treating interest on capital and partner salary as expenses deducted before net profit instead of appropriations after net profit.
  • Using the wrong discount rate (e.g., cost of debt instead of weighted average cost of capital) in DCF valuation of a partnership share.
  • Neglecting to adjust goodwill for the sacrifice/gaining ratio, leading to incorrect capital account balances on admission or retirement.
  • Assuming the mean proportional is always the arithmetic mean rather than the geometric mean.

These advanced topics complete the quantitative toolkit for competitive examinations.

Componendo and Dividendo in Ratio Equations

Derivation and Core Identities

When two ratios are equal, a : b = c : d, the componendo rule states that (a + b) : b = (c + d) : d. The dividendo rule gives (a − b) : b = (c − d) : d. Combining both yields the componendo‑dividendo identity (a + b) : (a − b) = (c + d) : (c − d). These transformations are valid provided the denominators are non‑zero and the quantities involved are positive, which is the usual case in competitive‑exam problems.

Typical Problem Patterns

Examiners often embed a hidden proportion inside a word problem. For example, “The sum of two numbers is 45 and their difference is 15. Find the numbers.” Setting the numbers as x and y gives x + y = 45 and x − y = 15. The ratio (x + y) : (x − y) = 45 : 15 = 3 : 1. By componendo‑dividendo, x : y = (3 + 1) : (3 − 1) = 4 : 2 = 2 : 1. Hence x = 30 and y = 15. This technique bypasses simultaneous equations and saves valuable seconds.

Extension to Three‑Term Ratios

If a : b : c = p : q : r, then (a + b + c) : (a − b + c) = (p + q + r) : (p − q + r) provided the expressions are defined. This extension is useful in mixture problems where three components are combined and the overall ratio of sum to a signed combination is given.

Common Pitfalls

  • Applying componendo‑dividendo when any term could be zero or negative, which invalidates the ratio.
  • Forgetting to revert the transformed ratio back to the original variables before answering the question.
  • Using the rule on non‑proportional expressions such as a/b = c/d + e.

Ratio in Time, Speed, and Distance Problems

Fundamental Ratio Relationships

Speed, time, and distance obey the simple proportion Distance = Speed × Time. When distance is constant, speed and time are inversely proportional: S₁ : S₂ = T₂ : T₁. When time is constant, distance and speed are directly proportional: D₁ : D₂ = S₁ : S₂. When speed is constant, distance and time are directly proportional: D₁ : D₂ = T₁ : T₂. Recognising which quantity is held constant converts a word problem into a pure ratio exercise.

Average Speed for Multiple Segments

For a journey split into two parts with distances d₁ and d₂ covered at speeds v₁ and v₂, the average speed is (d₁ + d₂) / (d₁/v₁ + d₂/v₂). If the distances are equal, the harmonic mean applies: 2 v₁ v₂ / (v₁ + v₂). If the times are equal, the arithmetic mean applies: (v₁ + v₂) / 2. Expressing the given data as ratios of distances or times often reveals which mean to use without memorising formulas.

Relative Speed and Meeting Problems

Two bodies moving towards each other with speeds u and v have a relative speed u + v. The time to meet equals the initial separation divided by u + v. If they move in the same direction, the relative speed is |u − v|. The ratio of distances covered until meeting equals the ratio of their speeds because the time is common. This insight turns many “when will they meet?” questions into a single ratio step.

Circular Track Scenarios

On a circular track of length L, two runners with speeds a and b (a > b) meet every L / (a − b) time units when running in the same direction, and every L / (a + b) when running opposite. The number of distinct meeting points on the track equals the numerator of the reduced fraction (a − b) / (a + b) or (a + b) / (a − b) depending on direction. This property is a direct consequence of the ratio of speeds expressed in lowest terms.

Worked Example: Meeting on a Circular Track
Two runners start together on a 400 m circular track. Their speeds are in the ratio 5 : 3. How many distinct points on the track will they meet if they run in the same direction?
Let the speeds be 5x and 3x. Relative speed = 5x − 3x = 2x. Time for first meeting = 400 / (2x) = 200/x. In that time the faster runner covers 5x × (200/x) = 1000 m, i.e. 2.5 laps. The meeting point is therefore half a lap (200 m) from the start. After each subsequent meeting the faster runner gains another 2.5 laps, so the meeting points repeat every two meetings. The reduced ratio of relative speed to sum of speeds is (5−3) : (5+3) = 2 : 8 = 1 : 4. The numerator 1 indicates a single distinct meeting point. Hence they meet at only one point on the track.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a time‑speed‑distance problem gives a ratio of speeds, immediately write the inverse ratio for times if the distance is common. For circular tracks, reduce the speed ratio to lowest terms; the numerator of the reduced relative‑speed ratio gives the number of distinct meeting points for same‑direction motion. This shortcut eliminates the need to compute absolute speeds or times.

Ratio in Work and Efficiency Problems

Efficiency as a Ratio Concept

Work problems treat “efficiency” as the amount of work done per unit time. If worker A completes a task in a days and worker B in b days, their efficiencies are in the ratio 1/a : 1/b = b : a. When several workers collaborate, the combined efficiency is the sum of individual efficiencies. The total time taken is the reciprocal of the combined efficiency multiplied by the total work (usually taken as 1 unit).

Fractional Work and Partial Participation

If a worker joins after k days or leaves early, the work done is split into segments. For each segment, compute the effective efficiency (sum of efficiencies of workers present) and multiply by the segment duration. The sum of work across segments equals 1. Expressing each segment’s contribution as a ratio of the total work often yields a linear equation in a single unknown.

Pipes and Cisterns as Work Problems

Inlet pipes have positive efficiency, outlet pipes negative. The net efficiency is the algebraic sum. If a pipe fills a tank in p hours and another empties it in q hours, the net rate is 1/p − 1/q = (q − p) / (pq). The time to fill the tank when both are open is pq / (q − p) provided q > p. This is a direct application of the ratio of rates.

Alternate Day Working

When two workers operate on alternate days, the work done in a two‑day cycle equals the sum of their daily efficiencies. If the total work is not an exact multiple of the cycle work, the remainder is completed by the worker whose turn comes next. The ratio of their efficiencies determines how many full cycles are needed and who finishes the job.

Ratio in Geometry: Section Formula and Similar Figures

Internal and External Division

A point P dividing the line segment joining A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m : n has coordinates ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)). For external division the formula becomes ((mx₂ − nx₁)/(m − n), (my₂ − ny₁)/(m − n)). The ratio m : n is taken as directed; reversing the order changes the sign of the denominator.

Centroid, Incentre, and Other Centres
