5. Economic Reforms since 1991 and External Sector

5.1 The Crisis of 1991 and the LPG Strategy

The balance of payments crisis of 1990-91, triggered by the Gulf War oil shock, loss of remittances from the Gulf, and political instability, brought India's foreign exchange reserves down to 1.1 billion dollars, barely enough for two weeks of imports. The Chandra Shekhar government pledged gold to the Bank of England and the Union Bank of Switzerland to secure emergency loans, and the incoming Narasimha Rao government, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, negotiated a structural adjustment programme with the IMF. The 1991 budget dismantled the licence raj by abolishing industrial licensing for all but eighteen industries, reduced the peak customs duty from 150 percent to 65 percent, announced automatic approval for foreign direct investment up to fifty-one percent in thirty-four high-priority industries, and initiated the phased reduction of the statutory liquidity ratio and cash reserve ratio to free resources for the private sector. This trinity of liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation shifted the development paradigm from state-led import substitution to market-oriented integration with the world economy.

5.2 Industrial Policy and Disinvestment

The 1991 Industrial Policy Statement reduced the number of industries reserved for the public sector from seventeen to eight and later to three: atomic energy, space, and defence equipment. The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act was amended to remove the threshold asset limit for large firms, eliminating the need for prior government approval for expansion, mergers, and new undertakings. Disinvestment began with the sale of minority stakes in public sector undertakings through auction and later through the Offer for Sale route on stock exchanges. The National Investment Fund was created in 2005 to channel disinvestment proceeds into social sector schemes. In 2021, the government announced a new Public Sector Enterprise Policy classifying sectors as strategic and non-strategic; in strategic sectors, a bare minimum presence will be maintained, while in non-strategic sectors, privatisation or closure will be pursued. The strategic sale of Air India to the Tata Group in 2022 marked the first full privatisation of a major airline in two decades.

5.3 Balance of Payments and Foreign Exchange Management

The Balance of Payments is a systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of India and the rest of the world in an accounting year. It comprises the current account, which records exports and imports of goods (trade balance), services (invisibles), primary income (investment income, compensation of employees), and secondary income (remittances, grants); and the capital and financial account, which records foreign direct investment, portfolio investment, external commercial borrowings, banking capital, and reserve assets. India has run a persistent merchandise trade deficit, financed by a surplus in services (especially software and business services) and private transfers (remittances), resulting in a current account deficit that averaged 1-2 percent of GDP in the pre-pandemic decade. The Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 replaced the draconian FERA 1973, shifting the focus from conservation to management of foreign exchange and making violations civil rather than criminal offences. The RBI manages the exchange rate through a managed float, intervening to curb excessive volatility without targeting a specific level.

5.4 Foreign Direct Investment versus Portfolio Investment

Foreign Direct Investment implies a lasting interest and significant influence over the management of an enterprise, typically defined as ownership of ten percent or more of voting power. FDI brings technology, managerial know-how, and access to global markets, and is considered stable because it involves physical assets. The government permits FDI under the automatic route (no prior approval) or the government route (approval required) depending on the sector; sensitive sectors such as defence, media, and multi-brand retail have caps and conditions. Foreign Portfolio Investment refers to investment in financial assets such as equity and debt securities without management control; it is more volatile, driven by global risk appetite and interest rate differentials. The SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations 2019 streamlined registration and investment limits. The distinction matters for policy: FDI is encouraged through liberalisation, while FPI flows are monitored for macro-financial stability, and the RBI may impose temporary restrictions on debt inflows during periods of excessive volatility.

6. Social Sector, Poverty Alleviation, and Key Institutions

6.1 Poverty Estimation Methodologies

Poverty measurement in India has evolved from the calorie-based poverty lines of the Alagh Committee (1979) and Lakdawala Committee (1993) to the consumption-expenditure-based lines of the Tendulkar Committee (2009) and the Rangarajan Committee (2014). The Tendulkar Committee shifted the reference basket from calories to a mixed basket of food, education, health, and transport, and used a uniform poverty line basket across rural and urban areas, yielding a poverty ratio of 21.9 percent for 2011-12. The Rangarajan Committee recommended higher expenditure thresholds and separate rural-urban baskets, estimating poverty at 29.5 percent for the same year. Since 2011-12, no official consumption expenditure survey has been finalised; the 2017-18 survey was withheld due to data quality concerns. The NITI Aayog introduced the Multidimensional Poverty Index in 2021, aligned with the global MPI, measuring deprivations across health, education, and living standards using twelve indicators; the 2023 progress review reported a decline in the multidimensionally poor from 24.85 percent in 2015-16 to 14.96 percent in 2019-21.

6.2 Employment Generation and Labour Reforms

The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 provides a legal guarantee of one hundred days of wage employment per year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work. The scheme is demand-driven, self-targeting, and creates durable assets such as water conservation structures and rural roads; wages are linked to the Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers. The Periodic Labour Force Survey, launched in 2017-18, replaced the quinquennial Employment-Unemployment Survey and provides annual estimates of labour force participation, worker population ratio, and unemployment rate by usual status and current weekly status.

Inflation Measurement, Targeting, and the Monetary Policy Committee

India’s headline inflation is tracked primarily through the Consumer Price Index (Combined) with base 2012 = 100, released monthly by the National Statistical Office. The Wholesale Price Index (base 2011‑12 = 100) continues to be published for industrial analysis but is no longer the policy anchor. In February 2015 the government and the Reserve Bank of India signed the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, committing to a flexible inflation target of 4 percent with a tolerance band of ±2 percentage points. The agreement gave statutory backing to the inflation‑targeting regime through the Finance Act 2016, which amended the RBI Act to create the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).

The MPC comprises six members: the Governor (chair), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one officer of the Bank nominated by the Central Board, and three external members appointed by the government for a four‑year term. Decisions are taken by majority vote; the Governor has a casting vote in case of a tie. The committee meets at least four times a year, and its resolution, including the policy repo rate, is published with the minutes after a 14‑day lag. The repo rate serves as the key signaling rate; the reverse repo rate, marginal standing facility (MSF) rate, and bank rate are aligned at fixed spreads (currently 0.25 percentage points below and 0.25 percentage points above the repo rate respectively).

Transmission of policy rates to lending rates has been strengthened by the external benchmark linking of floating‑rate loans (effective October 2019) and the introduction of the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) in April 2016. The RBI also conducts Open Market Operations (OMOs), variable rate repos/reverse repos, and the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) introduced in April 2022 to absorb surplus liquidity without collateral. The inflation‑targeting framework is reviewed every five years; the first review (2021) retained the 4 percent target and the ±2 percent band.

Key Indicators and Data Releases

  • CPI‑Combined (monthly, 12‑month YoY change) – primary gauge for MPC.
  • CPI‑Industrial Workers, CPI‑Agricultural Labourers, CPI‑Rural/Urban – used for wage indexation and specific scheme adjustments.
  • WPI (monthly) – monitored for input‑cost pressures in manufacturing.
  • Core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) – watched for persistence of demand‑side pressures.

Policy Response Toolkit

  1. Policy repo rate changes – conventional tightening/easing.
  2. Liquidity management – OMOs, variable rate repos, SDF, MSF.
  3. Macroprudential measures – loan‑to‑value caps, sectoral credit limits, countercyclical capital buffer.
  4. Forward guidance – MPC statements and minutes signal future stance.

Fiscal Federalism, the Finance Commission, and Centre‑State Financial Relations

The Constitution distributes fiscal powers through the Seventh Schedule: the Union List (e.g., customs, corporation tax), the State List (e.g., land revenue, state excise), and the Concurrent List (e.g., stamp duties). Article 280 mandates a Finance Commission every five years to recommend the vertical share of net proceeds of Union taxes to states (vertical devolution) and the horizontal distribution among states (horizontal devolution). The 15th Finance Commission (Chair: N. K. Singh), constituted in 2017, submitted its report for the award period 2021‑26.

Vertical devolution was fixed at 41 percent of the divisible pool, unchanged from the 14th Commission, but the 15th Commission introduced a performance‑based incentive for states that achieve reforms in health, education, and ease of doing business. Horizontal devolution weights: 45 percent for population (2011 Census), 15 percent for area, 15 percent for forest and ecology, 10 percent for income distance, 10 percent for demographic performance, and 5 percent for tax effort. The Commission also recommended grants for local bodies (₹4.36 lakh crore), disaster risk management (₹28,000 crore), and health sector (₹70,000 crore).

The Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council, a constitutional body under Article 279A, decides on rates, exemptions, and the compensation mechanism. The GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017 guaranteed states a 14 percent annual growth in protected revenue for five years (2017‑22), funded by a compensation cess on sin and luxury goods. The cess collection fell short during the pandemic; the Centre borrowed ₹1.1 lakh crore on behalf of states in 2020‑21 and 2021‑22, to be repaid from future cess collections. The compensation regime ended in June 2022, after which states rely solely on their share of GST revenues.

Emerging Issues

  • Revenue buoyancy of GST – structural rate rationalisation and compliance improvements needed to meet the 14 percent growth assumption.
  • Fiscal consolidation – the FRBM Act targets a combined debt‑to‑GDP of 60 percent (40 percent Centre, 20 percent states) by 2025‑26; current combined ratio exceeds 90 percent.
  • Off‑budget borrowings – state guarantees and public sector enterprise borrowings that bypass the FRBM ceiling.
  • Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) – shifting from input‑based to outcome‑based funding to improve expenditure efficiency.
Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which Finance Commission first introduced a performance‑based incentive for states in the horizontal devolution formula?" Many candidates answer the 14th Commission because it changed the population base to 2011 Census. The correct answer is the 15th Finance Commission, which added a 10 percent weight for demographic performance and a 5 percent weight for tax effort, explicitly linking a portion of the share to reform outcomes.
The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) introduced performance‑based incentives through the demographic performance (10 %) and tax effort (5 %) criteria in the horizontal devolution formula. The 14th Commission only updated the population base and adjusted weights for forest cover and area.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the 15th FC horizontal weights (population 45, area 15, forest 15, income distance 10, demographic performance 10, tax effort 5) and the vertical share (41 %). For GST compensation, recall the 14 percent protected growth, the five‑year period (2017‑22), and the borrowing mechanism used in 2020‑22. These numbers appear repeatedly in both prelims and mains.

Capital Account Convertibility, External Debt Management, and the Liberalised Remittance Scheme

India maintains a de‑facto partially open capital account. The current account has been fully convertible since 1994 (Article VIII of the IMF Articles of Agreement). Capital account liberalisation has proceeded in stages: the Tarapore Committee (1997) laid out pre‑conditions — fiscal consolidation, low inflation, a strong banking sector, and a market‑determined exchange rate. A second Tarapore Committee (2006) recommended a phased roadmap with quantitative ceilings for different categories of outflows and inflows.

Key elements of the present framework:

  • Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) – automatic route up to 100 percent in most sectors; government route with sectoral caps for defence (74 percent), telecom (100 percent with security clearance), and media (26 percent for news).
  • Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) – registered with SEBI; investment limits in corporate debt (currently 6 percent of outstanding stock) and government securities (currently 6 percent of outstanding stock, with a separate voluntary retention route for long‑term investors).
  • External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) – governed by the RBI’s ECB Framework (2018), which classifies borrowings into three tracks based on maturity and end‑use; all‑in‑cost ceilings linked to benchmark rates (e.g., 6‑month SOFR + 450 bps for Track I).
  • Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) – resident individuals may remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year for permissible current and capital account transactions (education, medical, investment in foreign securities, property purchase). The limit was raised from USD 200,000 in May 2015 and has remained unchanged since.
  • Non‑resident deposits – FCNR(B), NRE, and NRO accounts with interest rate ceilings linked to LIBOR/SOFR plus a spread.

India’s external debt stood at USD 620 billion (end‑March 2023), with a debt‑to‑GDP ratio of about 19 percent. The composition: commercial borrowings (≈ 38 percent), NRI deposits (≈ 24 percent), multilateral and bilateral loans (≈ 20 percent), and short‑term trade credit (≈ 18 percent). The RBI monitors the debt service ratio and the short‑term debt to reserves ratio (currently below 1.0) as early warning indicators.

Prudential Safeguards

  1. End‑use restrictions on ECB – prohibited for real estate, capital market speculation, and on‑lending to entities in restricted sectors.
  2. Hedging requirements – entities with ECB exposure above USD 20 million must hedge at least 70 percent of principal and interest.
  3. Capital flow management measures – the RBI can impose temporary restrictions (e.g., on short‑term debt inflows) under the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999.

Financial Sector Reforms: Basel Norms, NBFC Regulation, and the Payments Ecosystem

India adopted the Basel III capital framework in a phased manner beginning 2013, with full implementation of the Capital Conservation Buffer (2.5 percent), Countercyclical Capital Buffer (0‑2.5 percent), and the Leverage Ratio (3 percent) by March 2021. The RBI’s “Scale‑Based Regulation” (SBR) for Non‑Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), effective October 2022, classifies NBFCs into four layers — Base, Middle, Upper, and Top — based on asset size, interconnectedness, and supervisory assessment. The Top Layer (systemically significant NBFCs) faces bank‑like capital, liquidity, and governance requirements, including a Chief Risk Officer and a board‑level risk committee.

The IL&FS default in September 2018 exposed contagion risks from large NBFCs to mutual funds and banks. In response, the RBI tightened liquidity risk management (Liquidity Coverage Ratio for NBFCs from December 2020), mandated a minimum Net Owned Fund of ₹10 crore for new NBFCs, and introduced a Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework for NBFCs breaching capital or asset quality thresholds.

On the payments side, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) in April 2016, processes over 10 billion transactions per month as of 2023. The RBI’s “Payments Vision 2025” targets a 10× increase in digital payment volumes, interoperability across QR codes, and a regulatory sandbox (launched 2020) for fintech innovation. The Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS), the National Electronic Toll Collection (NETC), and the recently introduced Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) pilot (wholesale segment November 2022, retail segment February 2023) complete the evolving stack.

Regulatory Architecture

  • RBI – monetary authority, banking supervisor, payment system regulator.
  • SEBI – securities market regulator, oversees FPI, mutual funds, and listed NBFCs.
  • IRDAI – insurance regulator; coordinates with RBI on bancassurance.
  • PFRDA – pension fund regulator; manages NPS architecture.
  • Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) – apex inter‑regulatory forum chaired by the Finance Minister.

Public Debt Dynamics, Debt Sustainability, and the Debt Management Office

The combined (Centre plus states) general government debt‑to‑GDP ratio reached approximately 90 percent in 2022‑23, well above the FRBM Act’s medium‑term target of 60 percent (40 percent Centre, 20 percent states) by 2025‑26. The Centre’s debt is dominated by dated securities (≈ 85 percent), treasury bills (≈ 10 percent), and small savings (≈ 5 percent). States rely heavily on market borrowings (state development loans) and National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) loans.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Review Committee (2017, Chair: N. K. Singh) recommended a debt‑to‑GDP anchor, an escape clause for exogenous shocks, and the establishment of an independent Debt Management Office (DMO). The DMO was set up in 2022 under the Department of Economic Affairs to centralise cash management, issuance calendar coordination, and investor relations for both Centre and willing states. It publishes a quarterly issuance calendar, conducts buyback/switch operations to smooth the maturity profile, and manages the government’s cash balances through the Treasury Single Account (TSA) system.

Debt sustainability analysis (DSA) by the IMF and the RBI uses the primary deficit, interest‑growth differential (r − g), and the stock‑flow adjustment. As of 2023, the implicit interest rate on Centre’s debt is around 7.2 percent while nominal GDP growth averages 10‑11 percent, yielding a favourable r − g differential. However, contingent liabilities — guarantees to public sector enterprises, off‑budget borrowings, and state‑level guarantees — add an estimated 10‑12 percentage points to the effective debt ratio.

Key Policy Levers

  1. Lengthening maturity – shifting issuance to 10‑30 year bonds to reduce rollover risk.
  2. Interest rate risk management – using interest rate swaps and buybacks.
  3. Cash management – TSA and Ways and Means Advances (WMA) from RBI to smooth intra‑year mismatches.
  4. State coordination – the DMO assists states in issuing SDLs under a common calendar to avoid bunching.
  • Confusing the inflation target (4 percent) with the tolerance band (±2 percent) and stating the target as a range.
  • Attributing the 14 percent GST compensation growth guarantee to the 15th Finance Commission instead of the GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017.
  • Mixing up the LRS limit (USD 250,000) with the earlier USD 200,000 limit or the FPI debt limit.
  • Assuming Basel III was fully implemented in 2013; the capital conservation buffer and leverage ratio were phased in until 2021.
  • Believing the DMO was created by the 14th Finance Commission; it was established in 2022 on the recommendation of the FRBM Review Committee.
  • Stating that the current account has been fully convertible since 1991; the correct year is 1994 when India accepted Article VIII obligations.
  • Overlooking the distinction between the MPC’s statutory basis (Finance Act 2016) and the earlier technical advisory committee.
grammar/grammar-basics:
1. The Eight Parts of Speech and Their Functions

1.1 Nouns: Naming the World Around Us

Every English sentence begins with the need to name something, and the noun fulfills that need by identifying persons, places, animals, things, or abstract ideas. A common noun such as city or river labels a general class, while a proper noun like Delhi or Ganga singles out a unique entity and therefore always carries an initial capital letter. Collective nouns such as team, committee, or flock denote a group regarded as a single unit, yet they create persistent agreement problems because the same word can take a singular verb when the group acts in unison (The committee has submitted its report) and a plural verb when the members act individually (The committee are divided in their opinions). Abstract nouns name qualities, actions, or states that cannot be perceived by the senses — honesty, growth, childhood — and they never take a plural form. Material nouns such as gold, water, or cotton denote substances and are typically uncountable, though they may become countable when referring to distinct varieties (Indian teas versus tea as a substance). Countable nouns admit numbers and the indefinite article (a book, three books), whereas uncountable nouns require quantifiers such as some, much, or a piece of to express quantity. Recognising these sub-classifications is not merely taxonomic; it determines article choice, verb agreement, and the quantifiers that may precede the noun, all of which are tested directly in error-spotting and sentence-improvement items.

1.2 Pronouns: Standing in for Nouns

Pronouns reduce repetition by substituting for nouns already mentioned or easily inferred, but their utility depends on strict agreement in number, gender, and person with their antecedents. Personal pronouns distinguish three persons — first (I, we), second (you), and third (he, she, it, they) — and each person has distinct subject, object, and possessive forms; confusing he with him or his with he is a frequent source of case errors. Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself) must reflect back to a noun or pronoun in the same clause (She prepared herself), and they cannot stand alone as subjects or objects unless used emphatically (The director himself approved the plan). Demonstrative pronouns (this, that, these, those) point to specific items and imply proximity or distance in space, time, or discourse. Relative pronouns (who, whom, whose, which, that) introduce adjective clauses and must match their antecedents in animacy and case: who for people as subjects, whom for people as objects, whose for possession, and which or that for things. Interrogative pronouns (who, whom, whose, which, what) launch questions and follow the same case distinctions. Indefinite pronouns such as everyone, somebody, each, neither are grammatically singular even when they convey plural meaning, so they demand singular verbs and singular possessive pronouns (Each of the students has submitted his or her assignment). Mastery of pronoun case, antecedent clarity, and number agreement eliminates a large proportion of the sentence-correction errors that appear in competitive examinations.

1.3 Verbs: Action, State, and the Engine of the Sentence

The verb is the only part of speech that can constitute a predicate by itself, and every finite clause must contain a finite verb form that marks tense, number, and person. Main verbs express the core action (run, write, build) or state (be, seem, become), while auxiliary verbs — be, do, have — help form continuous, perfect, and passive constructions as well as questions and negatives. Modal auxiliaries (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to) convey modality such as ability, permission, obligation, or probability, and they never change form for person or number. Transitive verbs require a direct object to complete their meaning (She wrote a letter), whereas intransitive verbs do not (The child sleeps); many verbs function both ways depending on context (He runs a business versus He runs every morning). The distinction between finite and non-finite verb forms is structural: a finite verb (writes, wrote, will write) can serve as the main verb of an independent clause, while infinitives (to write), gerunds (writing), and participles (written, writing) cannot stand alone as predicates and therefore appear in phrases or dependent clauses. Tense, aspect, and voice together locate the action in time, depict its internal structure, and indicate whether the subject performs or receives the action; errors in tense sequencing, inappropriate passive voice, or confusion between been and being in perfect continuous forms are staples of grammar testing.

1.4 Adjectives and Adverbs: Modification and Degree

Adjectives qualify nouns or pronouns by answering the questions which one?, what kind?, or how many?; they appear attributively before the noun (a red balloon) or predicatively after a linking verb (The balloon is red). Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, or entire sentences, answering how?, when?, where?, to what extent?, or why?. The majority of adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective (quick → quickly), but flat adverbs such as fast, hard, early, late retain the same form as their adjective counterparts, and misidentifying them leads to errors like He runs quick instead of He runs quickly. Both adjectives and adverbs exhibit three degrees of comparison: positive (tall, quickly), comparative (taller, more quickly), and superlative (tallest, most quickly). One-syllable modifiers typically take -er and -est; two-syllable modifiers vary (happier but more careful); modifiers of three or more syllables always use more and most. Irregular forms such as good → better → best, bad → worse → worst, little → less → least, and much/many → more → most must be memorised. Double comparatives (more better) and double superlatives (most tallest) are ungrammatical. The placement of only, even, merely, and similar focusing adverbs changes the meaning of a sentence dramatically (Only she loves him versus She only loves him versus She loves only him), making adverb position a favourite testing point.

1.5 Prepositions, Conjunctions, and Interjections: Connecting and Expressing

Prepositions establish relationships of space, time, direction, agency, or manner between a noun or pronoun (the object of the preposition) and other words in the sentence. English prepositions are highly idiomatic; in denotes enclosure or large time spans (in the box, in July), on denotes surface contact or specific days (on the table, on Monday), and at denotes precise location or clock time (at the door, at 5 p.m.). The choice between between (two distinct entities) and among (more than two or a collective mass) is frequently tested, as is the distinction between since (point in time) and for (duration) with perfect tenses. Conjunctions join grammatical units of equal or unequal rank. Coordinating conjunctions — and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet — link words, phrases, or independent clauses of equal status and are remembered by the acronym FANBOYS. Subordinating conjunctions — because, although, if, since, while, unless, until — introduce dependent clauses and signal logical relationships such as cause, contrast, condition, or time. Correlative conjunctions — either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also, both…and — work in pairs and require parallel structure in the elements they connect. Interjections (Wow! Alas! Hurrah! Oh!) express sudden emotion and stand grammatically apart from the sentence, usually followed by an exclamation mark or a comma; they carry no syntactic function but appear in direct-speech narration and dialogue-based comprehension passages.

2. Sentence Architecture: Subjects, Predicates, and the Clause

2.1 The Subject-Predicate Relationship

Every complete sentence divides naturally into a subject — the person, place, thing, or idea that the sentence is about — and a predicate — everything that is said about the subject, always containing at least one finite verb. The simple subject is the head noun or pronoun stripped of modifiers (The bright morning star → star), while the complete subject includes all its modifiers. Similarly, the simple predicate is the verb or verb phrase alone (shines), and the complete predicate encompasses the verb plus objects, complements, and adverbial modifiers. Inverted order places the predicate or part of it before the subject (Into the room rushed the children, Rarely have I seen such courage), a structure common in literary writing and in questions. Compound subjects joined by and normally take a plural verb (Ravi and Priya are coming), but when the parts refer to the same person or thing, or express a single idea, the verb is singular (Bread and butter is his favourite snack). With correlative conjunctions (either…or, neither…nor) the verb agrees with the nearer subject (Neither the manager nor the employees are responsible). Indefinite pronouns such as each, every, either, neither take singular verbs even when followed by a plural noun in a prepositional phrase (Each of the boys has a bicycle). Understanding these agreement rules is essential because subject-verb disagreement is the single most tested error category in objective English papers.

2.2 Phrases: Word Groups Without Subject-Verb Pairing

A phrase is a group of related words that functions as a single part of speech but lacks a subject-finite verb combination; therefore it can never stand alone as a sentence. Noun phrases (the ancient banyan tree) act as subjects, objects, or complements. Verb phrases consist of a main verb plus its auxiliaries (has been waiting) and function as the predicate. Prepositional phrases begin with a preposition and end with its object (in the garden, after the meeting); they function adjectivally (The book on the table) or adverbially (We met after the meeting). Participial phrases use a present participle (walking down the street) or a past participle (exhausted by the journey) and function as adjectives; when they appear at the start of a sentence they must modify the grammatical subject, otherwise a dangling modifier results (Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful — incorrect because trees cannot walk). Gerund phrases (Swimming in the sea) function as nouns. Infinitive phrases (to win the match) can function as nouns, adjectives, or adverbs. Appositive phrases rename a neighbouring noun (My friend, a talented artist, painted this). Absolute phrases (The weather permitting, we shall depart) consist of a noun and a participle and modify the whole sentence. Recognising phrase types enables a candidate to spot misplaced modifiers, ensure parallelism in lists, and reduce wordy clauses to concise phrases during sentence improvement.

2.3 Clauses: The Building Blocks of Complete Thoughts

A clause is a group of words that contains its own subject and finite verb; this subject-verb pairing is what distinguishes a clause from a phrase. An independent (or main) clause expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence (The sun set). A dependent (or subordinate) clause cannot stand alone because it begins with a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun that marks it as incomplete (Because the sun set, who lives next door). Dependent clauses are classified by function: noun clauses act as subjects, objects, or complements (What he said is true); adjective (relative) clauses modify nouns (The book that you gave me); adverb clauses modify verbs, adjectives, or adverbs and answer questions such as when?, where?, why?, under what condition? (We left when the rain stopped). A relative clause may be restrictive (defining, no commas, The student who won the prize) or non-restrictive (non-defining, set off by commas, My brother, who lives in Mumbai, is visiting); the choice affects meaning and punctuation. Conditional clauses introduced by if, unless, provided that follow strict tense sequences: Type 0 (general truths) uses present in both clauses; Type 1 (real possibility) uses present in the if-clause and future in the main clause; Type 2 (unreal present) uses past in the if-clause and would + bare infinitive in the main clause; Type 3 (unreal past) uses past perfect in the if-clause and would have + past participle in the main clause. Mastery of clause types and their punctuation is indispensable for constructing complex sentences and for identifying fragment and run-on errors.

2.4 Classifying Sentences by Structure

Sentences are categorised structurally by the number and type of clauses they contain. A simple sentence contains exactly one independent clause and no dependent clauses (The tiger roared); it may have a compound subject (The tiger and the lion roared), a compound predicate (The tiger roared and prowled), or both, but it remains simple because it has only one subject-verb nexus. A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet), a semicolon, or a conjunctive adverb with a semicolon (The tiger roared; however, the deer escaped). A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause (Although the tiger roared, the deer escaped). A compound-complex sentence contains at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause (Although the tiger roared, the deer escaped, and the monkey chattered). The structural classification determines the punctuation rules that apply: compound sentences require a comma before the coordinating conjunction (unless the clauses are very short and closely related), complex sentences require a comma after an initial dependent clause but not before a final one, and compound-complex sentences combine both conventions. Examiners often test the ability to convert one structural type into another without changing meaning, a skill that demonstrates syntactic flexibility.

Worked Example: Structural Classification and Transformation
Question: Identify the structure of the following sentence and rewrite it as a complex sentence without altering its meaning: "The monsoon arrived late, so the crops failed, and the farmers suffered heavy losses."
Solution: The original sentence contains three independent clauses — "The monsoon arrived late", "the crops failed", and "the farmers suffered heavy losses" — joined by the coordinating conjunctions "so" and "and". There is no dependent clause, so the structure is compound. To convert it into a complex sentence, we must subordinate two of the ideas. One valid version: "Because the monsoon arrived late, the crops failed, causing the farmers to suffer heavy losses." Here "Because the monsoon arrived late" is a dependent adverb clause of reason, "the crops failed" is the independent clause, and "causing the farmers to suffer heavy losses" is a participial phrase modifying the main clause. The meaning is preserved, and the sentence is now complex.
Exam-Day Insight: Spotting Hidden Compounds
When a sentence appears simple but contains a subject-verb pair after a semicolon or a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, moreover), it is actually compound. Underline every finite verb; if you find more than one independent subject-verb pair not joined by a subordinating conjunction, the sentence is at least compound regardless of how short it looks.

3. Functional Classification: What Sentences Do

3.1 Declarative and Interrogative Sentences

Sentences are also classified by their communicative function, independent of their structural form. A declarative (assertive) sentence makes a statement of fact, opinion, or belief and ends with a full stop (The Parliament passes the bill). It may be affirmative or negative (The bill does not violate the Constitution). An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark. Yes-no questions invert the auxiliary and subject (Has the bill been passed?), while wh-questions begin with an interrogative word (When was the bill passed?). Tag questions attach a shortened question to a declarative clause, reversing polarity (The bill was passed, wasn't it?); the tag uses the same auxiliary and a pronoun matching the subject. Indirect questions embed a question within a declarative or interrogative frame without inversion (I wonder when the bill was passed, Can you tell me when the bill was passed?). In examination passages, the shift from direct to indirect speech often requires converting interrogative word order to declarative word order and adjusting pronouns, tenses, and time adverbials.

3.2 Imperative, Exclamatory, and Optative Sentences

An imperative sentence expresses a command, request, advice, or instruction and typically omits the subject you (Close the door, Please be seated). The verb appears in its base form; negative imperatives use do not or don't before the base verb (Do not touch). An exclamatory sentence conveys strong emotion — surprise, joy, anger, sorrow — and ends with an exclamation mark. It often begins with what or how followed by a noun phrase or adjective (What a magnificent building!, How beautifully she sings!). An optative sentence expresses a wish, prayer, or curse and usually begins with may or would that (May you live long!, Would that I were young again!). In formal grammar, optatives are a subset of exclamatories, but competitive examinations treat them as a distinct category. Transformation exercises frequently require changing a declarative into an exclamatory (It is a very hot day → What a hot day it is!) or an imperative into a polite request using a modal (Submit the form → Could you please submit the form?). Recognising the illocutionary force of a sentence helps in selecting the appropriate punctuation and in reporting speech accurately.

3.3 Transformation Between Functional Types

The ability to rewrite a sentence in a different functional form without changing its core meaning is a standard testing objective. Converting an assertive sentence into an interrogative often involves adding a negative tag or using a rhetorical question (Everyone knows the truth → Who does not know the truth?). Turning an interrogative into an assertive may require supplying the implied answer (Is he not a fool? → He is a fool). Imperatives can be reported as infinitives in indirect speech ("Leave the room," he said → He ordered me to leave the room). Exclamatories become declarative clauses with that and an intensifier ("What a tragedy!" she cried → She exclaimed that it was a great tragedy). Optatives are reported with wished or prayed followed by that and a modal ("May you succeed!" → He wished that I might succeed). These transformations rely on a secure grasp of clause structure, tense back-shifting, and pronoun adjustment, all of which are rooted in the foundational concepts covered in the preceding sections.

4. Agreement, Case, and Common Structural Errors

4.1 Subject-Verb Agreement Across Complex Subjects

Agreement errors arise when the verb fails to match the number of its subject, especially when intervening phrases obscure the true head noun. A singular subject takes a singular verb even when followed by a prepositional phrase containing a plural noun (The box of chocolates is open, not are open). Collective nouns take a singular verb when the group acts as a unit (The jury has delivered its verdict) and a plural verb when the members act individually (The jury are arguing among themselves). Nouns plural in form but singular in meaning — news, mathematics, physics, measles, economics, politics — take singular verbs (Mathematics is his favourite subject). Titles of books, films, or organisations are singular even when plural in form (The Canterbury Tales is a classic). Expressions of quantity — a lot of, a number of, the majority of — take their number from the noun that follows: A number of students are absent (plural) versus The number of students is small (singular). Fractions and percentages follow the same rule: Half of the cake is gone, Half of the cakes are gone. In inverted sentences the verb precedes the subject, but agreement remains with the subject (There is a book on the table; There are books on the table). Relative pronouns as subjects take verbs agreeing with their antecedents (He is one of the students who have passed — who refers to students, plural). These rules are not arbitrary; they reflect the logic of reference and are tested in every major English paper.

4.2 Pronoun Case and Reference Clarity

Pronoun case errors occur when a pronoun appears in the wrong case for its syntactic role. Subjective case (I, he, she, we, they, who) is required for subjects and subject complements after linking verbs (It is I, though It's me is accepted in informal usage). Objective case (me, him, her, us, them, whom) is required for direct objects, indirect objects, and objects of prepositions (Between you and me, never Between you and I). Possessive case (my, his, her, our, their, whose) shows ownership and precedes gerunds (His leaving early surprised us). Reflexive pronouns must have an antecedent in the same clause (She hurt herself); using a reflexive without an antecedent (Myself and Rahul went) is a common hypercorrection. Ambiguous reference arises when a pronoun could refer to more than one antecedent (Rahul told Amit that he had failed — who failed?). The remedy is to repeat the noun or restructure the sentence. Vague reference occurs when this, that, which, it refer to an entire clause or an implied idea rather than a specific noun (He missed the train, which annoyed him — which refers to the whole event). Examiners penalise both ambiguous and vague reference because they impair precision.

4.3 Modifier Placement and Dangling Constructions

A modifier must be placed as close as possible to the word it modifies; otherwise the sentence becomes ambiguous or absurd. Misplaced modifiers create unintended meanings: She only ate apples (she did nothing else with apples) versus She ate only apples (apples were the only food). Squinting modifiers sit between two possible heads: Running quickly improves health — does quickly modify running or improves? Dangling modifiers occur when the word modified is absent from the sentence, typically at the beginning: Walking down the road, a dog bit me (the dog was not walking). The correction supplies the appropriate subject: While I was walking down the road, a dog bit me or Walking down the road, I was bitten by a dog. Participial phrases, infinitive phrases, and elliptical clauses are the usual culprits. In sentence-improvement questions, the correct option will always attach the modifier to a logical subject, often by converting the phrase into a clause with its own subject and verb.

4.4 Parallelism in Coordination and Comparison

Parallelism requires that items joined by coordinating conjunctions, correlative conjunctions, or comparison markers share the same grammatical form. In a list, all elements must be nouns, gerunds, infinitives, or clauses — not a mixture (He likes reading, swimming, and to ride → reading, swimming, and riding or to read, to swim, and to ride). With correlatives, the structure after the first correlative must mirror the structure after the second: not only…but also demands not only did he sing but also did he dance (both clauses) or not only singing but also dancing (both gerunds). Comparisons using than or as must compare like with like: The climate of Mumbai is warmer than Delhi (illogical — climate compared to city) → The climate of Mumbai is warmer than that of Delhi or Mumbai is warmer than Delhi. Ellipsis in the second part of a comparison is permitted only when the omitted words are recoverable and the remaining elements are parallel: She runs faster than he (understood runs). Faulty parallelism is a hallmark of poorly constructed sentences and a reliable target for error-detection questions.

These foundational concepts — parts of speech, phrase and clause architecture, structural and functional sentence classification, and the agreement, case, modifier, and parallelism rules that govern well-formed sentences — constitute the grammatical bedrock upon which all higher-level language skills are built.

Finite and Non‑finite Verb Forms and Their Syntactic Roles

Finite verbs carry tense, person, and number, anchoring a clause in time and establishing agreement with the subject. A finite verb can stand alone as the predicate of an independent clause: She writes, They have arrived. Non‑finite verbs — infinitives, gerunds, and participles — lack these inflectional features and therefore cannot serve as the sole predicate of a finite clause. Their distribution is governed by the matrix verb, the presence of a complementizer, or the syntactic slot they occupy.

The infinitive appears in three guises: the bare infinitive after modal auxiliaries (can go), the to‑infinitive as a complement of verbs like want or adjectives like eager, and the perfect or progressive infinitives (to have finished, to be writing) which encode aspectual nuance without tense. Gerunds, the –ing form functioning as nouns, occupy subject, object, or prepositional complement positions: Swimming relaxes me, She enjoys reading, He is good at painting. Present participles head participial phrases that modify nouns or serve as adverbial adjuncts: The child crying in the corner, Walking home, he saw a fox. Past participles appear in passive constructions (The book was written) and perfect aspects (has written), and they also head reduced relative clauses: The documents signed yesterday.

Control and raising phenomena illustrate how non‑finite clauses interact with argument structure. In She tried to leave, the subject of the infinitive is controlled by the matrix subject (subject control). In She seems to be tired, the matrix subject is raised from the embedded clause (subject‑to‑subject raising). Object control occurs with verbs like persuade: They persuaded him to stay. Recognising whether a non‑finite clause has an overt subject (as in for him to go) or a PRO subject (unpronounced but syntactically active) is essential for parsing complex sentences and for spotting agreement errors in error‑detection items.

Non‑finite forms also participate in absolutive constructions: The meeting over, we left. Here the participle over (a past participle functioning adjectivally) combines with its own subject The meeting to form a clause‑like adjunct that modifies the whole sentence. Such constructions are frequent in formal writing and are a reliable source of sentence‑improvement questions where the test‑taker must choose between a dangling participle and a correctly attached absolute phrase.

Finally, the distribution of non‑finite forms is constrained by the lexical requirements of the governing head. Verbs of perception (see, hear) license bare infinitives or present participles with a subtle meaning shift: I saw him cross the street (complete event) versus I saw him crossing the street (ongoing). Verbs of causation (make, let, have) take bare infinitives: She made him apologize. Mastery of these subcategorisation frames enables rapid identification of ungrammatical patterns such as *She made him to apologize.

Subjunctive Mood and Conditional Constructions

The subjunctive mood expresses wishes, demands, suggestions, hypotheticals, and counterfactuals. In contemporary English the present subjunctive is morphologically identical to the base form for all persons (be, go, work) and appears in that‑clauses after verbs of mandate (insist, require, recommend) and adjectives of necessity (essential, imperative): The board insists that the report be submitted by Friday. The past subjunctive, historically distinct only for be (were for all persons), survives in conditional protases and optative formulas: If I were you, I would accept, Would that it were true.

Conditional sentences are classified by the reality status of the condition. The zero conditional uses present simple in both clauses for universal truths: If water reaches 100 °C, it boils. The first conditional pairs present simple in the if‑clause with will + bare infinitive in the main clause for likely future events: If it rains, we will cancel. The second conditional employs past simple (or past subjunctive were) in the if‑clause and would + bare infinitive in the main clause for present or future hypotheticals: If I knew the answer, I would tell you. The third conditional combines past perfect in the if‑clause with would have + past participle for counterfactual past situations: If she had studied, she would have passed. Mixed conditionals blend time references, e.g., If I had taken the job, I would be living in London now (past condition, present result).

Inverted conditionals omit if and front the auxiliary: Were I to win, I would travel (second conditional), Had they known, they would have acted (third conditional). This inversion is a hallmark of formal register and appears frequently in sentence‑reordering tasks. The subjunctive also surfaces in formulaic expressions such as God save the Queen, Long live the King, and in legal or bureaucratic language: The statute requires that the applicant be a citizen.

Common errors involve mismatched mood or tense: *If I was you, I would go (should be were), *The teacher suggested that he studies harder (should be study), *Had he not left early, he would miss the train (should be would have missed). Examiners test the ability to recognise the subjunctive in embedded clauses and to select the correct conditional form for a given temporal and epistemic context.

Worked Example: Subjunctive Selection
Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
A) The committee recommends that the proposal is approved.
B) The committee recommends that the proposal be approved.
C) The committee recommends that the proposal will be approved.
D) The committee recommends that the proposal would be approved.
The verb recommends triggers a mandative subjunctive in the following that‑clause. The present subjunctive uses the base form be for all persons, yielding that the proposal be approved. Option B matches this pattern. Options A, C, and D employ indicative or modal forms that are ungrammatical in a mandative context. Therefore B is correct.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a sentence contains a verb of demand, suggestion, or necessity followed by a that‑clause, immediately check whether the embedded verb is in the base form. If it is not, the sentence is almost certainly flawed. For conditionals, identify the time reference of the if‑clause first; then match the main‑clause auxiliary (will, would, would have) accordingly. Inverted conditionals are a quick signal of formal style — treat them as the same conditional type without if.

Ellipsis and Gapping in Coordination

Ellipsis is the omission of material that is recoverable from the linguistic context. In coordinated structures, three major types appear: gapping, stripping, and verb‑phrase ellipsis (VPE). Gapping deletes the verb (and sometimes the auxiliary) from the second conjunct while leaving two remnants, typically a subject and an object: Mary bought apples, and John pears. The missing verb bought is understood from the first conjunct. Stripping (or bare argument ellipsis) retains a single remnant, often with a focus particle: Mary likes coffee; John, tea or Only Mary arrived (where Only Mary is the remnant of Only Mary arrived). VPE elides an entire verb phrase after an auxiliary or modal: She will sing, and he will too (where too signals the elided sing).

Licensing conditions differ. Gapping requires a coordinate structure with a conjunction (usually and, but, or) and parallel syntactic categories in the two conjuncts. The remnants must be contrastive foci; non‑contrastive gapping is infelicitous: *Mary bought apples, and John bought. Stripping is licensed by a focus operator (only, even, also) or by a contrastive intonation contour. VPE is licensed by an auxiliary (including do support) that bears the tense and agreement features: They have finished, and we have too. The elided VP must be syntactically identical to the antecedent VP modulo permissible differences such as voice (active/passive) or bound anaphora.

Ellipsis interacts with binding theory. In John thinks he is smart, and Bill does too, the elided VP is smart can be interpreted either as Bill thinks Bill is smart (strict reading) or Bill thinks John is smart (sloppy reading). The availability of the sloppy reading demonstrates that the pronoun he is bound by the subject of the antecedent clause and that the ellipsis site contains a variable that can be reassigned. This phenomenon is a staple of advanced syntax questions that probe the candidate’s ability to predict possible readings.

Comparative ellipsis (or comparative deletion) removes the repeated standard of comparison: She runs faster than he does (where does stands for runs) or She runs faster than he (bare NP remnant). The latter is a case of gapping in a comparative clause. The comparative operator than licenses the ellipsis, and the remnant must be a constituent that can serve as the subject of the understood predicate. Errors arise when the remnant is not parallel: *She runs faster than his running.

In testing, ellipsis items often present a sentence with a missing auxiliary or verb and ask the examinee to select the form that restores grammaticality while preserving the intended meaning. Recognising the licensing head (conjunction, focus particle, auxiliary, comparative) and the parallelism requirement is the key to rapid resolution.

Nominalization: Gerunds, Infinitives, and Derived Nouns

Nominalization transforms verbs or adjectives into noun‑like expressions, enabling them to occupy argument positions (subject, object, complement) and to be modified by determiners, adjectives, and prepositional phrases. English employs three primary nominalizing strategies: the gerund (‑ing form), the to‑infinitive, and derivational suffixes (‑tion, ‑ment, ‑ance, ‑al, ‑ure). Each strategy carries distinct syntactic and semantic properties.

Gerunds retain verbal characteristics: they can take direct objects (Reading books improves vocabulary), be modified by adverbs (Reading quickly helps), and exhibit aspectual contrasts (Having finished the work, she left). They also accept possessive or objective subjects: His/Him leaving early surprised us. The choice between possessive and objective often reflects register; formal writing prefers the possessive. Gerunds can be the complement of prepositions (interested in learning) and can head noun phrases that function as subjects of passive sentences: Being ignored is frustrating.

Infinitival nominals (to‑infinitives) are more restricted. They cannot be preceded by a determiner (*the to go) and rarely take adverbial modifiers inside the infinitive phrase (to quickly decide is marginal). However, they freely occur as subjects (To err is human), extraposed subjects (It is easy to learn), and complements of adjectives (eager to help) or nouns (the decision to leave). The infinitive can also express purpose when adjoined to a clause: She called to ask a question.

Derived nouns (e.g., arrival, development, refusal) are fully lexicalised; they lose verbal argument structure and instead select prepositional complements: the arrival of the train, the development of the project, his refusal of the offer. They can be pluralised (arrivals), modified by adjectives (rapid development), and appear in measure phrases (two refusals). The semantic shift often adds a sense of result or event nominalisation rather than ongoing action.

Choosing among these forms is governed by the governing predicate’s subcategorisation frame and by information‑structure considerations. Verbs of cognition (remember, forget) alternate between gerund and infinitive with meaning change: I remember locking the door (past action) versus Remember to lock the door (future obligation). Verbs of emotion (like, hate) accept both with little semantic difference. In error‑detection tasks, the most frequent traps involve using an infinitive where a gerund is required after a preposition (*interested to learn) or using a derived noun where a gerund preserves the verbal argument (*the refusal the offer instead of refusing the offer). Mastery of the distribution of each nominal type enables precise sentence construction and reliable error spotting.

Information Structure: Topic, Focus, and Cleft Sentences

Information structure organises a sentence according to what the speaker assumes the hearer already knows (topic) and what constitutes the new, informative part (focus). English exploits several syntactic devices to manipulate this partition without altering propositional content. The canonical subject‑first order presents the subject as default topic. Passive voice shifts the object to subject position, promoting it to topic status: The cake was eaten by the children.

Cleft constructions — it‑clefts and wh‑clefts (pseudo‑clefts) — explicitly mark focus. An it‑cleft has the form It is/was X that/who Y, where X is the focused constituent and the relative clause presupposes the rest: It was Mary who solved the problem (focus on Mary). A wh‑cleft uses a free relative clause as subject and a copular clause for the focus: What Mary solved was the problem (focus on the problem). Reverse wh‑clefts place the focused element first: The problem is what Mary solved. These structures are frequent in written exposition and in test items that ask for the “most emphatic” or “most appropriate” reformulation.

Focus particles (only, even, also, just) associate with a constituent and generate alternative sets. Their placement determines the scope of focus: Only John read the book (no one else read it) versus John only read the book (he did nothing else with it). Misplacement creates ambiguity and is a classic error‑detection target. Intonation in speech mirrors syntactic focus; in writing, clefts and fronting serve the same function.

Topicalisation fronts a non‑subject constituent to topic position, often with a comma: That book, I have read. Left‑dislocation adds a resumptive pronoun: That book, I have read it. Both constructions signal that the fronted element is a discourse‑given topic. Right‑dislocation (post‑posing) occurs in informal registers: I have read it, that book. These patterns are less common in formal examinations but appear in reading‑comprehension passages where the author’s information‑flow choices affect interpretation.

Understanding information structure aids in answering questions on sentence improvement, paragraph coherence, and logical flow. When a sentence feels “awkward” despite being grammatically correct, the cause is often a mismatch between the intended focus and the syntactic form. Recognising whether a cleft, passive, or fronted construction better aligns with the discourse context allows the test‑taker to select the optimal version.

  • Assuming the present subjunctive is optional after verbs of recommendation; it is mandatory in formal English.
  • Treating if I was as acceptable in counterfactual conditionals; the past subjunctive were is required for all persons.
  • Using a bare infinitive after a preposition (e.g., *interested to learn) instead of the gerund.
  • Misplacing focus particles such as only, which changes the truth conditions of the sentence.
  • Confusing gapping with verb‑phrase ellipsis and therefore inserting an auxiliary where none is licensed.
  • Choosing a derived noun where the verbal argument structure must be preserved, leading to loss of the object.
  • Neglecting the parallelism requirement in comparative ellipsis, producing mismatched remnants.
grammar/tenses:
The Twelve Tenses

English has three main times (present, past, future) × four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) = twelve tenses. Each expresses when an action happens and whether it is complete or ongoing.

Key Verbs: V1, V2, V3

  • V1 (base): go, write, eat, see, take, give, know, come, do, make.
  • V2 (past): went, wrote, ate, saw, took, gave, knew, came, did, made.
  • V3 (past participle): gone, written, eaten, seen, taken, given, known, come, done, made.
  • Regular verbs: add -ed (walk → walked, play → played).
  • Irregular verbs: must be memorised (go-went-gone, see-saw-seen).

Signal Words

  • Present Simple: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day/week, generally.
  • Present Continuous: now, at present, at the moment, look!, listen!, today (with now).
  • Present Perfect: already, yet, just, ever, never, since, for, today, this week (unfinished).
  • Past Simple: yesterday, last night/week/month/year, ago, in 1999, once, then.
  • Past Perfect: already, before, by the time, when (earlier action), after (earlier action).
  • Future Simple: tomorrow, next week/month/year, soon, in 2026, probably.

Important Rules

  • Since vs For: since = point of time (since 2020, since Monday); for = period of time (for 3 years, for two hours). Used with perfect tenses.
  • Past Perfect for earlier action: When two past actions are mentioned, the earlier one takes Past Perfect (had + V3), the later one Past Simple. "The train had left before I reached the station."
  • No future tense in time/condition clauses: "If it rains, I will stay" (not "If it will rain"). "When he comes, we will start."
  • Present Perfect not used with definite past time: "I have seen him yesterday" (wrong) → "I saw him yesterday" (right).
  • Stative verbs usually not continuous: know, believe, love, hate, want, need, seem, understand — use simple, not continuous ("I know her," not "I am knowing her").
Technique: Choosing the tense
Question: "She ___ (work) here since 2020." Choose correct form.
Answer: "since 2020" = unfinished time starting in past → Present Perfect or Present Perfect Continuous. If focus on result: "has worked." If focus on duration: "has been working." Both acceptable depending on emphasis.
Technique: Earlier of two past actions
Question: "I ___ (reach) the station after the train ___ (leave)."
Answer: Two past actions — train left earlier (Past Perfect: had left), I reached later (Past Simple: reached). "I reached the station after the train had left."

Common Traps

  • Using Present Perfect with "yesterday/last year/ago" — wrong.
  • Using "will" in "if/when" clauses — wrong.
  • Confusing Past Simple and Past Perfect when only one past action is mentioned — use Simple, not Perfect.
  • Using continuous with stative verbs (know, believe, want) — generally wrong.
  • Subject-verb agreement with Present Simple third person singular (he/she/it + s/es).

Memory Tricks

  • 12 tenses: 3 times × 4 aspects. Perfect = completed effect; Continuous = ongoing.
  • Since = point; For = period.
  • V2 = finished past; had + V3 = earlier past.
  • will + V1 = future simple (decision/prediction).
Tense exam strategy
In error spotting, check signal words first (yesterday → past tense; since/for → perfect; every day → present simple). In sentence improvement, choose the tense that matches the time word. Don't overthink — most tense errors are basic form mistakes.

Sequence of Tenses in Reported Speech and Conditional Structures

When a speaker reports an utterance, the tense of the reported clause often shifts back one step in the temporal hierarchy. This backshifting follows a predictable pattern: present simple becomes past simple, present perfect becomes past perfect, past simple becomes past perfect, and future simple (will) becomes would. The rule applies when the reporting verb is in a past tense (said, told, asked) and the reported situation is not a universal truth or a still‑valid fact. For example, “She works here” reported after a past reporting verb becomes “He said she worked here.” If the original statement expresses a timeless fact — “The earth revolves round the sun” — the tense may remain unchanged because the proposition holds irrespective of the reporting time.

Conditional sentences exhibit a parallel tense logic. In the first conditional (real possibility), the if‑clause uses present simple and the main clause uses will + base: “If it rains, we will cancel.” In the second conditional (unreal present), the if‑clause shifts to past simple and the main clause uses would + base: “If it rained, we would cancel.” The third conditional (unreal past) pushes both clauses further back: past perfect in the if‑clause and would have + past participle in the main clause — “If it had rained, we would have cancelled.” Mixed conditionals combine these layers, e.g., “If I had studied harder, I would be a doctor now” (past perfect in the if‑clause, would + base in the main clause) to show a past counterfactual with a present result.

Exceptions arise with modal verbs that lack a past form (must, ought to, should). In reported speech, must often becomes had to when expressing obligation, but remains must when expressing logical deduction: “He must be tired” → “She said he must be tired.” Similarly, should and ought to are unchanged in indirect speech. The verb need behaves like a modal in negative and interrogative contexts (need not, need I?) but follows regular backshifting in affirmative reported clauses (needed to). Understanding these nuances prevents the common error of over‑backshifting modals that are historically present‑tense forms.

Non‑finite Verb Forms: Gerunds, Infinitives, and Participles in Complex Constructions

Gerunds (V‑ing) function as nouns, infinitives (to + V1) as verbal nouns or purpose adjuncts, and participles (present V‑ing, past V3) as adjectival or adverbial modifiers. The choice among them is governed by the matrix verb, the syntactic role, and subtle meaning differences. Verbs of perception (see, hear, watch) take either a bare infinitive or a present participle: “I saw him leave” (complete event) versus “I saw him leaving” (ongoing process). Verbs of preference (like, love, hate, prefer) accept both gerund and infinitive with a shift in focus: “I like swimming” (general enjoyment) versus “I like to swim every morning” (habitual routine).

Control structures determine whether the subject of the non‑finite clause is understood as the matrix subject (subject control) or the matrix object (object control). In “She promised to arrive early”, the understood subject of to arrive is she (subject control). In “She persuaded him to arrive early”, the understood subject is him (object control). Raising verbs (seem, appear, happen) differ: the matrix subject is not the semantic argument of the non‑finite verb — “He seems to know the answer” — the subject he is raised from the embedded clause.

Perfect and progressive non‑finite forms add temporal nuance. The perfect gerund having + V3 indicates anteriority: “Having finished the report, she left.” The perfect infinitive to have + V3 serves a similar function after verbs of expectation or regret: “He claims to have seen the document.” The progressive gerund being + V‑ing and progressive infinitive to be + V‑ing emphasize ongoingness at the reference time: “Being watched made him nervous” and “She appears to be working late.” Passive non‑finite forms (being + V3, to be + V3, having been + V3) allow the logical object to become the subject of the non‑finite clause: “Having been selected, the candidate was interviewed.”

Exam questions frequently test the distribution of gerunds versus infinitives after specific adjectives and nouns. Adjectives such as easy, hard, difficult, impossible license a for‑to infinitive with a passive interpretation: “The problem is easy to solve” (≈ “to solve the problem is easy”). Nouns like decision, attempt, plan, refusal select a to‑infinitive: “His decision to resign surprised everyone.” Conversely, nouns such as habit, chance, opportunity, reason often take a gerund or a prepositional gerund: “There is a chance of winning” or “He has a habit of arriving late.” Mastery of these collocational patterns is essential for sentence‑improvement and error‑spotting items.

Technique: Choosing the Correct Non‑finite Form
Select the appropriate form to complete the sentence: “The manager objected ___ (to propose / to proposing / proposing) the new policy without consultation.”
The verb object is followed by the preposition to and a gerund. Therefore the correct choice is to proposing. The completed sentence reads: “The manager objected to proposing the new policy without consultation.”
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a sentence contains a verb + preposition combination, identify the preposition first; the following verb must be a gerund. For verb‑only patterns, memorise the three major groups: (1) verbs taking only gerund (avoid, enjoy, mind), (2) verbs taking only infinitive (decide, hope, manage), (3) verbs taking both with meaning change (remember, forget, stop, try). Quick classification reduces hesitation in error‑spotting.

Perfect and Progressive Aspects: Interaction with Verb Classes and Aspectual Coercion

The perfect aspect (have + V3) signals that an event is viewed as completed relative to a reference time, while the progressive aspect (be + V‑ing) presents an event as ongoing at that reference time. Their interaction with lexical aspect — the inherent temporal structure of verbs — produces systematic patterns and occasional coercions. Stative verbs (know, believe, love, own) normally resist the progressive because they denote states without internal phases. However, in contexts where a temporary or deliberate interpretation is forced, the progressive appears: “I am loving this concert” (temporary enjoyment) or “He is being difficult” (volitional behaviour). This coercion is a hallmark of advanced usage and is frequently tested in sentence‑improvement items where the simple form would be marked as less appropriate.

Dynamic verbs subdivide into activities (run, write), accomplishments (build a house, write a letter), and achievements (recognise, reach). Activities and accomplishments readily combine with both perfect and progressive: “She has been writing for two hours” (progressive perfect) and “She has written three letters” (perfect). Achievements, being punctual, resist the progressive unless they are reinterpreted as a preliminary phase: “He is reaching the summit” implies the approach, not the instantaneous arrival. The perfect with achievements yields a resultative reading: “He has reached the summit” (current relevance of the achieved state).

Aspectual coercion also operates with the perfect progressive (have been + V‑ing). This form emphasises duration leading up to a reference point and is compatible with activities and accomplishments but odd with achievements unless a preparatory process is implied: “They have been reaching a decision” (extended deliberation). In exam contexts, the presence of duration adverbials (for three hours, since morning) strongly signals the perfect progressive, while result‑oriented adverbials (already, just, yet) favour the simple perfect. Recognising these collocations allows rapid elimination of incorrect tense choices.
