Special Noun Categories: Form versus Meaning

5.1 Nouns Plural in Form but Singular in Meaning

Several nouns end in -s — the typical plural marker — yet function as singular concepts and take singular verbs. These include names of academic disciplines (mathematics, physics, economics, politics, statistics, linguistics, ethics, civics), diseases (measles, mumps, rickets, shingles), games (billiards, darts, dominoes), and the word news. Mathematics is a difficult subject and The news was shocking illustrate the pattern. The plural form is a historical accident: many of these words derive from Greek or Latin neuter plurals that were reanalysed as singular in English. A few, notably economics and politics, can shift to plural when they refer to separate aspects rather than the discipline as a whole: The economics of the project are uncertain (meaning the financial details). Candidates should memorise the core list and the exceptional plural use for economics/politics.

5.2 Nouns Always Plural in Form and Agreement

Conversely, a set of nouns exists only in plural form and always governs plural verbs. These are typically items consisting of two joined parts (scissors, trousers, pants, shorts, jeans, spectacles, glasses, binoculars, tongs, pliers) or collective nouns lacking a singular counterpart (goods, clothes, alms, premises, thanks, regards, riches, wages, outskirts, surroundings, belongings). The scissors are blunt and His clothes are dirty are correct; The scissor is or A clothe is are impossible. To express singular quantity, English uses a pair of: A pair of scissors is on the table. Here the subject becomes the singular pair, so the verb shifts to singular. This pair of construction is a favourite examination device: A pair of trousers was bought versus The trousers were bought.

5.3 Expressions of Quantity: 'A Number of' versus 'The Number of'

The phrases a number of and the number of illustrate how the definite article can flip verb number. A number of functions as a quantifier meaning "several" or "many"; the true head is the plural noun following of, so the verb is plural: A number of students are absent. The number of refers to a statistical total; the head is the singular number, so the verb is singular: The number of students is fifty. The same contrast appears with a majority of (plural when meaning "most of the members") versus the majority of (singular when referring to the collective majority as a unit), though usage varies. The article test — a for plural, the for singular — provides a reliable heuristic for these expressions.

Inversion, Intervening Phrases, and Relative Clauses

6.1 Intervening Phrases and the Real Subject

A common source of concord error is the insertion of a prepositional phrase or other modifier between the subject and the verb. The verb must agree with the head noun of the subject phrase, not with the noun inside the intervening phrase. In The box of chocolates is expensive, the subject head is box (singular), so the verb is is; the plural chocolates is merely the object of the preposition of. Similarly, The quality of the mangoes is good takes is because quality is singular. Longer interruptions — The collection of rare stamps, which he inherited from his uncle, is valuable — do not change the rule. The grammatical reason is that agreement is a relation between the verb and the subject head; modifiers are structurally subordinate and cannot control verb form. Examination sentences often pile multiple phrases between subject and verb to test whether the candidate can isolate the head noun.

6.2 Inverted Sentences Beginning with 'Here' and 'There'

Sentences that open with here or there followed by a form of be (or occasionally other verbs) place the real subject after the verb. This inversion does not alter the agreement rule: the verb still agrees with the post-verbal subject. Here comes the bus (singular) versus Here come the buses (plural); There is a book on the table versus There are two books on the table. The expletive there is not the subject; it is a placeholder that allows the true subject to follow. In questions, the same principle applies: Where is the key? versus Where are the keys? Candidates must identify the noun after the verb and match the verb to it, ignoring the introductory here/there.

6.3 Relative Pronouns and Antecedent Agreement

When a relative pronoun (who, which, that) functions as the subject of a relative clause, its verb agrees with its antecedent — the noun or pronoun the relative clause modifies. In This is one of the best books that have been written, the antecedent of that is books (plural), so the verb is have. In This is the only book that has been written, the antecedent is book (singular), so the verb is has. The distinction between one of the (plural antecedent) and the only (singular antecedent) is a classic examination trap. The rule extends to other antecedents: He is one of those leaders who inspire confidence (plural leaders → inspire) versus He is the only one of the leaders who inspires confidence (singular one → inspires). The verb in the relative clause must reflect the number of the specific noun the relative pronoun refers to, not the number of the main-clause subject.

Mastery of subject-verb agreement requires not merely memorising rules but developing the habit of locating the true subject head in every sentence, regardless of intervening material, inversion, or quantifying expressions. The principles outlined here — basic number and person matching, coordination and proximity, collective noun nuance, indefinite pronoun invariability, quantifier dependence on the noun after of, form-meaning mismatches, and inversion or relative-clause structures — constitute the complete framework tested in competitive examinations. Consistent application of these principles, reinforced by practice with sentences that layer multiple complexities, will secure accuracy in this high-weight grammar topic.

Agreement with Complex Quantifiers and Partitive Constructions

Quantifying expressions that contain a partitive of phrase — such as a lot of, a majority of, a fraction of, a proportion of, a variety of, a range of, none of, all of, most of, some of, any of — follow a single governing principle: the verb agrees with the noun that immediately follows of. When that noun is plural, the verb is plural; when it is singular or uncountable, the verb is singular. For example, A lot of the evidence is circumstantial (uncountable evidence), but A lot of the witnesses are unreliable (plural witnesses). The same rule applies to a majority of: A majority of the committee has voted (collective singular sense) versus A majority of the members have voted (plural sense). In formal writing, none of traditionally takes a singular verb when the noun after of is singular or uncountable (None of the information is accurate) and a plural verb when the noun is plural (None of the candidates are qualified). However, modern usage increasingly accepts plural verbs with singular nouns in informal contexts; examiners usually expect the traditional singular agreement. All of and most of behave identically: All of the cake is gone (singular), All of the cakes are gone (plural). Some of and any of follow the same pattern. A frequent examination twist inserts a long modifier between the quantifier and the of phrase, e.g., A significant proportion of the students who applied for the scholarship are eligible. The head noun remains students, so the verb stays plural. Candidates must locate the noun after of and ignore intervening material.

Compound Subjects Linked by Additive Phrases

Additive phrases such as as well as, along with, together with, in addition to, besides, and including do not create a compound subject. The verb agrees solely with the first noun (the head subject). For instance, The captain, as well as the players, is ready — the head subject captain is singular, so the verb is singular. Reversing the order changes the agreement: The players, together with the captain, are ready. The same principle applies to not only … but also constructions, where the proximity rule governs: Not only the students but also the teacher is responsible (verb agrees with the nearer subject teacher). When the additive phrase is set off by commas, it is a parenthetical modifier and never controls verb number. A common trap places a plural noun in the additive phrase and a singular head subject, tempting the test‑taker to match the verb to the plural noun. The correct strategy is to underline the first noun before any additive phrase and match the verb to that noun alone. This rule holds regardless of the length or complexity of the additive phrase, and it also applies when the additive phrase precedes the subject: Along with the documents, the report was submitted.

Technique: Identify the Head Subject
Choose the correct verb: The director, along with the actors, ___ (is/are) attending the premiere.
The head subject is director (singular); the phrase along with the actors does not change number. Correct verb: is.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When you see additive phrases, underline the first noun and ignore the rest; match the verb to that noun only.

Elliptical and Comparative Structures in Concord

Ellipsis — the omission of words that are recoverable from context — frequently appears in comparative clauses introduced by than or as. The verb in the elliptical clause must agree with its own subject, even though the verb itself is omitted. In She runs faster than he, the full clause is than he runs; the subject he is singular, so the understood verb is singular. When the comparative subject is a plural pronoun, the understood verb is plural: They work harder than we (understood do). The same principle operates with as … as: He is as tall as she (understood is). In formal writing, the auxiliary may be retained for clarity: She runs faster than he does. A related construction is the reduced relative clause: The book (that) I read is interesting — the relative pronoun that is the object of read, so the verb in the main clause agrees with book. When the relative pronoun functions as subject, agreement follows the antecedent: The books that are on the shelf are mine. Examiners often test the distinction between than I and than me; the prescriptive rule requires the nominative pronoun because the elliptical clause contains a subject, but many modern tests accept the objective form in informal registers. Candidates should apply the formal rule unless the question explicitly signals a colloquial context.

Greek and Latin Plurals: Form‑Meaning Mismatches

English retains a substantial set of nouns borrowed from Greek and Latin that keep their original plural inflections. The most frequently tested pairs include criterion / criteria, phenomenon / phenomena, datum / data, medium / media, curriculum / curricula, syllabus / syllabi, appendix / appendices, index / indices, matrix / matrices, and vertex / vertices. In each case the singular form ends in -on, -um, -us, or -ex/-ix, while the plural ends in -a, -i, -ices, or -es. The verb must agree with the grammatical number of the form used: The criterion is clear (singular), The criteria are clear (plural). A persistent error is treating criteria or phenomena as singular because they look like singular nouns ending in -a. Data is a special case: in scientific and academic writing it remains plural (The data are significant), but in general usage it is often treated as a mass noun taking a singular verb (The data is inconclusive). Examiners typically expect the traditional plural agreement in formal contexts. Agenda, originally a plural of agendum, has become a singular noun in modern English (The agenda is long). Media as the plural of medium is still plural in formal writing (The media are reporting), though singular use appears in casual speech. Mastery of these forms requires memorising the singular‑plural pairs and applying the agreement rule without being misled by the unfamiliar endings.

Subjunctive and Conditional Mood Effects on Verb Number

The subjunctive mood in English uses invariant verb forms that do not change for person or number. In the present subjunctive (mandative), the base form be appears for all subjects: It is essential that he be present; It is essential that they be present. The past subjunctive (counterfactual) uses were for every person: If I were you; If she were here; If they were ready. Because these forms are invariant, the usual subject‑verb number agreement does not apply. Conditional sentences with would, could, should, or might also employ invariant modals, so number agreement is irrelevant in the conditional clause. However, the main clause of a conditional sentence follows normal agreement: If the plan were approved, the committee would meet (singular committee → would meet is invariant, but the committee meets would be singular). A common examination item mixes a subjunctive clause with a main clause that contains a collective noun, testing whether the candidate incorrectly forces plural agreement in the subjunctive. The rule to remember: subjunctive be and were never take an -s ending, regardless of the subject. This invariance also extends to the formulaic expressions be it, come what may, and so be it.

  • Treating a majority of as always plural, ignoring the collective‑unit sense.
  • Ignoring the noun after of when the quantifier is none in formal writing.
  • Applying the proximity rule to additive phrases instead of the head subject.
  • Using a singular verb with Greek/Latin plural forms such as criteria or phenomena.
  • Forgetting that subjunctive be and were are invariant for number.
  • Overlooking elliptical comparative clauses where the omitted verb must agree with the subject of the clause.
grammar/articles-prepositions:
Articles (a, an, the)

  • Indefinite article 'a/an': Used before singular countable nouns when mentioning something for the first time or when the noun is not specific. 'a' before consonant sound (a boy, a university — 'u' sounds like 'yu'), 'an' before vowel sound (an apple, an hour — 'h' silent, vowel sound). Choice depends on sound, not spelling letter.
  • Definite article 'the': Used before a particular person/thing already mentioned or known (the book I bought), unique things (the sun, the moon, the earth), superlatives (the best, the tallest), musical instruments (the piano), rivers/seas/ranges (the Ganga, the Indian Ocean, the Himalayas), newspapers (the Hindu), holy books (the Gita), and nationalities (the Indians).
  • Omission of articles: No article before proper nouns (Delhi, John), abstract nouns used generally (Honesty is best policy), material nouns (Gold is precious), languages (Hindi is easy), meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner), bed/church/college/hospital/prison/school when used for primary purpose (go to school = study; go to the school = visit building), plural countable nouns used generally (Cars are expensive).
  • 'A/an' vs 'The': 'A man and a woman were walking. The man was tall.' (first mention = a/an, second = the).

Prepositions

  • Time: at (exact point — at 5 o'clock, at noon, at night), in (period — in May, in 2024, in the morning), on (day/date — on Monday, on 15th August, on Christmas day). 'In' for longer periods, 'on' for specific days, 'at' for exact points.
  • Place: at (point — at the door, at the station), in (enclosed space — in the room, in Delhi, in the box), on (surface — on the table, on the wall, on the floor).
  • Movement/direction: to (towards — go to school), into (enter — go into the room), onto (on top — jump onto the bed), towards (direction — walk towards the market), through (pass from one side to other — walk through the tunnel), across (from one side to other — swim across the river), along (follow length — walk along the road), against (touching and opposing — lean against the wall), among (more than two — divide among three), between (two — divide between Ram and Shyam).
  • Instrument/agent: by (agent — killed by a thief; mode — travel by bus), with (instrument — cut with a knife; accompaniment — go with a friend), in (manner — write in ink), on (basis — depend on).
  • Other common prepositions: about (concerning — talk about politics), above (higher than — above the roof), below (lower than — below the poverty line), over (covering — a roof over the head), under (below — under the table), before (earlier than — before 5 pm), after (later than — after lunch), since (point in past — since Monday), for (duration — for 3 hours), from (starting point — from Monday to Friday), till/until (up to — wait till 6), during (within a period — during the holidays), within (before end — within a week), without (lacking — without water), unlike (different from — unlike his brother), like (similar to — like his father), beside (next to — sit beside me), besides (in addition to — besides English, she knows French), except (excluding — all except John), including (including — including tax).

Important Preposition Pairs/Rules

  • In vs On vs At (place): at (point) < in (enclosed) — I live at No. 5, in Delhi, in India.
  • In vs On vs At (time): at (exact) < on (day) < in (month/year) — at 5 pm, on Monday, in January.
  • Between vs Among: between = two (between you and me), among = more than two (distribute among the poor).
  • Since vs For: since = point (since 2010), for = duration (for 10 years). Both used with perfect tenses.
  • By vs With: by = agent/doer (killed by a thief), with = instrument (cut with a knife).
  • Beside vs Besides: beside = next to (sit beside me), besides = in addition to (besides English, she knows Hindi).
  • From vs Since: from = starting point (works from 9 to 5), since = point in past continued to present (works here since 2010 — with perfect tense).
  • Into vs In: into = movement entering (jump into the well), in = position (swim in the pool).
  • On vs Upon: upon is more formal/literary (once upon a time; upon reflection).
  • Above vs Over: above = higher than, no contact (flags above the building); over = covering/moving across (a roof over us, flew over the city).
  • Below vs Under: below = lower than, no contact (below the poverty line); under = directly below/contact (under the table).
  • Between vs From...to: between two points (between Delhi and Mumbai), from...to (from Monday to Friday).

Conjunctions

  • Coordinating conjunctions: join equal elements — and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet (FANBOYS).
  • Subordinating conjunctions: join dependent clause — because, although, though, since, if, unless, until, while, when, before, after, as, as if, as though, lest, so that.
  • Correlative conjunctions (pairs): either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or, scarcely...when, no sooner...than, rather...than.
  • Important rules:
    • No sooner...than (No sooner did he arrive than it started raining — inversion).
    • Scarcely/Hardly...when (Scarcely had he reached when it rained — inversion, past perfect).
    • Lest = that...not, followed by should (Walk carefully lest you should fall).
    • Unless = if not (Unless you work hard, you will fail — no 'not' with unless).
    • Both...and takes plural verb (Both Ram and Shyam are present).
    • Not only...but also — verb agrees with nearer subject (Not only the teacher but also the students were present).
Technique: Article choice
Question: "___ honest man is respected by all." Choose article.
Answer: 'honest' starts with silent 'h' but vowel sound /ɒn/ → use 'an'. "An honest man is respected by all."
Technique: Since vs For
Question: "She has been living here ___ 2015." Choose preposition.
Answer: 2015 is a point in time → 'since'. "She has been living here since 2015."

Common Traps

  • Using 'a/an' before uncountable nouns (a milk, a furniture — wrong; milk is uncountable).
  • Using 'the' before proper nouns (the Delhi — wrong; Delhi is correct).
  • Confusing 'in' and 'at' for time/place.
  • Using 'between' for more than two people/things.
  • Using 'unless' with 'not' (unless you don't work — wrong; unless you work — correct).
  • Using 'the' before names of meals used generally (I take the breakfast — wrong; I take breakfast — correct).

Memory Tricks

  • Articles: a/an = first mention, general; the = specific, unique, second mention.
  • Sound rule: 'a university' (consonant sound), 'an hour' (vowel sound) — depends on sound, not letter.
  • Preposition place/time: at → on → in (smallest → largest unit).
  • Between vs Among: Between = 2; Among = 3+.
Articles/prepositions exam strategy
In error spotting, check articles before countable nouns, preposition choice (since/for, in/on/at), and 'unless' without 'not'. Read the sentence for meaning — wrong prepositions often change meaning entirely.

Zero Article and Null Determiner Contexts

The zero article — the absence of any determiner before a noun — operates in a tightly constrained set of syntactic environments. Plural count nouns used generically (Dogs bark), uncountable nouns denoting substance or abstract quality (Water boils at 100 °C), proper nouns naming unique entities (Paris is beautiful), names of meals when referring to the routine event (We have breakfast at eight), names of languages (She speaks French), and institutional nouns such as school, college, hospital, prison, church when the focus is on the activity rather than the building (He goes to school) all trigger the zero article. The same nouns admit the when the speaker points to a specific instance (The dogs next door bark, The water in this bottle is cold, The Paris of my childhood, The breakfast we had yesterday, The French spoken in Quebec, The school on the hill). A further layer appears with nouns that alternate between count and mass senses: experience (uncountable) versus an experience (countable event), knowledge (mass) versus a knowledge of Sanskrit (specific body). Examiners test this by embedding a noun in a prepositional phrase that forces a generic reading (by car, on foot, at night) and then offering a distractor with a or the. The rule of thumb: if the noun denotes a class, substance, or routine activity without individuation, the zero article is mandatory; any determiner signals a shift to specificity or countability.

Prepositional Verbs and Phrasal Verbs: Particle vs Preposition

Distinguishing prepositional verbs from phrasal verbs is a recurring error‑spotting target because both surface as verb + small word, yet their syntactic behaviour diverges. A prepositional verb consists of a lexical verb and a preposition that licenses a noun phrase complement (depend on the weather, look at the map, refer to the manual). The preposition cannot move away from its object; adverbs cannot intervene (*depend carefully on the weather is marginal). In contrast, a phrasal verb pairs a verb with a particle that behaves like an adverb: the particle can follow a noun object (turn the light off) and must follow a pronoun object (turn it off, not *turn off it). The particle also admits stress and can be fronted in clefts (Off went the light). Diagnostic tests: (1) Movement — if the small word can appear after a full NP, it is a particle; (2) Pronoun placement — pronoun must precede particle; (3) Adverb insertion — adverbs may separate verb and particle (turn quickly off) but not verb and preposition (*depend quickly on). Common prepositional verbs tested: account for, adhere to, approve of, consist of, rely on. Frequent phrasal verbs: give up, put off, run into, set up, take after. Examiners often present a sentence where a prepositional verb is incorrectly treated as phrasal (He looked the document up — wrong; correct He looked up the document) or vice‑versa (She depends her brother on — wrong). Mastery of the three tests eliminates the majority of such traps.

Technique: Particle Identification
Identify the particle in the following sentence and rewrite the sentence placing a pronoun object correctly: "The manager turned down the proposal."
The particle is down. With a pronoun object the particle must follow the pronoun: "The manager turned it down." The prepositional‑verb test fails because down cannot precede a noun phrase (*turned down the proposal is acceptable only as phrasal). The movement test confirms particle status: The manager turned the proposal down is grammatical.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a verb + small word appears, first try substituting a pronoun for the object. If the pronoun must precede the small word, you have a phrasal verb; if the small word stays before the pronoun, it is a prepositional verb. Apply the three‑second movement test mentally before marking an answer.

Correlative Conjunctions in Complex Sentence Architecture

Correlative conjunctions impose strict parallelism across coordinated constituents. The pairs either…or, neither…nor, both…and, not only…but also, whether…or demand that the grammatical category following the first element matches the category following the second. Violations appear as mismatched parts of speech (Either you must study hard or playing games — incorrect; correct Either you must study hard or you must play games). Subject‑verb agreement follows the proximity rule for neither…nor and either…or: the verb agrees with the nearer subject (Neither the teacher nor the students are ready). With both…and the verb is plural because the conjunction creates a plural subject (Both the manager and the clerk are present). Not only…but also triggers inversion when the clause begins with Not only (Not only did he arrive late, but he also forgot the files). The pair scarcely…when and no sooner…than require past perfect in the first clause and inversion (Scarcely had the train left when the storm broke). Lest introduces a subjunctive‑like clause with should (Walk carefully lest you should slip). Examiners embed these structures in long sentences where a hidden agreement error or missing inversion lurks. The reliable checklist: (1) verify parallel form; (2) locate the nearest subject for agreement; (3) check for required inversion after negative fronting; (4) ensure lest is followed by should + bare infinitive.

Article Usage with Abstract Nouns and Generic Reference

Abstract nouns — beauty, honesty, information, progress — default to zero article when used generically (Honesty is the best policy). The definite article appears when the abstract noun is particularised by a following of-phrase, a relative clause, or contextual specificity (The honesty of the witness was questioned, The information you gave me is outdated). The indefinite article surfaces when the abstract noun is treated as a countable instance or a type (A deep sadness settled over the room, An unusual courage characterises her). Superlative and ordinal modifiers force the (The best advice, The first attempt). Certain fixed expressions retain the despite generic sense: the rich, the poor, the young, the old (adjectival nouns). Conversely, names of meals, diseases, and languages resist the unless specified (He has malaria vs The malaria he contracted was severe). Exam items often present a sentence where an abstract noun is preceded by a in a generic context (A knowledge of history is essential — wrong; correct Knowledge of history is essential) or where the is omitted before a particularised abstract noun (Honesty of the witness — wrong). The decision matrix: generic → zero; particularised → the; countable instance → a/an; superlative/ordinal → the.

Preposition Choice in Temporal and Spatial Metaphors

English extends concrete spatial prepositions into metaphorical domains, creating collocations that are opaque to learners. Temporal metaphors: in the long run, at the moment, on time, by then, during the process, within an hour. Spatial metaphors: under pressure, over budget, above suspicion, below standard, beside the point, beyond doubt. The governing principle is the underlying image schema: in for containment (periods, states), at for point‑like instants, on for surfaces or lines (deadlines, schedules), under for subjection, over for exceeding a limit, above for superiority without contact, below for inferiority, beside for irrelevance, beyond for transcendence. Errors arise when a learner selects the literal preposition instead of the metaphorical one (He is in pressure instead of under pressure; The project is at budget instead of over budget). A second trap is mixing metaphors: above the limit (acceptable) versus over the limit (also acceptable but with nuance of excess). Examiners test these by offering a sentence with a blank and four preposition options, only one of which matches the conventional metaphor. Mastery requires memorising the high‑frequency metaphorical collocations and recognising the image schema that licenses each preposition.

  • Using a zero article with a singular count noun in a generic statement (e.g., Tiger is endangered instead of The tiger is endangered or Tigers are endangered).
  • Treating a prepositional verb as a phrasal verb and moving the particle after a pronoun (e.g., She depended it on).
  • Failing to maintain parallel structure with correlative pairs (e.g., Not only he sings but also dances).
  • Omitting the definite article before a particularised abstract noun (e.g., Beauty of the sunset instead of The beauty of the sunset).
  • Selecting a literal preposition in a metaphorical collocation (e.g., in pressure for under pressure).
  • Neglecting inversion after fronted negative correlatives (e.g., No sooner he arrived than it rained).
  • Using lest without should or with a negative (e.g., Lest you fall instead of Lest you should fall).

Article Interaction with Quantifiers and Partitives

Quantifiers such as all, both, each, every, either, neither, many, few, several, a number of, a lot of impose distinct article requirements on the nouns they modify. When a quantifier precedes a plural count noun, the article is normally omitted: All students passed, Both options are viable. With singular count nouns, each and every take a zero article (Each candidate submitted a form), whereas either and neither require the singular noun without an article (Either answer is acceptable). The partitive construction of the forces the definite article: Many of the participants, Few of the books. However, a number of and a lot of behave as plural quantifiers and combine with zero article plural nouns (A number of errors were found). The quantifier some admits both article‑less plural (Some apples) and singular with a when indicating an unspecified singular entity (Some person called). Examiners frequently test the contrast between All the team (definite, specific group) and All team members (generic plural). A reliable decision matrix: (1) identify quantifier type; (2) check noun countability; (3) determine whether the noun phrase is specific (definite article) or generic (zero article).

Preposition Selection in Idiomatic Collocations and Register Variation

English prepositions often lose their spatial sense when they enter fixed collocations, and the register (formal, academic, journalistic, colloquial) determines which preposition is licensed. In formal writing, in respect of, with regard to, and by virtue of are preferred over their colloquial counterparts about, concerning, and because of. The preposition on appears in on condition that, on the grounds that, and on account of, whereas upon is restricted to elevated style (upon receipt, upon completion). The pair in/on with temporal nouns follows a register split: in the morning (neutral), on the morning of the exam (specific event). With abstract nouns, under signals subjection (under consideration, under review), while over signals authority or excess (over budget, over the limit). The preposition at is fixed in at risk, at stake, at variance; substituting in or on produces an error. A second dimension is the verb‑preposition complementation pattern: consist of, depend on, object to, subscribe to. Learners often replace the required preposition with a semantically similar one (depend *in*), which is a high‑frequency trap. Mastery requires memorising the top 150 verb‑preposition and adjective‑preposition collocations and recognising the register cue (e.g., in accordance with vs. according to).

Error‑Spotting Worked Example
Identify the error: The committee decided on the proposal in respect to the new guidelines.
The phrase in respect to is non‑standard; the correct collocation in formal register is in respect of or with respect to. The sentence should read: The committee decided on the proposal in respect of the new guidelines. The error is a preposition‑choice mistake driven by register mismatch.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a blank tests a preposition in a formal‑sounding sentence, first check whether the surrounding vocabulary signals elevated register (e.g., committee, guidelines, accordance, virtue). If so, select the preposition that belongs to the formal collocation set (in respect of, by virtue of, on condition that) rather than the everyday alternative.

Conjunction Coordination Across Clause Boundaries: Ellipsis and Gapping

Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet) can link not only full clauses but also reduced structures where material is omitted under identity. Gapping deletes the verb in the second conjunct when the verb is identical: She likes tea, and he coffee. Stripping retains only a single constituent (often a subject or object) with a conjunction: Only John passed; Mary, too. Ellipsis in not only … but also constructions permits omission of the auxiliary in the second clause when the first clause contains an inverted auxiliary: Not only did she arrive early, but she also prepared the agenda (no ellipsis) versus Not only did she arrive early, but also prepared the agenda (elliptical, acceptable in informal registers). With either … or and neither … nor, the verb may be omitted in the second conjunct if the modal or auxiliary is shared: You can either stay or leave (full) vs. You can either stay or leave (no ellipsis needed). However, examiners embed a hidden agreement error when the coordinated subjects differ in number: Neither the manager nor the clerks is available (incorrect; proximity rule demands are). The conjunction for (meaning because) coordinates independent clauses but never triggers inversion; it is often misidentified as a preposition. A checklist for coordination items: (1) verify parallel syntactic category; (2) apply proximity agreement for either/or, neither/nor; (3) confirm that any fronted negative element (not only, scarcely, no sooner) triggers subject‑auxiliary inversion in the first clause; (4) ensure that ellipsis does not create ambiguity (e.g., She likes him more than me vs. She likes him more than I).

Zero Article in Institutional and Title Contexts

Proper nouns that denote institutions, offices, or titles frequently appear without an article when used in a generic or role‑denoting sense. Parliament, Congress, Cabinet, Court, University, Hospital, School take zero article when referring to the institution as a concept: Parliament debated the bill. The definite article appears when the noun is particularised by a post‑modifier: The Parliament of 1998, The University where she teaches. Titles such as President, Prime Minister, Director, Professor drop the article when used as a vocative or role label: President signed the order, Professor Smith lectured. However, when the title functions as a common noun describing a person, the article returns: A president must be elected, The director of the department. Fixed expressions like at school, in hospital, at university (British usage) retain zero article, whereas American English prefers in the hospital, at the university. Examiners test this by presenting a sentence such as He was appointed Director of Finance (correct) versus He was appointed the Director of Finance (incorrect in role‑denoting context). The decision rule: if the noun denotes a unique office held by one person at a time and is used as a title, omit the article; if the noun is modified by a restrictive relative clause or an of-phrase that identifies a specific instance, insert the.

Prepositional Complementation of Adjectives and Nouns: Licensing Patterns

Adjectives and nouns license specific prepositions, and the choice is not predictable from semantics alone. Common adjective‑preposition pairs include aware of, capable of, dependent on, indifferent to, prone to, responsible for, similar to, superior to. Noun‑preposition pairs include advantage of, access to, attitude towards, cause of, effect on, exception to, increase in, reason for. Errors arise when learners substitute a semantically related preposition: interested *in* (correct) vs. interested *on*; good *at* (correct) vs. good *in*. Some adjectives accept two prepositions with a meaning shift: angry with (person) vs. angry about (situation); different from (standard) vs. different to (British informal) vs. different than (American informal). Nouns derived from verbs often retain the verb’s preposition: reliance on, insistence on, objection to. A high‑frequency trap is the noun preference, which licenses for (a preference for tea) not to. Another is solution, which takes to (solution to the problem) not for. Examiners embed these in long noun phrases: His insistence on the proposal was noted (correct) vs. His insistence *to* the proposal (incorrect). Mastery requires a memorised list of the 80 most tested adjective‑preposition and noun‑preposition collocations and the ability to spot the head adjective or noun that governs the preposition.

  • Using in respect to instead of in respect of or with respect to in formal register.
  • Omitting the required article after a partitive quantifier (e.g., Many of participants instead of Many of the participants).
  • Applying proximity agreement incorrectly with either … or when the nearer subject is plural (e.g., Either the manager or the clerks is responsible).
  • Failing to trigger inversion after fronted Not only (e.g., Not only she arrived late but also forgot the files).
  • Inserting an article before a role‑denoting title (e.g., The President signed when used as a title).
  • Choosing a semantically similar but unlicensed preposition with adjectives (e.g., interested on, good in).
  • Using preference to or solution for instead of the licensed preference for and solution to.

These advanced patterns complete the core toolkit for high‑stakes error‑spotting and sentence‑completion items.
grammar/sentence-correction:
1. Foundations of Sentence Structure

1.1 The Core Elements of a Sentence

A sentence in English is built around a subject and a predicate, and the relationship between them determines whether the construction is grammatically sound. The subject may be a simple noun phrase, a pronoun, a gerund phrase, or a clause, while the predicate must contain a finite verb that agrees with the subject in number and person. When a writer omits the subject, uses a non‑finite verb as the main verb, or inserts an extra clause without proper subordination, the result is a fragment or a run‑on that examiners flag as an error. Understanding that every complete sentence requires at least one independent clause, and that dependent clauses cannot stand alone, provides the diagnostic framework for spotting structural faults in error‑spotting questions.

1.2 Clause Types and Their Functions

Independent clauses express a complete thought and can function as standalone sentences, whereas dependent clauses — whether nominal, adjectival, or adverbial — rely on a main clause for meaning. Nominal clauses often serve as subjects or objects, adjectival clauses modify nouns, and adverbial clauses indicate time, cause, condition, or concession. Errors arise when a dependent clause is punctuated as a sentence, when a relative pronoun is omitted in a restrictive clause, or when a subordinating conjunction is used incorrectly, such as placing “because” at the start of a sentence without a following main clause. Recognising the syntactic role of each clause type allows a test‑taker to locate the exact point where the grammar breaks down.

1.3 Sentence Patterns and Word Order

English follows a relatively fixed Subject‑Verb‑Object (SVO) order, but variations appear in questions, inversions, and emphatic constructions. Inversion after negative adverbials (“Never have I seen such a mess”) or in conditional clauses without “if” (“Had he known, he would have acted”) is a frequent source of error because candidates often retain the declarative order. Similarly, misplaced adverbs can change the meaning of a sentence (“He only eats apples” versus “Only he eats apples”). Mastery of the standard patterns and their licensed deviations equips the learner to judge whether a given word order is permissible or constitutes a grammatical violation.

2. Agreement and Concord

2.1 Subject‑Verb Agreement with Simple Subjects

The most basic concord rule requires a singular subject to take a singular verb and a plural subject a plural verb. This principle operates even when the subject is separated from its verb by intervening phrases such as prepositional phrases (“The box of chocolates is open”) or relative clauses (“The student who won the prize is here”). The verb must agree with the head noun of the subject phrase, not with the noun nearest to it. Errors of attraction occur when the writer mistakenly matches the verb to the closer noun, producing forms like “The quality of the mangoes are good.” Recognising the head noun and ignoring distractors is the first line of defence in error detection.

2.2 Agreement with Compound and Collective Subjects

When two or more nouns are joined by “and”, the subject is usually plural and demands a plural verb (“The director and the producer have arrived”). However, if the coordinated nouns refer to a single entity or a unified concept, a singular verb is appropriate (“Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast”). Collective nouns such as “team”, “committee”, “family”, or “audience” can take either singular or plural verbs depending on whether the group is viewed as a unit or as individuals; British usage often prefers the plural (“The committee are divided”), while American usage leans toward the singular (“The committee is divided”). The test‑taker must infer the intended sense from context, because the exam rarely supplies an explicit cue.

2.3 Agreement with Indefinite Pronouns and Quantifiers

Indefinite pronouns fall into three categories: those that are always singular (“each”, “everyone”, “somebody”, “nothing”), those that are always plural (“both”, “few”, “many”, “several”), and those that vary with the noun they refer to (“all”, “any”, “most”, “none”, “some”). Quantifiers such as “a number of” take a plural verb (“A number of students are absent”), whereas “the number of” takes a singular verb (“The number of students is rising”). The distinction hinges on whether the phrase emphasises the individual members or the collective quantity. Misidentifying the category leads to errors like “Each of the boys have a pen” instead of “has”.

Indefinite Pronouns and Their Verb Agreement
PronounNumberExample
each, everyone, somebody, nothingSingularEveryone is ready.
both, few, many, severalPluralFew have arrived.
all, any, most, none, someDepends on referentAll of the cake is gone. All of the cakes are gone.

2.4 Proximity and Attraction Errors

Proximity attraction is the tendency of a verb to agree with a nearby noun rather than the true subject. This phenomenon appears frequently in sentences where a singular subject is followed by a plural noun in a prepositional phrase (“The list of items are long”) or where a plural subject precedes a singular noun in a relative clause (“The players who is injured”). The rule is absolute: the verb must agree with the grammatical subject, not with any noun that happens to be closer. Training the eye to locate the subject head noun before checking the verb eliminates the majority of attraction errors in competitive examinations.

Subject‑Verb Agreement with Intervening Phrase
Identify the error: "The bouquet of roses smell sweet."
The subject is "bouquet" (singular); the prepositional phrase "of roses" does not change the number. Correct sentence: "The bouquet of roses smells sweet."
Exam‑Day Insight
When a sentence contains a long modifier between subject and verb, mentally strip the modifier and test the core subject‑verb pair; this isolates attraction errors instantly.

3. Tense, Aspect, and Voice

3.1 Consistency of Tense within a Discourse

A coherent passage maintains a consistent time frame unless a shift is signalled by a time adverbial or a change in narrative perspective. Unmotivated tense shifts — such as moving from past simple to present perfect without a clear reason — create confusion and are marked as errors. For instance, “He entered the room and sees the letter” mixes past and present; the correct form is either “entered … saw” or “enters … sees”. The principle of tense consistency extends to subordinate clauses: when the main clause is in the past, subordinate clauses typically backshift (“She said she was tired”), except when expressing a universal truth (“He said the earth revolves around the sun”).

3.2 Sequence of Tenses in Reported Speech

Reported speech follows a systematic backshifting pattern: present simple becomes past simple, present perfect becomes past perfect, past simple becomes past perfect, and modal verbs shift to their past equivalents (“can” → “could”, “will” → “would”). The reporting verb’s tense governs the shift; a present reporting verb (“He says”) does not trigger backshift. However, if the reported clause contains a timeless fact or a still‑valid future arrangement, the original tense may be retained (“She said she will join us tomorrow”). Mastery of this sequence prevents the common error of leaving the reported verb in its original form when the reporting verb is past.

3.3 Conditional Structures and Their Time References

English conditionals are classified by the reality and time of the condition. The first conditional (real present/future) uses “if + present simple, will + base verb” (“If it rains, I will stay”). The second conditional (unreal present/future) uses “if + past simple, would + base verb” (“If I were you, I would go”). The third conditional (unreal past) uses “if + past perfect, would have + past participle” (“If he had studied, he would have passed”). Mixed conditionals combine time references, such as “If I had taken the job, I would be living in London” (past condition, present result). A frequent trap is inserting “will” or “would” into the if‑clause, which is never permitted in standard grammar.

3.4 Active and Passive Voice Transformations

Changing voice requires the object of the active sentence to become the subject of the passive, the verb to adopt a form of “be” plus the past participle, and the original subject to appear in a “by” phrase if retained. Errors arise when the past participle is omitted (“The letter was send”), when the auxiliary “be” does not match the tense (“The work is completed yesterday”), or when intransitive verbs are forced into passive (“The accident was happened”). Only transitive verbs with a direct object can be passivised, and the tense of the passive must mirror the tense of the active original.

4. Articles, Determiners, and Prepositions

4.1 Definite and Indefinite Articles with Countable and Uncountable Nouns

The indefinite article “a/an” appears only before singular countable nouns, signalling non‑specific reference (“a book”). The definite article “the” marks specific or previously mentioned nouns, whether countable or uncountable (“the water in this bottle”). Uncountable nouns never take “a/an” (“an advice” is incorrect; “advice” or “a piece of advice” is correct). Plural countable nouns use “the” for specific reference and zero article for generic reference (“Dogs are loyal” versus “The dogs next door bark”). Errors such as “The milk is spoilt” (when speaking generically) or “The Delhi is big” (proper nouns usually take zero article) stem from misapplying these rules.

4.2 Zero Article and Generic Reference

Zero article is used with plural countable nouns and uncountable nouns when making generalisations (“Gold is precious”, “Children need love”). It also appears with institutions and meals when they are referred to in their primary function (“at school”, “in hospital”, “at breakfast”). However, when the same nouns are particularised, “the” returns (“The school he attends is famous”). The distinction between generic and specific reference is a frequent source of error because the same noun can appear with or without an article depending on context.

4.3 Preposition Selection after Verbs and Adjectives

Many verbs and adjectives govern specific prepositions, and substituting another preposition changes meaning or creates an ungrammatical construction. “Depend on” (not “depend in”), “good at” (not “good in”), “interested in” (not “interested on”), “afraid of” (not “afraid from”) are fixed collocations. The preposition is part of the lexical entry of the verb or adjective; learning these collocations as whole units reduces errors. Some verbs allow two prepositions with a shift in meaning (“arrive at” a building, “arrive in” a city), and the test may probe this nuance.

4.4 Since versus For, In versus On versus At, Between versus Among

“Since” marks a point in time (“since 2010”), while “for” marks a duration (“for ten years”). “In” is used with months, years, seasons, and parts of the day (“in July”, “in the morning”), “on” with days and dates (“on Monday”, “on 15 August”), and “at” with precise times (“at 5 p.m.”). “Between” applies to two distinct entities (“between you and me”), whereas “among” distributes over three or more (“among the members”). Misusing these prepositions is a hallmark of non‑native writing and appears regularly in error‑spotting sections.

5. Pronouns, Modifiers, and Parallelism

5.1 Case Forms and Reflexive Pronouns

Pronouns must appear in the correct case: subjective (“I”, “he”, “she”, “we”, “they”) for subjects and subject complements, objective (“me”, “him”, “her”, “us”, “them”) for objects of verbs and prepositions, and possessive (“my”, “his”, “her”, “our”, “their”) for determiners. A common error is using the subjective case after a preposition (“between you and I”) where the objective “me” is required. Reflexive pronouns (“myself”, “yourself”, “himself”) are used only when the subject and object refer to the same entity (“I hurt myself”) or for emphasis (“The manager himself approved”). Using a reflexive as a subject (“Myself invited him”) is ungrammatical.

5.2 Relative Pronouns: Who, Whom, Which, That

“Who” and “whom” refer to people; “who” functions as subject, “whom” as object. In formal writing, “whom” appears after prepositions (“the person to whom I spoke”), but in everyday usage “who” often replaces it. “Which” refers to things and animals, and “that” can refer to both people and things in restrictive clauses. Non‑restrictive clauses require “who” or “which” and are set off by commas. Errors include using “which” for people, omitting the relative pronoun in a restrictive clause where it is the subject, or inserting a comma before “that”.

5.3 Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers

A modifier must be placed next to the word it modifies. A dangling modifier occurs when the intended subject is absent from the main clause (“Walking on the road, a dog bit him” implies the dog was walking). The correction supplies the correct subject (“While I was walking on the road, a dog bit me”). A misplaced modifier changes meaning (“He only eats apples” versus “Only he eats apples”). The adverb “only” is especially mobile; its position determines which element it limits. Careful placement of participial phrases, prepositional phrases, and adverbs eliminates ambiguity.

5.4 Parallel Structure in Lists and Correlative Conjunctions

Elements joined by coordinating conjunctions or correlative pairs (“not only … but also”, “either … or”, “neither … nor”) must share the same grammatical form. A list mixing gerunds, infinitives, and nouns (“She likes reading, to swim, and dancing”) violates parallelism; the corrected version uses a uniform form (“reading, swimming, and dancing”). With correlatives, the structure after each part must match (“not only honest but also hardworking” — both adjectives). Failure to maintain parallelism is a frequent error because writers focus on meaning rather than form.

6. Conditionals, Reported Speech, and Question Tags

6.1 First, Second, and Third Conditionals

The three canonical conditionals each encode a distinct degree of reality. The first conditional presents a likely future outcome (“If you study, you will pass”). The second conditional imagines a hypothetical present or future (“If I won the lottery, I would travel”). The third conditional regrets a past impossibility (“If she had called, I would have answered”). The verb forms are rigid: the if‑clause never contains “will” or “would”. Mixing the patterns — for example, “If I would know, I will tell you” — signals a fundamental misunderstanding of conditional logic and is always marked wrong.

6.2 Mixed Conditionals and Their Nuances

Mixed conditionals combine the time frames of the second and third conditionals. A past condition with a present result uses “if + past perfect, would + base verb” (“If I had taken the medicine, I would feel better now”). A present condition with a past result uses “if + past simple, would have + past participle” (“If he were smarter, he would have solved it”). These structures allow speakers to express counterfactual reasoning across time boundaries. The exam may test the ability to select the correct mixed form from distractors that misuse simple past or present perfect in the if‑clause.

6.3 Reporting Verbs and Backshifting Rules

Beyond “say” and “tell”, a variety of reporting verbs (“ask”, “wonder”, “promise”, “suggest”) govern different complement patterns: some take a that‑clause with backshift, others take an infinitive (“promised to come”), and others a gerund (“suggested going”). The tense of the reporting verb determines whether backshift occurs. When the reporting verb is in the past, the reported clause typically backshifts; when it is present or future, the original tense remains. Errors arise when candidates apply backshift indiscriminately or fail to adjust pronouns and time adverbials (“tomorrow” → “the next day”).

6.4 Formation and Inversion of Question Tags

A question tag mirrors the auxiliary of the main clause, reverses polarity, and matches the subject pronoun. Positive statements take negative tags (“He is coming, isn’t he?”), negative statements take positive tags (“She doesn’t know, does she?”). Special cases include “I am” → “aren’t I?”, imperatives → “will you?” or “won’t you?”, and “let’s” → “shall we?”. The tag must use the same auxiliary (or a form of “do” if none exists) and the appropriate pronoun. Errors such as “He can swim, can he?” (double positive) or “You’re ready, aren’t you?” (incorrect pronoun) are common.

7. Redundancy, Word Choice, and Common Confusions

7.1 Redundant Expressions and Pleonasms

Redundancy occurs when a word adds no new information because its meaning is already contained in another word. Phrases like “return back”, “revert back”, “free gift”, “past history”, “end result”, and “very unique” are pleonastic; the adverb or adjective repeats the inherent sense of the noun or verb. In formal writing and examinations, such constructions are considered errors of style and are corrected by deleting the redundant element (“return”, “revert”, “gift”, “history”, “result”, “unique”). Recognising these fixed collocations saves time during error spotting.

7.2 Adjective versus Adverb Forms

Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. The suffix “‑ly” typically forms adverbs from adjectives (“quick → quickly”), but some adjectives end in “‑ly” already (“friendly”, “lovely”) and have no adverbial form; they require a phrase (“in a friendly manner”). Conversely, flat adverbs (“fast”, “hard”, “late”) share the same form as their adjectives. Errors such as “She runs quick” (should be “quickly”) or “He is very fastly running” (should be “very fast”) reveal confusion between the two categories. The rule “very + adjective” never takes “‑ly” is a useful shortcut.

7.3 Frequently Confused Word Pairs

Certain word pairs differ by a single letter or by part of speech, yet their meanings diverge sharply. “Accept” (verb) versus “except” (preposition), “affect” (verb) versus “effect” (noun), “altar” (noun) versus “alter” (verb), “complement” (noun/verb) versus “compliment” (noun/verb), “stationary” (adjective) versus “stationery” (noun), “principal” (adjective/noun) versus “principle” (noun), “advice” (noun) versus “advise” (verb), “practice” (noun) versus “practise” (verb). The exam often embeds the wrong member of a pair in a sentence, requiring the candidate to spot the semantic mismatch. Learning each pair with a mnemonic sentence (“The effect of the medicine was immediate”) cements the distinction.

7.4 Comparative and Superlative Constructions

Comparatives of one‑syllable adjectives add “‑er” (“taller”), those of two syllables ending in “‑y” change “y” to “i” and add “‑er” (“happier”), and longer adjectives use “more” (“more beautiful”). Superlatives follow the parallel pattern (“tallest”, “happiest”, “most beautiful”). Double comparatives (“more better”) and double superlatives (“most tallest”) are always incorrect. When comparing two entities, “than” follows the comparative; when comparing more than two, “the” precedes the superlative and “of” or “in” indicates the group (“the tallest of the three”, “the best in the class”). Comparisons must be logical: “The climate of Delhi is better than Mumbai” is faulty because a climate is compared to a city; the correction inserts “that of” (“better than that of Mumbai”).
