The 2018 Ayushman Bharat programme launched two pillars: Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs) to deliver comprehensive primary care, and the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM‑JAY) providing ₹5 lakh annual hospitalisation cover for 10.74 crore vulnerable families (SECC 2011). The COVID‑19 pandemic (2020‑22) stress‑tested this architecture. The first wave saw a nationwide lockdown (March‑May 2020) and the rapid scaling of RT‑PCR testing from 1 lab to 2,500 labs by December 2020. The second wave (April‑June 2021) exposed oxygen supply chain failures, with the Supreme Court intervening in “In Re: Distribution of Essential Supplies” (April 2021) to mandate a national allocation formula. Vaccination rollout (January 2021 onward) achieved 2.2 billion doses by July 2023, yet NFHS‑5 (2019‑21) data reveal persistent inequities: institutional delivery 88.6 % nationally but 70 % in Bihar; full immunisation 76 % overall, 60 % among Scheduled Tribes. Medical pluralism shapes health‑seeking behaviour — 2018 NSSO 75th Round shows 69 % of outpatient visits to private allopathic providers, 12 % to AYUSH, and 9 % to informal practitioners. The 2020 Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, adopted by 11 states, attempts quality standardisation but faces enforcement gaps. Examiners expect candidates to integrate macro‑indicators (out‑of‑pocket expenditure 55 % of total health spending, 2021‑22 National Health Accounts) with micro‑studies of therapeutic itineraries, and to reference the 2022 “Global Health Security Index” (India rank 66) when discussing pandemic preparedness.

Sociology of Work: Gig Economy, Labour Codes, and Precarious Employment

The rise of platform‑mediated work — food delivery (Swiggy, Zomato), ride‑hailing (Uber, Ola), and micro‑tasking (Amazon Mechanical Turk) — has created a new labour segment estimated at 7.7 million workers in 2022 (NITI Aayog “India’s Gig Economy” report). These workers are classified as “partners” rather than employees, denying them statutory protections under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948, and the Employees’ Provident Funds Act, 1952. The Parliament responded with four labour codes passed in 2020: the Code on Wages, 2019 (effective 2022), the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, and the Code on Social Security, 2020. The Social Security Code extends coverage to gig and platform workers through a contributory fund financed by aggregators (1‑2 % of transaction value), but implementation rules were notified only in 2023, and state‑level registration portals remain uneven. The 2022‑23 Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) records a female labour force participation rate of 23 % and shows that 94 % of women workers are in informal employment, many in home‑based piece‑rate work linked to global value chains. Precariousness manifests as algorithmic control (dynamic pricing, deactivation risk), income volatility (median monthly earnings ₹12,000‑₹18,000 for delivery partners), and absence of collective bargaining — unions such as the Indian Federation of App‑Based Transport Workers (IFAT) have staged strikes in 2021‑22 demanding “employee” status. The 2021 Supreme Court judgment in “Gujarat Mazdoor Sabha v. State of Gujarat” affirmed that platform workers can claim minimum wages under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, if an employment relationship is established. Comparative insights from California’s Assembly Bill 5 (2020) and the EU’s Platform Work Directive (2024 proposal) illustrate regulatory trajectories. Examiners reward answers that juxtapose the four codes’ definitional ambiguities with ethnographic evidence of worker resistance, and that cite the 2023 “World Employment and Social Outlook” (ILO) on platform work growth rates.

Comparative Social Stratification: Caste, Class, and Race

Stratification in India is anchored in the caste system — a hereditary, endogamous hierarchy sanctioned by religious texts and reproduced through occupational specialization and ritual purity norms. The Mandal Commission (1980) identified 3,743 Other Backward Classes (OBCs) and recommended 27 % reservation in central government jobs, implemented in 1990 after the V.P. Singh government’s acceptance. The 2006 Sachar Committee documented Muslim socio‑economic deprivation comparable to SC/ST groups, prompting the 2008‑09 “Prime Minister’s New 15‑Point Programme”. Class analysis, drawing on Marx and later on N. K. Chandra’s “agrarian class structure”, maps landownership, tenancy, and wage labour onto caste categories — large landlords predominantly upper‑caste, middle peasants often OBC, landless labourers overwhelmingly Dalit and Adivasi. The 2011 Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) provides the most recent granular data: 21.9 % households headed by SC, 8.6 % by ST, 41.6 % by OBC. Race, while not a formal census category in India, operates through colourism, tribal marginalisation, and the “racialisation” of Northeastern migrants in metropolitan labour markets (studies by Dolly Kikon and Sanjay Barbora). Globally, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) has urged India to recognise caste‑based discrimination as a form of racial discrimination (General Recommendation 29, 2002). Intersectionality frameworks (Crenshaw, 1989; Rege, 2006) demonstrate that Dalit women experience compounded disadvantage — NFHS‑5 shows anaemia prevalence 58 % among Dalit women versus 45 % among upper‑caste women. The 2020 “National Education Policy” proposes a “Gender Inclusion Fund” and “Special Education Zones” for marginalised groups, reflecting policy recognition of overlapping axes. Examiners expect candidates to contrast the “closed” nature of caste with the “open” class mobility ideal, to cite the 2019 “World Inequality Report” (top 10 % hold 57 % of national income), and to evaluate whether affirmative action has altered structural reproduction or merely created a “creamy layer” within reserved categories.

  • Treating secularism as a static constitutional principle without analysing judicial‑legislative contests (Shah Bano, Ayodhya, CAA).
  • Equating Smart Cities’ ICT upgrades with inclusive urban development while ignoring eviction data from Yamuna Pushta and Mahul.
  • Presenting Ayushman Bharat as universal coverage without noting the 55 % out‑of‑pocket expenditure share and HWCs’ staffing gaps.
  • Describing gig workers as “entrepreneurs” and overlooking the 2021 Supreme Court ruling on minimum wages and the 2023 Social Security Code’s delayed rollout.
  • Reducing caste to a cultural relic and neglecting SECC 2011 quantitative evidence on asset ownership across caste‑class intersections.
  • Using pre‑2011 Census or pre‑NFHS‑4 data when the syllabus explicitly references the latest rounds.
  • Each of these traps can be avoided by anchoring every claim in a dated source and by linking macro‑policy to micro‑evidence.

Sociology of Education: Policy, Inequality, and the Digital Divide

The Right to Education Act, 2009 (RTE) made elementary education a justiciable right for children aged 6‑14 and mandated 25 % reservation in private unaided schools for economically weaker sections. Implementation data from the Unified District Information System for Education (UDISE+) shows that enrolment in elementary grades rose from 18.7 crore in 2009‑10 to 22.3 crore in 2021‑22, yet the gross enrolment ratio (GER) for secondary education remains below 80 %. The Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2022 records that only 42 % of Grade 5 children in rural India can read a Grade 2 level text, highlighting a learning crisis that persists despite near‑universal access.

Caste, gender, and regional disparities intersect with school quality. The 2019‑20 National Sample Survey (NSS) 75th round reveals that the attendance rate for Scheduled Tribe girls in secondary school is 58 % compared with 84 % for General‑category boys. The 2020 National Education Policy (NEP) proposes a 5+3+3+4 curricular structure, a National Mission on Foundational Literacy and Numeracy, and a Gender Inclusion Fund, but the policy’s financing roadmap remains contested — central allocation for school education stood at 2.7 % of GDP in 2022‑23, well short of the 6 % target set by the Kothari Commission (1966).

The COVID‑19 pandemic exposed a stark digital divide. The 2021 NSS 78th round on “Household Social Consumption: Education” reports that only 24 % of rural households owned a computer and 42 % had internet access, versus 56 % and 78 % in urban areas. The DIKSHA platform and PM e‑VIDYA channels reached an estimated 12 crore students, yet ASER 2021 found that 60 % of rural children had no regular contact with teachers during school closures. Examiners expect candidates to link macro‑policy (RTE, NEP) with micro‑evidence (ASER, NSS) and to critique the assumption that technology alone can bridge equity gaps.

Environmental Sociology: Climate Justice, Rural Livelihoods, and Policy Response

India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC), launched in 2008, comprises eight missions — solar, enhanced energy efficiency, sustainable habitat, water, Himalayan ecosystem, green India, sustainable agriculture, and strategic knowledge. The 2021‑22 Economic Survey notes that renewable energy capacity crossed 150 GW, yet coal still supplies 70 % of electricity generation. The Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, recognises community forest rights for Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers; as of March 2023, 2.1 million titles have been distributed covering 4.5 million hectares, but implementation gaps persist in states like Madhya Pradesh and Odisha where less than 30 % of claims are settled.

Climate vulnerability is uneven across social groups. The 2022 IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (Working Group II) identifies the Indo‑Gangetic plain and the western coast as hotspots for heat stress and cyclonic intensity. The 2021‑22 Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) shows that 68 % of agricultural workers are in the informal sector, with women constituting 73 % of the agricultural labour force in states like Bihar. The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) provided 2.5 billion person‑days in 2022‑23, yet wage rates remain below the statutory minimum in several states, limiting its adaptive capacity.

Policy responses increasingly invoke “climate justice”. The 2022‑23 Union Budget announced a Green Credit Programme and a National Green Hydrogen Mission (₹19,744 crore). The 2023 Supreme Court judgment in “M. C. Mehta v. Union of India” directed the Centre to formulate a time‑bound plan for phasing out single‑use plastics, linking environmental protection to Article 21. Candidates should juxtapose top‑down missions with grassroots movements such as the Chipko legacy, the Narmada Bachao Andolan, and recent farmer protests against the 2020 farm laws, analysing how social mobilisation reshapes state policy.

Answer‑Writing Technique: Concept‑Evidence‑Critique‑Diagram
“Critically examine the extent to which the National Education Policy 2020 addresses the digital divide in school education.” (15 marks)
Concept: Define digital divide (access, usage, quality) and NEP 2020 provisions (DIKSHA, NETF, digital infrastructure). Evidence: Cite NSS 78th round (24 % rural computer ownership), ASER 2021 (60 % no teacher contact), UDISE+ enrolment trends. Critique: NEP’s financing gap (2.7 % GDP vs 6 % target), lack of device‑distribution scheme, language‑barrier in digital content. Diagram: A two‑column table contrasting “Policy Intent” (universal broadband, teacher training) with “Ground Reality” (connectivity, device penetration, learning outcomes). Conclude with a balanced judgement: NEP sets direction but implementation architecture remains under‑specified.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “critical examination”, allocate 30 % of words to concept definition, 40 % to dated evidence (survey, judgment, budget figure), 20 % to critique (gap, contradiction, unintended consequence), and 10 % to a concise diagrammatic summary. Practice drawing the two‑column table on rough paper within 2 minutes.

Sociology of Science and Technology: Knowledge Production, Public Trust, and Governance

The Department of Science and Technology (DST) released the Science, Technology and Innovation Policy (STIP) 2020, aiming to double R&D expenditure to 2 % of GDP by 2030 and to create a National Research Foundation (NRF) modelled on the US National Science Foundation. As of 2023‑24, gross domestic expenditure on R&D (GERD) stands at 0.66 % of GDP, with the private sector contributing only 37 % — far below the 60 % share in OECD countries. The 2021‑22 “India Science Report” notes that India ranks third globally in scientific publications but 45th in citations per paper, indicating a quantity‑over‑quality trajectory.

Public trust in science became salient during the COVID‑19 pandemic. The 2021 Wellcome Global Monitor survey reported that 84 % of Indians trusted scientists “a lot” or “some”, yet vaccine hesitancy persisted in specific communities — NFHS‑5 data shows 12 % of rural women in Uttar Pradesh refused the first dose citing safety concerns. The 2022 Supreme Court order in “Dr. Jacob Puliyel v. Union of India” mandated transparency in clinical‑trial data for COVID‑19 vaccines, reinforcing the principle of informed consent under Article 21.

Governance of emerging technologies is evolving. The 2023 Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) establishes a Data Protection Board and mandates consent‑based processing, impacting AI‑driven health diagnostics and agritech platforms. The 2022 “National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence” (NITI Aayog) proposes sectoral “AI‑for‑All” hubs, but the absence of an algorithmic accountability framework leaves gaps in bias auditing. Examiners reward answers that connect institutional architecture (DST, NRF, DPDPA) with sociological concepts such as “boundary work” (Gieryn), “co‑production” (Jasanoff), and the “risk society” (Beck).

Political Sociology: State, Civil Society, and Democratic Deepening in India

The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) institutionalised Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), reserving one‑third of seats for women and proportionate seats for SC/ST. By 2022, 3.1 million elected representatives served in PRIs, of whom 46 % were women — the highest female representation in any legislative tier globally. However, the 2019‑20 “State of Panchayats” report by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj highlights that only 28 % of Gram Panchayats have functional Gram Sabhas meeting the mandated quarterly frequency.

Civil society operates within a shifting regulatory regime. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA), 2010, amended in 2020, tightened registration renewal, capped administrative expenses at 20 %, and barred sub‑granting. As of March 2023, 22,000 NGOs lost FCRA licences, affecting organisations working on tribal rights, environmental advocacy, and women’s health. The 2021 Supreme Court judgment in “Amnesty International India v. Union of India” upheld the government’s power to cancel FCRA registration but stressed procedural fairness.

Democratic deepening is also measured through electoral participation and accountability mechanisms. The 2019 General Election recorded a 67.4 % turnout, the highest ever, with women’s turnout (67.2 %) marginally exceeding men’s for the first time. The 2013 “Right to Information Act” (RTI) and the 2014 “Whistle Blowers Protection Act” provide transparency tools, yet the 2022 “Transparency International” Corruption Perceptions Index ranks India 85th of 180 countries. Candidates should analyse the tension between formal decentralisation, civil‑society space, and the concentration of executive power, using concepts of “political society” (Chatterjee) and “subaltern citizenship”.

Sociology of Migration: Internal Displacement, Remittances, and Urban Integration

India’s internal migrant population was estimated at 450 million in the 2011 Census (37 % of the total population), with the 2021‑22 PLFS indicating a rise to 520 million when short‑term circular migrants are included. The Inter‑State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979, mandates registration of contractors and provision of welfare facilities, but enforcement remains weak — only 12 % of inter‑state migrants were covered by any social security scheme in 2022.

Remittances constitute a critical livelihood buffer. The World Bank’s “Migration and Development Brief” 2023 records India as the top recipient of remittances globally at US $111 billion in 2022, surpassing FDI inflows. The 2020‑21 “National Sample Survey” on “Household Consumer Expenditure” shows that remittance‑receiving households in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have 18 % higher per‑capita consumption than non‑receiving peers. The 2021 “One Nation One Ration Card” (ONORC) scheme portability now covers 35 states/UTs, enabling migrant families to access subsidised grain across state borders.

Urban integration remains uneven. The 2022 “Urban India” report by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs notes that 35 % of urban households live in slums or informal settlements, with migrant workers over‑represented in construction, domestic work, and street vending. The 2020 “Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act” provides for Town Vending Committees, yet only 18 % of cities have constituted functional committees. The 2023 Supreme Court directive in “Migrant Workers v. Union of India” ordered states to register all migrant workers on the e‑Shram portal; as of December 2023, 28 crore workers are registered, but data on occupational categories and skill mapping remains incomplete. Examiners expect a linkage between macro‑data (Census, PLFS, World Bank) and micro‑ethnographies (e.g., Jan Breman’s “Footloose Labour”, Deshingkar & Akter on circular migration) to illustrate how structural constraints and agency co‑produce migrant trajectories.

  • Treating NEP 2020 as a finished reform without citing the 2.7 % GDP allocation gap and the absence of a device‑distribution budget.
  • Equating renewable‑energy capacity additions with climate justice while ignoring FRA implementation deficits and MGNREGA wage shortfalls.
  • Presenting STIP 2020 targets as achieved when GERD remains at 0.66 % of GDP and private R&D share is only 37 %.
  • Assuming Panchayati Raj reservations automatically translate into substantive participation without referencing Gram Sabha functionality data.
  • Citing remittance totals without disaggregating by corridor, gender, or end‑use, thereby missing intra‑household power dynamics.
  • Using pre‑2011 migration figures when the syllabus explicitly asks for the latest PLFS and e‑Shram portal statistics.
  • Overlooking the 2023 Supreme Court orders on platform‑worker minimum wages and migrant‑worker registration when discussing labour informality.

These traps can be avoided by anchoring every claim in a dated source and by linking macro‑policy to micro‑evidence.

Social Capital and Trust in Indian Society

Social capital refers to networks, norms and trust that enable collective action. In the Indian context three forms are analytically useful: bonding capital (strong ties within caste, kinship or religious groups), bridging capital (weaker ties across social cleavages) and linking capital (connections to formal institutions such as the state, NGOs or markets). Robert Putnam’s distinction between bonding and bridging capital, and James Coleman’s emphasis on closure and trustworthiness, provide the theoretical scaffold. Indian sociologists have operationalised these concepts through village‑level studies. André Béteille’s work on “social capital in rural India” shows that dominant caste networks often function as bonding capital that monopolises access to credit and irrigation, while the Self‑Help Group (SHG) movement, promoted by the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM) since 2011, creates bridging capital among women across caste lines. The 2011 Census recorded 8.6 % of the population aged 60 years and above; the 2021‑22 Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) reports that 62 % of elderly households rely on kin‑based support, illustrating the persistence of bonding capital in old‑age security. Conversely, the 2018 Kerala floods demonstrated bridging capital: inter‑community rescue teams, coordinated through local Kudumbashree neighbourhood groups, cut across religious and caste boundaries. Empirical measurement in UPSC answers should cite the “Social Capital Assessment Tool” used by the World Bank in the 2015‑16 India Human Development Survey, which found a positive correlation (r = 0.34) between bridging capital indices and household income diversification. Candidates must avoid treating social capital as an unqualified good; the same networks that facilitate micro‑finance can also enforce exclusionary norms, as documented in the 2019 study “Caste and Credit” by the Indian Institute of Dalit Studies.

Sociology of Disaster Management and Community Resilience

Disaster sociology examines how social structures shape vulnerability, response and recovery. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 created the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and mandated State and District Disaster Management Authorities. The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015‑2030), adopted by India, emphasises “building back better” and community participation. Empirical work on the 1999 Odisha super‑cyclone shows that villages with active Gram Panchayats and pre‑existing SHGs experienced 27 % lower mortality than comparable villages lacking such institutions (Government of Odisha, Post‑Disaster Needs Assessment, 2000). The 2018 Kerala floods illustrated the role of “social infrastructure”: the Kudumbashree network of 4.5 million women mobilised 1.2 lakh volunteers for relief distribution, while the state’s decentralized health system enabled rapid disease surveillance. In contrast, the 2020 Assam floods revealed that tea‑garden labour communities, organised under the Plantations Labour Act, 1951, had limited linking capital to district authorities, resulting in delayed evacuation. The 2021 “National Disaster Response Force” (NDRF) annual report notes that 68 % of deployed personnel were drawn from central paramilitary forces, underscoring a top‑down operational bias. For answer writing, candidates should juxtapose the “command‑and‑control” model (NDRF‑centric) with the “community‑based disaster risk management” (CBDRM) model advocated by the 2016 NDMA guidelines, and cite the 2022 “Community Resilience Index” developed by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, which scores districts on social cohesion, local leadership and access to early‑warning systems.

Comparative Case Analysis
Compare the role of bonding versus bridging social capital in post‑cyclone recovery in Odisha (1999) and Kerala floods (2018).
In Odisha, bonding capital within caste‑based fishing communities facilitated rapid mutual aid but limited access to external relief because dominant caste leaders controlled distribution channels. In Kerala, bridging capital generated by Kudumbashree’s cross‑caste women’s collectives enabled equitable relief delivery and coordinated volunteer labour across religious lines. The contrast shows that bonding capital accelerates immediate survival, while bridging capital sustains inclusive recovery. A high‑scoring answer would cite the 2000 Odisha PDNA mortality differential (27 % lower in villages with active Panchayats) and the 2018 Kerala volunteer mobilisation figure (1.2 lakh), then link each to Putnam’s typology and the NDMA’s 2016 CBDRM framework.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise a three‑column table: Disaster, Dominant Social Capital Type, Key Institutional Actor. Populate it with Odisha‑1999 (bonding, Gram Panchayat), Kerala‑2018 (bridging, Kudumbashree), Assam‑2020 (weak linking, tea‑garden unions). In the exam, reproduce the table in 30 seconds and use it to structure any disaster‑sociology question.

Sociology of Ageing and Elder Care in India

Population ageing is reshaping kinship, labour markets and welfare architecture. The 2011 Census recorded 104 million persons aged 60 years and above (8.6 % of total population). The United Nations “World Population Prospects 2022” projects this share to reach 12.5 % by 2030 and 19.5 % by 2050. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 legally obliges children and relatives to provide maintenance; the 2019 amendment extended the definition of “children” to include step‑children and adoptive children. The National Policy for Older Persons (NPOP), 2011, and its 2020 revision emphasise “active ageing”, health‑insurance convergence (Ayushman Bharat‑PMJAY covers 10 crore families, including senior citizens), and the creation of “Senior Citizen Welfare Funds” at state level. Empirical studies reveal a care gap: the 2017‑18 Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) found that 71 % of elderly women and 58 % of elderly men reported at least one functional limitation, yet only 12 % accessed formal home‑care services. The “Old Age Pension” schemes (IGNOAPS, state‑level variants) cover roughly 3.5 crore beneficiaries, but the monthly amount (₹200‑₹500) remains below the Tendulkar poverty line. Sociologically, the shift from joint to nuclear families, documented by the 2015‑16 National Family Health Survey (NFHS‑4) showing 54 % of households nuclear, intensifies the “care deficit”. Feminist scholars such as Leela Visaria argue that the burden falls disproportionately on daughters‑in‑law, reinforcing gendered intergenerational contracts. For UPSC, candidates should link demographic data (Census, LASI) to policy instruments (2007 Act, NPOP 2011/2020, Ayushman Bharat) and to theoretical lenses: structural functionalism (role disengagement), political economy (state withdrawal from universal pensions), and feminist care ethics.

Sociology of Media, Public Opinion and Democratic Discourse

Media sociology analyses how communication structures shape collective perceptions and political participation. The Press Council of India (PCI), established under the Press Council Act, 1978, functions as a quasi‑judicial body for print media ethics. The Information Technology Act, 2000 (amended 2008) and the 2021 Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules regulate digital platforms, mandating grievance redressal officers and traceability of originators. The 2019 “Digital News Report” by the Reuters Institute notes that 68 % of Indian internet users access news via smartphones, with WhatsApp and YouTube as primary distribution channels. Public‑opinion research in India is dominated by the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies (CSDS)‑Lokniti surveys, which have tracked electoral preferences since 1996. Their 2022 “National Election Study” shows a 12‑percentage‑point decline in trust in television news (from 62 % in 2014 to 50 % in 2022) and a rise in trust in “local WhatsApp groups” (23 %). The 2020 “Media Ownership Monitor” (Reporters Without Borders) documents that the top five conglomerates control 70 % of television viewership, raising concerns about pluralism. Sociologically, the “spiral of silence” (Noelle‑Neumann) and “agenda‑setting” (McCombs & Shaw) frameworks explain how concentrated ownership narrows the public sphere. The 2021 “Farmers’ Protest” illustrated counter‑publics: alternative digital platforms (Kisan Ekta Morcha’s YouTube channel, Twitter hashtags) bypassed mainstream media framing, creating a “networked public sphere” (Benkler). Answers should integrate legal‑regulatory milestones (PCI, IT Act, 2021 Rules), audience metrics (Reuters, CSDS), ownership data (Media Ownership Monitor) and theoretical concepts (public sphere, counter‑public, agenda‑setting) to evaluate democratic discourse quality.

Sociology of Legal Pluralism and Customary Law in India

Legal pluralism denotes the coexistence of multiple normative orders — state law, religious personal laws, tribal customary law and informal dispute‑resolution mechanisms. The Constitution recognises this through Article 372 (continuance of pre‑Constitution laws), Article 13 (laws inconsistent with fundamental rights void), and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules governing Scheduled Areas. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, and the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, constitute the major personal‑law regimes. Tribal customary law operates under the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA), which empowers Gram Sabhas to manage natural resources and resolve disputes according to tradition. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA) further recognises community forest rights and the authority of Gram Sabhas to adjudicate claims. Empirical work by the Indian Law Institute (2018) shows that in Jharkhand’s Santhal Parganas, 64 % of land‑dispute cases are settled by traditional “Manjhi” councils rather than formal courts. However, the 2020 Supreme Court judgment in “State of Karnataka v. Union of India” upheld the primacy of statutory law over customary practice when fundamental rights are violated, illustrating the tension between cultural autonomy and constitutional morality. The 2021 “Model Rules for Gram Nyayalayas” aim to institutionalise village‑level courts, yet only 12 states have operationalised them as of 2023. For answer writing, candidates should map the hierarchy: Constitution → Central statutes → State statutes → Personal laws → Customary norms, and cite the 2018 “Legal Pluralism in India” report (Law Commission of India, 267th Report) which recommends a “Uniform Civil Code” framework that respects pluralism while guaranteeing gender justice.

  • Treating social capital as uniformly beneficial without distinguishing bonding, bridging and linking forms.
  • Citing disaster‑management statutes (DM Act 2005, Sendai Framework) but ignoring community‑level evidence such as Kudumbashree or Gram Panchayat performance data.
  • Using outdated elderly‑population figures (pre‑2011 Census) while the syllabus expects LASI 2017‑18 and UN 2022 projections.
  • Equating media regulation (PCI, IT Rules) with media freedom, overlooking ownership concentration data from the Media Ownership Monitor.
  • Presenting legal pluralism as a static coexistence, neglecting Supreme Court rulings (e.g., 2020 Karnataka case) that re‑order the hierarchy of norms.
  • Omitting the 2021 IT Rules’ traceability requirement when discussing digital public sphere dynamics.
  • Failing to link the 2007 Maintenance Act amendments to the 2019 LASI functional‑limitation statistics in elder‑care answers.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the conceptual precision, empirical anchors and comparative lenses that differentiate high‑scoring sociology answers.

Sociology Paper I — Fundamentals of Sociology

Introducing Sociology

  • Emergence of sociology: Emerged in 19th century Europe due to industrial revolution, French Revolution, Enlightenment, scientific revolution. Key factors: industrialization, urbanization, secularization, rise of nation-states, colonialism.
  • Nature of sociology: Social science, empirical science, value-free (Weber), value-laden (Myrdal), interpretive vs positivist approaches.
  • Scope of sociology: Study of social relationships, social institutions, social groups, social institutions, social processes, social change, social problems.
  • Relationship with other social sciences: Anthropology (culture, primitive societies), Economics (production, distribution, consumption), Political Science (power, authority, state), Psychology (individual behavior), History (historical context), Geography (spatial distribution of population, resources).
  • Scope of sociology: Micro sociology (face-to-face interaction, small groups), Macro sociology (social institutions, social structure, social change), Micro-macro linkage.

Research Methods & Analysis

  • Scientific method: Observation, hypothesis formulation, data collection, data analysis, hypothesis testing, theory building, replication.
  • Research design: Experimental design, survey research, case study, ethnography, content analysis, historical-comparative research.
  • Data collection methods: Observation (participant, non-participant), interview (structured, semi-structured, unstructured), questionnaire, documents (primary, secondary sources), visual materials (photographs, films, videos).
  • Sampling: Probability sampling (simple random, stratified random, systematic, cluster, multi-stage), Non-probability sampling (convenience, purposive, snowball, quota).
  • Data analysis: Quantitative analysis (statistical analysis, descriptive statistics, inferential statistics), Qualitative analysis (thematic analysis, content analysis, discourse analysis, narrative analysis).
  • Ethics in social research: Informed consent, confidentiality, anonymity, voluntary participation, avoiding harm, debriefing, ethics committees.

Terms, Concepts & their Use in Sociological Analysis

  • Society: A group of people who share a common territory, interact with each other, and share a common culture.
  • Culture: Shared beliefs, values, norms, customs, practices, artifacts, symbols, language of a group or society.
  • Social structure: Patterned arrangement of institutions, groups, roles, statuses, and relationships that provide the framework for social interaction.
  • Social stratification: Hierarchical arrangement of individuals and groups based on wealth, power, prestige, prestige, education, occupation, race, ethnicity, gender.
  • Social groups: Primary groups (small, intimate, face-to-face interaction - family, peer group), Secondary groups (large, impersonal, task-oriented - organizations, bureaucracies, corporations).
  • Social institutions: Established patterns of behavior that satisfy basic human needs - family, education, religion, economy, polity, mass media.
  • Socialization: Process by which individuals learn the norms, values, beliefs, and behaviors of their society/culture - primary socialization (childhood, family), secondary socialization (adulthood, school, workplace, peer groups).
  • Social control: Mechanisms that encourage conformity to social norms - informal social control (gossip, ridicule, ostracism, social approval), formal social control (laws, police, courts, prisons).
  • Social mobility: Vertical mobility (upward or downward movement in social hierarchy), Horizontal mobility (movement within same social stratum), Intergenerational mobility (movement between generations), Intragenerational mobility (movement within one's lifetime).
  • Social change: Processes of change in social structure, social institutions, social relationships, social values, social norms - evolution, revolution, reform, diffusion, innovation, diffusion, cultural lag.

Social Institutions

  • Family: Primary social institution - functions: reproduction, socialization, economic support, emotional support, social control; types: nuclear family, extended family, joint family, single-parent family, blended family, same-sex marriage, live-in relationships; changes: declining fertility, rising divorce rates, increasing divorce rates, changing gender roles, decline of joint family, rise of nuclear family.
  • Marriage: Institution that regulates sexual relations, reproduction, child-rearing; types: monogamy, polygamy (polygyny, polyandry), endogamy (marriage within group), exogamy (marriage outside group), arranged marriage, love marriage, same-sex marriage; functions: reproduction, socialization of children, economic cooperation, emotional support, social status.
  • Kinship: System of social relationships based on blood, marriage, adoption; types: consanguineal kinship (blood relations), affinal kinship (marriage relations), fictive kinship (fictive kin relationships); descent rules: patrilineal, matrilineal, bilateral; residence patterns: patrilocal, matrilocal, neolocal, bilocal, avunculocal.
  • Religion: Belief system involving sacred things, rituals, rituals, moral codes; functions: social cohesion, social control, meaning and purpose, social control, explanation of suffering and death; theories: Durkheim (sacred and profane), Weber (Protestant ethic and spirit of capitalism), Marx (religion as opium of the people), Weber (charismatic authority, routinization of charisma).
  • Education: Formal education (schools, colleges, universities), informal education (family, peer groups, media), non-formal education (adult education, literacy programs), functions: socialization, social control, social placement, social integration, cultural transmission, social change.
  • Economy: Production, distribution, distribution, consumption of goods and services; types of economic systems: hunting and gathering, horticulture, pastoralism, agriculture, industrialism, post-industrialism; economic systems: capitalism, socialism, mixed economy, command economy.
  • Polity: Political institutions: state, government, political parties, interest groups, pressure groups, social movements; forms of government: democracy, authoritarianism, totalitarianism, monarchy, theocracy; political socialization, political participation, political culture.
  • Media: Mass media (print, broadcast, electronic media), social media, digital media, media effects (agenda-setting, priming, framing, cultivation theory, uses and gratifications), media ownership, media regulation, media ethics.

Social Stratification

  • Social stratification: Hierarchical arrangement of individuals and groups based on wealth, power, prestige, education, occupation, race, ethnicity, gender; types: caste system (India, endogamous, hereditary, ritual purity), class system (open, achievement-based, income, wealth, occupation), caste-class interface, ethnic stratification, gender stratification, racial stratification.
  • Theories of stratification: Functionalism (Davis & Moore - functional importance of positions, differential rewards), Conflict theory (Marx - class conflict, bourgeoisie vs proletariat, exploitation), Weberian theory (class, status, party - multidimensional stratification), Symbolic interactionism (symbolic meanings of status symbols, lifestyle, consumption patterns), Feminist theory (patriarchy, gender inequality, patriarchy as system of male domination).
  • Social mobility: Vertical mobility (upward or downward movement in social hierarchy), Horizontal mobility (movement within same social stratum), Intergenerational mobility (movement between generations - father to son), Intragenerational mobility (movement within one's lifetime), Absolute mobility (absolute change in position), Relative mobility (relative position compared to others).
  • Poverty: Absolute poverty (inability to meet basic needs - food, shelter, clothing), Relative poverty (income below 50% of median income), Multidimensional poverty (health, education, living standards - MPI), Chronic poverty, Transient poverty, Feminization of poverty (disproportionate representation of women among the poor), Urban poverty, Rural poverty.
  • Social exclusion: Exclusion from economic, social, political, cultural participation; mechanisms: discrimination, exclusion, marginalization, stigmatization, stereotyping, prejudice, discrimination.

Social Change

  • Social change: Changes in social structure, social institutions, social relationships, social values, social norms, social practices over time.
  • Factors of social change: Technological change (technology, communication, transportation), Demographic change (population growth, migration, urbanization), Economic change (industrialization, globalization, liberalization), Political change (democratization, revolution, reform), Cultural change (values, beliefs, norms, traditions), Environmental change (climate change, environmental degradation, natural disasters), War and conflict.
  • Theories of social change: Evolutionary theory (spencer, darwin - societies evolve from simple to complex), Cyclical theory (spengler, toynbee - rise and fall of civilizations), Conflict theory (marx - class conflict drives change), Modernization theory (rogers - traditional to modern societies), Dependency theory (dependency of peripheral countries on core countries), World systems theory (wallerstein - core, periphery, semi-periphery), Globalization (globalization of economy, culture, politics, culture).
  • Social movements: Collective behavior aimed at bringing about social change; types: reform movements (change specific aspects), revolutionary movements (complete transformation), resistance movements (resist change), expressive movements (express grievances), identity movements (identity politics - women's movement, dalit movement, environmental movement, LGBTQ+ movement), examples: civil rights movement, women's movement, environmental movement, dalit movement, farmers' movement, anti-globalization movement, anti-corruption movement.
  • Social movements in India: Nationalist movement (independence movement), Dalit movement (amitabh bachchan, b.r. ambedkar), Women's movement (sati abolition, widow remarriage, women's education, women's suffrage), Environmental movement (chipko movement, narmada bachao andolan, chipko movement), Farmers' movement (shekhar sangathan, bharatiya kisan union), Environmental movement (chipko movement, narmada bachao andolan, silent valley movement), Dalit movement (dr. b.r. ambedkar, dalit panthers, dalit panthers movement), Women's movement (sati abolition, widow remarriage, women's education, women's suffrage, dowry prohibition, domestic violence prevention), Environmental movement (chipko movement, narmada bachao andolan, silent valley movement, chipko movement).
Technique: Sanskritization
Question: 'Explain Sanskritization with examples.'
Answer: Sanskritization (m.n. srinivas) - process by which lower castes/tribes emulate customs, rituals, lifestyle of upper castes (vegetarianism, sanskrit names, rituals, endogamy) to claim higher ritual status. Examples: yadavs, kurmis, gonds adopting vegetarianism, sanskrit names, sanskrit rituals. Critique: doesn't alter structural hierarchy; reinforces sanskritic norms; ignores regional variations & dalit assertion (ambedkarite politics). Examples: yadavs claiming kshatriya status, kurmis claiming kshatriya status, gonds claiming rajput status.

Memory Tricks

  • Four pillars of sociology: Society, culture, social structure, social institutions - SSCI.
  • Major sociological thinkers: Auguste comte (father of sociology), karl marx (conflict theory), emile durkheim (social facts, division of labor, suicide), max weber (interpretive sociology, ideal types, bureaucracy), herbert spencer (social darwinism), herbert blumer (symbolic interactionism).
  • Social stratification: Caste (ascribed, closed, india), class (achieved, open, usa/uk), race (biological, ascribed), ethnicity (cultural, ethnic).
  • Social institutions: Family, marriage, kinship, religion, education, economy, polity - six basic institutions.
  • Social change: Sanskritization (caste emulation), Westernization (western influence), Modernization (industrialization, urbanization), Globalization (global integration).
Mains strategy
Sociology answers: concept → definition → theory/theorist → application → indian example → conclusion. Draw diagrams (social stratification pyramid, family lineage, caste hierarchy, social change models). Quote thinkers (comte, durkheim, marx, weber, spencer, simmel, mead, cooley, mead, blumer, merton, parsons, parsons, dahrendorf, collins, bourdieu, foucault). Data: india's population (~1.4 billion), sex ratio (943 females per 1000 males), literacy rate (77.7%), gender gap in literacy, sc/st population (16.6% sc, 8.6% st), urban population (~35%), rural population (~65%), unemployment rate (~7-8%), female labor force participation (~25-30%).

Sociology of Knowledge and Reflexivity

The sociology of knowledge examines how social conditions shape the production, validation, and circulation of knowledge. Classical foundations lie in the work of Karl Mannheim, who distinguished between relational and total conceptions of ideology, and in the phenomenological tradition of Alfred Schutz, which stresses the lifeworld as the taken‑for‑granted background of everyday understanding. In the late twentieth century Pierre Bourdieu introduced the concept of habitus and field to show that scientific knowledge is itself a form of capital contested within the academic field. Bourdieu’s Homo Academicus (1988) demonstrates how researchers’ positions influence problem selection, methodology, and interpretation.

Anthony Giddens extended reflexivity to the level of modernity itself, arguing in The Consequences of Modernity (1990) that late‑modern institutions constantly monitor and revise their own knowledge bases. This institutional reflexivity creates a feedback loop: expert knowledge informs policy, policy reshapes social conditions, and new conditions generate fresh expert claims. Ulrich Beck’s Risk Society (1992) further argues that scientific uncertainty becomes a political resource, making the sociology of knowledge central to understanding environmental and technological controversies.

Methodologically, reflexivity demands that the researcher disclose positionality, funding sources, and theoretical commitments. The reflexive turn in qualitative research (e.g., the work of Norman Denzin and Yvonna Lincoln) treats the research act as a co‑construction between investigator and participants. In quantitative work, reflexivity appears as sensitivity analysis and transparent reporting of model specifications. Examiners expect candidates to link these epistemological debates to concrete research designs, showing how reflexivity guards against both naïve objectivism and radical relativism.

Comparative Historical Sociology: State Formation and Social Policy

Comparative historical sociology (CHS) uses macro‑level, longitudinal comparison to explain large‑scale social outcomes such as state formation, welfare regimes, and revolutionary change. Theda Skocpol’s States and Social Revolutions (1979) pioneered a structural‑cultural approach, arguing that state autonomy, international pressures, and peasant rebellions jointly produce revolutionary outcomes in France, Russia, and China. Charles Tilly’s Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990) traces how war‑making and capital accumulation drove the emergence of national states in Europe, introducing the famous dictum “war made the state, and the state made war.”

Gøsta Esping‑Andersen’s The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism (1990) classifies welfare regimes into liberal, conservative‑corporatist, and social‑democratic types, linking each to distinct class coalitions and historical legacies. Subsequent scholarship (e.g., Kathleen Thelen on vocational training, Sven Steinmo on tax policy) shows how path dependence and institutional layering constrain contemporary reform. In the Indian context, scholars such as Atul Kohli and Pradeep Chhibber apply CHS to explain the divergent trajectories of state capacity in post‑colonial India versus East Asian developmental states.

CHS demands rigorous case selection, process tracing, and attention to counterfactuals. Examiners reward answers that juxtapose at least two cases, identify the causal mechanism (e.g., class coalition, geopolitical competition), and discuss the limits of generalisation. A common pitfall is treating historical description as explanation; the analytical core must be a theoretically informed causal narrative.

Technique: Structuring a CHS Answer
Question: “Compare the role of war in the formation of the French and Prussian states in the nineteenth century, using Tilly’s framework.”
Answer outline: 1) State Tilly’s thesis: war‑making extracts resources, builds bureaucracies, and legitimises central authority. 2) French case: Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars created a mass conscript army, centralised tax administration (the contributions directes), and a uniform legal code (Code Napoléon), producing a highly centralised bureaucratic state. 3) Prussian case: The Wars of Liberation (1813‑15) and later the Austro‑Prussian and Franco‑Prussian wars reinforced a militarised bureaucracy (the Generalstab), a landed‑officer elite (Junkers), and a fiscal system reliant on indirect taxes, yielding a “military‑bureaucratic” state. 4) Contrast: France’s war experience fostered civilian bureaucratic penetration; Prussia’s reinforced aristocratic military dominance. 5) Conclude: Both confirm Tilly’s mechanism but diverge in the social coalition that captured the state apparatus.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a comparative historical explanation, spend the first 30 seconds sketching a two‑column table (Case A | Case B) with the key variables (war, class coalition, fiscal system, bureaucratic outcome). This visual scaffold prevents omission of the comparative dimension and speeds up writing.

Network Analysis and Social Capital

Network analysis treats social structure as a set of nodes (actors) and ties (relations), enabling the measurement of structural properties such as centrality, density, and clustering. Mark Granovetter’s “The Strength of Weak Ties” (1973) demonstrated that acquaintances (weak ties) bridge otherwise disconnected clusters, facilitating the flow of novel information — a finding pivotal for labour‑market studies. Ronald Burt extended this with the concept of structural holes: actors who span non‑redundant contacts gain informational and control benefits, a mechanism he formalised in Structural Holes (1992).

James Coleman linked network closure to the creation of social capital, arguing that dense, multiplex ties generate trust, norms, and sanctions that lower transaction costs. Robert Putnam’s Bowling Alone (2000) popularised the distinction between bonding (inward‑looking, homogeneous) and bridging (outward‑looking, heterogeneous) social capital, showing a decline in associational life in the United States since the 1960s. In the Indian context, scholars such as Biju Rao and Vijayendra Rao have used village‑level network data to show how caste‑based closure both protects marginalized groups and limits access to state programmes.

Methodologically, network data can be collected via ego‑centric surveys, complete sociograms, or digital trace data (e.g., mobile‑phone call records). Analytical tools include UCINET, Gephi, and the igraph package in R. Examiners expect candidates to discuss the trade‑off between relational depth (qualitative ethnography) and structural breadth (quantitative network metrics), and to cite at least one empirical study that operationalises social capital as a predictor of outcomes such as health, migration, or political participation.

Gender and Intersectionality in Social Structure

Intersectionality, coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989), insists that categories such as gender, caste, class, race, and sexuality cannot be analysed additively; they intersect to produce distinct configurations of privilege and oppression. Patricia Hill Collins’ Black Feminist Thought (1990) develops the matrix of domination, showing how intersecting power relations operate at structural, disciplinary, hegemonic, and interpersonal levels. In Indian sociology, scholars like Nivedita Menon and Sharmila Rege apply intersectionality to reveal how Dalit women experience violence that is simultaneously gendered and caste‑based, a phenomenon invisible to single‑axis analyses.

Sylvia Walby’s Theorizing Patriarchy (1990) identifies six patriarchal structures — household production, paid work, the state, male violence, sexuality, and culture — and argues that their articulation varies across historical periods and welfare regimes. Comparative work by Joan Acker on “gendered organizations” demonstrates that bureaucratic rules, ostensibly neutral, embed gendered assumptions about the ideal worker. Recent scholarship on transnational intersectionality (e.g., Chandra Mohanty) traces how global care chains reconfigure gender, class, and nationality for migrant domestic workers.

For answer writing, candidates should (a) define intersectionality with reference to Crenshaw and Collins, (b) illustrate with an Indian case (e.g., the 2012 Delhi gang‑rape and the differential media treatment of victims by caste), (c) discuss methodological implications — the need for mixed‑methods designs that capture both macro‑structural patterns and lived experience — and (d) evaluate critiques (e.g., the risk of infinite fragmentation, the challenge of operationalising intersecting categories in survey research).

Environmental Sociology: Risk Society and Ecological Modernization

Environmental sociology interrogates the social drivers and consequences of ecological change. Ulrich Beck’s Risk Society (1992) argues that modern institutions produce “manufactured uncertainties” — nuclear contamination, chemical pollutants, climate change — that transcend national borders and class lines, yet their distribution remains socially stratified. Beck introduces the concept of reflexive modernization: societies increasingly confront the side‑effects of their own industrial logic, prompting new forms of political mobilization (e.g., anti‑nuclear movements in Germany, Chipko in India).

In contrast, the ecological modernization thesis (Arthur Mol, Gert Spaargaren, 1990s) posits that advanced economies can decouple economic growth from environmental degradation through technological innovation, market‑based instruments (carbon trading), and institutional redesign. Empirical support comes from the “green growth” trajectories of Nordic countries, while critics (e.g., John Bellamy Foster) argue that ecological modernization underestimates the structural imperative of capital accumulation and the metabolic rift identified by Marx.

Indian environmental sociology blends these perspectives. Ramachandra Guha’s Environmentalism: A Global History (2000) traces the genealogy of Indian movements from the Chipko Andolan (1973) to the Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985‑present), highlighting the role of subsistence communities, Gandhian ethics, and legal activism. Recent work on climate justice (e.g., by Sunita Narain) emphasizes differential vulnerability: smallholder farmers in Vidarbha face compounding risks from erratic monsoons, indebtedness, and inadequate insurance, illustrating Beck’s claim that risks are socially distributed.

Examiners reward answers that (i) contrast risk society and ecological modernization as competing theoretical lenses, (ii) cite at least one Indian movement with its specific demands and outcomes, (iii) discuss policy instruments (e.g., the National Action Plan on Climate Change, the Perform, Achieve and Trade scheme), and (iv) reflect on the limits of technological fixes without structural redistribution.

  • Confusing reflexivity (researcher self‑awareness) with institutional reflexivity (societal self‑monitoring) — they operate at different analytical levels.
  • Treating comparative historical sociology as mere narrative history; the core is causal mechanism identification, not chronological description.
  • Equating social capital with mere network size; bonding and bridging capital have opposite effects on inequality and innovation.
  • Applying intersectionality as a checklist of identities rather than a relational analysis of power structures.
  • Presenting ecological modernization as a proven universal trajectory; empirical evidence is mixed and context‑dependent.
  • Overlooking the role of the state in shaping risk distribution; risk society theory emphasizes state‑society feedback loops.
  • Using outdated data (e.g., pre‑2010 welfare regime classifications) without acknowledging recent regime shifts.

These advanced sections equip candidates with the conceptual depth, comparative rigour, and empirical specificity required for high‑scoring sociology answers.

Urban Sociology: Informal Economy and Spatial Segregation

Urban sociology examines how cities organise labour, housing, and social relations. The informal economy — unregistered enterprises, street vending, domestic work, and home‑based production — accounts for a substantial share of urban employment in the Global South. Classic studies by Keith Hart (1973) on Ghana and later by Jan Breman (1996) on India show that informality is not a residual sector but a structurally embedded mode of capital accumulation that supplies cheap labour and flexible services to formal firms. Spatial segregation reinforces this division: residential zones for the affluent are serviced by gated infrastructure, while low‑income settlements — often labelled “slums” or “bastis” — lack secure tenure, sanitation, and public transport. The 1995 UN‑Habitat definition of “slum” (lack of durable housing, sufficient living area, access to improved water, sanitation, and secure tenure) remains the benchmark for comparative research. In India, the 2001 Census identified 52 million slum dwellers; the 2011 Census raised the figure to 65 million, illustrating rapid urbanisation outpacing formal housing supply. Policy responses oscillate between eviction‑driven “slum clearance” (e.g., the 1970s Bombay Development Plan) and in‑situ upgrading (the 2005 Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission, later subsumed under the Smart Cities Mission). Empirical work by Gautam Bhan (2016) demonstrates that upgrading programmes that recognise residents’ property rights and involve participatory planning improve tenure security without displacing livelihoods. Examiners expect candidates to (a) contrast the dualist view of informality as “pre‑modern” with the structuralist view of informality as a permanent feature of capitalist urbanisation, (b) cite at least one Indian case (e.g., Dharavi’s recycling economy generating an estimated annual turnover of ₹1 billion), (c) discuss the role of municipal governance, land‑use regulations, and the 2017 Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act in shaping informal‑formal linkages, and (d) evaluate the gendered dimension — women dominate home‑based piece‑rate work and face intersecting vulnerabilities of caste, migration status, and lack of social protection.

Sociology of Health and Illness: Medicalization and Health Inequalities

The sociology of health interrogates how biological conditions become socially defined, managed, and stratified. Medicalization — the process by which non‑medical problems acquire medical definitions and treatments — was conceptualised by Peter Conrad (1992) and later expanded by Thomas Szasz’s critique of psychiatric imperialism. Classic examples include the re‑classification of homosexuality as a mental disorder (removed from DSM‑II in 1973), the expansion of ADHD diagnoses in children, and the pharmaceuticalisation of menopause. In India, the 2017 Mental Healthcare Act decriminalised attempted suicide and mandated community‑based care, reflecting a shift from institutional to rights‑based frameworks. Health inequalities follow the social gradient documented by the Whitehall Studies (Marmot, 1991): lower socioeconomic position correlates with higher morbidity and mortality, even after controlling for behavioural risk factors. Caste‑based disparities are stark — National Family Health Survey‑4 (2015‑16) shows infant mortality among Scheduled Tribes at 44 per 1,000 live births versus 29 for the general category. The concept of “structural violence” (Paul Farmer, 2004) captures how unequal access to nutrition, clean water, and health infrastructure produces avoidable suffering. The 2005 National Rural Health Mission (later subsumed under the National Health Mission) aimed to reduce maternal mortality through Janani Suraksha Yojana cash transfers; evaluations report a decline from 254 (2004‑06) to 113 (2016‑18) maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, yet gaps persist across states. Examiners reward answers that (i) define medicalization with reference to Conrad and Zola, (ii) illustrate with an Indian trajectory (e.g., the rise of private fertility clinics and the 2021 Assisted Reproductive Technology Regulation Bill), (iii) link health inequalities to intersecting axes of class, caste, gender, and region using NFHS data, and (iv) critically assess the limits of insurance‑based schemes such as Ayushman Bharat (launched 2018) in addressing out‑of‑pocket expenditures for chronic conditions.

Worked Answer Technique
“Explain how medicalization and structural violence intersect in shaping maternal health outcomes in rural India. Use relevant data and theory.”
Begin by defining medicalization (Conrad 1992) and structural violence (Farmer 2004). Show how childbirth, once a domestic event, became hospital‑centred through the Janani Suraksha Yojana, increasing institutional deliveries from 39 % (NFHS‑3) to 79 % (NFHS‑4). Argue that this medicalization improves access to skilled attendance but simultaneously marginalises traditional birth attendants and imposes biomedical protocols that may not respect cultural practices. Then introduce structural violence: caste‑based exclusion from quality facilities, distance to First Referral Units, and inadequate blood‑bank networks produce differential mortality — NFHS‑4 reports maternal mortality ratio of 174 for Scheduled Castes versus 113 for Others. Conclude that policy must combine medicalization (emergency obstetric care) with structural interventions (caste‑sensitive outreach, transport vouchers, community monitoring) to reduce inequities.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “intersection” of two concepts, structure the answer in three moves: (1) concise definitions with citations, (2) a concrete Indian illustration that shows the mechanisms linking them, (3) a critical evaluation of policy or theoretical limits. This pattern signals analytical depth and earns the full 15‑mark allocation.

Political Sociology: Power, Authority, and Social Movements

Political sociology analyses the distribution and exercise of power beyond formal institutions. Max Weber’s tripartite typology — traditional, charismatic, and legal‑rational authority — remains the analytical backbone. Steven Lukes’ three‑dimensional view of power (1974) adds the capacity to shape preferences and agenda‑setting, while Michel Foucault’s concept of governmentality (1991) extends power to dispersed techniques of self‑regulation. Social movements constitute collective challenges to existing power structures. Charles Tilly’s “repertoire of contention” (1978) and Sidney Tarrow’s “political opportunity structure” (1998) explain why movements emerge, mobilise, and achieve outcomes. In India, the Chipko movement (1973) exemplified ecological resistance rooted in subsistence livelihoods; the Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985‑present) combined legal petitions, mass mobilisation, and transnational advocacy to contest large‑dam displacement. The 2011 Anna Hazare anti‑corruption campaign illustrated the role of media‑mediated charismatic authority in pressuring legislative action (the 2013 Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act). Dalit movements, from the 1920s Mahad Satyagraha to the contemporary Bhim Army, deploy both legal‑rational strategies (reservation, SC/ST Act) and counter‑hegemonic cultural assertion. Examiners expect candidates to (a) differentiate authority types with Indian illustrations, (b) apply Lukes’ third dimension to explain how dominant narratives (e.g., “development” discourse) marginalise tribal land rights, (c) analyse a movement’s trajectory using Tilly’s repertoire and Tarrow’s opportunity structures, and (d) assess the state’s response — repression, co‑optation, or institutionalisation — with reference to the 1975‑77 Emergency and the 2020‑21 farmers’ protests against the three farm laws (later repealed).

Sociology of Education: Reproduction and Resistance

The sociology of education investigates how schooling systems reproduce social hierarchies and generate possibilities for resistance. Pierre Bourdieu’s concepts of cultural capital, habitus, and symbolic violence (1977) demonstrate that schools reward the linguistic and cultural dispositions of dominant classes, legitimising inequality as merit. Basil Bernstein’s “elaborated” versus “restricted” codes (1971) link language patterns to class‑based educational outcomes. Samuel Bowles and Herbert Gintis’ correspondence principle (1976) argues that the hidden curriculum mirrors workplace hierarchies, preparing students for stratified labour markets. In India, the 1968 Kothari Commission envisioned a common school system; the 1986 National Policy on Education and the 2009 Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (RTE) mandated 25 % reservation in private unaided schools for economically weaker sections. Empirical studies (e.g., PROBE Report 1999; ASER 2022) reveal persistent learning gaps: only 20 % of Grade 5 rural children can read a Grade 2 text. Caste‑based discrimination — separate seating, mid‑day meal exclusion — constitutes symbolic violence documented by the 2016 National Commission for Scheduled Castes report. Resistance appears in movements like the 1990s Dalit student unions demanding curriculum inclusion of Ambedkar, and the 2015 “Fee Hike” protests at Jawaharlal Nehru University that linked affordability to social justice. Examiners reward answers that (i) outline Bourdieu’s and Bowles‑Gintis’ theories with precise terminology, (ii) cite Indian data (ASER, NFHS, RTE compliance rates), (iii) discuss the tension between meritocratic rhetoric and structural barriers, and (iv) evaluate policy instruments — scholarship schemes, bridge courses, and the 2020 National Education Policy’s emphasis on multilingual foundational literacy — for their capacity to disrupt reproduction.

Globalization and Cultural Hybridity

Globalization reshapes cultural flows, producing hybrid forms that challenge essentialist notions of tradition and modernity. Arjun Appadurai’s “scapes” — ethnoscapes, mediascapes, technoscapes, financescapes, and ideoscapes (1996) — map the disjunctive movements of people, images, technology, capital, and ideas. Roland Robertson’s “glocalization” (1995) captures the simultaneous universalising and particularising tendencies. Homi Bhabha’s concept of the “third space” (1994) describes the interstitial zone where cultural meanings are negotiated, enabling subaltern agency. In India, the 1991 economic liberalisation accelerated satellite television, transnational advertising, and digital platforms. The rise of “Bollywood” as a global brand illustrates mediascape‑driven hybridity: films blend classical ragas, hip‑hop beats, and diaspora narratives, while overseas box‑office revenues exceed domestic earnings for major releases. The 2000s “fusion” music scene (e.g., Indian Ocean, Raghu Dixit) exemplifies technoscape‑mediated collaboration. Simultaneously, right‑wing cultural nationalism invokes “pure” tradition to police hybrid expressions — debates over Valentine’s Day, “love jihad” narratives, and the 2020 Citizenship Amendment Act protests reveal contested ideoscapes. Empirical work by Nandini Sundar (2011) on tribal media collectives in Chhattisgarh shows how community radio appropriates global formats for local language revitalisation. Examiners expect candidates to (a) define Appadurai’s scapes and Bhabha’s third space with citations, (b) illustrate hybridity through at least two Indian cultural domains (film, music, cuisine, digital activism), (c) analyse the power geometry — who controls production, distribution, and interpretation — and (d) critically assess whether hybridity empowers marginalised groups or becomes a commodified aesthetic for global markets.

  • Confusing medicalization with mere expansion of health services; medicalization specifically refers to the redefinition of non‑medical problems as medical issues.
  • Treating informal economy as a homogeneous sector; it comprises diverse forms (street vending, home‑based work, waste picking) with distinct regulatory challenges.
  • Equating social movements solely with protests; movements also involve institutional lobbying, legal strategies, and cultural production.
  • Presenting cultural hybridity as inherently progressive; hybrid forms can be co‑opted by market forces and reinforce existing hierarchies.
  • Using outdated census or NFHS rounds without noting the year; examiners penalise answers that cite 2001 data when 2011 or 2022 figures are available.
  • Overlooking the role of the state in shaping both risk distribution and cultural policy; state‑society feedback loops are central to risk society and glocalization analyses.
  • Neglecting intersectional analysis in education; caste, gender, and class operate simultaneously to produce differentiated schooling experiences.

Secularization, Fundamentalism, and the Public Sphere

The classical secularization thesis, articulated by Peter Berger and later refined by Steve Bruce, predicts that modernization — rationalization, differentiation, and societalization — inevitably erodes religious authority and confines faith to the private sphere. Berger’s 1967 formulation identified three mechanisms: the decline of religious institutions’ control over education and welfare, the rise of scientific explanations for natural phenomena, and the pluralization of worldviews that undermines taken‑for‑granted sacred canopies. Empirical work in Western Europe (e.g., the European Values Study 1999‑2008) shows falling church attendance and rising “no religion” identifiers, supporting the thesis for that region.

Jose Casanova’s 1994 critique, Public Religions in the Modern World, argues that deprivatization — religion’s re‑entry into public debate — is a global pattern, not an exception. He distinguishes three dimensions: (i) religious actors challenging state monopolies on moral legitimation, (ii) religious movements shaping public policy (abortion, education, bioethics), and (iii) the formation of transnational religious networks. Fundamentalist movements, whether Christian Right in the United States, Islamist parties in Turkey and Egypt, or Hindutva mobilisation in India, exemplify this deprivatization. They deploy modern media, electoral politics, and legal strategies to re‑sacralise the public sphere.

In India, the constitutional framework (Articles 25‑28) guarantees freedom of religion while mandating a secular state that maintains “principled distance” from all faiths (Rajeev Bhargava, 1998). Yet the public sphere witnesses recurring contests: the Shah Bano judgment (1985) and the subsequent Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act (1986); the Babri Masjid demolition (1992) and the 2019 Supreme Court verdict allocating the disputed site to a Hindu temple trust; the 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act protests framed as defence of secular citizenship. Scholars such as Niraja Gopal Jayal and Pratap Bhanu Mehta note that Indian secularism operates through state‑mediated regulation of religious institutions (e.g., temple management boards, waqf boards) rather than strict separation.

Examiners reward answers that (a) contrast the European secularization trajectory with the “multiple modernities” thesis (Shmuel Eisenstadt), (b) deploy Casanova’s deprivatization typology to analyse at least two Indian cases, (c) discuss the role of law in mediating religion‑state relations, and (d) evaluate whether fundamentalist mobilisation represents a reversal of secularization or a re‑configuration of religious authority in a plural public sphere.

Actor‑Network Theory and the Sociology of Scientific Practice

Actor‑Network Theory (ANT), developed by Bruno Latour, Michel Callon, and John Law in the 1980s, treats both human and non‑human entities — “actants” — as symmetrical participants in the construction of scientific facts. The core analytic moves are: (i) translation, the process by which actors define problems, enrol allies, and stabilise a network; (ii) inscription, the materialisation of knowledge in instruments, texts, and databases; and (iii) generalised symmetry, the refusal to privilege social explanations over technical ones. Latour’s Science in Action (1987) demonstrates how the Pasteurisation of milk became a fact only after a network of laboratories, veterinarians, farmers, and the French state aligned.

Callon’s “sociology of translation” outlines four moments: problematisation (defining the obligatory passage point), interessement (locking actors into roles), enrolment (defining identities), and mobilisation (speaking for the network). Law extends ANT to “heterogeneous engineering”, showing how the Brazilian nuclear programme (1970s‑1990s) required aligning uranium mines, German technology, IAEA safeguards, and domestic political coalitions. In India, the Green Revolution (1960s‑1970s) illustrates ANT: high‑yielding wheat varieties (IR8), irrigation bureaucracies, fertilizer subsidies, and farmer cooperatives formed a network that re‑defined agricultural productivity as a scientific fact.

Critics (e.g., Karin Knorr Cetina, Harry Collins) argue that ANT underplays power asymmetries and the role of institutionalised reflexivity. The “strong programme” in the sociology of scientific knowledge (Bloor, Barnes) insists on causal symmetry but retains a social‑explanatory focus. ANT scholars respond that power is an effect of network topology — actors gain influence by becoming obligatory passage points. Empirical studies of the Human Genome Project (1990‑2003) reveal how data‑sharing agreements, patent regimes, and bioinformatics tools co‑produced the “reference genome” as a stabilized object.

For examination, candidates should (i) define actant, translation, and inscription with precise terminology, (ii) trace a concrete scientific controversy (e.g., cold fusion 1989, CRISPR patent dispute 2015) through ANT’s four moments, (iii) compare ANT with the strong programme and with Bourdieu’s field theory, and (iv) discuss the policy relevance: how ANT informs responsible innovation frameworks and the governance of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence.

Worked Answer Technique
Question: Using Actor‑Network Theory, explain how the 1989 cold‑fusion claim became a contested scientific fact. Outline the translation moments and identify the obligatory passage point.
Answer: The cold‑fusion episode illustrates ANT’s translation process. Problematisation: Fleischmann and Pons positioned their electrolytic cell as the obligatory passage point for achieving room‑temperature nuclear fusion, promising limitless energy. Interessement: They enrolled the University of Utah, the US Department of Energy, and major media, locking these actors into roles of validator, funder, and publicist. Enrolment: Replication attempts by labs at MIT, Caltech, and Harwell defined new identities — “replicators” and “skeptics” — each with distinct experimental protocols. Mobilisation: The American Physical Society’s 1989 session became the forum where spokespersons (e.g., Steven Koonin) spoke for the network, declaring the claim unreproducible. The obligatory passage point — the specific palladium‑deuterium cell — failed to stabilise because the network could not maintain consistent inscriptions (calorimetry data, neutron counts). Consequently, the fact dissolved, demonstrating that scientific facts are network effects, not intrinsic properties of nature.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “a sociological analysis of a scientific controversy”, first name the theory (ANT, strong programme, Bourdieu), then structure the answer around the theory’s analytical moves (translation moments, symmetry principle, field positions). Use a single well‑known case (cold fusion, CRISPR, COVID‑19 modelling) and trace it step‑by‑step; examiners reward clear mapping of concepts to empirical detail over breadth.

Legal Pluralism and State Law in Postcolonial Contexts

Legal pluralism, as formulated by Sally Engle Merry (1988) and expanded by Boaventura de Sousa Santos (1995), denotes the coexistence of multiple normative orders — state law, customary law, religious law, and transnational regulatory regimes — within a single social field. Merry’s “semi‑autonomous social fields” concept highlights how non‑state arenas (village councils, caste panchayats, tribal assemblies) generate binding rules while remaining partially insulated from state enforcement. Santos’ “interlegality” stresses the productive friction when these orders intersect, producing hybrid legal consciousness.

In India, the colonial legacy created a dual system: Anglo‑Indian criminal and contract law applied uniformly, while personal laws (Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi) governed marriage, inheritance, and adoption. The Constitution (Articles 25‑28, 44) retains this pluralism but directs the state toward a Uniform Civil Code (UCC). Landmark Supreme Court judgments illustrate the tension: Shah Bano (1985) granted maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, prompting the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act (1986) that reinstated religious personal law; Sabarimala (2018) held that the exclusion of women of menstruating age violated constitutional equality, yet the review petition (2020) kept the issue alive; Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised consensual same‑sex relations, overriding colonial‑era Section 377.

Tribal customary law operates under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, granting autonomy to District and Regional Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act (1996) recognises Gram Sabha authority over natural resources, yet state forest laws frequently override it. Empirical work by Nandini Sundar (2007) on Chhattisgarh shows how Maoist insurgency, state counter‑insurgency, and customary dispute resolution produce a “legal bricolage” where villagers navigate multiple forums.

Examiners expect candidates to (a) define legal pluralism and interlegality with citations, (b) map at least three normative orders in a single Indian context (e.g., state criminal law, khap panchayat norms, and international human rights treaties in honour‑killing cases), (c) analyse how courts negotiate pluralism — “harmonious construction” versus “constitutional supremacy” — and (d) evaluate the UCC debate in light of Santos’ “subaltern cosmopolitanism”, which argues for a pluralist constitutionalism that recognises difference without hierarchy.

Transnational Migration, Remittances, and Diaspora Politics

Transnational migration studies, pioneered by Stephen Castles, Nina Glick Schiller, and Luis Eduardo Guarnizo, shift focus from assimilation to sustained cross‑border ties. The concept of transnationalism captures migrants’ simultaneous embeddedness in origin and destination societies through economic, political, and cultural practices. Social remittances (Levitt, 1998) — ideas, norms, and skills transferred alongside money — reshape gender relations, health behaviours, and democratic expectations in sending communities.

India has been the world’s largest recipient of remittances since the early 2000s (World Bank Migration and Development Brief, 2023). These flows finance household consumption, education, and real estate, but also fund community infrastructure — schools, temples, hospitals — in states such as Kerala, Punjab, and Gujarat.
