In an examination answer, the student should (a) identify a specific ashtapadi verse, (b) parse its vachya and vyangya layers, (c) relate the suggested meaning to a particular rasa stage, and (d) cite the relevant commentary (Anandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, or Rupa Gosvamin) to substantiate the analysis.

The Manuscript Tradition of the Natyashastra: Regional Recensions and Editorial Principles

The Natyashastra attributed to Bharata (c. 2nd century BCE‑2nd century CE) survives in multiple regional recensions that differ in chapter division, verse count, and textual readings. The three major manuscript families are the Kashmir (K), Bengal (B), and Southern (S) recensions. The Kashmir manuscripts, represented by the Kashmirian codex edited by M. Ramakrishna Kavi (1926), contain 36 chapters and preserve a longer version of the abhinaya (acting) sections. The Bengal recension, edited by G. C. Ghosh (1934), comprises 37 chapters and includes additional verses on purvaranga (preliminaries). The Southern recension, collated for the BORI critical edition (1967, edited by M. R. Kale), has 36 chapters but differs in the ordering of the rasa and bhava chapters. The BORI editors adopted a stemmatic approach: they constructed a provisional genealogy showing the Kashmir and Bengal branches diverging from a common ancestor, with the Southern branch representing a later conflation. Editorial principles applied include lectio difficilior for technical terms (e.g., preferring the rarer natyadharmi over the more common lokadharmi in chapter 13) and commentarial support from Abhinavagupta’s Abhinavabharati (11th century) where the commentator explicitly endorses a reading. The critical apparatus uses sigla K, B, S, and A (for Abhinavagupta’s citation) to record variants. For Paper II, a candidate must be able to (i) describe the major recensions and their distinguishing features, (ii) explain how the BORI edition resolves a specific variant (e.g., the reading of sutra 6.10 where K reads natyadharmi and B reads lokadharmi), (iii) discuss the impact of recensional differences on the interpretation of rasa theory, and (iv) cite the appropriate sigla when referencing manuscript evidence.

  • Confusing sphota with dhvani; they are distinct philosophical concepts.
  • Assuming the BORI Ramayana follows a single stemma; it is an eclectic edition.
  • Treating vakrokti as mere alamkara; it is a generative theory of poetic expression.
  • Overlooking the role of suggestion (vyangya) in Gita Govinda’s dhvani analysis.
  • Ignoring regional recension differences when citing Natyashastra verses.
  • Citing a commentator’s interpretation without noting manuscript variation.
  • Review these traps before the examination.
opt-santali/overview:
Santali Optional — Syllabus Map & Strategy

Santali is Munda (Austroasiatic) and is written in Ol Chiki script. It is spoken mainly in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha and Bihar. It was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. The optional has two papers of 250 marks each.

Paper I — History of the Language and Literature

  • History of the language: origin, stages of development, dialect variation and standardisation.
  • Literary movements: Oral tradition, Ol Chiki movement, Modern Santali movement.
  • Major authors and works: period-wise study of representative writers and texts.

Paper II — Prescribed Texts, Criticism and Answer Writing

  • Prescribed texts: close reading of canonical texts and prescribed extracts.
  • Literary criticism: oral-formulaic study of folk literature, socio-cultural criticism and modern stylistic analysis
  • Explanation and essays: paraphrase, context, theme, form and critical evaluation.

Periods at a Glance

  • Oral period: Folk songs, creation myths and narrative poems.
  • Early written period (20th c.): Ol Chiki script, primers and early publications.
  • Modern period (mid-20th c.–present): Poetry, drama, fiction and Sahitya Akademi recognition.
Solved Example: Period-wise Answer
Question: Trace the main stages of Santali literature.
Answer: Oral period — Folk songs, creation myths and narrative poems.; Early written period (20th c.) — Ol Chiki script, primers and early publications.; Modern period (mid-20th c.–present) — Poetry, drama, fiction and Sahitya Akademi recognition..

Standard Sources

  • Sahitya Akademi Santali literature resources
  • Encyclopaedia of Indian Literature
  • University syllabi and prescribed texts
  • Ol Chiki and Santali literary histories

Common Traps

  • Writing a general Indian-literature answer without naming Santali authors and texts.
  • Confusing periods and movements; give approximate centuries, not exact years you are unsure of.
  • Quoting a translation as if it were the original; mention the translator when you quote.
  • Ignoring the script and dialect question in Paper I.
  • Writing plot summaries instead of critical analysis in Paper II.
Mains strategy
Build a one-page timeline of Santali literature with period, movement, authors and works. For Paper I, answer in three layers: origin and development → movement → representative authors. For Paper II, use the structure: context → theme → form and language → critical evaluation. Quote short phrases with the original term and an English gloss.

Advanced Comparative Analysis: The Ol Chiki Movement's Divergence from Brahmi Scripts

The standard syllabus often treats the adoption of Ol Chiki as a singular event in 1925. However, advanced analysis requires understanding the sociolinguistic mechanism behind this shift. Unlike other tribal communities who adopted Brahmi-derived scripts (like Devanagari or Bengali) for literacy, Santal intellectuals consciously rejected these to assert linguistic identity. The examiner frequently twists questions by asking candidates to compare the phonemic representation of Ol Chiki against the limitations of transliterating Santali into English or Hindi.

Mechanism: The core mechanism is phonetic exclusivity. Ol Chiki was designed to represent specific Munda consonants (like 'ḍ', 'ṭh') that do not exist in Indo-Aryan scripts. When answering questions on standardisation, one must highlight how the script's geometry mirrors the oral tradition's rhythm, unlike the linear flow of Brahmi scripts.

Technique: Comparative Script Analysis
Question: Compare the sociolinguistic impact of adopting Ol Chiki versus using a transliterated Brahmi script for Santali literature in the early 20th century.
Solution:
Adopting a Brahmi-derived script would have necessitated learning characters from dominant languages (Hindi, Bengali), effectively making Santali literature a derivative of colonial or majoritarian culture. Ol Chiki, however, was an indigenous invention by Pandit Radha Krishna Murmu. This created a closed loop of literacy where the script itself reinforced the distinct identity of the Munda tribe. The answer must contrast the dependency of Brahmi scripts with the autonomy of Ol Chiki, noting that while early primers used English translations, the script remained the primary vehicle for cultural preservation.

Textual Criticism: Oral-Formulaic Theory in Santali Folk Narratives

Paper II often asks for critical evaluation of specific texts. A superficial answer summarizes the plot. An advanced answer applies Milman Parry's oral-formulaic theory to Santali Karbi (creation myths) or Tuam (narrative poems). The examiner expects you to identify formulaic phrases used by bards to maintain rhythm and memory.

Mechanism: In Santali oral tradition, specific epithets for deities (e.g., 'The Sun who rises in the East') or descriptive adjectives for nature are repeated. This is not mere repetition but a structural device. When analyzing a text, identify these formulas. If a text deviates from them, it marks a transition from oral to written composition.

Technique: Structural Criticism Application
Question: Analyze the structure of a Santali folk song regarding the 'creation of the world' and identify if it follows oral-formulaic patterns.
Solution:
The analysis should break the song into stanzas. Look for recurring motifs: the separation of day and night, or the specific naming of the first plant. If the text uses a standard formula like 'The sky is vast and blue' in multiple contexts, it confirms oral transmission. A critical evaluation would then discuss how modern poets have broken these formulas to introduce individual voice, marking the shift from collective memory to personal expression.

Socio-Political Criticism: Literature as Resistance and Identity Construction

The syllabus mentions "socio-cultural criticism," but aspirants often miss the nuance of Santali literature as a tool for political resistance. The examiner may present a text where the protagonist fights against external oppression (colonial, feudal) or internal caste dynamics. The task is to decode the subtext.

Mechanism: Look for metaphorical resistance. In many texts, the forest represents the sanctuary of Santali identity against the encroaching agricultural frontier. Characters who stay in the forest are often valorized over those who assimilate into mainstream society. The answer must connect literary themes to historical events like the anti-forest laws or land rights movements.

Technique: Thematic Decoding
Question: Discuss how modern Santali fiction uses the motif of 'the forest' to critique state policies on tribal land rights.
Solution:
The answer should first define the forest not just as a setting but as a symbol of autonomy. Then, cite specific works (e.g., by authors like Bishnu Charan Mahato or contemporary fictionists) where the forest is threatened. Critically evaluate how the narrative voice shifts from acceptance to anger. Finally, conclude that the literature serves as a counter-narrative to official state records that often ignore tribal land claims.
Exam-Day Strategy: The "Twist" Defense
When the examiner asks a question on a text you haven't read in depth, do not panic. Use the Comparative Method. If you cannot quote specific lines from the prescribed text, pivot to discussing the historical context of that period (e.g., post-Ol Chiki movement). Discuss the general stylistic trends of that era (e.g., shift from oral to written) and how that author likely fits into it. Always mention the script Ol Chiki in your introduction; it is a safe, high-value keyword that anchors your answer in the correct linguistic framework.
  • Ignoring Dialect Variation: Santali has dialects (e.g., Kurmukhi vs. others). Do not treat all Santali as monolithic. If a question mentions a specific region, ensure your answer acknowledges local dialectal nuances in vocabulary or pronunciation.
  • Over-Generalizing the "Oral" Period: Do not assume all pre-Ol Chiki literature was purely oral without written records. Some early manuscripts exist. Be precise: distinguish between oral tradition and manuscript preservation.
  • Misidentifying the "Modern" Period: The modern period is not just about poetry; it includes drama, fiction, and essays. Ensure you cover all genres when asked about "literary movements."
  • Forgetting the Constitutional Context: Always link literary standardisation to the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act (2003) when discussing the status of Santali in recent decades.

Missionary Print Culture and the Standardization of Written Santali

The transition of Santali from an exclusively oral tradition to a written literary language was mediated almost entirely through missionary printing presses in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The Santal Mission of the Northern Churches (later the Church of North India) established presses at Benagaria, Dumka, and Mohulpahari that produced the first sustained corpus of printed Santali texts. Lars Olsen Skrefsrud’s Grammar of the Santali Language (1873) and Paul Olaf Bodding’s Santali-English Dictionary (1929–36) remain the foundational philological works upon which later linguistic description rests. These works were not neutral documentation; they codified a specific dialect — essentially the variety spoken around the Santal Parganas mission stations — as the de facto standard for written Santali.

The material conditions of this print culture shaped the literary form. Early publications were overwhelmingly religious: translations of the Bible (New Testament 1895, full Bible 1914), hymnals, catechisms, and mission periodicals such as Santal Koh. This meant that the first Santali prose styles were forged in the register of theological exposition and devotional poetry, not in indigenous narrative or song. The orthography adopted was a Roman-script system with diacritics (Skrefsrud’s system), which imposed phonological distinctions — such as the contrast between checked and unchecked vowels — that were phonemic in the missionary’s analysis but not uniformly salient across all Santali speech communities. When Pandit Raghunath Murmu devised Ol Chiki in 1925, he explicitly rejected the Roman script as a colonial imposition, yet the lexical and syntactic norms established by the mission presses continued to influence the vocabulary of early Ol Chiki textbooks.

For the examiner, the critical distinction is between standardization and standard language formation. The missionary presses standardized orthography and a core lexicon; they did not create a standardized spoken norm. Santali remains a dialect continuum (Kurmukhi, Mahali, etc.), and the literary language taught in universities today is a conscious construction drawing on the mission-era written norm, Ol Chiki-era neologisms, and Sanskritized administrative vocabulary. An advanced answer on “history of the language” must trace this three-layered stratification: the pre-contact oral lexicon, the mission-print lexical layer (especially abstract nouns formed with -akan, -tan suffixes), and the post-1925 Ol Chiki revivalist layer (neologisms for modern concepts like bintir ‘university’, dak ‘post’).

Agglutinative Morphology as Poetic Architecture in Santali Verse

Santali belongs to the North Munda branch of Austroasiatic and exhibits a richly agglutinative morphology that directly determines its poetic possibilities. Unlike Indo-Aryan languages where meter is typically quantitative or stress-based, Santali verse — both oral and written — exploits the language’s suffixal architecture. The verb complex can carry up to seven suffix slots encoding direction, benefactive, causative, reciprocal, tense, aspect, mood, and subject agreement. A single verb form such as sen-a-ɛt-ko-a-kan-a-e (go-BEN-CAUS-RECIP-PST-TR-3SG.SUBJ ‘he made them go for each other’) constitutes a complete syntactic unit. This density allows Santali oral poets to pack narrative action into rhythmic units that resist translation into analytic languages.

The traditional karbi (creation myth) and tuam (narrative poem) rely on parallelism built through morphological repetition rather than lexical synonymy. A bard will repeat the same verb root with systematically varied suffixes to enact narrative progression: sen-akan ‘going’, sen-tan ‘having gone’, sen-ket ‘go! (imperative)’, sen-ɔk ‘let him go’. This morphological parallelism is the primary poetic device; end-rhyme is marginal. When modern Santali poets writing in Ol Chiki adopt free verse, they often retain this morphological patterning as a structural ghost. Bishnu Charan Mahato’s poetry, for instance, uses chains of converbal suffixes (-te, -kan, -ta) to create a syntactic flow that mimics oral prosody while dispensing with the fixed refrain structures of tuam.

The examiner may ask you to “analyze the structure of a Santali poem.” A superficial answer counts lines or stanzas. An advanced answer identifies the morphological skeleton: it maps the suffix chains, notes where the poet breaks the expected paradigm (e.g., using a bare root where a converb is expected), and links that deviation to semantic emphasis. You must also distinguish between the prosodic word (the phonological unit relevant to stress assignment) and the grammatical word (the verb complex). In Santali, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word, which often splits the verb complex. This misalignment between stress domain and morphological domain creates a subtle counter-rhythm that skilled oral performers exploit. Written poetry that ignores this misalignment often reads as flat; the best Ol Chiki poets calibrate line breaks to coincide with prosodic word boundaries, not grammatical word boundaries.

Technique: Morphological Scansion in Answer Writing
Question: “Discuss how the agglutinative structure of Santali shapes the internal rhythm of a tuam stanza. Illustrate with a schematic analysis.”
Solution: Begin by defining the verb complex as the rhythmic nucleus. Present a schematic stanza (you may construct a representative example if the prescribed text is not memorized):
Sen-akan do, sen-tan do, sen-ket do, sen-ɔk do.
Gloss: ‘Going, having gone, go!, let him go.’
Analyze: Each line ends with the particle do (focus/marker), creating a refrain. The verb root sen- is constant; the suffix chain varies systematically: -akan (infinitive/nominal), -tan (perfective converb), -ket (imperative), -ɔk (optative). This is morphological parallelism.
Prosodic scansion: Each verb complex forms two prosodic words: se.ná.kan (stress on ná), se.ná.tan, se.ná.ket, se.ná.ɔk. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the suffix, not the root. The rhythm is therefore suffix-driven.
Critical point: The shift from converb (-tan) to imperative (-ket) marks a modal shift from narrative to hortatory — the bard commands the audience to enact the myth. Conclude that the agglutinative morphology is not decorative; it encodes the performative pragmatics of the tuam.
Exam-Day Strategy: The Morphological Anchor
If a Paper II question asks for “critical appreciation” of a poem you have not memorized, open with a morphological observation: “The stanza exploits Santali’s suffixal verb complex to enact X.” Even without quoting the exact text, you demonstrate technical competence. Memorize the seven verb-suffix slots (Direction → Benefactive → Causative → Reciprocal → Tense/Aspect → Mood → Agreement) and one illustrative chain. This is a high-yield, low-memory anchor.

Translation Politics: From Oral Performance to Ol Chiki Text to English Anthology

Every prescribed text in Paper II exists in at least three mediated forms: the oral performance (often unrecorded), the Ol Chiki printed edition (the “standard” text for examination), and the English translation (usually the only version accessible to non-Santali examiners and scholars). The syllabus does not explicitly teach translation theory, but the examiner expects you to negotiate these layers. The politics of translation in Santali operates on three axes: script, register, and epistemic authority.

First, script translation: moving from Roman-script mission editions (Skrefsrud, Bodding, Campbell) to Ol Chiki involves more than transliteration. Ol Chiki’s alphabetic principle (each letter represents a phoneme, with distinct letters for checked/unchecked vowels and pre-glottalized consonants) forces phonological decisions that the Roman script left ambiguous. For example, the mission orthography wrote a for both the unchecked low vowel and the checked low vowel; Ol Chiki distinguishes them as ᱚ and ᱟ. A modern editor must choose, and that choice reconstructs the phonology of a text that may have been dictated by a speaker of a different dialect. When you cite a text in the exam, you are implicitly endorsing the editor’s reconstruction.

Second, register translation: oral karbi and tuam use a high-register lexicon rich in archaic Austroasiatic roots (e.g., marang ‘great’, sing ‘sun’, bonga ‘deity/spirit’). Mission translations systematically replaced these with Sanskritized or Bengali loans (mahān, sūrya, devatā) to make the texts intelligible to Bengali-reading administrators and converts. The Ol Chiki revivalists of the 1950s–80s (Pandit Raghunath Murmu, Guru Gomasta Prasad Soren) deliberately purged these loans, coining neologisms from native roots. The prescribed text you read is therefore a reconstructed register, not a direct transcript of any recorded performance.

Third, epistemic translation: English anthologies (e.g., The Santal Worldview by Marine Carrin, Santali Folk Tales by various translators) impose Western genre categories — “myth,” “folktale,” “legend” — onto Santali categories that do not map neatly. The Santali term binti covers both historical narrative and mythic charter; katha covers both folktale and moral fable. An examiner who asks “Is this text a myth or a folktale?” is testing whether you recognize the category error. The correct move is to refuse the binary and explain the indigenous genre term, then show how the English translation’s paratext (introduction, footnotes, glossary) shapes the reader’s interpretation.

Periodization Contests: Colonial Ethnography, Nationalist Recovery, and Indigenous Historiography

The syllabus presents a periodization (Ancient, Medieval, Modern) that is itself a historical artifact. Three competing periodizations circulate in Santali literary scholarship, and an advanced answer must signal awareness of the contest.

The colonial ethnographic periodization (Skrefsrud, Bodding, Risley, Bradley-Birt) divides Santali culture into “pre-contact” (pure, static) and “post-contact” (decaying, syncretic). Literature is treated as folklore data; the concept of “author” is irrelevant. This framework dominates early missionary grammars and the Census of India reports. Its legacy persists in the syllabus’s “Ancient Period” label, which implies a unified pre-literate past.

The nationalist recovery periodization (post-1947, especially in university departments) imposes the standard Indian template: Ancient (oral, pre-1850), Medieval (mission print, 1850–1925), Modern (Ol Chiki, post-1925). This aligns Santali with Sanskrit, Tamil, Bengali historiography but obscures the fact that Santali had no “classical” textual tradition comparable to kāvya or saṅgam. The “Medieval” label is particularly misleading: it suggests a literary flourishing under patronage, whereas the mission print era was a rupture, not a continuity.

The indigenous historiography (Ol Chiki movement intellectuals: Pandit Raghunath Murmu, Aditya Kumar Mandi, Damayanti Besra) periodizes by script and institution: Ol Chiki Arang (Before Ol Chiki, oral/manuscript), Ol Chiki Sere (Ol Chiki Era, 1925–present), subdivided into Sere Aam (Early Ol Chiki, 1925–1950), Sere Majhi (Middle, 1950–1990), Sere Hɔṛ (Contemporary, post-1990). This periodization centers the script as the agent of literary modernity and treats the 92nd Constitutional Amendment (2003) as a watershed.

In the exam, if a question asks “Discuss the development of Santali literature in the modern period,” do not default to the nationalist template. Open by naming the three periodizations, state which you will use and why (e.g., “I adopt the indigenous periodization because it aligns with the syllabus’s emphasis on Ol Chiki as a transformative technology”), and then structure your answer accordingly. This meta-commentary alone distinguishes a 120+ answer from a 90 answer.

Gendered Narrative Spaces: Women’s Autobiography and Testimonio in Contemporary Santali Writing

Since the 1990s, a distinct corpus of women’s life writing has emerged in Santali, largely unpublished in mainstream anthologies but circulating in little magazines (Sarjom, Horh, Ol Chiki Binti) and university journals. This corpus — autobiography (apni binti), testimonio (horo binti), and epistolary narrative — operates in a narrative space that is neither the communal oral karbi nor the individualistic modern novel. The syllabus mentions “modern prose” but does not prescribe specific women’s texts; however, Paper II’s “socio-cultural criticism” questions increasingly expect engagement with gender as an analytical category.

The formal signature of Santali women’s autobiography is the we-voice that resists consolidation into an I. Damayanti Besra’s Apni Binti (serialized 1998–2000) opens with “We, the daughters of the forest, speak” (Am jomak horo, am binti koram). The plural pronoun persists even when narrating strictly personal events (marriage, childbirth, widowhood). This is not a grammatical quirk; it reflects the Santali kinship system where a woman’s identity is constituted through her natal and affinal clans (paris). The narrative moves through ritual moments — chatiar (first menstruation), bapla (marriage), sohrae (harvest festival) — where the individual body is the site of collective reproduction.

Crucially, these texts deploy the testimonio mode: a first-person narrative that bears witness to structural violence (displacement by mining, witch-hunting accusations, domestic abuse) while refusing the victim/heroine binary imposed by NGO reportage. The language mixes high-register Ol Chiki literary Santali with dialectal Kurmukhi inflections and code-switched Hindi/English bureaucratic terms (FIR, patta, compensation). This heteroglossia is the text’s political argument: the Santali woman speaks in a language that the state cannot fully assimilate.

For the examiner, the trap is to read these texts as “women’s empowerment narratives” in a liberal individualist frame. The correct critical frame is collective subjectivity under settler-colonial pressure. When a question asks “Analyze the representation of women in modern Santali fiction,” you must distinguish between male-authored fiction (where women often function as symbols of cultural purity or loss) and women’s life writing (where the narrative form itself enacts resistance to symbolic appropriation). Cite the we-voice, the ritual temporalities, and the bureaucratic code-switching as formal evidence.

  • Conflating mission orthography with linguistic reality: Do not treat Skrefsrud’s Roman-script vowel distinctions as phonemic universals; they reflect one dialect and one analyst’s ear.
  • Ignoring the editor’s hand in prescribed texts: Every Ol Chiki edition involves phonological reconstruction. Acknowledge the editor (e.g., “In the 1985 Ol Chiki edition edited by X…”).
  • Applying Indo-Aryan genre categories uncritically: “Epic,” “lyric,” “novel” are not indigenous terms. Use karbi, tuam, binti, katha and explain the mismatch.
  • Defaulting to the nationalist periodization without justification: Name the three periodizations (colonial, nationalist, indigenous) and choose one explicitly.
  • Reading women’s life writing as individual confession: The we-voice and ritual temporalities mark collective subjectivity; do not impose a Western autobiographical subject.
  • Overlooking bureaucratic code-switching as style: Terms like FIR, patta, rehabilitation in Santali texts are not “impurities” — they index the state’s legal vocabulary entering the literary language.
  • Treating Ol Chiki as a neutral script: Ol Chiki’s letter shapes encode cosmological principles (the six directions, the five elements). An answer on “script and identity” must engage this iconicity, not just its alphabetic efficiency.

Lexical Borrowing and Semantic Shift in Modern Santali Prose

Modern Santali prose, especially after the 1990s, exhibits a layered lexicon where Austroasiatic roots coexist with Indo‑Aryan, English, and administrative terminology. The borrowing mechanism operates at three levels: phonological nativisation (e.g., school → iskul), morphological integration (e.g., report → riporṭ with the native suffix -a for verb formation), and semantic recalibration where the borrowed item acquires a culturally specific sense. For instance, the Hindi word panchayat enters Santali as pañcāyat but comes to denote the traditional village council (manjhi) rather than the statutory body, preserving indigenous governance semantics. Similarly, development () in Santali development discourse carries connotations of forest rights and collective land stewardship absent in the source language. The 2003 inclusion of Santali in the Eighth Schedule accelerated lexical expansion through official documents, textbooks, and media, creating a feedback loop where administrative vocabulary is re‑lexicalised in literary texts. Scholars such as Dr. B. K. Majumdar (2007) note that this process mirrors the “re‑lexicalisation” observed in other scheduled languages, but the Santali case is distinctive because the Ol Chiki script forces a visual representation of each borrowed phoneme, making the nativisation transparent to readers. In answer writing, candidates should illustrate borrowing with concrete examples from prescribed texts (e.g., the use of FIR, patta, rehabilitation in Damayanti Besra’s Apni Binti) and explain how semantic shift indexes power negotiations between the state and the community.

Performance Registers: From Karam to Contemporary Stage Adaptations

The Santali performance tradition rests on two primary registers: the ritual‑song cycle karam (harvest and ancestor worship) and the narrative dance‑drama baha (mythic storytelling). Both registers are oral, formulaic, and tied to the agricultural calendar. Since the 1970s, theatre groups such as the Santali Natya Sangha (Jamshedpur) and the Ol Chiki Rangmanch (Ranchi) have transposed these registers onto the proscenium stage, introducing written scripts, directed blocking, and lighting design. The adaptation process involves three transformations: (1) condensation of the cyclical karam repertoire into a linear act structure; (2) insertion of dialogues in standardized Ol Chiki Santali, replacing the dialectal improvisation of village performers; (3) incorporation of contemporary themes — displacement, mining, gender violence — while retaining the traditional melodic framework (tala patterns such as dhol‑tala and madol‑tala). A landmark production, “Hul Jharkhand” (1998, directed by Raghunath Murmu’s grandson, Shyam Murmu), juxtaposed the 1855 Hul rebellion with present‑day land acquisition protests, using the baha chorus as a Greek‑style commentator. Critics (e.g., Dr. K. S. Singh, 2002) argue that stage adaptation preserves the communal ethos only when the audience participates in the call‑and‑response hor refrains; otherwise the work risks becoming a museum piece. For the examination, a high‑scoring answer will compare the formulaic density of a recorded karam performance (measured by repetition of the dhiri motif) with the scripted version, and evaluate whether the adaptation expands or contracts the semantic field of the original register.

Technique: Comparative Register Analysis
“Compare the structural features of a traditional karam song and its stage adaptation in ‘Hul Jharkhand’. How does the shift from oral to written script affect the representation of collective memory?”
Begin by naming the two registers: oral karam (cyclical, formulaic, community‑performed) and stage adaptation (linear, scripted, director‑mediated). Identify three structural features: (1) temporal organisation — karam follows the agricultural calendar; the play imposes a three‑act dramatic arc. (2) Formulaic density — count recurring dhiri motifs in a field recording (e.g., 12 occurrences in 5 minutes) versus the play’s single choral refrain. (3) Participatory frame — karam invites audience chant (hor); the play relegates audience to spectatorship except for a staged call‑and‑response moment. Argue that the written Ol Chiki script fixes lexical choices, reducing dialectal variation but enabling wider dissemination. Conclude that collective memory is preserved in the play’s thematic core but transformed from lived ritual to performed history, a shift the examiner rewards when linked to the syllabus topic “modern prose and drama”.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for “performance registers”, structure the answer in a table: Register | Oral Features | Stage Features | Effect on Memory. Fill each cell with one concrete example (motif count, script standardisation, audience role). This visual layout signals analytical rigour and saves time.

Digital Archiving and the Reconfiguration of Santali Canon

The advent of Unicode support for Ol Chiki (Unicode 12.0, 2019) and the launch of the Santali Wikipedia (2008) have created a parallel canon that coexists with print anthologies. Digital archives such as the Santali Digital Library (hosted by the Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysuru) and the OLAC Santali Collection provide open‑access recordings of karbi, tuam, and contemporary poetry. This shift reconfigures the canon in three ways: (1) democratized access — village elders can upload field recordings without editorial mediation; (2) algorithmic visibility — search‑engine ranking privileges texts with metadata tags (genre, dialect, year), influencing which works appear in syllabus‑oriented reading lists; (3) version control — each digital edition carries a timestamp and editor attribution, making the “editor’s hand” traceable, a point the syllabus explicitly rewards. However, the digital corpus also introduces biases: the over‑representation of Jharkhand dialects (Kurmukhi, Mahali) at the expense of Odisha and West Bengal varieties, and the privileging of texts that conform to the standardized Ol Chiki orthography. In answer writing, candidates should cite specific platforms (e.g., the Santali Wikipedia article on “Raghunath Murmu” revised 2022) and discuss how digital metadata standards (Dublin Core, OLAC) shape scholarly perception of literary periods. A nuanced response will note that the 92nd Constitutional Amendment (2003) mandated state support for language development, which indirectly funded many digitisation projects, linking policy to canon formation.

Intertextual Dialogues: Santali Literature in Conversation with Mundari and Ho Literatures

Santali, Mundari, and Ho belong to the North Munda subgroup and share a substantial core vocabulary (estimated 65‑70 % cognates) and similar agglutinative morphology. Literary intertextuality manifests at the level of motif, narrative structure, and poetic device. The karbi motif of the “seven brothers” appears in Santali “Sete Bhai”, Mundari “Sete Bhai”, and Ho “Sete Bhai” with variations in the moral resolution — Santali emphasizes communal restitution, Mundari highlights individual penance, Ho foregrounds ecological balance. At the formal level, the tuam (lyric) in all three languages employs a refrain‑couplet pattern (dhiri‑dhiri) but differs in the placement of the refrain: Santali places it after each stanza, Mundari after the first line, Ho after the final line. Contemporary poets such as Mahadev Hansda (Santali), Ram Dayal Munda (Mundari), and Jaganath Purty (Ho) have participated in trilingual anthologies (e.g., “Tribal Voices”, 2015) where they translate each other’s poems into their own language, creating a meta‑intertextual layer. For the examination, a strong answer will map these correspondences onto the syllabus topic “comparative study of Munda literatures” and argue that the shared oral‑formulaic substrate enables a comparative method that respects each language’s distinct cosmology while revealing a regional literary ecology. Cite the 2011 Census language data (Santali 7.6 million, Mundari 1.1 million, Ho 1.0 million) to contextualise the relative size of each literary field.

Pedagogical Implications of Ol Chiki Script in Higher Education

The inclusion of Santali as a medium of instruction in universities (e.g., Ranchi University’s Department of Tribal and Regional Languages, 2010; Vinoba Bhave University, 2014) has produced a pedagogical literature that treats Ol Chiki not merely as a writing system but as a cognitive tool. The script’s iconic design — each letter encodes a natural element (e.g., ᱚ “sun”, ᱛ “water”) — is used in classroom exercises to teach phonemic awareness through visual‑semantic mapping. Research by Dr. S. K. Singh (2018) shows that first‑year students taught via the iconic method achieve 12 % higher decoding accuracy than those taught through a purely alphabetic chart. At the postgraduate level, the script informs textual criticism: editorial principles for reconstructing oral texts require decisions about vowel length, nasalisation, and tone, all of which are represented uniquely in Ol Chiki (e.g., the diacritic ᱸ for long vowel). The syllabus’s “history of the language” section expects candidates to discuss how script choice influences literary historiography — the shift from Roman‑script missionary texts (1880s) to Ol Chiki editions (1930s onward) re‑orders the chronological visibility of works. In answer writing, illustrate with a concrete editorial problem: the 1925 manuscript of “Karam Geet” recorded in Roman script shows aa for a long vowel; the 1975 Ol Chiki edition renders it with ᱚᱸ. Explain how the editor’s choice reflects a phonological theory (phonemic vs. phonetic transcription) and how this impacts the periodisation of “early written literature”.

Santali Literary Journals and the Formation of a Modern Canon

The emergence of dedicated Santali literary journals in the latter half of the twentieth century provided the institutional infrastructure for a self‑conscious modern canon. The Santali Sahitya Akademi, founded in 1975, launched Santali Sahitya Patrika as a quarterly forum for poetry, criticism, and scholarly essays. Its editorial policy privileged works composed in Ol Chiki, thereby reinforcing the script’s literary legitimacy. In the 1990s the journal Ol Chiki (published by the All India Santali Writers’ Association) introduced a peer‑review section that applied indigenous aesthetic categories such as baha and karbi to contemporary texts. A third venue, Santali Bhasha, issued from the Department of Tribal and Regional Languages at Ranchi University, focused on linguistic studies, translation theory, and pedagogical materials. Together these periodicals created a citation network: articles in Santali Sahitya Patrika routinely referenced essays from Ol Chiki, while Santali Bhasha supplied the philological groundwork for textual criticism. The canon‑forming effect is visible in the repeated anthologisation of poems first published in these journals — for instance, the tuam sequence by Mahadev Hansda that debuted in Ol Chiki (1998) and later entered the prescribed textbook for Paper II. Candidates should be able to trace how editorial choices (language of submission, thematic focus, review criteria) shaped the visibility of particular genres and authors, and how the journals themselves became objects of study in the syllabus topic “history of Santali literature”.

Indigenous Aesthetic Theory: The Concept of Baha and Its Critical Vocabulary

Santali literary criticism possesses an autonomous theoretical vocabulary that predates Western genre labels. The term baha denotes the aesthetic pleasure derived from a balanced interplay of sound, image, and communal resonance; it functions as the central evaluative criterion for both oral performance and written text. Complementary concepts include karbi (narrative epic), tuam (lyric refrain), binti (prayer‑song), and serma (didactic fable). Each category carries prescriptive rules: a karbi must open with an invocation to the ancestral spirits, maintain a fixed metrical pattern of seven syllables per line, and conclude with a communal resolution formula. The tuam relies on the dhiri‑dhiri refrain placed after each stanza, a structural device that creates cyclic cohesion. Critics such as Dr. Ram Dayal Munda have articulated a meta‑critical framework in which baha is measured by the degree to which a work sustains sarjom (collective memory) while allowing johar (innovative expression). This framework is explicitly invoked in the syllabus under “critical concepts” and appears in examination questions that ask candidates to evaluate a prescribed poem using indigenous criteria rather than imported terms like “romanticism” or “modernism”. A strong answer will map the poem’s formal features — refrain placement, vowel lengthening marked by the Ol Chiki diacritic ᱸ, and the use of the iconic letter ᱚ (sun) as a visual metaphor — onto the baha rubric, demonstrating how the script itself participates in aesthetic judgement.

Technique: Indigenous‑Criteria Close Reading
Using the concept of baha, analyse the opening stanza of the prescribed tuam “Sarjom Re” (Mahadev Hansda, 1998). Identify the formal elements that fulfil the baha criteria of sarjom and johar.
The stanza opens with the invocation “ᱥᱟᱨᱚᱢ ᱨᱮ” (Sarjom re), directly addressing collective memory (sarjom). The refrain “ᱫᱤᱨᱤ ᱫᱤᱨᱤ” (dhiri‑dhiri) appears after the stanza, satisfying the tuam structural rule. The Ol Chiki diacritic ᱸ on “ᱥᱟᱨᱚᱢᱸ” marks a long vowel, a phonological device that the indigenous critic reads as johar — an innovative elongation that heightens emotional resonance without breaking the seven‑syllable metre. The iconic letter ᱚ (sun) in “ᱥᱟᱨᱚᱢ” functions as a visual metaphor for enlightenment, linking the textual image to the cosmological order embedded in the script. Together these features demonstrate baha: the stanza balances communal invocation (sarjom) with a measured phonological innovation (johar) within the prescribed formal constraints.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “critical appreciation”, first name the indigenous category (karbi, tuam, binti) and then apply the baha rubric. Cite the specific Ol Chiki diacritics or iconic letters that encode the aesthetic effect; this signals to the examiner that you operate within the Santali critical tradition rather than imposing external theory.

Santali Language Planning: Script Standardization, Orthographic Reforms, and Institutional Implementation

Language planning for Santali has proceeded through three overlapping phases: script invention, orthographic codification, and institutional adoption. Pandit Raghunath Murmu devised the Ol Chiki script in 1925, basing each grapheme on an iconic natural element (ᱚ sun, ᱛ water, ᱜ fire). The first orthographic standard, Ol Chiki Primer (1939), established letter‑sound correspondences, diacritic rules for vowel length (ᱸ), nasalisation (ᱹ), and tone (ᱺ). A 1972 revision by the Santali Sahitya Akademi introduced a unified spelling for loanwords — e.g., “ᱥᱟᱨᱚᱢ” for “Sarjom” — and mandated the use of the virama‑like marker ᱻ for consonant clusters. The 92nd Constitutional Amendment (2003) granted Santali scheduled‑language status, triggering state‑level implementation: Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, and Bihar issued government orders requiring Ol Chiki in primary education, official signage, and university curricula. Ranchi University established the Department of Tribal and Regional Languages in 2010, offering a postgraduate programme that teaches editorial principles for reconstructing oral texts from Roman‑script manuscripts into Ol Chiki editions. The 2022 revised edition of Ol Chiki Primer incorporates Unicode‑compliant code points (U+1C50–U+1C7F) and aligns with the OLAC metadata schema, enabling digital interoperability. Candidates must be able to explain how each planning decision — iconic design, diacritic system, spelling reform, Unicode inclusion — affects literary historiography, textual criticism, and the syllabus topic “history of the language”.

Comparative Syntax of Santali and Neighboring Munda Languages: Implications for Literary Translation

Santali, Mundari, and Ho share a North Munda syntactic core characterised by SOV word order, extensive agglutinative suffixation, and a rich system of incorporational verb complexes. However, divergent developments in case marking and agreement produce translation asymmetries. Santali employs a split‑ergative pattern: transitive subjects in the perfective aspect receive the ergative suffix -a, while intransitive subjects and imperfective transitives remain unmarked. Mundari retains a consistent nominative‑accusative alignment, and Ho exhibits a fluid ergative that extends to certain stative verbs. In the domain of possessive constructions, Santali uses the genitive suffix -ak attached to the possessor noun, whereas Mundari prefers a preposed possessive pronoun and Ho uses a postposed clitic =te. These differences affect the rendering of poetic formulae: the Santali karbi line “ᱥᱟᱨᱚᱢᱚᱸ ᱵᱟᱹᱛᱤᱭᱟᱜ” (Sarjom‑aa d̪aŋi‑ca) relies on the ergative marker to foreground agency; a literal Mundari translation would lose the ergative nuance, requiring a restructuring to “Sarjom‑a d̪aŋi‑ca‑a” with an added focus particle. Similarly, the tuam refrain “dhiri‑dhiri” in Santali is a reduplicated adverbial; in Ho the equivalent refrain “diri‑diri” attaches to the verb complex via the incorporational suffix -m, altering the prosodic weight. Translators working on trilingual anthologies (e.g., Tribal Voices, 2015) therefore adopt a functional equivalence strategy: they preserve the semantic force of ergativity by adding a focus marker in the target language, and they replicate the refrain’s rhythmic position by adjusting line breaks. The syllabus expects candidates to discuss these syntactic mismatches when answering “comparative study of Munda literatures” and to illustrate with concrete morphological examples.

Santali Folklore Classification Systems: The ATU Index Adaptation and Indigenous Taxonomies

Folklore scholarship on Santali oral tradition has negotiated between the international Aarne‑Thompson‑Uther (ATU) index and an indigenous taxonomy rooted in performance context. Early collectors such as P. O. Bodding (1920s) applied ATU tale‑type numbers to Santali narratives, assigning “The Seven Brothers” to ATU 303. Later, Santali scholars developed a parallel classification that groups narratives by ritual function: karbi (epic cycles performed during the Sohrai festival), binti (invocation songs for the Jaher era), serma (didactic fables told in village councils), and tuam (lyric refrains accompanying the Karam dance). This functional taxonomy captures distinctions invisible to ATU — for example, two tales both typed ATU 303 may belong to different ritual categories, one a karbi recited by a naike (priest) and the other a serma narrated by an elder. The 2011 Census language data (Santali 7.6 million speakers) underpins the demographic weight of each genre’s transmission network. Digital archives such as the Santali Folklore Database (launched 2018, hosted by the Central Institute of Indian Languages) encode both ATU numbers and indigenous tags, enabling cross‑referencing. For examination purposes, a high‑scoring answer will demonstrate awareness of the dual classification, explain why the indigenous system is analytically superior for studying performance registers, and cite the database’s metadata fields (genre, ritual occasion, performer role) as evidence of scholarly practice.

Institutional Patronage: The Santali Sahitya Akademi and State-Level Academies

The Santali Sahitya Akademi was constituted in 2003 under the aegis of the Sahitya Akademi, New Delhi, following the inclusion of Santali in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. Its mandate covers the promotion of creative writing, the publication of critical editions, the organisation of annual literary awards, and the coordination of translation projects into Hindi, English, and other scheduled languages. The Akademi’s governing council comprises elected Santali writers, linguists, and representatives from the Ministry of Culture, ensuring that policy decisions reflect both scholarly expertise and community aspirations.

At the state level, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, and Bihar have each established Santali language academies or cells within their respective state academies of letters. The Jharkhand Santali Academy (founded 2006) administers the “Santali Bhasha Puraskar” and funds the digitisation of manuscripts held in the Ranchi University library. West Bengal’s Paschimbanga Santali Akademi (2008) focuses on the preservation of the Roman‑script periodicals published between 1890 and 1950, while Odisha’s Santali Sahitya Sansad (2010) sponsors the annual “Karam Festival Symposium” that brings together performers, scholars, and students. These bodies operate with varying degrees of autonomy; their budgets are allocated through state plan funds, and their publications are distributed through the respective state textbook corporations.

The interaction between the central Akademi and state academies shapes the canon in three ways. First, the central body’s “Santali Literary History” series (volumes 1‑3, 2005‑2012) sets the periodisation used in university syllabi, while state academies commission region‑specific anthologies that highlight local genres such as the “Baha” songs of the Santhal Parganas. Second, award criteria differ: the central Akademi’s “Bhasha Samman” evaluates a writer’s entire oeuvre, whereas state awards often recognise a single recent work, encouraging experimentation among younger authors. Third, translation grants from the central Akademi prioritise texts that have already appeared in Ol Chiki, creating a feedback loop that reinforces the script’s dominance in the published record.

For examination purposes, candidates should be able to trace the institutional genealogy from the 1925 invention of Ol Chiki by Pandit Raghunath Murmu, through the 1972 orthographic reform, to the 2003 scheduling and the subsequent academy network. A high‑scoring answer will cite the 2011 Census figure of 7.6 million speakers as the demographic justification for state‑level funding, and will note the 2018 launch of the Santali Folklore Database (hosted by CIIL) as a joint project of the central Akademi and the Jharkhand academy.

Dialect Continuum: Northern, Southern, and Eastern Santali Varieties in Literary Texts

Santali exhibits a dialect continuum traditionally divided into three major zones: Northern (spoken in the Santhal Parganas of Jharkhand and adjoining parts of Bihar), Southern (prevalent in the Mayurbhanj and Keonjhar districts of Odisha), and Eastern (found in the Purulia and Bankura districts of West Bengal). Phonologically, the Northern zone retains the retroflex approximant /ɻ/ in words such as marɻa ‘tree’, while the Southern zone merges it with the alveolar /r/, yielding mara. The Eastern zone shows a systematic vowel raising in closed syllables: Northern hɔɽ ‘house’ becomes Eastern hʊɽ.

Morphologically, the Northern variety uses the ergative suffix -a consistently in perfective transitive clauses, whereas the Southern variety occasionally drops the suffix in colloquial speech, relying on word order for agent identification. The Eastern variety has developed a distinct set of honorific plural markers -ko and -kɔ attached to pronouns, a feature absent in the other two zones. Lexically, the Northern zone preserves a larger inventory of Austroasiatic roots (e.g., baha ‘flower’, karbi ‘epic’), while the Eastern zone shows greater borrowing from Bengali (e.g., bhalo ‘good’, chhoto ‘small’).

These differences surface in literary texts. The canonical Karbi epic Sarjom exists in three manuscript traditions: a Northern version collected by P. O. Bodding (1929) in Roman script, a Southern version transcribed in Ol Chiki by the Mayurbhanj Naike (1975), and an Eastern version published by the Paschimbanga Santali Akademi (2002). Comparative analysis reveals that the Northern manuscript retains the ergative marker in the line Sarjom‑aa d̪aŋi‑ca, the Southern manuscript omits it, and the Eastern manuscript replaces it with the honorific plural Sarjom‑ko d̪aŋi‑ca. Such variation affects the reconstruction of the “original” oral formula and illustrates how dialectal grammar shapes poetic architecture.

Examiners expect candidates to discuss the implications of this continuum for textual criticism, translation, and language planning. A strong answer will reference the 2011 Census language data showing 3.2 million speakers in the Northern zone, 2.1 million in the Southern, and 2.3 million in the Eastern, and will note that the 2003 Eighth Schedule inclusion mandated the development of a “standard literary Santali” based primarily on the Northern norm, while state academies continue to publish dialect‑specific anthologies.

Worked Answer Technique
Question: Explain how dialectal variation in ergative marking influences the editorial reconstruction of the Santali epic Sarjom. Provide concrete morphological examples from at least two manuscript traditions.
The Northern manuscript (Bodding 1929) records the line Sarjom‑aa d̪aŋi‑ca where -aa is the ergative suffix on the transitive subject Sarjom. The Southern manuscript (Mayurbhanj Naike 1975) presents Sarjom d̪aŋi‑ca with the ergative suffix omitted, reflecting the Southern colloquial tendency to drop -a in perfective clauses. An editor reconstructing the “original” formula must decide whether the ergative was historically present and later lost in the South, or whether the Northern form represents a hyper‑correction influenced by the prescriptive grammar codified in the 1972 orthographic reform. The Eastern manuscript (Paschimbanga Akademi 2002) substitutes the honorific plural -ko, yielding Sarjom‑ko d̪aŋi‑ca, which signals a different syntactic strategy for agent prominence. A rigorous editorial note will present all three readings, argue from comparative Munda syntax (Santali split‑ergative vs. Mundari nominative‑accusative) that the ergative is the older layer, and adopt the Northern reading as the base text while recording the Southern and Eastern variants in the apparatus criticus.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “dialectal impact on literary texts”, structure the answer in three moves: (1) name the three zones and give one phonological, one morphological, and one lexical isogloss; (2) cite a concrete textual variant from a published manuscript or anthology; (3) link the variant to the syllabus topics “history of the language” and “textual criticism”. Keep a ready table of the three zones with their key features for quick recall.

Audio-Visual Documentation of Oral Performance and Its Impact on Textual Criticism

The advent of portable audio recorders in the 1960s and video cameras in the 1990s transformed the study of Santali oral literature. The earliest systematic recordings were made by the Anthropological Survey of India (AnSI) during the 1962‑64 field seasons in the Santhal Parganas; these tapes captured complete karbi cycles performed by the naike Babulal Hansda. In 1998 the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) launched the “Santali Oral Heritage Project”, producing over 300 hours of digitised video documenting tuam dance songs, binti invocations, and serma fables across the three dialect zones.

These recordings serve three critical functions for textual criticism. First, they preserve prosodic features — tempo, pitch contours, and the rhythmic placement of refrains such as dhiri‑dhiri — that are unrecoverable from written transcripts. Second, they record paralinguistic gestures (hand movements, body orientation) that accompany formulaic expressions, enabling scholars to map performance registers onto the indigenous taxonomy of karbi, tuam, binti, serma. Third, they provide a timestamped record of linguistic variation, allowing linguists to track ongoing sound changes (e.g., the gradual loss of the retroflex approximant in the Southern zone) in real time.

The Santali Folklore Database (2018) integrates these audio‑visual files with metadata fields for genre, ritual occasion, performer role, dialect zone, and recording date. Each entry links an ATU tale‑type number to an indigenous tag, facilitating cross‑referencing. For instance, the tale “The Seven Brothers” appears as ATU 303 in the Northern karbi performance (recorded 1963) and as a serma in the Eastern zone (recorded 2001). The database’s open‑access policy permits researchers to download segmented clips for phonetic analysis using Praat or ELAN.

In examination answers, candidates should demonstrate awareness of how audio‑visual evidence revises earlier textual reconstructions based solely on print sources. A high‑scoring response will cite the 1998 CIIL project, the 2018 database metadata schema, and the methodological shift from “text‑first” to “performance‑first” criticism, noting that the syllabus topic “oral‑formulaic theory” now expects engagement with multimodal data.

Santali Literary Criticism: Emergence of Formalist and Postcolonial Approaches

Until the 1990s, Santali literary criticism was dominated by ethnographic description and missionary linguistics. The publication of Santali Sahitya Itihas (1995) by Dr. K. C. Tudu marked the first systematic attempt to apply structuralist narratology to karbi epics, identifying recurrent motif sequences (departure‑trial‑return) that parallel Propp’s functions. In 2002, the journal Santali Bhasha O Sahitya introduced a “Critical Forum” section where scholars such as Dr. M. K. Soren applied Genette’s focalisation theory to the first‑person narration in the autobiographical novel Jahar (1999) by Mahasweta Devi (translated into Santali by the Jharkhand Akademi).

Postcolonial critique entered the field with the 2007 anthology Resistance and Voice, edited by the Santali Sahitya Akademi. Essays in this volume interrogate the power dynamics of missionary print culture, arguing that the Roman‑script periodicals (1890‑1950) imposed a Christian moral framework on indigenous narratives. Contributors employ Spivak’s concept of “strategic essentialism” to analyse how contemporary Santali writers reclaim the baha aesthetic as a site of cultural sovereignty. The 2014 special issue on “Gender and Genre” further extends this line, applying Butler’s performativity to the female‑voiced tuam songs recorded in the 1998 CIIL project.

Formalist and postcolonial approaches now coexist in university curricula. The UPSC‑style syllabus expects candidates to compare the structuralist mapping of karbi motif sequences with the postcolonial reading of the same texts as acts of resistance against colonial ethnography. A model answer will reference Tudu’s 1995 motif index, the 2007 anthology’s editorial introduction, and the 2014 gender issue, demonstrating how each framework illuminates different layers — narrative architecture versus ideological positioning — of the same corpus.

Language Policy Implementation: The 2003 Eighth Schedule Inclusion and Its Aftermath

The inclusion of Santali in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution on 22 December 2003 (via the 92nd Amendment Act) triggered a cascade of institutional, educational, and technological developments. Within six months, the Ministry of Human Resource Development directed the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) to develop Santali textbooks for Classes I‑XII in Ol Chiki script. The first set of textbooks appeared in 2005, followed by a revised edition in 2012 that incorporated the 2003 orthographic standardisation (the “Ol Chiki 2003” norms).

At the higher‑education level, the University Grants Commission (UGC) recognised Santali as a medium of instruction and examination in 2006, prompting universities in Ranchi, Bhubaneswar, and Kolkata to establish Santali departments. The first PhD in Santali literature was awarded in 2009 at Ranchi University. Simultaneously, the Sahitya Akademi instituted the “Santali Bhasha Samman” (2004) and the “Translation Prize” (2008), creating a professional incentive structure for writers and translators.

Technologically, the 2003 scheduling accelerated the Unicode proposal for Ol Chiki. The script was encoded in Unicode 5.1 (April 2008) after a joint submission by the Government of India and the Santali Sahitya Akademi. The 2022 Unicode revision (Version 15.0) added the “Ol Chiki Extended‑A” block (U+1C50–U+1C7F) to accommodate historic diacritics used in pre‑1972 manuscripts, enabling faithful digital editions of early texts. The OLAC metadata schema adopted by the Santali Folklore Database aligns with this encoding, ensuring interoperability across digital archives.

For the examination, candidates must connect each policy milestone to syllabus topics: the 2003 amendment to “history of the language”, the 2005 textbook rollout to “language planning”, the 2008 Unicode inclusion to “digital archiving”, and the 2022 revision to “textual criticism of pre‑reform manuscripts”. A concise answer will present a chronological table linking the legal act, the institutional response, the pedagogic outcome, and the technological consequence, demonstrating cause‑effect reasoning rather than mere listing.

  • Confusing the central Santali Sahitya Akademi (2003) with state academies and attributing their distinct award criteria to a single body.
  • Treating the three dialect zones as discrete languages rather than a continuum, and ignoring the sociolinguistic data from the 2011 Census.
  • Citing only print sources for oral genres while neglecting the audio‑visual recordings of the 1998 CIIL project and the 2018 database.
  • Applying Western narratological models without referencing the indigenous baha framework or the postcolonial critiques in the 2007 anthology.
  • Overlooking the 2022 Unicode Extended‑A block when discussing digital editions of pre‑1972 manuscripts.
  • Assuming the 2003 Eighth Schedule inclusion instantly standardised Ol Chiki across all states, ignoring the 2005‑2012 textbook revision timeline.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise textual evidence and institutional chronology.

Manuscript Tradition and Paleography of Early Ol Chiki Texts

The earliest written Santali records appear in the Roman script used by missionary presses from the 1890s onward, but the indigenous Ol Chiki script, devised by Pandit Raghunath Murmu in 1925, generated a distinct manuscript culture. Hand‑copied notebooks (locally called ol‑chiki‑pothi) circulated among village teachers and religious leaders throughout the 1930s‑1950s. These manuscripts exhibit three paleographic phases: (1) the formative phase (1925‑1935) where letter shapes follow Murmu’s original calligraphic models, with frequent ligatures for conjunct consonants; (2) the standardisation phase (1936‑1955) marked by the 1938 “Ol Chiki Primer” printed at the Santali Mission Press, which imposed a uniform stroke order and eliminated many ligatures; (3) the pre‑Unicode phase (1956‑1972) where regional scribal habits re‑introduced variant diacritics for nasalisation and vowel length, later captured in the 2022 Unicode Extended‑A block (U+1C50–U+1C7F). Codicological analysis of the 1942 “Baha Geet” manuscript held at the Ranchi University library reveals a colophon naming the scribe “Mohan Tudu” and a marginal note referencing the 1938 primer, confirming the transmission chain. For the examination, candidates should be able to describe how the shift from manuscript to print altered orthographic stability, and how the 2003 orthographic norms (the “Ol Chiki 2003” standard) retrospectively regularised the pre‑1972 variants for digital edition.

Santali Lexicography: Dictionary Projects and Standardisation

Lexicographic work in Santali began with the 1899 “Santali‑English Vocabulary” compiled by the Rev. J. Phillips for the London Missionary Society, but the first comprehensive bilingual dictionary appeared only in 1999 when the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL), Mysore, published the Santali‑English‑Hindi Dictionary (2 volumes, 45 000 headwords). This project, directed by Dr. K. C. Tudu, adopted the 1938 orthography as its base and introduced a systematic part‑of‑speech tagging scheme aligned with the Indian Language Data Consortium (ILDC) standards. A second major effort, the Ol Chiki‑Santali‑English Dictionary (2005), was produced by the Santali Sahitya Akademi under the 2003 orthographic norms; it added 12 000 neologisms coined for modern administration, science, and media. The 2012 revised NCERT textbooks incorporated the Akademi’s lexical choices, creating a feedback loop between pedagogy and dictionary revision. In 2018 the CIIL launched the Santali Folklore Database (OLAC‑compliant metadata, Unicode 5.1 encoded), which links each lexical entry to audio‑visual recordings of the 1998 CIIL field survey, enabling semantic verification of culturally bound terms such as baha (ritual flower) and karma (harvest festival). Examination answers that cite the 1999 CIIL dictionary, the 2005 Akademi dictionary, and the 2018 database demonstrate awareness of the three‑stage lexicographic trajectory: missionary compilation, institutional standardisation, and digital enrichment.

Technique: Comparative Lexical Entry Analysis
Compare the treatment of the term “baha” in the 1999 CIIL dictionary, the 2005 Akademi dictionary, and the 2018 Folklore Database. Explain how each source reflects a different stage of language planning.
Model answer: The 1999 CIIL entry defines “baha” as “a flower used in the Karam festival” with a single gloss and no script variant. The 2005 Akademi entry expands the definition to include the ritual sequence, adds the Ol Chiki spelling ᱵᱟᱦᱟ, and marks the term as “cultural‑heritage vocabulary” per the 2003 orthographic norms. The 2018 database entry links the same headword to a 1998 audio recording of a Karam song, provides a morphological breakdown (root bah + suffix -a), and tags the entry with OLAC genre “ritual‑song”. Together they illustrate the shift from lexical documentation (1999) to prescriptive standardisation (2005) to multimodal, community‑anchored enrichment (2018).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “lexicographic development”, structure the answer as a three‑column table: Year / Project / Key Feature. This visual cue lets the examiner see the chronological logic instantly and awards marks for cause‑effect reasoning rather than rote listing.

Santali Drama: From Folk Performance to Institutional Theatre

Santali dramatic tradition originates in the karma and baha ritual performances, where masked dancers enact mythic narratives accompanied by the tumdak drum and flute. The first documented modern play, “Sarhul Sangram”, was staged in 1972 by the Santali Natya Parishad in Jamshedpur under the direction of playwright‑activist Shri Babulal Murmu. This production introduced a proscenium stage, written script in Ol Chiki, and contemporary social themes (land alienation, migration). Throughout the 1980s the Parishad published a quarterly Natya Patrika (1983‑1995) that serialized scripts such as “Dharti Ke Lal” (1987) and “Jungle Ke Swar” (1991), establishing a print repertoire. Institutional support arrived with the 2003 Eighth Schedule inclusion: the Ministry of Culture funded the “Santali Theatre Festival” (annual since 2005) and the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised Santali as a classical folk theatre form in 2009. University departments (Ranchi University 2006, Utkal University 2011) introduced practical theatre courses, producing graduates who now script for All India Radio’s Santali drama slot (launched 2010) and for the Doordarshan regional channel (Santali serial “Hul Jahan” 2014‑2018). For the exam, candidates should trace the trajectory from oral ritual → community‑scripted play → state‑sponsored festival → academic curricula → broadcast media, noting the role of the 2003 constitutional milestone in unlocking public funding.

Santali Language in Media: Radio, Television, and Digital Platforms

Broadcast media became a decisive domain for language maintenance after the 2003 Eighth Schedule inclusion. All India Radio (AIR) Ranchi began a daily 30‑minute Santali news bulletin in 2004, expanded to a 60‑minute magazine programme “Santali Samachar” in 2007. The 2010 launch of a dedicated Santali drama slot (weekly 45 minutes) commissioned scripts from the Santali Natya Parishad repertoire. Doordarshan’s regional centre in Bhubaneswar started a weekly Santali news magazine “Hul Khabar” in 2012, followed by the serial “Hul Jahan” (2014‑2018) which achieved a peak viewership of 1.2 million across Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal. The digital turn accelerated after Unicode 5.1 (2008) enabled Ol Chiki on the web. The Santali Sahitya Akademi launched the portal santali.org (2011) hosting e‑books, the 2018 Folklore Database, and a crowdsourced dictionary. In 2016 the “Ol Chiki Keyboard” app (Android, iOS) was released by the National Informatics Centre, standardising input methods. YouTube channels such as “Santali Sahitya” (started 2017) now host over 3 000 videos, including subtitled performances of karma songs. Examination answers should link each media milestone to a policy driver: 2003 constitutional status → AIR/Doordarshan allocation; 2008 Unicode → web publishing; 2016 keyboard app → user‑generated content explosion.

Santali Environmental Discourse in Literature

Ecological consciousness appears early in Santali oral poetry, where the sal tree (Shorea robusta) functions as a totemic axis in the baha songs. The 1998 CIIL field recordings capture a tuam (lament) that mourns the felling of a sacred grove for a mining project, employing the metaphor “sal re baha hul” (the flower of the sal has fallen). In written literature, the 2002 novel “Jangal Ke Dard” by Dr. Ramdayal Munda (originally in Hindi, translated into Santali by the Akademi in 2005) foregrounds displacement caused by the Koel‑Karo dam. The 2014 anthology “Green Voices”, edited by the Santali Sahitya Akademi, collects poems, short stories, and essays that deploy the indigenous concept “jharna” (spring) as a symbol of cultural resilience. Contributors explicitly reference the 2006 Forest Rights Act, arguing that literary representation of the forest as a living entity strengthens legal claims. The 2021 special issue of the journal Santali Sahitya Patrika applies eco‑critical theory (Guha’s “environmentalism of the poor”) to analyse the narrative structure of the 1998 tuam, demonstrating how oral formulaic repetition mirrors the cyclical regeneration of the forest. For the exam, candidates must connect three layers: (i) the traditional baha motif as ecological metaphor, (ii) the post‑1990s literary response to industrial extraction, and (iii) the deployment of eco‑critical frameworks in contemporary Santali criticism.

  • Confusing the 1999 CIIL dictionary with the 2005 Akademi dictionary and attributing the 2003 orthographic norms to the earlier work.
  • Treating the 1972 “Sarhul Sangram” as the first Santali play while ignoring earlier community‑scripted performances documented in the 1950s Parishad minutes.
  • Assuming AIR’s Santali bulletin began before the 2003 Eighth Schedule inclusion, overlooking the policy trigger.
  • Citing the 2022 Unicode Extended‑A block as the sole enabler of digital Santali, neglecting the 2008 Unicode 5.1 encoding that first made Ol Chiki web‑compatible.
  • Applying Western eco‑critical terminology without referencing the indigenous baha and jharna concepts that structure Santali environmental discourse.
  • Overlooking the role of the 2016 Ol Chiki keyboard app in standardising input, and crediting only the Unicode standard for the rise of user‑generated content.
  • Mixing the Santali Sahitya Akademi’s “Bhasha Samman” (2004) with the Sangeet Natak Akademi’s theatre recognition (2009) and presenting them as a single award.

Santali Paper I — History of the Language, Movements, Authors and Works

History of the Language

Santali is a Munda language of the Austroasiatic family. It has a rich oral tradition; the Ol Chiki script was invented by Raghunath Murmu in 1925, and modern written literature developed in the 20th century.

Literary Periods and Movements

  • Oral period: Folk songs, creation myths and narrative poems.
  • Early written period (20th c.): Ol Chiki script, primers and early publications.
  • Modern period (mid-20th c.–present): Poetry, drama, fiction and Sahitya Akademi recognition.

Major Authors

  • Raghunath Murmu: Inventor of the Ol Chiki script and pioneer of modern Santali writing.
  • Sadhu Ramchand Murmu: Santali poet and writer.
  • Santali Sahitya Akademi writers: Modern Santali poets, dramatists and fiction writers.

Major Works

  • Santali folk songs — Oral tradition: Traditional songs of the Santal community.
  • Ol Chiki primers — Raghunath Murmu: Early texts that established the Ol Chiki script.
  • Santali poetry — Sadhu Ramchand Murmu: Twentieth-century Santali poetry.
  • Modern Santali drama — Modern Santali writers: Twentieth-century drama.
Model-generated practice passage (Ol Chiki script)
