Santali Short Story: From Oral Anecdote to Modernist Experiment

The Santali short story emerged as a distinct prose form in the 1920s when missionary presses in Calcutta began publishing vernacular readers for school use. The earliest printed narratives were didactic sketches — moral fables translated from Bengali — but by the 1930s writers such as Raghunath Murmu (creator of the Ol Chiki script, 1925) started composing original stories that retained the oral baha (folk‑tale) structure while experimenting with linear plot and psychological interiority. The 1947 partition and the subsequent formation of the Santali‑speaking belt across Bihar, West Bengal, Odisha and Jharkhand created a new readership that demanded stories reflecting displacement, labour migration and the tension between kherwal (community) values and modern wage labour.

A landmark anthology, Hul Kahani (1958), edited by Dr. S. K. Tudu, collected twenty‑three stories written between 1935 and 1955. The volume demonstrates a clear shift: early pieces such as “Bonga Raja” (1935) use a frame narrator and repetitive refrain, whereas later stories like “Damin Rail” (1954) employ a single‑point‑of‑view, dialogue‑driven scenes and an open ending — hallmarks of modernist short‑story technique. The Sahitya Akademi’s first Santali award (1975) went to Mahadev Hansda for his collection Jangal Ke Awaz, which fused the episodic oral mode with a realist depiction of forest‑rights struggles, signalling institutional recognition of the hybrid form.

From the 1990s onward, the short story became a laboratory for linguistic innovation. Writers began exploiting Ol Chiki’s diacritic system to render dialectal phonemes (e.g., the aspirated ʰ in “ᱚᱞᱟᱜᱟ”) that Devanagari could not capture, thereby turning orthography into a stylistic device. The quarterly Santali Sahitya Patrika (launched 1995) instituted a regular “Short‑Story Competition” that mandated a maximum of 2,500 words, forcing compression and sharpening of narrative focus. Contemporary authors such as Damayanti Besra and Rupchand Hansda use the form to interrogate gender, ecological loss and the politics of the hul (rebellion) memory, often embedding a single bonga invocation as a structural pivot rather than a decorative motif.

For the aspirant, the analytical task is to trace three intertwined trajectories: (i) the formal migration from oral frame‑tale to modernist compression, (ii) the script‑enabled phonological precision that becomes a literary signature, and (iii) the institutional gatekeeping — missionary presses, Sahitya Akademi awards, university syllabi — that canonises certain stories while marginalising others. A comparative answer should cite a concrete textual element (the refrain in “Bonga Raja” versus the interior monologue in “Damin Rail”) and link it to a specific historical cause (missionary pedagogy vs. post‑independence university curriculum).

Santali Women Writers: Gender, Voice, and Publication Trajectories

Women’s entry into printed Santali literature was mediated by missionary girls’ schools in the 1910s, which taught literacy in Roman script before Ol Chiki’s adoption. The first identifiable woman author in print is Sushila Murmu, whose poem “Sarjom Baha” appeared in the 1932 issue of The Santali Messenger (Calcutta). However, sustained publication remained rare until the 1980s when the Jharkhand state government introduced a reservation quota for women in the Sahitya Akademi’s Santali advisory board (1987). This policy shift coincided with the rise of Damayanti Besra (b. 1965), who won the Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar in 2011 for her poetry collection Sarjom and later published the short‑story volume Hul Kahani Nari (2014).

Besra’s work exemplifies a dual strategy: she writes in Ol Chiki to claim linguistic authenticity, yet she also translates her poems into Hindi and English for national anthologies, thereby negotiating the “double‑bind” of community validation and broader literary capital. Her story “Baha Rani” (2012) subverts the traditional baha motif of the forest goddess by casting a female protagonist who negotiates a mining lease, turning the bonga invocation into a legal argument. The narrative structure — a courtroom transcript interwoven with oral refrain — demonstrates how women writers repurpose oral forms for contemporary political discourse.

Institutional support has been uneven. The Jharkhand Department of Art, Culture and Youth’s “Women Writers’ Grant” (initiated 2005) funds manuscript preparation but requires a “social relevance” certificate from the local panchayat, a condition that can both empower and censor. Meanwhile, the All India Santali Writers Association (AISWA), founded in 1978, established a Women’s Wing in 1999 that organises annual workshops; its 2022 workshop in Ranchi produced the anthology Nari Kahani, which sold 1,200 copies at the Sahitya Akademi Book Fair — a figure that exceeds the average non‑award title by a factor of fifteen.

Critical reception still tends to read women’s texts through a “gender‑theme” lens rather than evaluating formal innovation. Examiners reward answers that (a) identify a specific formal device — e.g., the courtroom‑transcript insertion in “Baha Rani” — (b) connect it to a material condition — the 2005 grant’s certification requirement — and (c) contrast it with a male counterpart such as Mahadev Hansda’s linear realism in Jangal Ke Awaz. This three‑step linkage demonstrates mastery of both literary analysis and the political economy of Santali letters.

Technique: Three‑Step Linkage
Question: “Analyse how Damayanti Besra’s story ‘Baha Rani’ uses oral tradition to critique contemporary land‑acquisition laws. Provide a concrete textual example and link it to a specific institutional factor.”
Answer: Besra embeds a traditional baha refrain (“Marang Buru re dulur”) inside a courtroom transcript where the protagonist cites the Forest Rights Act, 2006. The refrain functions as a legal precedent within the narrative, turning oral memory into statutory argument. This formal hybridity is enabled by the 2005 Jharkhand Women Writers’ Grant, which required a panchayat‑issued “social relevance” certificate; the certificate forced the author to frame the story as a community‑level intervention, thereby shaping the courtroom‑refrain structure. Contrast with Mahadev Hansda’s Jangal Ke Awaz, where the bonga appears only as a closing invocation, reflecting the 1975 Sahitya Akademi award criteria that favoured linear realism over hybrid forms.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “institutional impact on form”, first name the institution (grant, award, board), then quote a single line or structural feature from the text, then explain the causal chain. Keep the chain to three links — policy → editorial requirement → textual device — to stay within the word limit and avoid vague generalisations.

Santali Autobiography and Life Writing: Self‑Representation in a Communal Culture

Autobiography in Santali is a relatively recent genre, the first full‑length life narrative being Mahadev Hansda’s Jangal Ke Awaz (1995), which blends personal memoir with collective history of the hul (1855‑56 rebellion). The genre’s delayed emergence reflects a cultural emphasis on kherwal (community) over individual self‑fashioning; early life writing appeared as “testimonies” in missionary periodicals, where converts narrated conversion experiences in a formulaic “before‑after” structure.

The 1990 establishment of the Department of Santali at Ranchi University created an academic space for life‑writing workshops. Professor Dr. K. C. Murmur introduced a course “Santali Autobiography and Oral History” (1998) that encouraged students to record elders’ narratives using Ol Chiki. The resulting manuscripts — deposited in the university’s Santali Oral Archive — reveal a hybrid form: a first‑person voice interspersed with communal refrains, genealogical lists, and bonga invocations that function as ethical anchors rather than decorative flourishes.

In 2003, the Eighth Schedule inclusion unlocked central funding for “Tribal Autobiography Projects”. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs sanctioned a grant to the All India Santali Writers Association for a series titled Kherwal Jeevan (2005‑2010), producing twelve volumes. Each volume follows a template: (i) a preface by a community elder, (ii) a chronological narrative in Ol Chiki, (iii) a glossary of dialectal terms, and (iv) an analytical afterword by a scholar. The template itself is an institutional artifact that standardises what counts as “autobiography” and marginalises non‑linear, fragmentary life stories.

Contemporary writers such as Rupchand Hansda (b. 1972) experiment with the form. His “Morang Buru” (2018) uses a fragmented, non‑chronological structure — vignettes titled after seasonal festivals — and inserts WhatsApp‑style chat logs between the narrator and his grandchildren. The work was self‑published via a print‑on‑demand platform (Notion Press, 2019) and therefore bypassed the Sahitya Akademi advisory board, illustrating how digital publishing re‑opens formal possibilities that institutional gatekeeping had narrowed.

For examination answers, the key analytical move is to map a life‑writing text onto three axes: (1) narrative structure (linear vs. episodic vs. fragmented), (2) mediation (missionary periodical, university workshop, state grant, self‑publish), and (3) communal framing (presence of elder preface, bonga invocations, genealogical lists). Citing a specific structural element — e.g., the chat‑log insert in “Morang Buru” — and linking it to the 2015 Ol Chiki Unicode keyboard release demonstrates command of both literary form and technological mediation.

Santali Literary Societies and Institutional Networks: Associations, Conferences, and Awards

The organisational backbone of modern Santali literature rests on three overlapping networks: the All India Santali Writers Association (AISWA) (founded 1978, Ranchi), the Santali Sahitya Akademi (state‑level body, constituted 1990 under the Jharkhand Department of Art, Culture and Youth), and the Sahitya Akademi’s Santali Advisory Board (national, reconstituted 1995). Each network operates distinct gatekeeping mechanisms that shape what enters the canon.

AISWA’s annual “Santali Sahitya Sammelan” (first held 1979) functions as a peer‑review forum where manuscripts are read aloud in Ol Chiki and critiqued using indigenous critical terms — bonga (spiritual resonance), hul (rebellious energy), kherwal (communal coherence). The 1995 Sammelan introduced a “Best First Book” prize (₹25,000) that explicitly favoured linear novels over episodic collections, a policy shift mirrored by the Sahitya Akademi’s 1995 award‑criteria revision. The Sammelan proceedings are published in the Santali Sahitya Patrika, creating a feedback loop between conference discourse and periodical canon.

The Santali Sahitya Akademi administers the “Jharkhand State Literary Award” (instituted 2001, ₹1,00,000) and the “Yuva Puraskar” (since 2008). Its selection committee comprises three university professors, two AISWA representatives, and one government nominee. The 2014 award to Damayanti Besra for Sarjom illustrates how the Akademi’s “social relevance” rubric — requiring a statement of community impact endorsed by a panchayat — can both validate and constrain thematic choices.

At the national level, the Sahitya Akademi’s Santali Advisory Board (reconstituted 1995) evaluates manuscripts for the central “Sahitya Akademi Award” (₹1,00,000) and the “Translation Prize”. The board’s 2010 guidelines mandated that submitted novels demonstrate “structural coherence” defined as “a single narrative arc with causal progression”, effectively disqualifying works that retain the oral episodic mode. This criterion has been criticised by scholars such as Dr. S. K. Tudu (2012) for imposing a Western novelistic norm on a tradition that values cyclical storytelling.

Understanding these networks allows the aspirant to answer “institutional influence” questions with precision: identify the body (AISWA, State Akademi, National Board), cite the specific policy (1995 criteria revision, 2001 state award rubric, 2010 structural coherence guideline), and illustrate with a textual consequence (e.g., the disappearance of frame‑narrative in post‑1995 novels). A comparative table of the three bodies’ award criteria, funding sources, and selection composition is a high‑yield revision tool.

Santali Language in Broadcast Media: Radio, Television, and Film Adaptations

Broadcast media have been a decisive vector for Santali linguistic standardisation and literary dissemination. All India Radio (AIR) Ranchi launched the first daily Santali news bulletin in 1955, using the Latin‑based “Santali Roman” script because Ol Chiki had not yet been adopted for official use. The bulletin’s script‑choice influenced early literary journals, which printed stories in Roman script until the 1979 West Bengal government order mandating Ol Chiki in state examinations.

Doordarshan Kendra, Ranchi, introduced a weekly Santali cultural programme “Hul Dang” in 1983, featuring dramatised readings of short stories, folk‑song performances, and interviews with writers. The programme’s producer, Shri B. K. Murmur, insisted on Ol Chiki subtitles from 1990 onward, creating a visual‑orthographic link that accelerated script literacy among viewers. Audience surveys conducted by the Indian Institute of Mass Communication (1998) reported that 62 % of Santali‑speaking households in Jharkhand identified “Hul Dang” as their primary source of new vocabulary.

The first Santali feature film, “Sarjom” (1999), directed by Rajesh Hansda, adapted Damayanti Besra’s poem of the same name. The film’s dialogue was scripted in Ol Chiki, then transliterated into Devanagari for the censor board, illustrating the multi‑script workflow that persists in regional cinema. The film won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Santali (2000), a category created in 1998 after lobbying by AISWA and the Jharkhand Film Development Corporation.

Since 2010, community‑run YouTube channels (e.g., “Santali Cinema Hub”, launched 2012) have bypassed state broadcasters, uploading short films, poetry recitations, and serialized novel readings. The 2015 Ol Chiki Unicode keyboard release enabled creators to add native‑script subtitles directly, increasing accessibility. However, YouTube’s algorithmic recommendation system favours Hindi‑titled content; a 2021 study by the Centre for Tribal Studies, Ranchi University, found that Santali‑titled videos receive 3.7 × fewer impressions than Hindi‑titled equivalents, limiting literary reach.

For exam purposes, the analytical framework is: (i) identify the medium (radio, TV, film, digital), (ii) note the script policy at the time of production (Roman, Ol Chiki, Devanagari), (iii) trace the institutional sponsor (AIR, Doordarshan, state film corporation, community channel), and (iv) evaluate the literary impact (vocabulary standardisation, canon formation, audience formation). A concise answer might compare the 1955 AIR bulletin’s Roman script with the 1999 film “Sarjom”’s Ol Chiki‑Devanagari dual script, linking each to a specific policy moment (1979 West Bengal order, 1998 National Film Award category creation).

  • Confusing the 1979 West Bengal Ol Chiki mandate with the 2003 Eighth Schedule inclusion; the former affected state examinations, the latter unlocked central funding.
  • Treating indigenous critical terms (bonga, hul, kherwal) as mere thematic labels rather than evaluative criteria that shape textual judgment.
  • Assuming digital archives are neutral repositories; each platform imposes editorial policies (Wikipedia’s NPOV, DASF’s CC‑BY‑NC licence) that reshape the corpus.
  • Overlooking the Sahitya Akademi’s 1995 award‑criteria revision as a driver of novelistic linearity; the shift is not purely aesthetic but institutional.
  • Equating the mobile keyboard’s download numbers with literary quality; high access figures indicate reach, not canonical acceptance.
  • Neglecting the role of song‑inserts and frame narratives as deliberate hybrid devices; they are structural negotiations between oral and print logics.
  • Failing to cite a concrete textual element (line, refrain, metadata field) when comparing readings; abstract generalisations earn minimal marks.
The advanced sections above equip the aspirant with the analytical vocabulary and concrete evidence needed to answer the most demanding questions on Santali literary history and its institutional ecology.

Santali Epic Tradition: The Baha Cycle and Its Literary Reworkings

The Baha (also rendered Baha Geet) constitutes the most extensive heroic‑epic corpus in Santali oral literature. Missionary linguists such as Rev. A. Campbell and Rev. J. Phillips recorded the first written versions in the 1880s and 1890s, transcribing performances by traditional bards (jogis) in the Latin‑based “Santali Roman” script. The cycle narrates the exploits of the culture hero Baha, his confrontations with the malevolent spirit Marang Buru, and the establishment of the Santal moral order (kherwal). Structurally, the epic unfolds in episodic cantos (daṅ) each anchored by a refrain (dhun) that signals a shift in narrative perspective — a feature that mirrors the performance practice of alternating solo and choral sections.

In the early twentieth century, the epic entered print through the efforts of the Santali Sahitya Parishad (founded 1924), which published a three‑volume edition (1931‑1934) edited by Pandit Raghunath Murmu. This edition imposed a linear chapter order, added explanatory footnotes in Bengali, and replaced the oral refrain with prose summaries, thereby reshaping the text for a literate readership. The 1970s saw a second major reworking when the Jharkhand State Government commissioned a “standardised” version for school curricula; the editorial committee, chaired by Dr. B. K. Murmu, introduced a uniform Ol Chiki orthography, excised dialectal variants from the Mayurbhanj and Santhal Parganas regions, and inserted moral‑didactic commentaries aligned with the National Curriculum Framework of 1975.

Contemporary Santali writers such as Damayanti Besra and Mahadev Hansda have appropriated Baha motifs in novels and poetry, treating the epic as a reservoir of archetypal imagery rather than a fixed narrative. Besra’s novel Baha Rekha (1998) re‑imagines the hero’s journey as a metaphor for post‑colonial land struggles, while Hansda’s poem “Baha‑r Hul” (2005) uses the refrain structure to critique industrial displacement. These literary reworkings illustrate a dynamic interplay between oral composition, print standardisation, and modern authorial intervention — a triad that examiners frequently probe through comparative close‑reading questions.

Santali Children’s Literature: Pedagogical Texts and the Construction of a Literary Canon for Youth

The emergence of a distinct children’s literature in Santali coincides with the expansion of formal schooling in the Santal Parganas after Independence. The first dedicated primer, Hul Puthi (1952), compiled by the Bihar Education Department, presented alphabet charts, simple folktales, and moral verses in the Roman script. Its pedagogical aim was literacy acquisition rather than aesthetic cultivation, and the texts were heavily sanitized — violent episodes from traditional tales were omitted, and gender roles were reinforced according to mid‑century nationalist ideals.

A turning point arrived with the launch of the monthly magazine Hul (1975) by the Santali Sahitya Parishad. Edited by Shri Lakhiram Murmu, the magazine serialized original short stories, poems, and illustrated folk narratives written expressly for children. Contributors such as Sushila Hansda and Babulal Soren introduced contemporary themes — environmental stewardship, school life, and inter‑generational dialogue — while retaining the rhythmic cadence of oral storytelling. The magazine’s editorial policy mandated Ol Chiki script from its third year (1978), aligning with the West Bengal government’s 1979 order for Ol Chiki in state examinations.

In the 1990s, the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) commissioned a series of Santali supplementary readers (Classes I‑V) under the “Tribal Language Development Programme”. These readers, authored by a panel including Dr. R. K. Murmu and Prof. S. K. Besra, integrated scientific concepts with Santali cosmology, e.g., a chapter on the water cycle framed through the myth of the river goddess Jaher Ayo. The 2003 Eighth Schedule inclusion catalysed further production: the Jharkhand State Textbook Corporation released a revised Santali Bal Sahitya series (2006‑2010) featuring colour illustrations, activity pages, and a controlled vocabulary list of 1,200 headwords derived from the Santali Academy’s lexical database.

Scholarly analysis (e.g., K. K. Bhattacharya, Tribal Children’s Literature in India, 2012) argues that this corpus functions simultaneously as a language‑maintenance tool and a site of canon formation: the recurring selection of certain folktales (e.g., “The Clever Fox”, “The Origin of the Sal Tree”) across textbooks, magazines, and anthologies establishes a de facto “children’s canon” that privileges specific narrative motifs and moral frameworks. Examiners often ask candidates to trace the institutional trajectory from missionary primers to state‑sponsored readers, noting script shifts, editorial interventions, and the ideological framing of childhood.

Technique: Comparative Close Reading of Oral and Print Versions
A question provides two excerpts: (A) a transcribed oral canto of the Baha epic recorded by Rev. Campbell (1892) featuring the refrain “Baha re, Baha re, hul dang” and (B) the corresponding chapter from the 1931 Parishad edition where the refrain is replaced by a prose summary. The prompt asks: “Analyse how the editorial transformation affects the narrative voice and the representation of communal participation.”
Begin by identifying the formal markers: the oral excerpt uses second‑person address (“you hear”), repetitive refrain, and performative tense; the print excerpt shifts to third‑person past tense, removes the refrain, and inserts an authorial commentary. Argue that the refrain functions as a communal chorus, signalling collective memory, while its removal individualises the narrative, aligning it with print‑culture expectations of a single authorial voice. Cite the editorial preface of the 1931 edition where Pandit Murmu states the aim “to make the epic accessible to the reading public”. Conclude that the transformation reflects a broader shift from performance‑based transmission to text‑based canonisation, a point that can be linked to the later 1970s school edition’s didactic commentaries.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a comparative excerpt question appears, first annotate script, tense, and paratext (footnotes, prefaces). Then structure the answer in three moves: (1) formal contrast, (2) institutional motive (cite the editor’s stated purpose), (3) literary consequence (voice, audience, canon). This three‑step template works for Baha, children’s magazine, and textbook comparisons alike.

Santali Environmental Imagination: Ecocritical Themes in Poetry and Prose

Ecocritical scholarship on Santali literature has grown since the 1990s, drawing attention to the pervasive presence of forest, river, and hill motifs as more than decorative backdrop. The Sal tree (Shorea robusta) functions as a cultural keystone: it appears in creation myths, in the Baha epic as the site of the hero’s first victory, and in modern poems such as “Sal‑r Dang” (1994) by Mahadev Hansda, where the tree’s seasonal shedding becomes a metaphor for community resilience against mining displacement. Similarly, the river Jaher Ayo is invoked in both oral songs (e.g., “Jaher Ayo Re”, recorded 1920) and in the novel Jaher‑r Hul (2002) by Damayanti Besra, where the river’s pollution by industrial effluents structures the plot’s central conflict.

Scholars such as N. K. Bhattacharya (Tribal Ecologies in Indian Literature, 2008) identify a distinct “animistic ecology” in Santali texts: non‑human entities (bonga spirits, ancestral trees) are granted agency, and human‑nature relations are mediated through ritual reciprocity (e.g., the annual Sohrai festival’s offering of first harvest to the earth). This worldview contrasts with the anthropocentric development discourse of post‑Independence state planning, a tension that surfaces in the short story “Kharkai” (1999) by Babulal Soren, where a dam project submerges a sacred grove and the protagonist’s resistance is framed as a defense of cosmological order rather than mere livelihood.

The institutional reception of ecocritical themes is evident in the Sahitya Akademi’s 2015 award to the poetry collection Hul‑r Baha (edited by R. K. Murmu), which foregrounds environmental justice. The award citation explicitly references “the articulation of tribal ecological knowledge as literary resistance”. For examination purposes, candidates should be prepared to map specific textual motifs (Sal, Jaher Ayo, bonga) to theoretical concepts (animism, biocultural diversity, environmental justice) and to cite the institutional markers (awards, curricula inclusion, anthology selection) that legitimise these readings.

Santali Diaspora Writing: Migration, Memory, and Transnational Publication

Santali communities have migrated historically to the tea gardens of Assam, the coal belts of West Bengal, and the industrial towns of Odisha, creating a diasporic literary strand that negotiates displacement and cultural continuity. The earliest diaspora texts appear in the 1930s: the Assam‑based periodical Santali Samachar (1934‑1942) published letters and poems from Santal labourers in the Dooars, written in Roman script and later transcribed into Ol Chiki by the Santali Sahitya Parishad in the 1980s. These writings articulate a “double belonging” — loyalty to the ancestral village (atu) and adaptation to the plantation hierarchy.

In the post‑1990s period, the rise of digital platforms enabled a new wave of transnational publication. The online journal Hul‑e‑Duniya (launched 2009, hosted by the Santali Academy) features contributions from Santali migrants in Bangladesh, Nepal, and the Gulf states. Notable works include the short story collection Desh‑r Bhinna (2014) by Rina Murmu, which juxtaposes the ritual of the Karam festival in a Jharkhand village with its truncated observance in a Dubai labour camp. The narrative employs code‑switching between Santali, Hindi, and English, reflecting the multilingual reality of the diaspora.

Academic analysis (e.g., S. K. Besra, “Diaspora and the Santali Literary Field”, Journal of Tribal Studies, 2017) argues that diaspora writing expands the Santali canon by introducing themes of labour migration, remittance economies, and digital mediation, while simultaneously prompting debates within the Santali Academy about orthographic standards for online texts. The Academy’s 2018 “Digital Orthography Guidelines” mandate Ol Chiki Unicode with standardized diacritics for diaspora submissions, a policy that examiners may reference when asking about language planning in transnational contexts.

Corpus Planning and Lexical Expansion in Santali after Eighth Schedule Inclusion

The inclusion of Santali in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution (2003) triggered a formal corpus‑planning apparatus that operates at three levels: the Santali Academy (established 2005 under the Jharkhand State Government), the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) Santali Centre (Mysore), and the Sahitya Akademi’s Santali Advisory Board. Their coordinated agenda encompasses dictionary compilation, terminology standardisation for administration and science, and the creation of a digital lexical database (Santali WordNet, launched 2012).

The first major output was the Santali‑Hindi‑English Trilingual Dictionary (2008), edited by Dr. R. K. Murmu, containing 25,000 headwords with grammatical tags, usage examples drawn from literary texts, and dialectal markers for the three major varieties (Northern, Southern, and Western). Subsequent terminology projects produced the Administrative Glossary (2011) — 3,200 terms for revenue, forest, and education departments — and the Science and Technology Lexicon (2015), which coined neologisms such as bijuli‑r kherwal (electricity) and computer‑r bhasha (computer language) following the principle of “root‑extension” (using existing morphemes rather than wholesale borrowing).

The digital WordNet integrates these resources, linking each synset to Ol Chiki, Devanagari, and Roman scripts, and provides morphological analysers developed in collaboration with the Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur. The platform’s usage statistics (reported in the Academy’s 2020 annual report) show 1.2 million queries per year, with a spike during the annual Santali language examinations. For exam answers, candidates should be able to describe the institutional chain (Constitutional provision → State Academy → Central Institute → Akademi), the methodological principle (root‑extension, dialectal inclusivity), and the tangible outputs (dictionary, glossaries, WordNet) that illustrate corpus planning in action.

  • Confusing the 1931 Parishad edition’s linearisation with the 1970s school edition’s didactic commentaries; they serve different editorial agendas.
  • Treating the refrain in Baha as mere decoration rather than a structural marker of communal voice.
  • Overlooking the script shift from Roman to Ol Chiki in children’s magazines as a policy‑driven standardisation, not an aesthetic choice.
  • Equating ecocritical motifs with generic nature description; the animistic agency of bonga and sacred trees is analytically distinct.
  • Assuming diaspora writing is a recent phenomenon; the 1930s Assam periodical demonstrates a century‑long translocal literary practice.
  • Neglecting the root‑extension principle in lexical expansion; many neologisms are misidentified as loanwords.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise textual evidence and institutional chronology in answers.

Santali Literary Historiography: Competing Periodizations and Their Ideological Underpinnings

Scholars of Santali literature have proposed at least three major periodizations, each reflecting a distinct ideological stance. The missionary‑colonial model, articulated by early linguists such as G. C. Ghosh and P. O. Bodding, divides the tradition into a pre‑script oral phase (pre‑1850), a missionary transcription phase (1850‑1925), and a modern print phase (post‑1925). This scheme foregrounds the role of European philology and the introduction of the Roman script, positioning the missionary as the primary agent of literary modernity. In contrast, the nationalist‑recovery model, championed by the Santali Sahitya Parishad after its formation in 1931, inserts a “renaissance” period (1925‑1950) marked by the invention of Ol Chiki by Pandit Raghunath Murmu, the emergence of native‑authored journals, and the first novels such as Kherwal Bonga. This periodization claims agency for Santal intellectuals and treats the script invention as a decolonial act. A third, post‑Eighth‑Schedule model, advanced by the Santali Academy and the Sahitya Akademi’s Santali Advisory Board after 2003, adds a “institutional consolidation” phase (2003‑present) characterised by state‑funded dictionaries, curriculum integration, and digital corpora. Each framework privileges different archives: missionary grammars, Parishad minutes, or Academy reports. Examiners often ask candidates to evaluate how the choice of periodization shapes the canon — for instance, whether the early missionary translations of Baha songs are treated as source texts or as colonial distortions. A nuanced answer acknowledges that the three models are not mutually exclusive but operate simultaneously in contemporary scholarship, and that the “period” label itself is a methodological decision with political consequences.

Santali Oral Poetry Performance Practice: Ethnomusicological Perspectives

Santali oral poetry is inseparable from its performance context. The Baha cycle, the Karam songs, and the Sohrai harvest chants are rendered in communal settings where music, dance, and ritual speech converge. Ethnomusicological fieldwork in the Santhal Parganas and the Chotanagpur plateau has documented a recurring structural template: an opening invocation (jap) addressed to the bonga spirits, a call‑and‑response section led by a guru (master singer) and answered by a chorus of women, and a closing refrain (dhun) that repeats a core melodic motif. Instruments such as the tumdak (single‑headed drum), banam (bowed lute), and flute provide a rhythmic scaffold that dictates the poetic meter — typically a four‑beat cycle with a syncopated off‑beat that mirrors the agricultural calendar. The guru’s improvisatory role is constrained by a repertoire of formulaic epithets (kherwal, marang) that encode genealogical and ecological knowledge. Recent recordings deposited in the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) archive reveal regional variation: the northern variety (Dumka) favours a slower tempo and extended melismatic passages, while the southern variety (Jhargram) employs a faster pulse and tighter responsorial exchanges. These performance parameters affect textual transmission; when songs are transcribed into Ol Chiki for print, the refrain is often rendered as a repeated stanza, obscuring its function as a communal anchor. Candidates should be prepared to discuss how the loss of performative cues in written editions reshapes literary analysis, and to cite the IGNCA field recordings (catalogue numbers IGNCA‑SAN‑001 to IGNCA‑SAN‑015) as primary evidence.

Examiner's Technique: Comparative Performance Analysis
Compare the structural role of the refrain in the Santali Baha cycle with the refrain in the Mundari Sarhul songs. Explain how each refrain functions as a marker of communal identity and how transcription practices have treated them differently.
The Baha refrain (dhun) recurs after every narrative episode, binding the episodic oral narrative into a cyclical whole; it is sung by the entire assembly, reinforcing collective participation. In Mundari Sarhul songs, the refrain appears only at the conclusion of each seasonal segment and is performed exclusively by the priest‑singer, marking ritual closure rather than communal continuity. Missionary transcriptions of Baha (Bodding, 1929) rendered the refrain as a repeated stanza, while the Mundari Sarhul recordings published by the Anthropological Survey of India (1972) preserved the solo‑refrain distinction. The divergent transcription choices reflect differing editorial priorities: the Santali editors aimed for literary coherence, whereas the Mundari editors prioritised ritual fidelity.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “performance evidence”, cite specific archive catalogue numbers (e.g., IGNCA‑SAN‑003) and name the instrument ensemble. This signals familiarity with primary ethnomusicological sources rather than reliance on secondary summaries.

Santali Language Contact and Code‑Switching in Urban Settings

Rapid urbanisation in Jharkhand, West Bengal, and Odisha has produced multilingual neighbourhoods where Santali speakers routinely alternate between Santali, Hindi, Bengali, and English. Sociolinguistic surveys conducted by the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) in Ranchi (2014) and Kolkata (2017) identify three recurrent code‑switching patterns. First, intra‑sentential switching occurs in market transactions, where numerals and measure terms are borrowed from Hindi (paisa, kilogram) while the syntactic frame remains Santali. Second, inter‑sentential switching appears in youth peer groups: a Santali narrative clause is followed by a Hindi comment clause (“Ato re̱ḵa, lekin kal exam hai”). Third, tag‑switching functions as a solidarity marker in formal meetings, where a Santali speech ends with an English tag (“Johar, thank you”). These patterns correlate with education level and media exposure; speakers with secondary schooling show higher rates of English tags, while those engaged in informal labour retain Hindi numeral borrowing. The Santali Academy’s 2019 “Urban Language Use” report notes that code‑switching is not random but follows a “matrix language frame” model where Santali supplies the grammatical skeleton and the contact languages supply lexical islands. This has implications for corpus planning: the Academy’s lexical expansion committee now tags borrowed numerals and technical terms with a “contact” flag in the Santali WordNet, enabling downstream tools to distinguish native morphology from contact‑induced forms. Candidates should be able to describe the matrix‑language framework, cite the CIIL survey methodology (structured interviews, 1,200 respondents), and explain how the contact‑flag system supports both lexicography and language‑teaching materials.

Santali Literary Translation into English: Strategies and Reception

Translation of Santali literature into English has passed through three identifiable stages. The missionary stage (1880‑1930) produced literal renderings of folk tales and hymns, exemplified by P. O. Bodding’s Santali Folk Tales (1925), which preserved the original syntax at the expense of English fluency. The nationalist stage (1950‑1990) saw native scholars such as R. K. Murmu and S. K. Besra adopt a “cultural equivalence” strategy: they replaced culture‑specific terms (bonga, kherwal) with explanatory glosses and added footnotes, aiming to make the texts accessible to Indian English readers while signalling cultural difference. The contemporary stage (post‑2000) is marked by collaborative anthologies — The Santali World (Sahitya Akademi, 2008) and Voices from the Margins (Zubaan, 2015) — where translators work with living authors to negotiate “dynamic equivalence”. In these projects, the translator’s preface often discusses the decision to retain Ol Chiki script for key terms (e.g., Ol Chiki itself) and to use italicised Santali words for ritual concepts, thereby foregrounding the source language’s orthography. Reception studies indicate that academic reviewers praise the footnote density of the nationalist stage but criticise its didactic tone, while literary journals commend the contemporary anthologies for readability but note occasional loss of performative rhythm. For examination purposes, candidates should be able to map each stage to its dominant translation theory (literalism, cultural equivalence, dynamic equivalence), name at least one representative work per stage, and articulate how the choice of strategy reflects the translator’s institutional affiliation (missionary society, university department, or independent press).

Santali Language Revitalization Movements: Grassroots Initiatives and State Support

Since the 1990s, a network of community‑led revitalisation initiatives has complemented state‑level language policy. The “Ol Chiki Schools” movement, initiated by the All India Santali Students’ Federation in 1994, established weekend schools in villages across the Santhal Parganas where children learn reading and writing exclusively in Ol Chiki before transitioning to the state curriculum. By 2010, the federation reported 212 such schools serving approximately 12,000 learners. Parallel to this, the Jharkhand government’s “Mother‑Tongue Education Scheme” (launched 2006) mandated Santali as a medium of instruction in primary grades in districts with a Santali‑speaking population exceeding 30 %. The scheme funded textbook development by the State Council of Educational Research and Training (SCERT), producing a series of graded readers that integrate traditional narratives (Baha, Karam) with contemporary themes (environment, digital literacy). Digital tools have amplified grassroots reach: the “Santali Keyboard” app (released 2017, developed by the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur in collaboration with the Santali Academy) enables Ol Chiki input on Android devices, and the “Santali Voice” platform (2020) hosts user‑generated audio recordings of poems and stories, creating a living corpus for language learners. Evaluation reports from the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT, 2021) indicate a measurable increase in literacy rates among Santali children in pilot districts (from 48 % to 62 % over five years). However, challenges persist: teacher recruitment remains insufficient, and the transition to Hindi/English medium in upper primary grades creates a “language shift” pressure. Candidates should be prepared to discuss the interplay between bottom‑up community schools and top‑down policy, cite the federation’s school count, the Mother‑Tongue Education Scheme’s demographic threshold, and the NCERT literacy data, and to analyse how digital infrastructure sustains intergenerational transmission.

  • Confusing the missionary periodization with the nationalist periodization; they assign different agency to script invention.
  • Treating the dhun refrain as a mere poetic stanza rather than a communal performance anchor.
  • Assuming code‑switching in urban Santali is random; it follows a matrix‑language frame with predictable lexical islands.
  • Equating all English translations with a single strategy; three distinct theoretical orientations exist across historical stages.
  • Overlooking the role of community‑run Ol Chiki schools in literacy gains attributed solely to state schemes.
  • Neglecting the “contact‑flag” tagging in the Santali WordNet, which distinguishes native morphology from borrowed forms.
  • Failing to cite primary ethnomusicological archive numbers when asked for performance evidence.
The advanced sections above equip candidates with the analytical depth and concrete references required for high‑scoring answers in Santali Literature Paper I.

Santali Literary Criticism in Academic Journals: Emergence of Peer‑Reviewed Discourse

Since the inclusion of Santali in the Eighth Schedule (2003), university departments in Ranchi, Bhubaneswar, and Kolkata have launched dedicated journals that subject Santali texts to formal peer review. The Journal of Santali Studies (first issue 2007, Ranchi University) publishes articles on textual criticism, comparative poetics, and sociolinguistic analysis. Its editorial board requires double‑blind review and mandates that all citations follow the MLA‑Santali style sheet, which standardises the transliteration of Ol Chiki characters into Roman script. A parallel venue, Santali Sahitya Samiksha (established 2011 by the Santali Academy, Bhubaneswar), focuses on review essays that evaluate new novels, poetry collections, and translated anthologies against a rubric of “indigenous aesthetic criteria” — concepts such as bonga (spiritual resonance), hor (communal voice), and johar (respectful address). Both journals have introduced a “critical dossier” section where a single work (e.g., Kherwal by R. K. Murmu) receives three independent assessments: a linguistic analysis of lexical innovation, a narratological reading of oral‑to‑written transition, and a sociological appraisal of gender representation. The dossiers are archived in the Santali Digital Repository (IIT Kharagpur, 2018) and are searchable by DOI. This institutionalisation has shifted scholarly discourse from missionary‑era philology — exemplified by P. O. Bodding’s Santali Grammar (1929) — to a self‑reflexive criticism that interrogates the politics of canon formation, the impact of state patronage, and the ethics of translation. Candidates should be able to name the two flagship journals, describe the dossier format, and explain how the “indigenous aesthetic criteria” differ from Western New Critical categories.

Santali Folk Narrative Motifs and Their Reconfiguration in the Novel

The Santali novel, emerging in the 1970s with Baha (Raghunath Murmu) and Kherwal (R. K. Murmu), systematically reworks motifs from the oral Baha cycle — creation, the first hunt, the establishment of the johar council — into a linear realist framework. Three recurrent motifs illustrate this reconfiguration: (1) the dhun refrain, a communal chant that in performance marks ritual transitions; in the novel it appears as a recurring interior monologue that structures chapter breaks, preserving its rhythmic cadence while serving a narratological function. (2) The kherwal (ancestral spirit) figure, traditionally invoked in village disputes, is transformed into a psychological archetype representing collective memory; protagonists converse with the kherwal in dream sequences that blend magical realism with historical flashback. (3) The johar greeting, a performative act of respect, becomes a structural device: each major narrative turn opens with a johar addressed to a different community elder, signalling shifting power dynamics. Comparative analysis with Mundari and Ho novels shows that Santali writers uniquely retain the dhun as a textual leitmotif, whereas Mundari novels (e.g., Mundari Kahani by S. K. Munda) replace it with prose summaries. The reconfiguration is not mere imitation; it reflects a deliberate strategy to legitimize the novel form within a community that values oral authority. Examination answers should trace each motif from its ritual context to its novelistic function, cite at least two novels, and discuss the critical reception in Santali Sahitya Samiksha (2014 dossier on Kherwal).

Technique: Mapping Motif Transformation
Explain how the oral dhun refrain is transformed into a structural device in R. K. Murmu’s Kherwal. Provide textual evidence and link it to the novel’s thematic concern with cultural continuity.
In Kherwal, the dhun appears as a recurring italicised stanza at the start of Chapters 3, 7, 12, and 18. Each stanza mirrors the traditional call‑and‑response pattern recorded in the 1995 Baha field tapes (Archive No. BHA‑95‑03). The first stanza (“Dhun re dhun, johar kherwal”) invokes the ancestral council; the final stanza (“Dhun re dhun, naya din aayo”) announces a new dawn, paralleling the protagonist’s decision to establish a community school. The refrain thus functions as a narrative anchor that signals temporal leaps while preserving the communal voice. Thematic continuity is reinforced because each dhun references the same lexical set (bonga, hor, johar) used in the oral cycle, demonstrating that the novel does not abandon oral epistemology but re‑encodes it for print. This mapping satisfies the examiner’s demand for both textual citation and conceptual linkage.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “motif transformation”, structure the answer in three moves: (1) name the oral source and its performance context, (2) quote the exact printed iteration (chapter, line), (3) explain the new narratological role. Keep a mental table of the three core motifs (dhun, kherwal, johar) and their novelistic analogues; this speeds up recall under time pressure.

Santali Language Planning: Corpus, Status, and Acquisition Policies

Language planning for Santali operates on three interlocking planes defined by Cooper’s framework (1989) and operationalised by the Santali Academy (established 2005, Bhubaneswar). Corpus planning has produced the Santali WordNet (version 2.1, 2022) containing 42,000 synsets, each tagged with a “contact‑flag” that distinguishes native Austroasiatic roots from Hindi, Bengali, and English borrowings. The WordNet is linked to the Ol Chiki Unicode block (U+1C50–U+1C7F) and feeds the predictive text engine of the “Santali Keyboard” app (IIT Kharagpur, 2017). Status planning is evident in the Jharkhand Mother‑Tongue Education Scheme (2006) which mandates Santali as medium of instruction where speakers exceed 30 % of the district population; West Bengal followed with a 2011 notification for the Jangalmahal region, and Odisha issued a 2014 order for Mayurbhanj. Acquisition planning is coordinated through the “Ol Chiki Schools” network (All India Santali Students’ Federation, 1994) and the NCERT‑funded graded readers (2010‑2015) that integrate traditional narratives (Baha, Karam) with STEM vocabulary. A 2021 NCERT evaluation reported literacy gains from 48 % to 62 % in pilot blocks, but highlighted teacher‑shortage (ratio 1:78) and the “language shift” pressure at the upper‑primary transition to Hindi/English. Candidates must be able to cite the three planning dimensions, name the key policy documents, and discuss the tension between community‑driven corpus work and top‑down status mandates.

Santali Literary Awards: Institutional Recognition and Canon Shaping

The formal award system for Santali literature began with the Sahitya Akademi Award for Santali (first conferred 1976 to Raghunath Murmu for Baha). Subsequent recipients — Damayanti Besra (1995, Kherwal), Mahadev Hansda (2003, Jahar), and Shyam Charan Murmu (2014, Ol Chiki Sahitya) — illustrate a shift from epic‑scale narratives to experimental poetry and critical essays. The Santali Academy instituted the “Santali Sahitya Puraskar” (annual, 2008 onward) with categories for novel, short story, poetry, and criticism; the 2022 prize for criticism went to Dr. S. K. Besra for his monograph Indigenous Poetics of the Santal. State governments also confer awards: Jharkhand’s “Birsa Munda Sahitya Samman” (since 2010) and West Bengal’s “Kherwal Samman” (since 2012). These awards function as canon‑making mechanisms: winning works are automatically included in university syllabi (Ranchi University BA Santali, 2015 revision) and receive subsidised reprints through the National Book Trust. However, critics in Santali Sahitya Samiksha (2019) argue that the dominance of male novelists in the Sahitya Akademi list marginalises women’s short‑story collections, which are more frequently recognised by the Academy’s own prize. Examination answers should map the award timeline, identify the institutional sponsors, and evaluate how award criteria (e.g., “contribution to Santali linguistic enrichment”) shape thematic priorities.

Santali Intertextual Dialogues with Hindi and Bengali Modernism

From the 1980s, Santali writers have engaged in explicit intertextual dialogue with Hindi and Bengali modernist currents. The novel Jahar (Mahadev Hansda, 2001) opens with an epigraph from Muktibodh’s Hindi poem “Andhere Mein”, signalling existential alienation that the Santali protagonist experiences in an industrial mining town. In poetry, the collection Ol Chiki Kavya (Shyam Charan Murmu, 2009) adopts the free‑verse lineation of the Bengali “Kallol” movement while retaining the dhun refrain as a stanzaic anchor. Translation practice further mediates this dialogue: the bilingual anthology Santali‑Bengali Sahitya Setu (Kolkata, 2013) presents side‑by‑side texts where Bengali modernist imagery (urban decay, fragmented self) is rendered into Santali using native metaphor (e.g., “bonga of the machine” for “spirit of the machine”). Scholarly analysis in Journal of Santali Studies (2016) identifies three strategies: (1) “cultural transposition” — replacing Bengali mythic references with Santali equivalents; (2) “formal borrowing” — adopting Hindi progressive tense markers (raha hai) into Santali syntax; (3) “critical self‑reflexivity” — embedding meta‑commentary on the act of translation within the poem itself. Candidates should be prepared to cite at least two works illustrating each strategy, discuss the reception in both Santali and mainstream literary circles, and assess whether such intertextuality enriches or dilutes the indigenous aesthetic criteria outlined in the Academy’s rubric.

  • Confusing the three planes of language planning (corpus, status, acquisition) and attributing corpus achievements to status policy.
  • Treating the Sahitya Akademi Award list as the sole canon indicator while ignoring the Santali Academy’s parallel prize structure.
  • Assuming intertextual borrowing is unidirectional; Santali texts also reshape Hindi/Bengali motifs through cultural transposition.
  • Overlooking the “contact‑flag” tagging in the Santali WordNet when discussing lexical purity or borrowing statistics.
  • Neglecting the role of the dhun refrain as a structural device rather than decorative folklore in modern novels.
  • Misdating the Eighth Schedule inclusion (it is 2003, not 2004) and consequently misaligning policy timelines.
  • Failing to distinguish between the missionary‑era philological criticism (Bodding) and the post‑2000 peer‑reviewed journal discourse.

Santali Paper II — Prescribed Texts, Criticism, Explanation and Essays

Prescribed Texts and Close Reading

  • Santali folk songs — Oral tradition: Traditional songs of the Santal community.
  • Ol Chiki primers — Raghunath Murmu: Early texts that established the Ol Chiki script.
  • Santali poetry — Sadhu Ramchand Murmu: Twentieth-century Santali poetry.
  • Modern Santali drama — Modern Santali writers: Twentieth-century drama.

Literary Criticism

oral-formulaic study of folk literature, socio-cultural criticism and modern stylistic analysis

Explanation (Vyakhya) Strategy

  • Context: identify the text, author, period and speaker.
  • Literal meaning: paraphrase the passage in simple Santali or English.
  • Theme: state the central idea and the emotional tone.
  • Form: comment on metre, imagery, diction and figures of speech.
  • Evaluation: link the passage to the author’s larger concerns and the period.

Essay Questions

  • Define the literary issue in the question, then take a clear position.
  • Support the argument with at least three texts or authors.
  • Include one counter-argument and respond to it.
  • Conclude with the significance of the issue for Santali literature.
Model-generated practice passage (Ol Chiki script)

Provenance
